allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
By 1877 Allen's Encyclopaedia had reached its sixth volume, still adding remedies and symptoms at full length. The editorial rule never bends: report everything the provers reported, and trim nothing for neatness. Allen trusts the reader to weigh strong signs against weak ones, as a prescriber must.

That trust made the set a foundation stone for the school's later classics. Hering's guiding marks and Kent's repertory grades both rest on records like these. Volume VI also shows the wide spread of homeopathy itself, with proving reports drawn from two continents. The archive, not the argument, is the point.

Volume VII of Allen's Encyclopaedia, from 1877, adds another thick slice of the proving archive. Remedy by remedy, symptoms accumulate in their fixed bodily order, entry after long entry. Timothy Field Allen gathered them from the whole printed record of his school, plus reports sent to him directly by doctors.

A modern reader may find the lists overwhelming, and that flood is itself the lesson here. Nineteenth-century homeopaths built drug knowledge by mass watching, and this set is their storehouse. Volume VII keeps faith with the plan announced in the first volume: pure materia medica, whole and unsifted.
american-notes-pg977: Rudyard Kipling's 1891 letters from America, written during a coast-to-coast tour. The young imperialist admires American energy while mocking its manners, politics, and press with sharp colonial wit. Americans were not amused, but the letters are vivid journalism and a fascinating record of the young nation through foreign eyes.
articles-of-confederation-1777:
The Continental Congress adopted the Articles of Confederation in 1777, giving the young United States its first frame of government. Thirteen jealous states, fighting a war together, wanted a league strong enough to win and too weak to rule them. Ratification took until 1781, as Maryland held out over western lands.

The Articles call the union a firm league of friendship among sovereign states. Congress could wage war and borrow money, but it could not tax, pay its debts reliably, or stop states from fighting over trade. Disorder after the war, capped by Shays' Rebellion, convinced many leaders that the league was unworkable. It gave way to the Constitution of 1787. Liberty's first American charter was noble in aim and flawed in form, a lesson its framers learned by governing under it.
arxiv-2510-00177:
Shuyue Stella Li and six colleagues published this 2025 paper on a gap in how language models serve individual users. Models are trained first for correct answers, then tuned toward average human preferences. A correct answer can still miss what a particular user needs, though. The authors name the missing skill personalized reasoning, and they build a test for it called PrefDisco.

PrefDisco turns fixed benchmarks into interactive tasks with psychologically grounded personas. The same question can demand different reasoning for different users in these tasks. Across 21 frontier models and ten tasks, naive personalization often backfired badly. Nearly three in ten such attempts aligned worse than a plain generic answer would. Yet generic answers also underserve individuals, the authors stress. They argue personalization must be developed and measured directly, not assumed to emerge.
arxiv-2510-00277:
M. Huerta-Sandoval and four colleagues wrote this 2025 physics paper on the paraxial wave equation, the standard model of laser beam travel. Beam modes such as Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss resemble quantum oscillator states, yet their width grows as they propagate. The authors recast beam propagation through propagation-dependent unitary transformations tied to the Lewis-Ermakov invariant. That invariant is a conserved quantity for oscillators whose settings change over time.

Within their framework, free-space travel maps exactly onto motion inside a quadratic gradient-index medium. A finite-energy beam's Gaussian envelope acts like a harmonic trap on itself. Only an infinitely wide beam could escape that effective confinement, they show. Standard mode families then emerge as modes of one effective system in the right coordinates. The approach unifies mode derivations across rectangular, round, and elliptical coordinate systems. It also ties beam optics to the zero-frequency Ermakov equation.
arxiv-2510-00777:
Choi and six co-authors at POSTECH propose in-place feedback in this 2025 arXiv paper on human-AI interaction. In multi-turn reasoning, users correct a language model by sending a new message describing the error. Models integrate such messages unreliably: they fix the wrong span, leave the error standing, or break previously correct content. The authors instead let the user edit the model's previous response, and the model then continues from that edited text.

Across reasoning benchmarks, in-place feedback beat conventional multi-turn feedback while using about seventy-nine percent fewer tokens. Controlled experiments on the ZebraLogic puzzle suite isolated why: precise edits land exactly on the erroneous part of the response. The paradigm needs no model changes, only an interface that treats the last answer as editable. The authors expect gains in document editing and code writing too, and they flag misuse risks for safety filters.
arxiv-2510-01077:
Bifolco and four co-authors present CodeGenLink in this 2025 arXiv paper, a tool that traces the likely origin and license of AI-generated code. Developers now accept amounts of model-written code, but unlike code from the web it arrives with no provenance. Nobody can judge its trustworthiness or whether reusing it breaks a copyright or license. CodeGenLink plugs into Visual Studio Code as a GitHub Copilot extension to close that gap.

The tool asks a language model with web search to propose source links for a generated snippet. It then runs similarity analysis between the generated code and each candidate, which discards unrelated pages. Where a license can be identified, the tool reports it beside the link. Preliminary results showed the filtering works well, though only some tasks yielded a similar candidate. Licenses were accurate when found, but many pages exposed no clear license.
arxiv-2510-01177:
Wurm asks whether the coming glow of neutrinos from every past supernova can reveal stars that died invisibly. Some collapsing stars form black holes without any optical flash, yet they shine brightly in neutrinos first. A new generation of detectors stands close to measuring this diffuse background at last.

Early spectra will mix many unknowns, so outside observations must pin down the visible supernova share. Spectral differences between visible and invisible collapses then expose the hidden fraction. The author maps how well first data could detect invisible supernovae and size their population. Results hinge on how the black-hole-forming component's spectrum is modeled. Two detectors, one running gadolinium-loaded and one starting up, frame the timing. Astronomy supplies what neutrino spectra alone cannot disentangle. Invisible collapses still count in the cosmic star-death budget. Cooperation across disciplines carries the interpretation from the start.
arxiv-2510-01277:
Christopher, at The American College in Madurai, derives a single recurrence pattern that works for any arithmetical function at all. Euler's pentagonal theorem famously turns the partition counting function into a self-referencing sum. Lambert series supply the bridge that generalizes that trick far beyond partitions.

Feeding different generating functions through the same machinery yields matching recurrences automatically. Sum-of-divisors functions and several partition variants receive their Euler-style relations as corollaries. Product identities of Jacobi and Gauss extend the reach further. One classical interplay thus organizes a whole family of number-theoretic computations. Pentagonal numbers mark the sparse indices where the weights live. Distinct-part partitions receive the same treatment through parallel identities. A congruence for the generalized counts falls out immediately. Recurrences convert infinite products into finite computations. Euler's eighteenth-century insight keeps organizing new results. One theorem, many functions served.
arxiv-2510-01377:
He, Ren, Mao, and Larsson spread a fashionable matrix-based optimizer across a network of cooperating machines. The Muon optimizer, built on orthogonalized matrix updates, has impressed in centralized training. Decentralizing it over a communication graph, without losing its guarantees, is the paper's problem.

Their method, DeMuon, keeps the orthogonalization step and adds gradient tracking to tame differences between machines' data. Even under heavy-tailed noise, its iteration complexity matches the best centralized bounds. Early experiments on decentralized transformer pretraining beat popular rivals across network shapes. Better connectivity helped, but the margin persisted throughout. Newton-Schulz iterations perform the orthogonalization without heavy decompositions. Heterogeneity among local objectives is the decentralization tax being paid down. Approximate stationary points are the guarantee's destination. Topology experiments vary connectivity to stress the method. First-of-kind claims rest squarely on the complexity proof.
arxiv-2510-01577:
Miao, Zhao, and Kang measure how fragile a study design is when researchers borrow data from one population to learn about another. Such generalization assumes the two groups differ only in measured ways, an assumption no dataset can verify. Hidden differences can quietly invalidate the borrowed conclusions.

Their measure, SLOPE, scores a design's sensitivity to small local breaks in that assumption. It blends causal sensitivity analysis with a classic influence-function idea from robust statistics. Designers can compare candidate studies before collecting data and pick the sturdier one. Honest sensitivity numbers should replace false confidence in cross-population claims. Design-level scoring shifts the question from analysis fixes to planning choices. Influence functions contribute the local-derivative machinery behind the score. Two design characteristics get tracked, the target quantity and its estimator behavior. Robust designs forgive the assumptions reality breaks. Generalization earns a stress test.
arxiv-2510-01777:
Capozziello and Iosifidis extend non-local gravity into a broader geometric framework in this 2025 theoretical physics paper. Non-local gravity adds terms that smear curvature over spacetime, which may fix problems at very small and very large scales. Most versions treat the metric as the only geometric field. Metric-affine theories instead let the metric and the connection vary independently.

The authors build metric-affine versions of well-studied non-local gravity models. Solving the connection equations shows one such theory matches a scalar-tensor theory on shell. Its scalar field carries higher-order derivative terms that the non-locality generates. They generalize the construction to infinite-derivative gravity with an analytic function of the wave operator. They also propose new non-local metric-affine theories with no Riemannian counterpart at all. Cosmological applications close the paper, showing how the framework could describe the early and late universe.
arxiv-2510-01977:
Powis, Corona Rivera, Khrabry, and Kaganovich start plasma simulations from machine-learned guesses in this 2025 paper. Kinetic plasma codes crawl through long startup transients before reaching their quasi-steady state. That burn-in wastes most of the computing time in engineering studies. The authors train networks to predict the final state directly from device settings.

Three model families were trained across driving frequency and operating pressure for capacitively coupled discharges. The models blend perceptrons, principal component analysis, and convolutional networks. They output time-averaged ion density profiles and velocity distributions as starting points. Measured offline, the generated starts cut convergence time by a factor of about seventeen on average. An online procedure still delivered more than a fourfold speedup. Convolutional networks performed best of the three families. The paper sketches a loop where each run improves the generator, aiming at full digital twins of plasma devices.
arxiv-2510-02377:
Agrawal and co-authors pick the best answer from several language models using calibrated confidence. Their 2025 paper addresses a practical selection problem. Asking many models yields diverse candidate answers. Cheap settings rule out human judges and pricey verifiers. Single model voting wastes the diversity on offer. The team scores each answer with a calibrated log-likelihood. The score reflects how strongly models back the answer. Normalizing per token removes length and scale distortions. One fixed formula then compares answers fairly across models.

Tests covered math, knowledge, and reasoning benchmarks. Gains ran near four, three, and five percent across the sets. Both debate and best-of-N setups improved under the method. The approach needs no extra trained judge. Multi-model systems often trail single model voting today. A principled confidence score closes that gap cheaply.
arxiv-2510-02577:
Holm, Hu, and Wang study a modified shallow water system with odd wave behavior. Their 2025 mathematical physics paper examines the BKBK equations. The system tweaks how water transports itself. Transport speed depends on the slope of the wave surface. That shift adds backward diffusion terms scaled by a parameter. Remarkably, the system stays integrable as a Hamiltonian system. At one imaginary parameter value, it becomes the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The authors probe its Lie algebraic and variational structure. Simulations then test regularized versions in one and two dimensions.

The same shift that enriches the system also destabilizes it. Short waves grow at rates that explode with wavenumber. Real parameter values therefore make solutions ill posed. Imaginary values would remove that instability entirely. The work maps where the model helps and where it breaks. Water wave theory gains a bridge to nonlinear optics. Complementary viewpoints often unlock solution methods.
arxiv-2510-02877:
Palmer argues that quantum mechanics may carry a hidden information limit. His idea follows John Wheeler's hunch about Hilbert space. The smooth, endless space of quantum states may be an idealization. A discrete structure may sit underneath it. Palmer defines a qubit information capacity for any quantum system. Past a size near five hundred to one thousand qubits, the states demand more values than the qubits can supply. Gravity, in his framework, sets that discrete scale.

The claim leads to a sharp, testable forecast. Quantum speedup should stop growing near a thousand logical qubits. Shor's factoring method would then stall at that scale. Breaking RSA-2048 codes would stay out of reach in practice. Palmer says the test should come within the next decade. A confirmed limit would reshape thinking on measurement and nonlocality. It would also push theory toward a blend of quantum physics and gravity.
arxiv-2510-03077:
Neumann and co-authors use circuit cutting to stretch small quantum computers. Cutting splits a big circuit into pieces that fit small hardware. The pieces run apart, then their results are stitched back. Algorithms with many rounds can drown in extra runs that way. The team tests a second stitch based on full outcome patterns. Their test bed is a variational classifier, a trainable quantum model.

Two training orders were compared head to head. One trains first and cuts later, which often cannot be done. The other cuts first and trains the pieces, a far easier flow. The cut-first flow still learned well in practice. Hardware runs then compared cut and uncut versions directly. The cut circuit reached higher fidelity than the whole one. Extra randomness from cutting did not sink the result. Bigger circuits and other algorithm types come next.
arxiv-2510-03777:
Handa and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper making repeated sampling from language models explore different solutions instead of duplicates. Sampling answers helps problems, but models tend to retry the approach, wasting the budget. GuidedSampling splits inference into two phases. An exploration phase names concepts that could crack the problem. A generation phase then solves the problem once per concept, forcing variety into the candidates. The authors derive theoretical bounds and test the method across reasoning benchmarks.

GuidedSampling improved the base model's pass at fifty score by twenty two percent on average over repeated sampling. The gains reached thirty five percent. Models fine tuned on its trajectories improved, gaining ten percent at pass at five over models trained on samples. Concepts per problem nearly doubled, from one point seven to three. Inference budgets are now a scaling lever for models. Spending them on diversity rather than repetition is a simple win.
arxiv-2510-04277:
Flynn presents this 2025 arXiv paper introducing relative information gain as a sharper way to measure the complexity of kernel learning problems. Sample complexity for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space is commonly described by information gain or effective dimension. Information gain has a clear probabilistic meaning, but effective dimension usually yields better convergence rates. Flynn defines relative information gain as the sensitivity of information gain to observation noise and shows that it bridges the two quantities.

The new measure interpolates smoothly between effective dimension and ordinary information gain, while growing at the same rate as effective dimension. It then appears naturally in a new PAC-Bayesian excess risk bound for Gaussian process regression. Spectral bounds on relative information gain combine with that risk bound to produce minimax-optimal convergence rates. The work gives kernel methods a complexity measure that retains an information-theoretic interpretation without sacrificing sharp statistical guarantees.
arxiv-2510-04377:
Jiarui Li and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on how the immune system spots threats. T cells check small protein pieces held by a carrier molecule, and that check starts the immune response. Computer models can guess which pieces a T cell will bind, but the best models act like black boxes. They give a score and no reason for it. The team built model layers that show their reasoning by design.

The new layers are called TCR EML, and they plug into large protein language models. They work from known contact patterns at the binding site. In tests, the models matched top methods on accuracy and handled new protein pieces well. On a benchmark built for explanations, they beat older methods. A case study showed the contact patterns lined up with real binding biology. Clearer models could help vaccine and cancer work.
arxiv-2510-04477:
Soo Yong Kim and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching AI models to reason about medical images. Doctors answer questions about scans by pointing at a lesion and explaining each step. Models that answer directly give no such visible reasoning, which limits clinical trust. The team built a pipeline, MedCLM, that creates such data on its own.

The pipeline starts from detection data sets that already mark lesion boxes. It links each box to organ maps and structured explanations, then writes question and answer pairs with step by step reasoning. Training follows a three stage curriculum built on that data. The easy stage shows the lesion box openly, and the medium stage hides it so the model must find the spot itself. The hard stage asks for weakly supervised reasoning with little guidance. Models trained this way reached top scores on several medical question benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-04677:
Foucher and a team of coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a disk seen edge on. The disk circles a star, SSTTau042021, and its tilt lets telescopes slice it by height. The team combined archive data from ALMA with views from the NOEMA array. They tracked carbon monoxide in forms plus the ion HCO plus. A model turned those signals into temperature and density maps.

The mid plane runs cold, near seven to eleven degrees above absolute zero. The molecular layer above it sits near sixteen degrees, and the atmosphere reaches about thirty one degrees. The ion data set a bound on gas density at one to two disk heights. Gas appeared along the mid plane beyond where the dust ends, past three hundred astronomical units. The disk holds a few percent of a solar mass. The authors call this the first evidence of vertical layering in such a disk.
arxiv-2510-04877:
Anton Alekseev, Matthias Christandl, and Thomas Fraser wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on a three dimensional cousin of a classic eigenvalue puzzle. The Horn problem asks which eigenvalues matrices can have when the third is the sum of the first two. The tetrahedral version ties six matrices along the edges of a tetrahedron, with sum rules on its faces. The authors derive inequalities that eigenvalue lists must obey. The inequalities are stated through Schur polynomials of the eigenvalues.

They prove the converse up to error. If the inequalities hold up to some degree, approximate matrix solutions exist, with error shrinking as the degree grows. The bridge runs through eigenvalue estimation tools from quantum information theory. The geometry controls the size of 6j symbols, which encode how representations recombine. Those symbols are mild, falling like a power, or tiny, falling exponentially. Which case holds depends on whether the tetrahedron of matrices exists.
arxiv-2510-05877:
The TREX-DM team demonstrates an ultra-low energy threshold for light dark matter searches. TREX-DM is a high-pressure time projection chamber hunting low-mass WIMPs. Calibration at sub-keV energies is essential and notoriously difficult. Their 2025 work implants an argon-37 source inside the detector itself.

Fast neutron activation of calcium oxide powder produced the source in Spain. Its activity reached roughly a kilobecquerel, enough for full characterization. A combined GEM-Micromegas readout preamplified signals fifty to sixty times. Both characteristic emissions appeared, at two point eight keV and two hundred seventy electronvolts. Detecting the tiny L-shell peak is the headline achievement. Spatial analysis confirms a homogeneous response across the active volume. The threshold approaches argon's single-electron ionization energy. Light WIMP searches live or die by exactly this threshold. Gas detectors rarely reach such low energies cleanly.
arxiv-2510-06077:
Luo and co-authors show that step-by-step thinking can mislead video models in a 2025 study from UT Austin, UC Berkeley, and Bespoke Labs. The team tested chain-of-thought prompting across 10 video benchmarks and 20 question-answering subtasks. They found a failure they call visual thinking drift, where long reasoning traces drift away from the footage.

During drift, a model invents visual details, leans on outdated frames, and talks itself out of answers it would give directly. The authors explain the pattern with a Bayesian account in which reasoning amplifies language priors over visual evidence. Their fix is Visual Evidence Reward, a reinforcement learning method that pays for reasoning steps verifiably tied to the video. The trained model, Video-VER, reached top performance across the benchmark suite. The lesson is that video models must keep looking while they think.
arxiv-2510-06177:
Pearse and Bondell uncover a double life for the functions behind phi divergences in a 2025 statistics paper. Copulas join separate variables into a joint distribution, keeping each variable's behavior intact. Archimedean copulas are built from one convex generator. They show that, under one convention, phi-divergence functions also generate Archimedean copulas in at least two dimensions.

As a special case they develop the power-divergence copulas. They map the family in depth: which members are absolutely continuous, which carry a singular component, and how it is ordered. Limiting cases reach the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds, with Kendall's tau and tail-dependence coefficients derived. Some extend to three or more dimensions. In an application, the new copulas fit a Danish fire insurance dataset covering two kinds of business losses. Several benchmark families failed that fit, making the new class useful for actuarial dependence modeling.
arxiv-2510-06277:
Shahriar and seven co-authors use dynamic object masks as goals for visual robot learning in a 2025 robotics paper. Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning promises one policy for many tasks, but most methods assume exact goal states or positions. Real robots in warehouses, farms, and labs rarely enjoy such privileged information.

They instead specify goals as image masks updated at every timestep. A goal detector builds each mask from image processing, task recognizers, or pretrained detectors like Detic and Grounding DINO. The mask marks the spatial target without naming the object, keeping the method object-agnostic. Learning became more stable and sample-efficient in their experiments. Agents reached training and novel objects at a ninety-nine percent success rate on Franka and UR10e arms. Simulated navigation learned faster with mask goals. They demonstrated learning from scratch and sim-to-real transfer on both arms.
arxiv-2510-06377:
Ranjan and nine co-authors present the Relational Transformer, a step toward foundation models for relational data, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Pretrained transformers transfer zero-shot across sequence tasks, but relational databases resist the recipe. Their schemas, structures, and dependencies vary much between datasets.

The architecture specifies tasks through a task table prompt, so no fine-tuning or retrieval is needed. Cells are tokenized with their table and column metadata. Pretraining uses masked token prediction across databases. A Relational Attention mechanism attends over columns, rows, and primary–foreign key links. Pretrained on RelBench tasks such as churn and sales forecasting, the model reached ninety-three percent of fully supervised AUROC on binary classification in a single forward pass. A much larger twenty-seven-billion-parameter language model managed only eighty-four percent by the same measure. Fine-tuning delivered state-of-the-art results with sample efficiency.
arxiv-2510-06477:
Queipo-de-Llano and six co-authors unify two puzzling language model phenomena as effects of one mechanism in a 2025 machine learning paper. Attention sinks dump attention onto the first token inexplicably. Compression valleys squeeze middle-layer representations, reducing their information. The two effects had been studied in isolation.

Both trace to massive activations in the residual stream. The authors prove such activations necessarily produce representational compression. Their proof bounds the resulting entropy reduction. Experiments across models from small to huge confirm the shared origin. When the first token develops extreme middle-layer activation norms, sinks and valleys emerge together. Targeted ablations validate the predictions. The team proposes a Mix-Compress-Refine theory of information flow. Models mix broadly early, compute compressed mid-depth, then refine selectively late. That explains why embedding tasks peak mid-depth while generation needs full depth.
arxiv-2510-06577:
Jiaogen Zhang studies a geometry problem about shaping the curvature of a space. His 2025 paper works with compact spaces that curve negatively everywhere, in three or more dimensions. The question is whether a new metric can be found with a prescribed curvature pattern. The curvature measure here sums parts of a modified tensor that tracks how the space bends.

Zhang proves that such a metric exists within the same conformal family as the original. In the simplest case, the new metric has constant values for that curvature measure. That case recovers a known result by Gursky and Viaclovsky. The proof relies on careful advance estimates for a nonlinear equation of Monge-Ampère type. Results like this one extend the classic Yamabe problem, a central question in modern geometry. They show which curvature patterns negatively curved spaces can actually realize.
arxiv-2510-06677:
Yisha Wu and five co-authors build a note-taking assistant for customer support agents. Their 2025 paper describes a system that summarizes conversations while they happen. Support agents juggle phone, chat, and email threads at once. Writing summaries afterward wastes time and invites missed details.

The system decides on its own when to add a short bullet note during a conversation. A fine-tuned Mixtral model writes the notes, and a DeBERTa classifier filters out trivial content. Agent edits feed back into the system, both live and in regular retraining. The tool was deployed in real production support work. Overall case handling time fell by three percent compared with after-the-fact summaries. For highly complex cases, handling time fell by up to nine percent. Agents also rated the system highly in satisfaction surveys. Steady, small notes beat one big summary written at the end.
arxiv-2510-06777:
Maciej Piróg and Filip Sieczkowski work in category theory, an abstract field behind programming languages. Their 2025 paper extends a device called the codensity monad. Monads package effects, such as state or continuations, in functional languages. Codensity monads build them from simpler pieces called functors.

The classical version starts from functors with one input slot. Many natural examples need two slots that vary in opposed directions. The authors introduce dicodensity monads for those mixed cases. Their construction rests on strong dinaturality, also called Barr dinaturality. It echoes continuation monads that appear in models of polymorphic languages, like the Church coding of lists. They give conditions under which a monad matches the dicodensity monad of a chosen bifunctor. Important examples come from sets of homomorphisms between algebras. Those examples yield fresh forms of several known monads.
arxiv-2510-07277:
Arellano and Orlando test whether big foundation models actually help detect diabetic macular edema, a swelling that steals vision from people with diabetes. Their 2025 paper compares two retinal foundation models, RETFound and FLAIR, against a compact standard network. All were tried across training regimes on three eye-image data sets. Annotated medical data is scarce, so foundation models promise relief. The results complicate that promise for this fine-grained task.

The compact EfficientNet model ranked first or second on most measures in most settings. RETFound shone only on one data set. FLAIR, though, showed strong zero-shot skill when prompted well, needing no task training at all. The authors conclude that foundation models are no universal fix here. Small convolutional networks remain sturdy because the task rewards their built-in bias toward local detail. Clinics with little data should benchmark simple models before paying for scale.
arxiv-2510-07377:
Chen, Monni, Pang, Vita, and Zhu open a systematic study of multi-point correlation functions in gauge theories at a special kinematic limit. Their 2025 letter works in quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force. At the sequential light-cone limit, these correlation functions simplify dramatically. The authors prove a factorization theorem using soft-collinear effective theory. The theorem reveals a duality: the singular parts of the correlation function equal a polygonal Wilson loop dressed by universal jet and form-factor pieces borrowed from collider physics.

With the theorem in hand, they compute the singular terms of a four-current correlation function through three loops. No result beyond one loop existed before. The calculation yields, for the first time, the symmetry-breaking terms caused by the running coupling of the strong force.
arxiv-2510-07577:
Martin settles a web of conjectures about Markoff-type equations over finite fields by reducing them to one checkable computation. The 2025 paper studies triples solving a deformed Markoff equation in the special linear group over a finite field, and the Nielsen equivalence classes of generating pairs there. Conjectures by McCullough and Wanderley from 2013 describe these classes completely, with the undeformed case going back to Baragar in 1991. Martin proves the classification conjecture at the center of the web implies all the others.

The remaining primes are handled by an algorithm: for each modulus, the conjecture reduces to checking invertibility of a modest matrix over a polynomial ring. Implementations in SageMath verify the needed cases, with the author reporting true outputs for all prime powers below thirteen. The work blends structural group theory with certified computation, a modern proof style.
arxiv-2510-07777:
Dongre and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on context drift in long conversations with language models. Across many turns, replies can wander away from the user's goals. That slow divergence differs from a single-turn mistake and escapes static tests. The authors model drift as a moving quantity rather than a death spiral. They compare each turn's output distribution against a goal-consistent reference model.

Experiments on synthetic rewriting tasks and a realistic agent benchmark told a consistent story. Drift settled into stable, noise-limited equilibria instead of growing without bound. Simple reminder interventions reliably pulled divergence back down, as their model predicted. Several open-weight models showed the same pattern when acting as user simulators. The authors frame drift as a controllable equilibrium process. That view gives builders a way to measure long-run behavior and to design interventions that keep agents on goal over extended interactions.
arxiv-2510-07877:
Sayeedi and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on bias and uneven quality in multilingual translation by language models. Models now translate fluently across hundreds of languages. Quality still varies sharply by language family and subject domain. Bias from training data can also leak into translations, hurting low-resource languages most. The authors introduce Translation Tangles, a framework and dataset for measuring both quality and fairness in open-source models.

They benchmark twenty-four bidirectional language pairs across several domains. A hybrid pipeline hunts bias by combining rules, semantic filtering, and model validation. Human judges annotated a bias-labeled dataset from over fourteen hundred translation pairs. The study shows where models serve some languages well and others poorly. It also shows that fluent output can still carry systematic bias. The released tools give researchers a shared way to push translation toward equity, not just accuracy.
arxiv-2510-08377:
Cong Wei and co-authors unify video understanding, generation, and editing in one model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Unified multimodal models already mix these skills for still images. Video, with its motion over time, has lagged behind that trend. Their framework, UniVideo, aims to close the gap with a dual-stream design.

One stream is a multimodal large language model that reads instructions and visual inputs. The other is a multimodal diffusion transformer that generates the actual video frames. Joint training covers in-context editing, in-context generation, image-to-video, and text-to-video tasks. UniVideo matched or beat specialized baselines across these tasks in their experiments. The unified design also composed skills, such as editing plus style transfer in one instruction. It even transferred image editing skill to free-form video editing tasks it was never trained on.
arxiv-2510-08977:
Tan and co-authors diagnose why language models that grade their own work stall below models graded by answer keys, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Self-rewarding training promises endless unlabeled practice data, yet lags verifiable-reward training, which checks answers against truth. The team traces the gap to a system bias: a model tends to declare its own confident attempts correct, so its rewards drift toward generosity as training proceeds.

They measure the bias with three gauges covering reward noise, self-favoritism, and imbalance between over- and under-rewarding. The self-favoritism gauge proved dangerous: it amplifies updates of right and wrong answers alike and destabilizes rewards. Their remedy pools rewards from several diverse models, blending them adaptively and selecting practice attempts carefully. The pooled system gained about fourteen percent over the best self-rewarding baseline, nearly matched the answer-key method, and scaled steadily on unlabeled problems.
arxiv-2510-09277:
Thomas Lawrence and Jason Semeraro prove a conjecture in pure mathematics in their 2025 arXiv paper. Their subject is fusion systems, algebraic structures that record how a group and its subgroups fit together. For such a system they study its character table, a square grid of values built from the system's stable characters, which are special counting functions on the group.

The authors prove a guess made earlier by Semeraro, linking the size of that table to the orders of certain centraliser subgroups. A centraliser collects the elements that commute with a given element. They first give a direct proof when the system comes from a finite group. Then they settle the general case with an averaging tool in a double Burnside ring, showing the character lattice is self-dual and one key equality holds for every suitable element.
arxiv-2510-09477:
Conor Hassan and eight co-authors, among them Samuel Kaski and Luigi Acerbi, speed up a class of probabilistic models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Set-based transformers for amortised inference, such as neural processes, predict in one pass. But many tasks need joint predictions for several targets, and set-based models must re-encode the whole context at each step, scaling badly.

Their fix is a causal autoregressive buffer. The model encodes the context a single time and caches the result, while a light buffer tracks dependencies among targets generated. Each prediction attends to both the cached context and the buffer. Training mixes the set-based mode with the autoregressive one through masked attention, at minimal extra cost. Across synthetic functions, brain signals, model comparison, and tabular regression, it nearly matched re-encoding. It sampled up to twenty times faster and used up to seven times less memory.
arxiv-2510-09577:
Xiao Yu and eight co-authors, among them Jianfeng Gao, teach AI agents to imagine before acting in a 2025 arXiv paper. Reasoning models shine at maths and coding but falter at long interactive tasks such as web navigation or phone use. Drawing on human cognition research, the authors argue that agents need vicarious trial and error: mentally simulating alternative futures before choosing a move.

Their framework, Dyna-Mind, trains agents in two stages. The first stage, ReSim, builds reasoning traces from search trees grown out of real interactions, grounding the agent's thinking in faithful world dynamics. The second stage, Dyna-GRPO, uses online reinforcement learning with both final rewards and intermediate states as feedback. On two synthetic benchmarks, the puzzle game Sokoban and the household world ALFWorld, and on the realistic AndroidWorld benchmark, the stages proved effective at instilling simulation ability and strengthening decisions.
arxiv-2510-09677:
Ebrahim Rahimi and Clara Maathuis review how artificial intelligence is used to teach computational thinking in universities in a 2025 arXiv paper. Computational thinking, the problem-solving skill set behind programming, is increasingly vital for students facing a technology-driven workplace. Research on teaching it has boomed in schools but stayed thin in higher education, leaving university teachers with little overview or support.

The authors run a systematic literature review focused on artificial intelligence initiatives in higher education courses on computational thinking. They catalogue the benefits and challenges reported, the instructional strategies used, which components of computational thinking the initiatives cover, and which AI techniques and models they employ. The review weighs the promise that AI could reshape this teaching against its risks. It offers educators an inventory of working initiatives and gives the research community a map of the field's current state and gaps.
arxiv-2510-10277:
Jeanine Van Order derives new formulas for special values tied to elliptic curves in this 2025 arXiv paper. L-functions are number-theory tools that encode deep facts about curves, and their derivative values at the central point carry key information. She studies curves defined over the rational numbers, moved to a real quadratic field and twisted by ring class characters, which are labels drawn from that field's arithmetic.

Van Order presents these central derivative values through new integral formulas. The values become sums taken along geodesics tied to the class group of the field. The terms in the sums are automorphic Green's functions attached to certain divisors on Hilbert modular surfaces. She also connects the sums to Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer constants and to periods. Those constants sit at the heart of a famous open conjecture about elliptic curves, so explicit formulas for them are valuable.
arxiv-2510-10377:
Martinez breaks down polysymmetric functions in this 2025 arXiv paper in combinatorics. These functions, due to Asvin G. and Andrew O'Desky, link combinatorics with algebraic geometry, using motivic measures valued in the Grothendieck ring of varieties. They refine the classical theory of symmetric functions.

Building on work of Khanna and Loehr, Martinez studies the polysymmetric algebra's non-tensor bases. He brings in a new basis and derives explicit expansions among the main basis families. Stack partitions, counting objects that index these bases, organize the expansions. Explicit changes of basis are the working tools of the field: they let a problem be moved into the basis where it becomes solvable.
arxiv-2510-11077:
Tom Kimpson, Nicholas J O'Neill, Patrick M Meyers, and Andrew Melatos release Argus, a software package for hunting gravitational waves with pulsars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Pulsar timing arrays watch many ultra stable pulsars for tiny timing shifts caused by nanohertz gravitational waves, ripples far too slow for ground based detectors. Argus provides a complete Bayesian inference framework built on state space models. It evaluates likelihoods with Kalman filtering, a recursive technique borrowed from control engineering, instead of traditional frequency domain methods.

The package is written in Python on top of JAX, which supplies just in time compilation, GPU acceleration, and automatic differentiation. That makes gradient based samplers fast. The state space design scales linearly with the number of pulse arrival times, a real advantage as datasets grow for decades. It also handles non stationary processes naturally, meaning noise that changes character over time needs no special patching.
arxiv-2510-11877:
Xiaohang Tang, Zhuowen Cheng, and Satyabrat Kumar harden a popular way of teaching agents against adversaries. The Decision Transformer learns behavior from sequences, aiming at a desired return like following a script. Nobody had checked how such sequence-based policies hold up when an opponent actively tries to exploit them. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces CART, the Conservative Adversarially Robust Decision Transformer.

CART treats each stage of play as a small game between hero and adversary. The stage payoff looks ahead to the best expected value over later states, which folds in the randomness of the world. The transformer is then conditioned on the Nash equilibrium value of those stage games, the value neither side can improve alone. This makes its policies both harder to exploit and cautious about uncertain transitions. In tests, CART estimated minimax values more accurately and earned better worst-case returns.
arxiv-2510-12077:
Einar Urdshals and four co-authors test whether a network's compressibility betrays its complexity. The minimum description length rule gauges complexity by the shortest code that captures a model. It stumbles on neural networks, whose singularities break classical statistics. This 2025 arXiv paper repairs the principle using singular learning theory, Watanabe's extension of the field to such models.

The bridge number is the local learning coefficient, a singular-learning measure of effective complexity around a solution. The team compresses models from the Pythia suite by rounding weights, splitting matrices, and other techniques, then checks achieved compression against the coefficient. The scores track compressibility closely, in some cases in a straight line. That link matters because it turns a folk hunch, simpler models squash further, into a law one can measure. The authors frame the result as a path toward hard limits on model compression.
arxiv-2510-12177:
Anthony J. Pahl and thirteen co-authors measure how well early galaxies make ionizing photons, with dust finally handled with care. The rate at which galaxies produce ionizing photons drives reionization models, but dust dimming corrupts its estimates. Using the JWST AURORA survey, their 2025 arXiv paper studies sixty-three star-forming galaxies at redshifts one point five to six point nine, many with their own measured nebular dust curves.

Those curves vary a lot in shape and strength, and using them shrinks systematic uncertainty in the galaxies' true ionizing output. Efficiency rises with redshift, with oxygen emission strength, and with ionization gauges. It falls with stellar dimming, ultraviolet brightness, stellar mass, and direct-method metallicity. Swapping in common shortcuts, a Galactic extinction curve or equal stellar and nebular dimming, lowers the inferred dimming and can flatten real trends. The AURORA curves reveal hidden ionizing output that simpler recipes miss.
arxiv-2510-12577:
Hays and Richardson build a web application that simulates how heart scar tissue remodels in real time, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The extracellular matrix, the scaffold between cells, remodels constantly in health and disease. Predicting that remodeling is hard, because its controlling reaction networks are complex and spread over space and time. Cardiac fibrosis, excess scarring, drives many forms of heart failure.

Their ECMSim platform simulates a large cardiac fibroblast signaling network across a spatial array of ten thousand cells. It solves over a million coupled equations in real time, covering inputs, receptors, signaling cascades, matrix production, feedback loops, and molecular diffusion between cells. The simulation core is compiled code running through WebAssembly in the browser. Users can paint inputs onto selected cells, drag parameter sliders, and watch coupled visualizations at several scales. They present it as a tool for testing disease conditions, hypothetical scenarios, and candidate drug effects.
arxiv-2510-12677:
Roy, Pousset, and Royer improve the decoding of quantum error correction for logical qubits stored across several harmonic oscillators, in a 2025 arXiv quantum physics paper. Gottesman Kitaev Preskill codes encode a qubit into an oscillator's continuous values, and multimode versions spread it across several oscillators for protection against decoherence. Steane type error correction measures errors using auxiliary states, themselves noisy in practice.

Standard decoders ignore that auxiliary noise. The proposed decoder tracks the correlations between errors on different modes as they spread through the error correction circuit. It also uses the links between measurement results and the actual error on the encoded state. Using this information decreased the logical error rate by at least a factor of ten in their analysis. More faithful decoding of noisy measurements is a practical step toward fault tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2511-00177:
Hiba Ahsan and Byron Wallace test whether sparse autoencoders can reveal and mitigate racial bias in language models used in healthcare. Models may spuriously rely on patient race when predicting, worsening existing disparities. They identify autoencoder traits in Gemma family models that correlate with Black individuals, checking when those traits activate on reasonable inputs such as clear demographic terms.

The study then assesses whether those traits can be controlled to reduce biased associations with stigmatizing concepts. Health AI readers get a concrete audit technique. Finding the internal traits tied to race is a first step toward models that use clinical facts instead.
arxiv-2511-00477:
Aditya Parikh, Sneha Das, and Aasa Feragen audit age bias in medical image segmentation, where models outline structures in scans. In breast cancer segmentation, models perform worse for younger patients, a gap usually blamed on denser breast tissue. The team audits the MAMA-MIA dataset and quantifies the bias in its automated labels, uncovering a biased ruler effect: flawed validation labels can misstate a model's true bias.

Controlled experiments then test where the bias comes from. It does not stem from label quality sensitivity, nor from an imbalance in case difficulty counts, and balancing training data by difficulty fails to close the gap. Younger cases appear intrinsically harder to learn. Training on biased machine-made labels teaches and amplifies the disparity, a warning for automated annotation pipelines.
arxiv-2511-00677:
Robert Ghrist and Cassie Ding rebuild persistent homology with a new yardstick: precision instead of scale. Classic persistence tracks how topological features are born and die as geometry grows, summed up in barcodes. Working over the p-adic integers, the authors define arithmetic barcodes for network sheaves, where each bar marks the precision level at which a cohomology class stops lifting through finer and finer approximations.

Their central Digit-SNF Dictionary shows hierarchical precision data from maps between successive levels encodes exactly the Smith normal form exponents of the coboundary operator. For rank-one sheaves, loop holonomy fixes bar lengths through p-adic valuation, and stability holds under small shifts that respect precision. Torsion becomes the signal, not a nuisance, with uses from quantized consensus to sensor synchronization.
arxiv-2511-00877:
Yuanceng Xu, Li Li, and Wei-Jia Li look inside anti-de Sitter black holes in holographic axion models, which describe strongly coupled materials that break translation symmetry. They strain these solids by shearing them and ask what happens to the black hole interior.

Shear, they find, always removes the inner Cauchy horizon. The bridge like structure inside collapses there, the geometry turns sharply anisotropic, and the interior heads toward a spacelike singularity. For power law axion potentials, strong shear can also create a domain wall with a scaling region near the boundary and a Kasner style epoch near the horizon. Deeper inside, the dynamics settle into anisotropic Kasner behavior, sometimes alternating between epochs as the singularity nears.
arxiv-2511-00977:
Kristiyan Sakalyan and colleagues introduce NicheFlow, a generative model for tracking how cell neighborhoods change over time in tissue. Spatial transcriptomics can now map gene activity across tissue slices at several time points, but most models follow single cells and miss how whole local communities develop together.

NicheFlow treats each local neighborhood as a point cloud and learns how both cell states and their positions evolve between slices. It combines optimal transport with variational flow matching to make that inference. On data sets ranging from embryonic development to brain development, the model recovers both the large scale tissue layout and the local mix of cell types. That offers a way to study development and disease as moving ecosystems, rather than isolated cells.
arxiv-2511-01077:
David McCoy, Yulun Wu, and Zachary Butzin-Dozier argue, in a position paper, that progress in large language models should be measured as capability per unit of resource, not by scale alone. They criticize what they call scaling fundamentalism, pointing to environmental costs and widening inequality in who can afford to build models.

Their framework uses gradient influence patterns to guide where resources go. In transformers, a small share of parameters carries outsized influence. They argue that updating only high influence parameters beats full tuning per unit of resource. Simple gradient norms can find those parameters cheaply. Pairing parameter selection with data selection multiplies the gains. They propose gradient blueprints, shared metadata about which parameters matter, to spread the method.
arxiv-2511-20177:
Dai, Chen, Shu, and colleagues feed language-model world knowledge into sequential recommenders carefully. Their 2025 paper proposes GRASP for predicting users' next actions. Recommenders read past behavior to guess what comes next. Collaborative signals alone are often too thin. Language models add rich world knowledge about items.

That knowledge arrives with hallucinations attached, though. Prior work trusted model output far too readily. GRASP retrieves similar users and items as auxiliary context. Generation-augmented retrieval synthesizes helpful item descriptions. Holistic attention then weighs knowledge at several levels. Noisy guidance gets filtered instead of obeyed blindly. Two public benchmarks plus one industrial dataset were used. The industry set held one hundred thousand interactions. GRASP reached state-of-the-art results across diverse backbones. Gains held when paired with varied base models. The design deploys as a front-end feature module. Deployed systems can adopt it without surgery.
arxiv-2511-20277:
Zhang, Wu, Xu, Wu, Xu, Drew, and Niu speed up neural training by reading the whole landscape. Their 2025 paper introduces HVAdam, a full-dimension optimizer. Adam-like methods tune each parameter's step separately. Per-dimension tuning ignores the global loss shape. Valleys then trap training in slow zigzags.

HVAdam tracks a hidden vector across all dimensions. That vector captures the loss surface's trend direction. Updates align with the trend instead of fighting it. A restart strategy refreshes the trend estimate. Convergence is proved for convex and non-convex cases. Toy functions show it reaching optima fastest. Image classification tasks confirmed faster convergence. Image generation and language tasks agreed with the trend. Gains were largest on GAN training benchmarks. Wasserstein GAN variants improved especially clearly. Accuracy and stability rose together in tests. Extra memory overhead is the admitted cost.
arxiv-2511-20377:
Kunnawalkam Elayavalli maps fifty unsolved questions about limits of matrix algebras. The 2025 paper collects open problems on ultraproduct II-one factors. Von Neumann algebras extend matrices to endless dimensions. An ultraproduct glues endless many into one limit object. Their theory hides many basic mysteries still.

Problems span classification, embeddings, and group algebras. One asks how many classes matrices produce. Another probes embeddings with small commutants. Ioana and Popa posed that embedding question. One family asks whether free group factors mimic matrices. For rank two and above it remains open. Non-pseudocompact examples are known to exist already. Partial progress covers rigid group factors. Entropy bounds give another solved corner. Each problem carries notes and references. The list updates an earlier ultraproduct collection. Operator algebraists get a shared to-do list. Connes's embedding legacy runs through many items. Newcomers can find entry points quickly.
arxiv-2511-20477:
Issifu, Konstantinou, da Silva, and Frederico spin up hypothetical stars made of quarks. Their 2025 paper compares two models of strange quark matter. Such stars would be self-bound balls of up, down, and strange quarks. Rotation changes their masses, shapes, and observable signals. Two equations of state give competing predictions to test.

The vector MIT bag model includes repulsive interactions between quarks. The density-dependent quark mass model lets quark masses vary with density. General relativistic calculations spun both kinds of stars uniformly. The MIT model supports stars above 3.3 solar masses. Its spin frequencies exceed about 1,450 hertz before breakup. The rival model caps near 2.8 solar masses with larger radii. Its surface redshift peaks near 0.59 versus 0.88 for MIT stars. A full energy budget decomposition is presented for rotating stars. Mass, radius, and spin together can discriminate the models.
arxiv-2511-20677:
Saleh Almohaimeed and colleagues present in 2025 Ar-SParC, the first Arabic dataset for text-to-SQL conversations that unfold over several linked turns. Users question a database in plain words while software writes the SQL, the language databases understand. Work existed for English and Chinese but not Arabic, despite more than 400 million Arabic speakers worldwide. The team modelled their set on the English SParC benchmark.

Ar-SParC contains 3,450 question sequences, averaging about three linked questions each, for a total of 10,225 questions with matching queries. They are spread over 160 databases in 116 domains. Using the set, the authors ran 40 experiments with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4.5-turbo across ten prompting techniques. Their new GAT corrector, a checking step that repairs model output, improved every experiment. It added 1.9 percent in execution accuracy under zero-shot settings, where the model sees no examples first, with smaller gains under example-based prompting.
arxiv-2511-20977:
Junkai Hu and Li Xia tackle in 2025 how clusters of microgrids should trade power with the main grid without a central controller. Each microgrid updates its own energy policy, yet the cluster is judged jointly: cheap operation matters, and so does reliability, measured by how wildly the exchanged power swings. They capture both goals with the mean and variance of exchange power, framing management as a mean-variance team stochastic game. Standard reward-maximising methods cannot handle the variance term.

Two algorithms follow. For known models, a fully distributed independent policy gradient method comes with rigorous convergence analysis. For large, unknown settings, a deep reinforcement learning version learns from data. Numerical experiments in two scenarios validate both approaches. The authors claim the first fully distributed, risk-sensitive cooperative learning scheme with guarantees for heterogeneous multi-agent energy systems, balancing cost against operational steadiness.
arxiv-2511-21377:
Ben Anson and Laurence Aitchison stabilize the training of transformer language models by watching the right quantity, in 2025. During training, the query and key weights inside attention tend to balloon, and the scores they produce, the attention logits, can blow up and wreck learning. The standard fix, QK norm, rescales queries and keys, but it clashes with Multi-Latent Attention, an efficient design that never fully builds those matrices at inference time.

Anson and Aitchison argue that what matters is not the logits' size but how fast they change per training step. They bound that change and control it with parameter-dependent learning rates assigned to the query and key weights, a cheap change they call QuacK. The intervention lets the whole network train at a higher base learning rate. It beats rival stabilizers in the Multi-Latent Attention setting and matches QK norm under ordinary multi-head attention.
arxiv-2511-21577:
Kexin Li, Xiao Hu, Ilya Grishchenko, and David Lie strip the watermarks from AI-generated audio under realistic attacker conditions, in 2025. Watermarks are the main defense against voice-cloning fraud and misinformation, but earlier removal attacks assumed impractical knowledge of the scheme or heavy computation, flattering the defenses. HarmonicAttack needs only one ability: generating watermarked samples from the targeted scheme, nothing about its internals.

From such samples the team trains a general removal model, a dual-path autoencoder working in time and frequency domains under adversarial training. It learns to separate watermark from content and erase the former. Against three leading schemes, AudioSeal, WavMark, and SilentCipher, HarmonicAttack outperformed prior attacks while keeping the cleaned audio high-quality. It neutralized the watermarks with attack success near 100 percent at near-real-time speed. Watermark designers now have an honest yardstick: robustness claims must survive a closed-box attacker.
arxiv-2511-21877:
Petrovic and colleagues present a workflow using large language models to write automotive code from plain-language requirements, with guardrails. Car software is safety-critical, and language models often invent nonexistent signal names. Their system first retrieves real signals from the Vehicle Signal Specification catalogue, a master list of car signals, and feeds only those into the prompt.

The retrieved signals are mapped and checked, then arranged into event chains, diagrams that encode what causes what and how long each step may take. Those chains constrain generated code, enforcing timing and behaviour beforehand. In an emergency braking case study, the workflow achieved valid signal usage and consistent code generation without retraining the language model at all in the authors' tests. Generated code was even run on a modified Volkswagen ID. Buzz test vehicle, where hazard lights switched on when a camera detected a person.
arxiv-2511-22177:
Yu, Kothawade, Xie, Wu, and Fei improve text-to-image generation without touching the model's weights: they retime it. A diffusion sampler spends its step budget along a fixed schedule, yet a prompt demanding rendered text needs different pacing than one asking for three oranges. Their method learns an instance-level schedule, conditioned on the prompt and the starting noise, output in a pass by a Dirichlet policy trained with the REINFORCE algorithm. A novel James-Stein shrinkage reward baseline with provably lower estimation error stabilizes it.

Across Stable Diffusion and Flux, rescheduled samplers improve text-image alignment, including text rendering and compositional control. A five-step Flux-Dev sampler with learned schedules matches the quality of distilled few-step models like Flux-Schnell. The authors pitch scheduling as a model-agnostic post-training lever, complementary to fine-tuning and distillation, that unlocks quality in pretrained samplers.
arxiv-2511-22277:
Princis, Sharma, and David, computer scientists, stop asking language models nicely and start constraining them mechanically. Prompted code generators routinely emit programs violating syntax, style, or execution constraints. TreeCoder frames decoding itself as a tree search over candidate programs in which decoding strategies and constraint functions, style, syntax, even execution checks, are first-class, tunable components. So the whole configuration can be explored systematically and optimized automatically with standard techniques instead of hand-tweaked per model.

On the MBPP Python benchmark and the Spider SQL benchmark, TreeCoder improves accuracy across open-source models including CodeLlama, Mistral, and DeepSeek, beating their unconstrained baselines by margins, without retraining any of them. The authors present the framework as the most general testbed yet for a practical question practitioners face daily. Given a fixed model, how much correctness is hiding in better decoding and properly enforced constraints?
arxiv-2511-22377:
Flaminio, Godo, and Rosella study if-then statements, called conditionals, and how their probabilities connect to ways of updating beliefs. A selection function picks the closest worlds where the if-part holds, and conditionals built this way cover many familiar kinds, including counterfactuals. The question is whether updating beliefs after learning something can always be read as the probability that some conditional holds.

The team proves that the probability of a selection-function conditional can be described exactly using updated belief functions from Dempster-Shafer theory, a framework for reasoning with partial evidence. In contrast, ordinary Bayesian updating cannot be captured as the probability of such a conditional, except in one narrow case where the set of closest worlds has a single member. So a broad family of updates cannot be read as betting on an if-then statement, which narrows the search for operators that could represent them.
arxiv-2511-22477:
Xu, Lin, and Zhang settle a decades-old question about ice: whether two crystal forms of frozen water hold exactly the same residual entropy, the disorder remaining even near absolute zero. In ice, hydrogen atoms sit between oxygens under rules leaving many arrangements possible. Hexagonal ice, the everyday form, was proven to have at least as much residual entropy as cubic ice, with numbers suggesting the two are extremely close but not proven equal.

The authors encode the ice rules into tensor networks, turning the entropy into the largest eigenvalue of a transfer operator. They show that if this operator is normal, a standard matrix property, equality follows directly, and variational tensor network calculations verify that normality. Finally, their split corner transfer matrix algorithm computes both entropies directly at high precision, together providing rigorous evidence that the two residual entropies are indeed equal.
arxiv-2511-22877:
Kim, Wieser, and Yang prove a local-global principle for quadratic form representation. A binary form, in two variables, is represented by a quaternary form, in four variables, when a linear map between the lattices intertwines them exactly. Representation everywhere locally is clearly necessary; whether it is sufficient drives the arithmetic of quadratic forms, and in this dimension range classical means did not settle it.

The proof's engine is ergodic theory: a recent Einsiedler-Lindenstrauss measure rigidity theorem for diagonalisable actions on quotients of products of SL2. With rigidity, the problem reduces to showing that limits of uniform measures on the associated rank-one adelic toral packets carry more than half the maximal entropy. That bound is proved with the Siegel mass formula and the determinant method of Bombieri, Pila, and Heath-Brown. The result ties a concrete question to deep machinery in homogeneous dynamics.
arxiv-2511-23477:
Rasheed and colleagues change how multimodal models reason about video. From thinking about a video in text after one passive encoding pass to thinking with the video through active manipulation. Their model Video-CoM works through a chain of manipulations, repeatedly rewatching, refocusing on segments and frames, and verifying evidence. In effect instead of treating the visual input as a fixed context that reasoning can drift away from.

Training combines an 18 thousand example instruction dataset built for multi-step manipulation reasoning with reinforcement learning whose rewards grade intermediate reasoning steps, not just final answers. Across nine video reasoning benchmarks Video-CoM improves average performance by 3.6 percent over recent state-of-the-art models while training on only 25 thousand supervised and 3 thousand reinforcement samples. Far fewer than comparable large-scale systems, and ablations credit the step-level rewards for accuracy and interpretability in the study.
arxiv-2512-00277:
Angles need special statistics, because a direction of zero degrees and one of three hundred sixty are the same. Andrew Cooper and co-authors develop robust wrapped Gaussian process inference for noisy angular data in 2025. Angular responses arise wherever data have a directional or orientational component.

One popular approach wraps real-valued functions around the unit circle with a modulo transformation. The authors aim to make such inference robust when the angular data are noisy. Reliable directional models serve fields from wind forecasting to neuroscience, where directions and phases are the measurements that matter. Wrapped distributions are the standard trick the authors aim to make more reliable. Gaussian processes bring flexible curves plus honest uncertainty estimates to the task.
arxiv-2512-00377:
Memecoins are crypto assets born from internet culture rather than new technology. Yuexin Xiang and co-authors measure the fragility of memecoin ecosystems in 2025. Their prices move with viral social media diffusion, celebrity influence, and speculative inflows more than with utility.

The team presents what they call the first Memecoin Ecosystem Fragility Framework, designed to capture these special weak spots. A fragility measure could warn holders and regulators how quickly such markets might collapse. The work treats memecoins as a social phenomenon with financial consequences, not just as a trading curiosity. Fragility here means exposure to sudden sentiment swings, not weakness of the code. A framework gives exchanges and researchers a shared vocabulary for that exposure. For folks who hold such coins, the gain is a gauge. It can warn when a crowd's mood is the sole prop left, and the floor may give way soon.
arxiv-2512-00777:
Nitin Singh, Arie Syulistyo, Yuichiro Tanaka, and Hakaru Tamukoh build a lighter sign language reader in a 2025 paper. Sign language recognition turns hand signs into text or speech, helping deaf and hearing people talk with each other. Deep learning systems do this well but demand heavy computing power.

That cost rules out cheap, small devices. The team instead pairs MediaPipe, which tracks hand joint positions, with an echo state network using bidirectional reservoir computing. Reservoir methods train only a small part of the network, saving effort. Their design aims for accurate signing recognition on modest hardware.
arxiv-2512-01077:
Neha Joshi and a large team present ELR-1000 in a 2025 paper on endangered languages. Many Indic indigenous languages have few speakers and almost no digital resources. Without data, language technology cannot serve the communities that speak them.

The dataset holds over a thousand traditional recipes crowdsourced from rural communities across remote parts of Eastern India. It spans ten endangered languages and pairs text with other media, grounded in local culture. Collection used a mobile interface designed for contributors with low digital literacy. Recipes carry rich, everyday vocabulary, making them a natural vessel for preserving both language and food heritage.
arxiv-2512-01377:
Ryosuke Hirai studies pairs of white dwarf stars that pass mass between them. Some pairs hold two helium white dwarfs. When one feeds the other in a stable way, the pair can become an AM CVn system. How many such pairs exist in our galaxy is not known.

Hirai works out when that mass flow stays stable. His tests treat each dwarf as cold and fully packed. The count of stable pairs sets the birth rate of AM CVn systems. That rate helps scope hunts for their faint light and for the waves they send through space.
arxiv-2512-01777:
Jack Homans and co-authors set out the MAQRO-PF white paper on macroscopic quantum resonators. Optically levitated particles serve many experiments. They probe fundamental physics and sense tiny forces. Quantum mechanics at large scales is a key open field for them.

The Pathfinder paper maps a route to test quantum acts with big resonators. It lays out goals, hardware needs, and key risks. A shared road map lets labs align their steps. Tests at that scale could show where quantum rules give way to classical ones, if they do. Levitated tests are table-top in scale, which lets many labs join the pathfinder program without space mission budgets or launch slots.
arxiv-2512-02177:
Crater 2 is a sprawling, extremely faint dwarf galaxy whose stars are being pulled apart by the Milky Way's tides. Guilherme Limberg and a large collaboration report in 2025 the results of a spectroscopic campaign around Crater 2 and its tidal tails, part of the Southern Stellar Stream Spectroscopic Survey.

Spectroscopy measures the stars' motions and chemistry, showing how the galaxy is dissolving and what it was made of. Crater 2 is a case study in how diffuse dwarf galaxies form in the Local Group. Its unraveling also probes the Milky Way's gravitational field, since tidal streams trace the gravity that shapes them.
arxiv-2512-02877:
Bruno Barton-Singer, Anusree Navallur, and Stavros Komineas track magnetic whirlpools that remember where they stopped. Skyrmions are tiny swirling patterns in a magnet, here living in a bilayer with antiferromagnetic coupling between layers. A magnetic field gradient sets the pair in motion.

The skyrmions move almost sideways to the gradient, then halt at a set distance apart. That positional memory, found by simulation and analysis, is the core effect studied. Controllable skyrmion placement matters for proposed memory devices that store bits in these stable magnetic swirls. A pair that stops at a set gap is a pair that can be parked. Parked bits are the base of a store that holds.
arxiv-2512-03177:
Fluid flow data may be hard or easy for quantum methods. Antonio Francesco Mello, Mario Collura, Miles Stoudenmire, and Ryan Levy measure that difficulty in this 2025 work. Their data come from simulations of two-dimensional shear flow that repeats in space.

The team encodes the data in a compact form and measures entanglement and non-stabilizerness. Those two traits show how much quantum resource a solver would need. The measures span several flow regimes, from calm to turbulent. The results help judge when quantum or tensor methods can handle fluid problems well. Flow regime matters, since turbulent data carry far more structure than smooth laminar cases.
arxiv-2512-03877:
Some particle decays happen so rarely that measuring them takes billions of collisions. The BESIII Collaboration reports one such measurement in a 2025 experimental preprint: the weak radiative decay of the Xi-zero hyperon into a photon and a Sigma-zero hyperon. The data come from the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider in China.

The team produced the hyperons through decays of J/psi particles, collecting more than ten billion such events. From that sample they extract an absolute branching fraction for the decay, a few parts in a thousand, with statistical and systematic uncertainties stated separately. A full angular analysis of the cascade decay chain also yields the decay asymmetry parameter, which comes out large and negative. Numbers like these test theories of how hyperons decay and how the weak force acts inside strange particles.
arxiv-2512-04177:
Cosmic inflation is usually pictured as beginning arbitrarily early, with no observable first moment. Rashmish K. Mishra, Michael Nee, and Lisa Randall ask what changes if inflation had a finite start, in a 2025 physics preprint. Their stage is a five-dimensional warped space with two branes; the fifth dimension grows as inflation proceeds.

The authors derive the ultraviolet brane's motion through the bulk and the resulting four-dimensional effective action. Early evolution is driven by the radion rolling fast; late evolution, by the inflaton rolling slowly. The action matches a two-field hyperbolic inflation model, whose holographic dual pairs an inflaton with a strongly coupled confining sector. The infrared brane leaves fingerprints: deviations from the near-de Sitter background, a blue tilt in the large-scale scalar spectrum, and oscillations in the tensor spectrum. Numerical fits to the scalar spectrum feed microwave background analysis.
arxiv-2512-04377:
Gabriel Ribeiro, Renan Magalhães, and Luís Crispino study black holes that wear extra fields, nicknamed hair, and ask how those fields change the waves a hole can swallow. The three hairy solutions they test come from a method called gravitational decoupling. Each solution obeys a distinct energy rule: weak, strong, or dominant. Their 2025 arXiv paper tracks massless scalar waves as the holes absorb them.

In some hairy setups under the weak energy rule, waves can linger in quasibound states near the hole. Those states stamp sharp, bell-shaped spikes on the absorption spectrum, like spectral lines. The spikes trace back to stable rings of light in the space around the hole. Such rings are more often linked to star-like objects with no horizon. The team shows how the decoupling knobs create new light rings and shift the lines, with numbers that match known approximations.
arxiv-2512-04477:
Tian Qiu, Wenting Wang, Sergey Koposov, and co-authors count how many stars in the dwarf galaxy Ursa Minor travel in pairs. Binary stars sway as they orbit, and that sway shows up as shifts in their measured speed along our line of sight. The team used repeated readings from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument's Milky Way Survey. Their 2025 arXiv paper covers hundreds of member stars watched over about a year.

With more than two thousand readings on hundreds of stars, the team fit the share that must be binaries to explain the speed jitter. Two classic models of orbital traits gave binary shares near six tenths and seven tenths. Splitting stars by metal content showed a slightly higher pair share among metal-rich stars. Such counts test how stars form in a tiny, dark-matter-rich galaxy, and they clean up mass estimates that binaries can distort.
arxiv-2512-04677:
Yubo Huang, Hailong Guo, Fangtai Wu, and co-authors present Live Avatar, a system that streams a talking digital face in real time with no length limit. Audio-driven avatars must answer live, keep streaming, and hold a steady identity for hours. Diffusion models fight all three demands: they denoise step by step in sequence and drift over long runs. Their 2025 arXiv paper co-designs the algorithm and the hardware layout to break that knot.

A two-stage pipeline distills a large bidirectional model into a causal, few-step streaming one. Extra strategies stop identity drift and visual glitches across runs past ten thousand seconds. On the system side, each graphics processor owns one fixed denoising step, turning the chain into an asynchronous spatial pipeline. The split lifts throughput while cutting delay. Live, endless avatars could serve streaming hosts and virtual assistants.
arxiv-2512-04777:
Alexander Shlapunov and Alexander Polkovnikov study a cousin of the Navier-Stokes equations built from complex analysis instead of the usual gradient operators. The classical equations govern incompressible fluids through gradient, divergence, and curl. Their system swaps those for the Cauchy-Riemann operator in several complex variables, its adjoint, and the matching Dolbeault complex.
