Their 2025 arXiv paper poses the start-value problem for this system on a time band and asks what can be proved.

The structural kinship with Navier-Stokes carries the day. Working in specially built Bochner-Sobolev spaces, the authors prove that weak solutions exist. They also prove an open mapping theorem on that scale of spaces. A criterion sorts out when a strong solution can exist at all. Such parallel systems test which parts of fluid theory depend on the exact operators and which flow from structure alone, sharpening both fields.
arxiv-2512-04977:
Oem Trivedi and Venkat Venkatasubramanian argue that black holes and the universe as a whole play by different rules of heat and disorder. A settled black hole, they show, fits the classic picture worked out by Bekenstein and Hawking, where disorder grows with the area of the horizon. The expanding universe, by contrast, does not fit that picture at all, and forcing it to do so leads theory astray.

Their alternative is teleodynamics, a framework in which a system carries a memory of its past. They argue that such memory is unavoidable in cosmology but has no place for a settled black hole. Built-up memory, they argue, explains why the universe drifts away from the simple area rule. The upshot is that quantum gravity should stop stretching black hole rules to cover the cosmos and instead treat horizon memory as a basic ingredient.
arxiv-2512-05477:
Motohiko Ezawa reviews quantum geometry — the differential geometry that quantum mechanics itself supplies — and turns it on a trendy family of magnets. Quantum geometry governs how electrons respond in transport and optics, and its Zeeman generalization, which includes spin, controls cross-responses between charge and magnetism. Ezawa lays out the framework's extensions to non-Hermitian systems and to density matrices, where the quantum Fisher information of information theory appears as a metric.

The applications target X-wave magnets, a family that includes the altermagnets alongside p-wave and f-wave cousins. Across the family, universal behaviour shows up in Hall responses, tunnelling magnetoresistance, and the planar Hall effect. Ezawa adds magneto-optical conductivity, magnetic circular dichroism, and Friedel oscillations to the list. He derives analytic formulas for two-band models. The paper is a progress report on a young field and a source of new results for these magnets.
arxiv-2512-06177:
Jiahan Xie, Evan Williams, and Adrian Sampson build a bridge from the world's most popular machine learning framework to custom silicon. Models are written in PyTorch; accelerators want hardware descriptions. Their toolchain compiles PyTorch to SystemVerilog via Allo and Calyx. Custom passes partition memory for parallelism.

The FPGA designs perform reasonably against Vitis HLS. An open toolchain now stands within sight of the commercial one. Compiler infrastructure shapes who gets to design accelerators. Open paths let small teams experiment instead of renting a black box. The toolchain runs end to end and is open source.
arxiv-2512-06877:
Mohammed Q Alkhatib, Ali Jamali, and Swalpa Kumar Roy design a compact neural network that labels aerial and satellite scenes, sorting images into types of land use and land cover. The task is harder than it looks: the same kind of place can appear at many scales, angles, and orientations, with cluttered backgrounds. Heavy transformer models do well but cost much computation, limiting their use on modest hardware.

Their model, SceneMixer, alternates two cheap operations. One mixes information across nearby positions at several scales, catching fine detail and broad context. The other mixes across the network's channels using simple pointwise steps. Tested on two public benchmarks of overhead imagery, the design reached accuracy close to far larger rivals while keeping size and computing needs low. The authors frame the trade-off as a practical win for Earth observation groups with limited resources, and plan to share the code.
arxiv-2512-06977:
Laurentius Valdy and co-authors rebuild full three-dimensional images from deliberately incomplete scans, a shortcut that speeds up medical and scientific imaging. Taking fewer measurements makes the puzzle ill-posed: many images could fit the same data. Heavy generative models can fill the gaps, but running them across many slices at once eats memory on each graphics card.

Their framework splits the job. A diffusion model supplies learned expectations about what slices should look like, applied in partitions to keep memory low. Hard physics constraints from the scanner keep the result honest. Tests span two very different tools: magnetic resonance imaging of the body, and a four-dimensional electron microscopy method for materials. The partitioned approach beat both physics-only reconstruction and full multi-slice baselines. It also stayed accurate on data unlike its training set, a sign the physics guardrails help when the learned expectations falter.
arxiv-2512-07177:
Fanjun Bu and co-authors ask how a service robot can tell whether a nearby person wants to talk to it. In a five-day field deployment, a mobile robot worked a university cafe while human operators secretly steered it, a Wizard-of-Oz setup. Watching how patrons signaled readiness through glances and body positioning, and how the expert operators read those cues, the team mapped the nonverbal grammar of starting an interaction.

Their pipeline saves the expensive judgment for the right moments. Lightweight detectors track gaze shifts and personal distance continuously, and only when those cues turn meaningful do they trigger a video-capable vision-language model to reason about the scene. On replays of the field interactions, two prompting strategies for the big model were compared.
arxiv-2512-07277:
Srihari Bandarupalli and co-authors shrink speech recognition for languages the industry underserves, using Persian, Arabic, and Urdu as the proving ground. Recognizers starve where labeled recordings are scarce, and the biggest models demand computing that low-resource settings cannot supply. The team's lever is unlabeled speech: a scalable pipeline gathers thousands of hours of raw audio in the Perso-Arabic family. And continual pretraining teaches the model the sounds of these languages before any transcripts are needed.

Combined with tokenization that respects how these languages build words, the recipe yields a model a fifth the size of the leading commercial-scale rival. On Persian it beats that rival outright, and on Arabic and Urdu it stays competitive, despite far fewer parameters and much less labeled data.
arxiv-2512-08077:
Jaron Cohen, Alexander G Hasson, and Sara Tanovic, a team working where machine learning meets chemistry, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is language models trained for chemistry, which predict how molecules behave and design new ones well. What these models know inside, and how that knowledge is laid out, has stayed poorly understood.

The team uses sparse autoencoders, a tool that pulls a model inner features apart into parts a person can read. Working with a foundation model called SMI TED, they extract latent features and track when each fires across many sets of molecules. The features line up with real ideas in the field, such as common building patterns in molecules, traits of matter, and drug classes. The same method works on other such models, and could help scientists trust and steer tools now guiding drug and materials work.
arxiv-2512-08177:
Debasis Mishra, Sanket Patil, and Alessandro Pavan, economists, posted a theory paper on arXiv in December 2025 about buying goods under a cautious approver. A Bayesian designer plans the purchase, but a non Bayesian authority must approve the deal. The authority shares the designer goal yet is unsure of the good value and the supplier cost.

The designer may only pick mechanisms that give the authority the largest guaranteed payoff. That worst case requirement changes the usual balance between efficiency and keeping supplier rent down. It reduces buying from sellers with mid range costs, yet can increase buying from high cost sellers. When the good is resold in a market, the paper compares two tools. Quantity regulation wins when markups are large in the designer model, while price regulation wins when demand uncertainty is large.
arxiv-2512-08377:
Marcus Schoenfelder, a mathematician in combinatorics, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. His subject is domino tilings of the Aztec diamond, a region tiled by two by one dominoes. Using a shuffling algorithm that generates tilings uniformly at random, he studies the chance of a domino at one specific spot.

He proves this placement probability always takes a neat form. It is one quarter, plus a rational function of the domino position, scaled by a factor set only by the diamond size. That structure yields explicit counting formulas far more compact than earlier results. As a direct use, he derives formulas counting the tilings of Aztec diamonds with two by two square holes punched at arbitrary positions. The paper adds exact knowledge to a classic model where random tilings show striking patterns, such as the famous arctic circle phenomenon.
arxiv-2512-08677:
Mayara Antunes, Bernardo Carvalho, and Welington Cordeiro prove a result about shadowing for maps on compact metric spaces and for the maps they induce on collections of subsets. A homeomorphism has the L shadowing property when approximate orbits can be closely followed by true orbits in a set sense. The question is whether that property passes to the induced hyperspace map.

The authors show the property holds for the original map exactly when it holds for the induced map. In the proof, shadowing alone yields points with a local product structure whose iterates approach at a uniform rate. That uniformity is notable, because many maps with this shadowing property lack uniform contraction on their stable and unstable sets.
arxiv-2512-08877:
Ryan LeRoy and Jack Kolb study whether a common multi agent reinforcement learning method learns the game itself or merely learns its training teammates. In self play, agents often share one policy and train with identical partners. That setup can hide overfitting to specific partner behavior, which would hurt deployment with new teammates.

The study uses a challenge environment with two distinct agent types that have complementary abilities, an observer and a drone. The authors introduce rotating policy training, which cycles in teammate policies from different learning algorithms during training. That rotation exposes the agent to a broader range of partner strategies. When tested with a withheld teammate policy, the rotating method matches a standard self play baseline. That result suggests the baseline already generalizes to novel teammates in this setting. A diverse training regimen, designed to force generalization, proves not to be necessary here.
arxiv-2512-09177:
Murman Gurgenidze and colleagues revisit a proposed origin for the first magnetic fields in the universe. In a plasma of electrons and their antimatter partners, an imbalance between right-handed and left-handed particles can grow a twisting magnetic field. This process is called the chiral plasma instability.

Standard reasoning says the idea fails once the early universe cools below a very high temperature, because scattering reactions then erase any handedness imbalance. The authors show that a steady source of new imbalance changes the verdict. With such a source, the instability can keep working at lower temperatures. Using both analysis and direct computer simulation, they derive predictions for the twist, or helicity, of the magnetic field that results. The work reopens a possible route to primordial magnetism and gives concrete features that future models must match.
arxiv-2512-09277:
Yanpeng Yu leads a systems team working on mixture-of-experts language models, in which each piece of text is routed to a few specialist subnetworks. Spreading those experts across many graphics processors lets the models grow huge. The usual fix for uneven workloads is to balance the number of tokens each processor handles.

The authors show that this fix backfires when serving is limited by memory, as often happens while generating text. Balancing tokens activates more experts per processor, and loading those experts strains memory further. Their routing algorithm, METRO, instead balances the number of activated experts. It gathers global routing knowledge cheaply and keeps routing quality near optimal. In tests on real and simulated hardware serving Qwen3 and DeepSeek-V3, METRO cut generation delays and raised throughput, in some settings several-fold, compared with the standard load balancer.
arxiv-2512-09377:
Lidan Xu and colleagues ask a question about drone transport: can two drones carrying a bar between them know the load's pose without sensors? Suspended aerial transport is buffeted by aerodynamic effects and thrust errors. Existing methods add sensors to measure cable directions or the payload's pose, which raises cost.

Focusing on the two-drone-bar system, the authors prove with the observability rank criterion that the whole system is observable from the drones' odometry alone. That holds as long as no more than two types of lumped disturbances act at once. They state this is the first such result. To back it up, they build a composite disturbance filter for disturbances acting only on the drones. It combines a disturbance observer with an error-state Kalman filter on the system's natural geometry. Simulations and experiments confirm that state and disturbances can both be estimated from odometry only.
arxiv-2512-09477:
Guillem Arias and colleagues study how color is stored inside Stable Diffusion, the widely used image generation model. Such models produce strikingly faithful images, yet how they represent traits like color and shape inside is poorly understood. Knowing that structure could make models easier to understand and edit.

Using controlled synthetic datasets, principal component analysis, and similarity measures, the team mapped the model's latent space. Color turns out to be encoded along circular, opponent axes, carried mainly by two of the latent channels, while intensity and shape live mostly in the other two. That layout mirrors efficient coding schemes found in perception science: the latent space organizes information in a readable way rather than scattering it at random. The authors present their findings as a foundation for work on model understanding, editing tools, and designing generative models whose internal factors are more cleanly separated.
arxiv-2512-09777:
Simone Manti leads the VIP team in upgrading event choice for their detector at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. The experiment searches for radiation from collapse processes and for atomic jumps that would violate the Pauli exclusion principle, tests of quantum mechanics needing quiet. The detector records X-rays and gamma rays across a wide energy range.

Their machine learning pipeline first runs a denoising autoencoder that suppresses electronic and microphonic noise and reconstructs pulse shapes, then a convolutional neural network classifies waveforms as normal events or anomalies. Validated on more than twenty thousand recordings, the classifier reached ninety-five percent accuracy. Applying it lowers the detectable energy to about ten thousand electronvolts and improves the signal-to-background ratio and energy resolution on spectral lines, boosting the hunt for rare low-energy signals.
arxiv-2512-09877:
Bappaditya Bhowmik, Deblina Maity, and Toshiyuki Sugawa extend a classical inequality of complex analysis to a wider family of maps. The maps are meromorphic and univalent on the unit disk, meaning they are one to one but may blow up at a single simple pole inside the disk. The map also extends continuously to part of the boundary circle. The classical Gehring-Hayman inequality compares lengths of competing paths under such mappings.

The authors prove that the length of the image of a diameter, divided by the length of the image of a boundary arc, stays bounded. The bound depends only on where the pole sits. They then generalize the comparison from that diameter to any hyperbolic geodesic, and to Jordan curves sharing its endpoints. These results carry the classical inequality into the meromorphic setting. They also settle a conjecture that Bhowmik and Maity had posed in earlier work.
arxiv-2512-10177:
Shamil Asgarli, Sara Krehbiel, and Simon MacLean study graphs built out of graph colorings. Given a graph and a number of colors, the Bell coloring graph has one vertex for every partition of the original vertices into that many independent sets, allowing empty parts. Two partitions are joined when one move of a single vertex transforms one into the other. The authors ask which graphs can arise this way, and how much the coloring graph remembers about its parent. They first classify the cliques inside these graphs.

Every tree and every cycle can be realized as a Bell coloring graph. A small near complete graph cannot, and larger near complete graphs cannot even appear inside one, beyond a small threshold. Reconstruction results cut the other way: the Bell three coloring graph is a complete invariant for trees, meaning it determines the tree entirely.
arxiv-2512-10277:
A team led by Dibya Bharati Pradhan tests which signs of life future telescopes could actually detect on an Earth like planet ten parsecs away. They model reflection and thermal emission spectra across ultraviolet, visible, near infrared, and mid infrared bands. Temperature and pressure profiles come from weather model data of Earth's own atmosphere, fed into a photochemical model. Two flagship mission concepts are modeled: a large optical telescope and a mid infrared interferometer. Surface conditions encoding biology and geology are varied.

Ozone is detectable by both mission types, the most robust biosignature in the study. Water needs specific humidity levels, firmly for the interferometer and only possibly for the telescope. Carbon dioxide is detectable by the interferometer. Nitrous oxide and methane need continuous surface outgassing to show at all, and methane also needs dry surface conditions so water features do not mask it.
arxiv-2512-10477:
Timur Ishuov and co-authors present Symphony, a learning algorithm for teaching humanoid robots to move from scratch. They open with a complaint about expectations: children take years to learn movement, yet robots are often asked to learn in far fewer steps than real hardware can safely spare. Training must therefore be sample-efficient and gentle on motors and gearboxes.

Symphony combines several ideas toward that end. A swaddling rule restrains action strength, limited noise keeps motion smooth while entropy still grows safely, and a fading replay buffer blends recent and long-term memory. A temporal advantage measure lets the actor and critic update in a single pass, even merged into one object. The authors report empirically safer training for both the robot's mechanisms and its surroundings, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-10577:
Md Fahad Equbal and M Ahsan ask how holes pair up in the Hubbard model, the standard toy model of electrons that repel each other on a lattice. Pairing of the missing electrons, called holes, is a clue to superconductivity, and it competes with magnetic and charge patterns. The authors solve the model exactly, by brute-force diagonalisation, on a small cylindrical lattice.

In the plain model they find weakly bound hole pairs held together by magnetic correlations at middling repulsion, with no sign of the holes clumping into separate phases. Adding a neighbour interaction changes everything by sign. Attraction drives multi-hole clusters and phase separation with local magnetism switched off, while repulsion stabilises a charge-density wave that hosts bound pairs inside a patterned magnetic background. Real-space correlation maps show the two binding mechanisms at work.
arxiv-2512-11077:
Hyuna Kwon and colleagues present one unified model that cleans noisy atomic data, labels crystal phases, and measures how ordered a structure is. Simulations produce huge amounts of noisy structural data, and existing tools usually handle only a few crystal types and split those three jobs apart. Their probabilistic framework compares each atom's surroundings against known crystal prototypes.

The model assigns scores for each prototype, then combines them into a single smooth landscape over atomic positions. Its slope defines a denoising field that nudges atoms toward cleaner structures, while the scores give local phase labels and order measures. Trained on database crystals with added synthetic noise and strain, it handled stronger noise, hot disordered samples, defects, ice water mixtures, and shocked titanium. It also flagged uncertain regions near defects and phase boundaries.
arxiv-2512-11177:
Andrea Capa Salinas and a large team map how charge patterns and superconductivity interact in a layered kagome metal, a crystal whose atoms form a woven lattice. The material hosts both a charge density wave, where electrons settle into a repeating pattern, and superconductivity. Adding tin removes electrons and gradually melts the charge order, revealing two separate domes where superconductivity appears.

With light doping, a fragile charge pattern and superconducting fluctuations fade together. Heavier doping kills the long range charge order but leaves short range, almost one dimensional correlations that survive across the second dome. Those correlations vanish at exactly the doping where superconductivity ends, suggesting they are essential to it. The authors propose that local pairing of vanadium atoms into dimers explains the surviving pattern, with symmetry broken locally even without long range order.
arxiv-2512-11477:
Pierre Fima and Yigang Qiu study free wreath products in quantum group theory, where symmetry objects can be noncommutative. A compact quantum group generalises the symmetries of a space, and wreath products combine such symmetries with permutations, as when identical subsystems are shuffled. Bichon's free wreath products paired quantum groups with the free permutation group. Fima and Qiu build a parallel family using duals of finite groups instead.

For the resulting object they derive an explicit formula for its Haar state, the canonical averaging operation that plays the role of uniform integration. Under natural assumptions of Kac type and factoriality, they decompose the associated operator algebras into central summands. Those pieces turn out to be well behaved factors of a standard type, or simple algebras carrying a unique trace. The results extend the structural understanding of free wreath constructions in noncommutative geometry.
arxiv-2512-11577:
Sergei Stepanenko and co-authors extend Guarded Interaction Trees, a formal tool for proving facts about programs with side effects. The tool lives inside the Rocq proof assistant. It handled many effects well, but not ones whose meaning depends on context, such as call/cc or the shift and reset controls.

The extension adds those tricky effects while keeping all old proof rules intact for plain effects. The team uses it to give exact meanings to languages with call/cc and with bounded continuations, and proves the meanings match how the programs run. They also add preemptive concurrency, with atomic steps such as compare and swap, for proving facts about shared data.
arxiv-2512-11677:
A A Gunyaga, M V Durnev, and S A Tarasenko work out how shaped light beams drive electric currents in atom thin Dirac materials. Such sheets, like graphene, host electrons that act as if they have no mass. Twisted or patterned light can inject charge flow and sort electrons by spin and valley.

The team derives general formulas for current density and for how light creates electrons across momentum, space, and spin valley traits. They sort out the roles of local and non local effects. Named effects include alignment by straight polarized light, sorting by round polarized light, and photon drag that feels the beam shape. The theory guides future light controlled electronics.
arxiv-2512-11777:
Sinyoung Park, Matthew Nunes, and Sandipan Roy propose a new way to group nodes in sparse networks. Spectral clustering reads a network through its connection matrix or Laplacian. It works well on dense nets but can falter on core periphery shapes, where a rich core links to a sparse fringe, and on sparse data in general.

Their Doubled Adjacency Spectral Embedding squares the connection matrix before embedding, so weak two step ties count more. Theory backs the method with consistency proofs for sparse community finding. Broad simulations on directed and undirected nets show gains on sparse and dense cases alike. Tests on jobs and transport data show the method at work in practice.
arxiv-2512-11877:
Jeongwon Ho argues that recovering information from a black hole is the same act as sliding through space. The claim, Teleportation equals Translation, says the dual of info recovery is a geometric shift in the spacetime that emerges from the hole. Ho proves it for general local quantum field theories.

The proof builds a smooth unitary path linking step by step teleportation to steady modular flow. A snag with Type III algebras, the failure of dynamic idempotency, is fixed by lifting to a Type II envelope via a crossed product build. The generator of that path turns out to be exactly twice the geometric modular momentum. The result frames the black hole information paradox in clean operator terms.
arxiv-2512-12177:
Aydin Ayanzadeh and Tim Oates present Floorplan2Guide in a 2025 paper on indoor navigation for blind and low vision users. Finding a route inside a building is hard without sight. Most aids need sensors placed in the building, which limits where they work and how they handle change.

Floorplan2Guide uses a large language model to read a floor plan and build a map graph, then writes route steps in plain words. On the MP-1 floor plan, Claude 3.7 Sonnet scored 92.31, 76.92, and 61.54 percent on short, medium, and long routes with five examples. Graph based maps beat direct image reasoning by 15.4 percent in success rate.
arxiv-2512-12677:
Amirhossein Yousefiramandi and Ciaran Cooney compare two ways to fine tune causal language models for text classification in a 2025 paper. Resources are tight, so they combine 4-bit quantization with LoRA adapters to train models up to 8 billion parameters on one GPU. The question is whether a classification head on the final token embedding beats instruction tuning in a prompt to response format.

Two patent benchmarks were used. One was a 5 class internal corpus, and the other was the public WIPO-Alpha set with 14 categories. On them, the embedding head matched or beat fine tuned BERT on single label tasks. It also trained 10 to 30 times fewer parameters. Instruction tuning was competitive only on multi-label data, and only with at least 100 million trainable parameters.
arxiv-2512-12777:
Mosh Levy, Zohar Elyoseph, Shauli Ravfogel, and Yoav Goldberg argue that reasoning tokens in language models are better read as state than as story in a 2025 paper. Models often write chain of thought tokens before a final answer, and those sequences look like human thought. Evidence shows they do not faithfully explain the model's actual process, though, leaving a gap between appearance and function.

Their State over Tokens framework treats the tokens as externalized computational state: the only persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. That explains how tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation as text. The authors urge research to decode tokens as state rather than read them as narrative, and list questions this view opens.
arxiv-2512-13077:
Md Awsafur Rahman and co-authors introduce LikeBench, a benchmark for how likable a personalized language model feels over time. A good personal assistant should remember user facts and use them well. The authors argue that a third quality, likability, is just as central and far less measured.

In LikeBench, a model chats with a simulated user across sessions and learns tastes only from the dialogue. After each turn, the same simulated user rates likability on seven dimensions, from emotional fit to humor fit. Splitting likability into parts makes failures easier to diagnose. The framework tests whether models truly adapt to a person over time.
arxiv-2512-13277:
D. L. Neuhauser and co-authors re-examine three claimed links between historical sky records and nova shells: events in BC 48, 483, and 1645. Matching ancient guest star reports to modern remnants matters for tracing how shells and cataclysmic variables evolve. Only firm matches can be trusted.

They combine fresh translations of Chinese texts with brightness, decay, and shell age calculations. The BC 48 report sits far from the cluster M22 and was likely a comet. The 483 event fits a bolide better, and its shell looks like a planetary nebula. The 1645 text most likely meant Mars in motion. All three exact age claims fail.
arxiv-2512-13577:
Lokendra Kumar, Neelesh S. Upadhye, and Kannan Piedy use math optimization to assign staff to software tasks. Their model uses Mixed Integer Linear Programming, a method that picks whole-number choices under set limits. It takes in each worker's efficiency, task difficulty, and past performance scores.

The model aims at two goals: fair workloads matched to skill, and the lowest total project cost. It also updates efficiency values as new performance data comes in. In tests on simulated data, the method beat standard assignment plans on both fairness and cost. The authors present it as a scalable tool for project staffing in software work and beyond.
arxiv-2512-13777:
Alison Warman and Sakura Schäfer-Nameki build constant-depth quantum gates at any Clifford hierarchy level in two dimensions. Topological phase gates are prized for fault tolerance, but a theorem by Bravyi and König limits shallow circuits on standard stabilizer codes. Their construction bypasses that limit with non-Abelian surface codes.

A logical qubit is encoded in the quantum double of a non-Abelian group on a triangular patch. The gate stacks a symmetry-protected topological phase on the region, with boundary counter-terms, in constant depth. For dihedral groups, they realize fine phase gates in the logical basis. They also develop a non-Abelian stabilizer formalism and discuss code-switching to complete a universal gate set, at the cost of the non-Abelian code.
arxiv-2512-13877:
Ian M. Hayes and co-authors use heat transport to locate nodes in the superconducting gap of uranium ditelluride. UTe2 shows many superconducting phases under pressure and field, each likely with a distinct gap symmetry. None has been firmly identified, a recurring hurdle for unconventional superconductors.

They measure thermal conductivity in the low-field, low-temperature state while rotating a magnetic field in the b-c plane. Clear oscillations with field angle point to point nodes in the gap. Using the known Fermi surface, they model all candidate gap structures and match the nodes to the crystallographic b-axis. That places the order parameter in the B2u representation. The clear result should speed identification of the other UTe2 phases.
arxiv-2512-14277:
Panayiotis Smeros and four coauthors present SPARQL LLM in a 2025 paper on turning plain questions into SPARQL queries. SPARQL is the query language for knowledge graphs, and most people cannot write it. Language models can, but many systems ignore speed, cost, and use across many data stores.

SPARQL LLM is open source, works with any triplestore, and uses lightweight metadata to index sources, build prompts, and run queries. On a leading challenge with multilingual questions it beat the second best system by up to 59 percent in F1 score. It was also up to 27 times faster, at a maximum cost of 0.01 dollars per question. It handles English, Spanish, and German well.
arxiv-2512-14377:
Xiongfeng Ma introduces reality steering in a 2025 paper on quantum measurement. Measurement ties a superposition to an observer memory, so the local reality seen by the observer becomes single and definite. The global state, by contrast, stays coherent.

Reality steering would let an observer reach a different reality that the initial state already supports. It does so without reversing decoherence in the wider world. The trick is to erase the which outcome data stored locally in the observer memory. Success needs coherent help from observer counterparts across branches. Any switch also looks just like no switch, since memory records in the new reality fit it well. Tools beyond standard theory could in principle make such moves checkable.
arxiv-2512-14577: Global solution curves for a super-critical reaction equation are computed and analyzed here. The problem is posed on the unit ball, with the solution held at zero on the boundary. The model mixes a diffusion term with two power growth terms, scaled by a parameter. Analysis and computation together trace how the full set of solutions changes as that parameter varies. That is a standard way to study equations whose solutions can bend, branch, or disappear.
arxiv-2512-15177:
Davar Khoshnevisan and a coauthor find special points where a noisy heat equation stays unusually calm. The equation is a parabolic stochastic partial differential equation driven by space time white noise, starting from a flat profile of one. Near time zero, the solution at any fixed point behaves almost like a Gaussian.

The authors prove that random points exist where the fluctuations near time zero are almost surely of sharp order t to the one quarter power. Such points are slow growth points, spots where the solution stirs far less than typical. The work loosely echoes the study of slow points of Brownian motion, but the infinite dimensional setting brings real new challenges. The result adds fine detail to what is known about the wild, rough paths of stochastic heat flow.
arxiv-2512-15477:
Alisha Vasan and co authors characterize a persistence effect in the JWST MIRI detector in a 2025 paper. Persistence means a bright source leaves a lingering imprint on later images. For MIRI it appears as a flux deficit, a faint dark ghost, and it was poorly measured at the longest wavelengths.

The team studies full field images at 21 microns after a bright nearby star saturated the detector. They measure a persistence level of 1.69 percent shortly after saturation, and model its decay over hours. The paper then warns that such ghosts can mimic exoplanets or spoil background subtraction in direct imaging, and it outlines ways to avoid those traps.
arxiv-2512-15577:
Zhipeng Du and co authors present MoonSeg3R for online 3D instance segmentation from a single camera in a 2025 paper. Segmenting objects in 3D as video streams in is useful, but prior methods need posed RGB-D sequences. A phone or robot with one RGB camera gets neither depth nor poses handed to it.

MoonSeg3R draws geometric priors from CUT3R, a reconstructive foundation model, using only the RGB stream. A query refinement module turns 2D masks into 3D queries, a query index memory keeps identities steady across frames, and a state token strengthens cross frame fusion. On ScanNet200 and SceneNN it rivals RGB-D systems, a first for online monocular 3D segmentation.
arxiv-2512-15777:
Suraj Kumar Sah and Love Kumar Sah present a Variable Record Table for runtime security in a 2025 conference paper, dated December 14. Modern processors face memory corruption, speculative execution attacks, and control flow hijacking. Defenses built one threat at a time add overhead and still leave gaps between them.

Their unified hardware framework enforces spatial memory safety, back edge control flow integrity, and speculative attack detection through one protection table. Runtime instructions supply memory addresses, bounds data, and control flow signatures to build it. Across MiBench and SPEC benchmarks, the design detects all tested attack variants with no extra instruction overhead. Memory stays below 25 kilobytes for 512 entries.
arxiv-2512-15977:
Earl Ranario and Mason Earles benchmark vision language models for farm image classification in a 2025 paper. Such models are proposed as general purpose visual tools, yet their reliability for agricultural decisions was poorly tested. The team uses 27 data sets from the AgML collection, spanning 162 classes and 248,000 images.

Tasks cover plant disease, pest and damage, and species identification. Zero shot vision language models fall well short of a supervised YOLO11 baseline on every task. The best model, Gemini-3 Pro, reaches about 62 percent average accuracy under multiple choice prompting, while open ended answers score far lower. Plant and weed species prove easiest, and pest and damage hardest. The verdict: assistive use only, for now.
arxiv-2512-16277:
Jialiang Wang, Xueyan Bao, and Hao Wu refine a data completion method in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. High-dimensional, incomplete data, like user ratings with most entries missing, is often summarized by latent factor models that learn hidden traits for each row and column. A second-order variant works well but is hard to optimize because its objective is bilinear and non-convex.

The authors merge that model with sharpness-aware minimization, a training trick that seeks flat minima for better generalization. Their SSLF model gathers curvature information through Hessian-vector products and injects a sharpness term into that curvature by design. On several industrial data sets, SSLF consistently beat state-of-the-art baselines. The work shows that geometry-aware training can stabilize a notoriously touchy optimization.
arxiv-2512-16477:
Nikolay Kozyrev constructs exotic quantum mechanics models in a short note published on arXiv in 2025. Superconformal mechanics describes a particle with both supersymmetry and conformal symmetry. Such models are prized test beds for deeper theories. Kozyrev targets two symmetry supergroups, SU(1,1|n) and OSp(6|2). The interactions are carried by non-Abelian bosonic currents.

He shows that beyond four supersymmetries, the currents cannot be free. They must obey algebraic equations of their own. The note discusses general methods for solving those equations. In the solutions found, currents are expressed through semi-dynamical variables called harmonics. In one case they use ordinary coordinates and momenta instead. The work extends the catalogue of superconformal models. Theorists can use these models to probe supersymmetric dynamics.
arxiv-2512-16577:
Nico Albert Disch and seven co-authors forecast medical scans in their 2025 arXiv paper. Doctors track disease through repeated 3D imaging, but visits come at irregular times, and most prediction models demand a single prior scan or fixed time grids. Voxel-level forecasting under such messy sampling stayed out of reach.

Their framework, CRONOS, takes several past scans and predicts the volume at any chosen time, discrete or continuous, within one model. It learns a spatio-temporal velocity field that carries earlier volumes toward the target, working directly in 3D voxel space. Tests spanned three public data sets: cardiac cine MRI, perfusion CT, and longitudinal brain MRI. CRONOS beat the baselines on all three while staying computationally competitive. The team will release code and evaluation protocols for reproducible benchmarking.
arxiv-2512-16977:
Hao Li and coauthors present Endo-SemiS. It is a semi-supervised method that segments endoscopy video frames when hand labels are scarce. Two clinical uses drive the work. One is kidney stone laser work in ureteroscopy. The other is polyp screening in colonoscopy.

Four tricks share the load. Two networks teach each other. Unsure zones are filtered from pseudo-labels by confidence. Trusted pixels from both labels are pooled for joint supervision. Mutual learning at feature and image levels cuts variance. A separate fix-up network uses space-time cues from the video. On both clinical data sets, Endo-SemiS beat top rivals by a wide margin, with few labels in hand.
arxiv-2512-17277:
Saeed Ebrahimi and five co-authors tackle a familiar problem at Pinterest: new posts have almost no history, so the system that picks what users see tends to bury them. Such cold-start items rely on content traits alone, get low scores, and carry very few labels to learn from. The team studied live traffic to name each failure mode.

For each snag they add a cheap fix. A side path lifts the weight of content traits, a score rule stops new items from sinking, and a mixing trick stretches the sparse labels. Together the fixes add only 5 percent more parameters. Fresh content engagement rose by 10 percent, and the system now serves over 570 million users.
arxiv-2512-17677:
Riccardo Di Sipio argues that a question-answering system earns trust by knowing when to say it does not know. Bayesian methods give a neural network a confidence score with its answer, by tracking a spread of plausible settings instead of one best guess. Di Sipio climbs a ladder of systems, from a tiny network on the classic Iris flower data to adapted transformer language models on CommonsenseQA.

At each rung he compares a full Bayesian treatment, via the Laplace approximation, against a single-point estimate. The Bayesian versions judge their own certainty more honestly, so they can abstain on shaky questions instead of bluffing. The paper frames that honesty as an ethical feature, not a luxury, for systems people rely on.
arxiv-2512-17777:
T. Torres and ten coauthors study how light waves behave inside a nonlinear optical fiber when the system is driven far from equilibrium. Their work joins theory with lab experiments. The setup is described by two coupled nonlinear Schrödinger equations that track how the polarization of light evolves as it travels.

The team finds two sharply different regimes. In one, the waves slowly thermalize in an irreversible way that matches wave turbulence theory and a steady growth of entropy. In the other, strong phase links appear on their own and drive fast, reversible swings instead. Experiments confirm that both regimes really occur.
arxiv-2512-17877:
Tim Whittaker and four coauthors tackle a grid problem in weather models. Over steep mountains, height based layers bend and can stir up fake winds in the forecast. The usual fixes rest on hand tuned curves that stay fixed once set.

Their idea lets the model learn its own vertical grid inside a solver that can be trained end to end. Exact grid terms come from automatic differentiation, which removes a source of math error. On standard tests the learned grid cut errors by a factor of 1.4 to 2 and erased the fake vertical wind stripes over steep ground. Better grids mean cleaner forecasts near mountains.
arxiv-2512-18177:
Midhat Urooj, Ayan Banerjee, and Sandeep Gupta present NEURO-GUARD, a medical imaging system built to be accurate and explainable at once. Image based diagnosis often rests on black box models that learn from data alone, which limits trust and hurts performance on new kinds of scans.

The framework pairs Vision Transformers with language driven reasoning grounded in clinical guidelines. A retrieval augmented loop lets a large language model write, test, and refine the code that extracts features from the images, checking its own work against expert knowledge. On diabetic retinopathy grading across four datasets, APTOS, EyePACS, Messidor 1, and Messidor 2, accuracy reaches 84.69 percent against 78.4 percent for a Vision Transformer alone. The system also gains 5 percent in domain generalization, and tests on MRI based seizure detection confirm the gains carry across domains.
arxiv-2512-18277:
Alba Sendón Blanco studies shapes nested inside shapes, like a surface sitting in a solid that itself sits in a larger space. Cobordism asks when two such nests can be joined by a smooth bridge one level up. Her work builds a nested version of a classic bridge counting tool, the Pontryagin-Thom construction.

When the outer shape carries a framed direction in its side space, she finds stand in spaces that match the nested tool's behavior. Those spaces tie nested nests to links, the tangles of loops in space, up to the same bridging idea. Known link measures then yield new nested measures for free. She also gives a fresh proof of Wall's result on how the stable nested groups split apart.
arxiv-2512-18477:
Wenjun Lin and three co-authors present STORM, a framework that helps robots plan manipulations by imagining what their actions will look like. Earlier vision-language-action models reason in hidden, abstract codes. STORM instead grounds planning in explicit video rollouts, and the work was posted to arXiv in December 2025.

Three parts work together. A diffusion-based policy proposes varied candidate actions. A generative video model predicts each action's visual outcome and reward. Monte Carlo tree search then refines the plan by looking ahead. On the SimplerEnv benchmark STORM reaches a 51.0 percent average success rate, a new best, beating systems such as CogACT. Its reward-aware video prediction cuts the Frechet Video Distance by over 75 percent, and the system replans well after failures.
arxiv-2512-18577:
Nitya Ravi, Kelly A. Douglass, and Regina Demina extend a classic galaxy law. The baryonic Tully-Fisher relation links a spiral galaxy's rotation speed to its total ordinary mass, and it doubles as a test of the standard cosmology against alternatives like MOND. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and submitted to The Astrophysical Journal, builds the relation from 5,743 SDSS MaNGA galaxies.

Spirals get rotation curves from hydrogen-alpha light; ellipticals, which do not rotate the same way, get masses from stellar velocity spread and an effective rotation speed to match. The joint fit gives a slope of 3.54, close to the 3.57 found in the IllustrisTNG simulation for galaxies above a billion solar masses. At these masses the data agree with both standard cosmology and MOND. Only a lower-mass sample can separate the two theories.
arxiv-2512-19277:
Ashley Guo, Sam Wilken, Dov Levine, and Paul Chaikin report strange phases in a flat layer of identical disks that only push each other apart. When disks overlap, each gets a random repulsive kick, up to a size set by one driving parameter. No attraction, no friction, no energy-entropy contest drives the behavior.

Small kicks let the disks settle into a still, disordered absorbing state. A sharp second-order change then yields an active hexagonal crystal whose particles diffuse in rings. Stronger kicks melt it, through a first-order change, into an active liquid. Large kicks in fact prevent order, reversing the usual story of phase changes.
arxiv-2512-19477:
Sofia Blomqvist, Christian Ecker, Tyler Gorda, and Aleksi Vuorinen ask whether neutron stars can come in twins: same mass, different size. Twins arise when matter inside the star jumps through a first-order phase transition. Their Bayesian analysis stays model-agnostic, mixing first-principles constraints with telescope observations of the matter equation of state.

Allowing sharp transitions and then searching, they find current data exclude nearly every twin family. Two classes survive: one with a very early transition, and one where a fast crossover at higher density precedes the jump, with the sound speed peaking twice. The classic story tying twins to quark deconfinement is firmly ruled out.
arxiv-2512-19677:
Letizia Iannucci and three co-authors hunt for online accounts that move as a pack. In influence drives, no single account looks odd on its own. The tell is that many accounts act in sync. Their framework models online activity as a multiplex network. Each type of action gets its own layer in the network.

On top sits a time-aware model of joint work. It credits acts done together again and again over time. A decay curve makes old joint acts count for less. The team tested the method on several sets of coordinated activity. The full model found the groups better than past methods. The aim is to catch campaigns early, as groups, not one account at a time.
arxiv-2512-19777:
Antonio Tarizzo, Mohammad Kazemi, and Deniz Gündüz redesign how wireless devices pool their learning. In federated edge learning, devices train a shared model with no raw data shared. But sending each update clogs the airwaves. Over-the-air aggregation uses the way radio waves add up. Devices send at once, and the sum is the update. Digital versions add toughness, yet they falter when signals are weak.

Their learned scheme pairs a random-access codebook with vector quantization. A decoder built by unrolling a message-passing method is trained end to end with it. The pooled result can be more than a mean. Trimmed means and majority rules are also covered. On mixed device data, the scheme stayed sound far deeper into weak-signal ground. It did so at the same uplink cost as the best past methods.
arxiv-2512-19877:
Gurtej Kanwar and Octavio Vega bring diffusion models to lattice field theory. Diffusion models drive much of today's image synthesis. Lattice work needs huge sets of field configurations, and making them is its central cost. Learned samplers promise relief. Their framework trains diffusion models that live on the SU(N) group manifold. Score matching is reshaped to respect that curved space.

The trained models matched several target densities well. They gave precise, unbiased mean values, the coin of lattice work. The authors frame this as a step toward diffusion sampling of full SU(N) gauge theories. Lattice QCD is the prize case in view. The work was presented at the LATTICE 2025 symposium. Code is public.
arxiv-2512-20077:
Anthony Etim and Jakub Szefer ask a physical security question about quantum computers: what happens if someone glitches the machine-learning models inside them? Neural networks now discriminate multi-qubit readouts, correct readout errors, and decode error-correcting codes, placing them inside the trusted control stack. Nobody had tested their resistance to fault injection, deliberate voltage glitches meant to corrupt computation.

Using a ChipWhisperer Husky glitcher with automated parameter search, they attacked a fully connected readout-correction network and a convolutional decoder for the distance-five surface code. Susceptibility varied sharply by layer, with early layers failing most in the first model. One well-timed glitch in the decoder crashed its accuracy from perfect to barely a fifth correct, with structured rather than random corruption. The authors urge treating these models as security-critical components.
arxiv-2512-20377:
Linfei Li, Lin Zhang, Zhong Wang, and Ying Shen compress ultra-high-resolution images with a trick borrowed from three-dimensional graphics. Gaussian splatting represents scenes with many soft blobs; adapted to flat images, it can be extremely compact. Earlier two-dimensional versions, though, traded away too much fidelity at high resolutions and strong compression.

SmartSplat allocates its Gaussians using image-aware cues such as gradients and colour variance. A guided variational sampling strategy plus an exclusion-based uniform scheme spread the primitives without wasteful overlap. A scale-adaptive scheme initializes colours well across resolutions. Jointly optimizing layout, scale, and colour lets few Gaussians capture both detail and texture. On DIV8K and a new sixteen-thousand-pixel dataset, the method beats current leaders at matched ratios.
arxiv-2512-20477:
Ilias Aarab returns to his Aligned Economic Index, this time asking what it is worth to a practising investor. His earlier work showed the index predicts United States stock returns across economic regimes, switching state with the yield curve slope. Statistical significance, though, is not the same as money earned.

Aarab computes the gains for a mean-variance investor using the index inside the state-switching model. The added benefit is substantial in every market state, during expansions as well as recessions. That breadth matters because expansions last far longer. Extending the data through September 2020 covers the COVID-19 turbulence, where the index again delivered sizable gains over traditional approaches. The index can be maintained in real time.
arxiv-2512-20577:
Leslie Barrett and Michael W Sherman treat data labelling as a manufacturing process with quality control. Hand-tagged examples feed countless machine learning systems, yet tagging quality varies wildly between exercises and the literature barely studies it. The authors propose statistical ways to measure and improve that quality before models ever train.

Agreement metrics become trustworthy when tracked over repeated tagging iterations; declining variance in those recordings signals genuinely improving data. The paper also shows how a project can collect high-quality data without paying for multiple tags on every item. A caution follows: a simple burn-in period for new taggers may not suffice to minimize their errors. For teams buying or building training data, the methods offer an audit trail.
arxiv-2512-20677:
Zhang Wei and a large team teach machines to attack language models before criminals do. Red-teaming today leans on expert-written prompts and fixed suites, while real failures are rare, context-sensitive, and spread across threat categories. The authors recast red-teaming as constrained adversarial search and automate it with learning.

Starting from curated safety seeds, the approach expands attacks through meta-prompt guidance and evolutionary search. Lexical, semantic, and behavioural detectors score every prompt-response pair hierarchically. On one twenty-billion-parameter open model across six threat categories, the system found dozens of validated vulnerabilities, including high-severity and novel patterns, at several times the manual discovery rate under matched budgets. Diversity and coverage constraints, not prompt volume, drive the gains.
arxiv-2512-20877:
Shivraj Singh Bhatti measures what each design choice buys a small language model when computing power is tight. Starting from a bare linear next-token predictor, he adds one ingredient at a time: nonlinearity, self-attention, then full multi-layer transformers. Each variant trains on Tiny Shakespeare at character level, plus two word-level datasets.

Scoring weighs accuracy against parameter count and training cost. Attention models beat plain feed-forward networks in accuracy per unit of compute, even at tiny sizes. Extra depth or context length hurt when the training budget could not support them. One caution stands out: rotary position embeddings, a hit in large models, did not reliably transfer to small ones.
arxiv-2512-21077:
Abhijeet Kale, Rohit Batra, and four co-authors let an algorithm decide which two-dimensional materials deserve expensive physics calculations. The prize is spin Hall conductivity, the efficiency with which a material converts charge current into spin current for spintronic devices. First-principles values come from density functional theory with tight-binding Hamiltonians and spin-orbit coupling, far too costly to run across the roughly two thousand candidate materials.

Active learning closes the loop: models trained on an initial twenty-four diverse systems nominate the most promising next calculations, and three rounds grow the dataset to forty-one computed cases. The best candidate found shows a conductivity nearly twenty-three times the initial round's champion. Feature analysis then explains the wins, pointing to orbital symmetry near the Fermi level, atomic species, covalent radii, and electronegativity. The dataset is public for the spintronics community.
arxiv-2512-21477:
Ethan Andersson and Valeri Frumkin show that topology, the mathematics of global shape, can steer a single moving particle. Topology usually controls waves spread across a system, giving robust transport in electronic and photonic materials. Whether it could direct one localized particle, coupled to the field guiding it, was largely unexplored.

Their test system is a walking droplet, a small oil drop that bounces on a vibrating fluid surface and is propelled by its own waves. By structuring the wave environment, the authors make band gaps exclude the droplet from whole regions. Edges guide its motion along chosen paths. Its orbital motion depends on chirality, through an emergent gauge structure in the wave field. Here global geometric design acts directly on a particle's path, not just on waves. The results suggest new ways to direct matter without pushing it locally.
arxiv-2512-21577:
Emmy Liu, Varun Gangal, and their co-authors argue that the many competing definitions of AI hallucination fold into one. Hallucination, in their proposal, is simply inaccurate internal world modeling that becomes visible to the user. A stated fact contradicting a knowledge base counts, and so does a summary contradicting its source.

Earlier definitions appear as special cases once two choices are explicit: which reference world model the output is judged against, and what policy decides when a mismatch counts as a conflict. The unified view forces evaluations to state their assumed reference world. It also separates true hallucinations from planning mistakes and reward errors, different failure modes needing different fixes. The authors connect the framework to HalluWorld, a companion benchmark that spells out its reference worlds completely for stress-testing models.
arxiv-2512-22377:
Sajjad Taravati introduces temporal Bragg gratings as a new class of optical amplifiers. These are layered photonic forms, periodic in space, whose refractive index is varied in time near the Bragg frequency. Through careful simulations, Taravati varies where the time-variation sits, in high-index or low-index layers, and how its frequency and amplitude change the gain spectrum and field behavior.

Both layer choices produced strong parametric gain, with high-index modulation giving higher gain at comparable depth. The gain peaks can be tuned across a broad frequency range, making the device frequency-agile. Amplification is asymmetric: below the Bragg frequency, far stronger modulation is needed than above it. In the extreme low-frequency limit, discrete sidebands merge into a broadband gain continuum.
arxiv-2512-22677:
Trung Hieu Giang and Ngoc Quynh Nguyen study what happens to a curved-shell model as the shell flattens into a plate. Their subject is the nonlinear shallow shell model associated with Donnell, Vlasov, Mushtari, Galimov, and Koiter, a classic description of thin curved forms under load. The question is asymptotic: do minimizing solutions of the shell model settle into the solutions of the corresponding plate model as curvature disappears?

The authors prove that they do, and their result allows general applied forces. That generality matters because the earlier reference result assumed the tangential components of the applied forces vanish, a key restriction. Removing it substantially widens the class of loading conditions under which the shell-to-plate limit is now justified.
arxiv-2512-22777:
Kasra Jalaldoust and Elias Bareinboim ask when knowledge learned in one domain can be carried to another by recombining pieces. Drawing on causal transportability theory, they picture a target predictor as a circuit assembled from causal mechanisms, each learned from source data. Two levels are defined: a single mechanism that transfers directly, and full circuits composed from several transferred modules, which can even predict labels no single source mechanism predicts.

The authors give conditions for learning such circuits from source data alone when the causal structure of both domains is known. They then loosen the requirements, adding a supervised adaptation scheme that uses a little target data and no explicit causal graph. The few-shot error ends up tied to the size of the smallest target circuit buildable from source modules. A gradient-based version of the circuit search behaves as the theory predicts in experiments.
arxiv-2512-22877:
Ju-Hsuan Weng, Jia-Wei Liao, Cheng-Fu Chou, and Jun-Cheng Chen benchmark how well image generators can be made to forget a concept. Text-to-image models sometimes produce harmful or copyrighted content, so erasure methods try to remove ideas. Nearly all testing, however, only attacks the model through text prompts. Real uses such as image editing feed information through other channels that can smuggle the erased concept back in.

Their benchmark, M-ErasureBench, tests erasure through text prompts, learned embeddings, and inverted image latents, under white-box and black-box access. Current methods hold up against prompts but mostly fail against the other channels. Erased concepts reappear at very high rates in the white-box case. The authors answer with IRECE, an inference-time add-on that finds the concept through cross-attention and disturbs the matching latents during generation, cutting reappearance while keeping image quality.
arxiv-2512-23077:
Saraswati Soedarmadji, Yunyue Wei, Chen Zhang, Yisong Yue, and Yanan Sui use vision-language models to discover reward functions for controlling simulated bodies with muscles. Musculoskeletal systems have hundreds of actuators, and nobody knows how to write a reward that turns a phrase like walking forward with upright posture into coordinated motion. People can judge movement by eye, though, and modern vision-language models can share that judgment.

Their framework, MoVLR, loops between control optimization and model feedback. A controller tries to move the body, the vision-language model assesses the resulting motion against the stated goal, and that assessment is converted into structured guidance that refines the reward. Through repeated rounds, rewards emerge that produce physically coordinated locomotion and manipulation in high-dimensional musculoskeletal models. The results suggest vision-language models can ground abstract motion descriptions in the implicit principles that govern real motor control.
arxiv-2512-23377:
Shuangyang Li and co-authors introduce faster-than-Nyquist signaling, a technique that packs symbols more tightly in time than the classic Nyquist criterion allows. Future wireless networks need far higher throughput, and simply widening the channel is not always possible. Faster-than-Nyquist signaling sends more symbols through the same resources by accepting controlled interference between them and untangling it at the receiver.

The article is a structured tutorial and roadmap rather than a single new result. It lays out the principles and theory, then presents promising results for coded faster-than-Nyquist systems. An application is integrated sensing and communications, where one waveform must both carry data and probe the area, an important function for next-generation networks. The authors close by mapping open research challenges, including receiver cost and interference control, and the directions they judge most promising.
arxiv-2512-23477:
Yao Ma, Yong-Liang Ma, and Lu-Qi Zhang model the matter inside neutron stars with a baryonic extended linear sigma model. A framework that includes baryons and the explicit breaking of chiral symmetry. Using a relativistic mean field approximation, they ask whether such a model can describe both ordinary nuclear matter and stars heavy enough to contain hyperons, particles with strange quarks.

The model reproduces hadron masses and nuclear matter properties near saturation density well. Matching the observed mass-radius relation of neutron stars, however, requires the pion-nucleon sigma term to take a value far from its measured vacuum range. The authors read this tension as a hint that the model's low-energy constants change with density, and they call for calculations beyond the leading-order mean field treatment.
arxiv-2512-23577:
Jing Fu Hu, Hang Lu, and Bao Yuan Sun ask how much dark matter a neutron star could contain without contradicting observations. A star with dark matter mixed in, alongside ordinary nuclear matter, would have different mass, radius, and tidal response. Recent measurements by NICER and the LIGO-Virgo gravitational-wave detectors make it possible to bound that hidden component.

The team built equations of state from twelve nuclear matter models plus a self-interacting fermionic dark matter model, then solved the two-fluid structure equations. For each model they found the largest allowed dark matter fraction, and noticed it correlates almost perfectly with the star's maximum mass. Turning that correlation into a probability statement, they bound the dark matter mass inside such stars at a level near a tenth of a solar mass.
arxiv-2512-24177:
Yun-Xuan Lu and four colleagues report a compact cold-atom source. It produces two species at once. The species are lithium-6 and rubidium-87. Such sources underpin work on quantum mixtures and molecules. Dual-species setups are traditionally bulky and complex. This design strings two-dimensional magneto-optical traps in series. Efficient Zeeman slowing works over a short distance.

The performance sets records. Lithium loading reached billions of atoms per second. The oven temperature stayed moderate. The rate was forty-four times higher than without the slowing light. Rubidium streamed in at a comparable rate. Its oven sat at room temperature. The whole vacuum system fits in a small volume. The science cell is included in that size. The authors offer the setup as a fast starting point. Double-degenerate mixtures and ultracold molecules are the targets.
arxiv-2512-24977:
Barna Zajzon, Younes Bouhadjar, Maxime Fabre, and others introduce SymSeqBench, a unified approach for creating and studying rule-based symbolic series. Sequential structure supports language, motion, and choice-making, and AI systems must learn it too. Their tools, including SymSeq, strictly create ordered symbolic data sets with known rules.

The approach is domain neutral while linking tasks to formal theories of computation and computability. Cognitive science and AI readers get benchmarks where the true rule behind a sequence is known, so learning can be judged exactly. Controlled symbolic series help split genuine rule learning from pattern rote recall.
arxiv-2601-06677:
Zohaib Khan, Omer Tafveez, and Zoha Hayat Bhatti test small-model reasoning on a micro-budget in 2026. Recent reasoning advances typically rely on massive scale, they observe. They ask whether strong reasoning can be induced in small models instead.

Their models hold at most one and a half billion parameters. Training runs on a single A40 graphics card for under a day. They use reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for that training. Low-rank adapters keep the trainable footprint small and cheap to store. The paper frames this as plasticity against rigidity in adaptation. Small teams get a recipe for reasoning models without giant clusters. Results would matter for schools and labs with one good GPU.
arxiv-2601-06777:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Ali Lotfi and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers normalized difference layer. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Normalized difference indices have been a staple in remote sensing for decades. They stay reliable under lighting changes produce bounded values and connect well to biophysical signals.

Even so, they are usually treated as a fixed pre processing step with coefficients set to one. Which limits how well they can adapt to a specific learning task. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-06877:
Donghuo Zeng, Roberto Legaspi, and Kazushi Ikeda wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on chat agents that aim to persuade. A good agent of this kind shifts its plan to fit each user. It tracks how the mood and aims of the user change as the chat goes on. The team trains its agent with reinforcement learning, where the agent learns from rewards.

The method has three main parts. One part picks the next move from a set plan and pulls past text that fits the chat. A pull rule called Maximal Marginal Relevance keeps the text on point and fresh. A second part learns a sketch of the user. That sketch has 81 parts and mixes kinds of facts. A third part, named in the full text, ties the sketch to the plan the agent picks.
arxiv-2601-06977:
Zhengjie Xiong and Yangyang Xu wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a fast way to solve hard math tasks in parts. The way is called the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, or ADMM. The tasks in view split into two blocks of choice. Each block has its own aim, and the aims add up to one shared aim.

Rules bind the two blocks as one. Some rules bend, in the sense that they are not straight lines. Some rules are straight and tie the blocks to each other. Tasks of this shape show up in real work. One case is how to share scarce goods or power across a network. A second case is machine learning with rules the model must obey. The paper gives a form of ADMM that fits this class of tasks.
arxiv-2601-07777:
Linda Albanese and colleagues revisit how a neural network model recalls patterns, comparing serial and parallel updating. Blume-Emery-Griffiths networks are fully connected models for pattern recognition and associative memory. They generalize the standard Hopfield network. Past studies treated them heuristically, mainly with the replica trick under a replica symmetric assumption. Their 2026 notes first rebuild that picture rigorously.

The rigorous route uses Guerra interpolation, a method from spin glass theory. With the existing picture secured, the authors can compare recall modes on firm ground. Serial recall updates neurons one by one; parallel recall updates them together. The difference can change what the memory retrieves. Statistical physicists studying neural networks are the readers. The work replaces heuristic confidence with proof for a classic model.
arxiv-2601-08277:
Yizhuo Rao and co-authors speed up particle-in-cell simulations by using matrix units on modern CPUs. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that these simulations spend most cycles on particle-grid interactions. Fine-grained atomic updates become a severe bottleneck on traditional many-core chips.

New CPUs add matrix processing units built for efficient outer-product operations. Matrix-PIC reshapes the particle-grid work to harness those units. Plasma and fusion researchers rely on particle-in-cell runs that can take huge compute budgets. Cutting the core bottleneck could shorten design cycles for devices modeled this way. The work shows a path to gains without moving to special accelerators.
arxiv-2601-08477: Francesco Dettori and co-authors envision verified empathy for therapy chatbots. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that conversational agents increasingly support mental therapeutic pathways. Empathy is a key non-functional requirement in such settings, with real societal impact. Current chatbot practice gives no systematic way to specify or verify empathy, though. The authors propose a framework joining natural language processing with formal verification. Verified empathy claims could help clinics and regulators judge whether a support bot behaves as promised with vulnerable users.
arxiv-2601-08677:
Serena Dipierro and three co-authors study flat fronts in a type of energy with long range pulls. Think of a wall that splits two states of a stuff. Far parts of the stuff still pull on the wall, and a wave like force acts on it at a set pace. The team asks if flat walls can be the best shape for such energy.

They show flat front forms do exist that give the least energy. They also show what shape the energy takes when seen from far off. At large scale it looks like a local wall cost with a slant that shifts by place. A reader in this math field gets two gains. Flat fronts are real in this long range case, and the large scale cost is now known.
arxiv-2601-09577:
MD Nazmul Alam Shanto, Md. Tanzeem Rahat, and Md. Manzurul Hasan speed up a classic string search. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies permutation pattern matching, also called jumbled or Abelian matching. The task: find a spot in a text where the letter counts match a pattern's counts exactly.

Letter counts are captured by the Parikh vector, one tally per symbol. The authors give linear-time detection under a Parikh budget, plus packing and disjoint selection variants. Jumbled matching shows up in bioinformatics and music search, where order is loose but content matters. Linear time keeps the method usable on very long texts.
arxiv-2601-09677:
Guillermina Senn and four co-authors scale up a hard image problem: sharpening pictures when the blur itself is unknown. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Bayesian semi-blind deconvolution at scale. In blind deconvolution, both the true image and the blur kernel must be guessed from the data.

Semi-blind versions use extra knowledge about the image or the blur to narrow the search. The Bayesian frame tracks uncertainty instead of betting on one answer. Scaling that care to large images is the paper's challenge. Sharper recovery matters in astronomy, microscopy, and medical scans.
arxiv-2601-09777:
An ALICE collaboration paper uses short-lived particles to probe the final stage of heavy-ion collisions. The 2026 arXiv paper studies the hadronic phase through how resonances spread in momentum and angle. Resonances decay so fast that their yields carry fingerprints of the medium they died in.

After the quark-gluon plasma cools, hadrons keep colliding for a while in a hadronic phase. New collisions can destroy resonance signals, while fresh reactions rebuild them. The balance shapes the yields physicists measure. The paper also uses resonances to probe the internal structure of exotic states. Together, the measurements test how matter behaves as it freezes out.
arxiv-2601-09977:
Rikizo Ikuta studies how light grains clash in groups of two and three. When two light grains meet, their clash rate drops in a known dip. That dip is the Hong Ou Mandel effect. More noise in the light tends to make the dip less sharp.

Ikuta asks if the same trend holds for three grains. He finds that it does not. In a circuit with a fair shape, the trend can break. Noise can shift the clash rate in a way that two grain tests would not hint at. The result warns that rules from two grain tests do not scale in a plain way.
arxiv-2601-10077:
Francesco Maria Iudica lifts a classic lift into p-adic form. The Cogdell lift maps cycles on Picard surfaces to forms on the elliptic side. Such maps link two worlds of forms. A p-adic form lets the map bend with a prime p.

Iudica gets more than one result. In part one, he lifts the adjoint Kudla lift. He uses a p-adic Kudla lift built in past work. The paper then works out what the lift yields. Maps of this kind aid the study of L values and cycles. They show how forms on one side cast light on the other side.
arxiv-2601-10277:
Evangelos Kolyvas, Alexandros Antonov, and Spyros Voulgaris speed up how blocks spread in a chain net. Chain nets have been built for over a decade. Yet their rate stays low. Each block must reach all nodes in the net. Slow spread caps the whole rate.

Nodes in such nets link at random. That random web adds lag. The team made SCRamble, a self tuning overlay. It reshapes links as the net runs. It seeks a web that spreads blocks fast. The work tests the overlay in sims of chain nets. A faster web could lift the rate cap.
arxiv-2601-10477:
Yu Wang and co authors cut city scenes by what places mean, not just how they look. A city holds homes, schools, parks, roads, and more. From a sky shot, plain tools can find built forms with ease. They can mark blocks, roofs, and water well. Social forms are more hard.

A school and an office can look the same from the sky. Their split is in use, not in shape. The team use sight and text thought to make that split. Their tool reads cues of use in the shot. It aims for maps that serve real city tasks, like plan and care work.
arxiv-2601-10877:
Ludovic Righetti and Vincent Boulanin ask whether open robotics innovation threatens peace and security. Open access to papers, software, and hardware is central to robotics. It lowers entry barriers, supports reproducible science, and speeds reliable system building. The same openness, they note, sharpens the dual-use risk built into robotics research.

Open tools lower the bar for states and non-state actors to build robots for military or harmful ends. The authors weigh that risk against the clear gains of openness. Their essay speaks to researchers, funders, and policymakers who must set the terms of sharing. It asks the field to face its security shadow without giving up what makes it thrive.
arxiv-2601-10977:
Haoran Xu proposes a scheme for parabolic equations that keeps solutions positive. Parabolic equations model heat, diffusion, and option prices. The scheme spreads wide, using a broad stencil, and it is built on the Feynman-Kac formula. That formula writes the solution as a conditional expectation over a diffusion process.

Rather than the usual compact Markov chain shortcuts, Xu approximates that expectation directly with the wide stencil. The design aims to be accurate and positive at once. Staying positive matters because negative values are nonsense in the models it targets. The scheme serves financial work, the author's home field, where prices must stay sensible.
arxiv-2601-11277:
Gauhar Abbas works through hadronic tau decays at higher orders in QCD. The 2026 preprint is an introduction-style work from IIT-BHU. QCD is the theory of the strong force in particle physics. Its strength is set by one key number, the strong coupling.

That number, alpha-s, rules strong dynamics at all energy scales. Tau decays give a clean place to measure it well. The tau is a heavy cousin of the electron. When it decays to hadrons, QCD shapes the outcome. Higher-order terms sharpen the link between data and alpha-s. The work sets out that link in step-by-step form.
arxiv-2601-11477:
Itauany do Nascimento Barroso and Hermano Velten model dark matter as a condensate. Their 2026 preprint adds a Kapitza potential to the setup. Bose-Einstein condensate dark matter is a studied alternative model. It casts dark matter as a vast quantum fluid.

A Kapitza potential was just realized in a lab BEC. That first realization drives fresh theory work on the system. The team asks what such a potential does in galaxies. Their focus is a core-tail structure in galactic halos. A dense core with a long tail is a known BEC trait. The Kapitza term may reshape that profile in testable ways. The work links tabletop quantum optics to galactic scales.
arxiv-2601-11977:
Ren He, Yinliang Xu, Jinfeng Wang, Jeremy Watson, and Jian Song forecast power prices in one shot while data stay private. Power forecasts use series with complex links across sites. Rules on privacy bar full data share between regions.

Past tools need much expert input and fail to move well to new sites. Pre-trained series models help, but their zero-shot skill on such tasks is weak.
