europmc-pmc9188077: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on intermittent theta-burst stimulation improves motor function by inhibiting neuronal pyroptosis (a fiery form of cell death) and regulating microglial polarization. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9330677: A fresh look at clinical (in patients) application (use) of stem cell in regenerative medicine: a narrative review arrived with this 2022 review paper. The multipotency property of stem cells has attained worldwide consideration because of their immense for immunomodulation and their treatment function. A good review shows what is solid, what is shaky, and where the next study should look.
europmc-pmc9349777: Published in 2022, this research paper takes on evolution (gradual change) of the SARS-CoV-2 omicron variants ba-1 to ba-5: implications (what the findings mean) for immune escape and spread. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. Each solid result like this one becomes a stepping stone for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc9832677: Zhao and co-authors published this review paper in 2023 on insulin resistance (cells ignoring insulin) in polycystic ovary syndrome across various tissues: an updated review of pathogenesis (how the disease develops), testing. The authors pull together the key findings from across the field. Results like these feed the work that turns lab findings into future treatments.
europmc-pmc9942077: Published in 2023, this research paper takes on lung cancer immunotherapy (treatment that boosts the immune system): progress, pitfalls, and promises. The authors lay out their methods and results in full. If later work backs it up, the finding could open a new path for treating the illness.
flaubert-simple-soul-1877:
Flaubert opens A Simple Soul in the town of Pont-l'Eveque in Normandy. For half a century, he writes, local housewives envied Madame Aubain her servant Felicite. For a hundred francs a year, Felicite cooked, cleaned, washed, ironed, and mended for her mistress.

Madame Aubain, widowed in 1809 with two children and many debts, was not an easy woman. Felicite stayed loyal all the same, through a plain and narrowing life. She pours her pure love on a nephew, an old man, and at last on Loulou, her parrot. Flaubert finds the sublime in that humble heart, with tenderness and quiet irony.
flaubert-three-short-works-1877:
Three short works share this Flaubert volume, and their span may surprise readers. The Dance of Death, a prose poem of 1838, comes first. The Legend of Saint-Julian the Hospitaller and A Simple Soul follow it.

In the opening piece Death speaks at night among cold tombs in winter. Death claims to have reaped countless generations with a scythe, like a nurse of earth itself. Saint Julian retells a medieval tale of sin and pardon in rich style. A Simple Soul then finds grandeur in a poor servant's plain life, and many call the late tales the finest short fiction in French.
freeman-ottoman-power-europe-1877:
Edward Freeman wrote The Ottoman Power in Europe in 1877, amid the Eastern Crisis. His history of Turkish rule in the Balkans doubles as a polemic. He argues that Ottoman power in Europe is alien and doomed to fall.

Atrocity reports and great-power rivalry heat his pages throughout. Freeman the liberal pleads the cause of the Balkan Christians with passion. Modern readers will find his views partisan and dated in places. Yet the book vividly shows Victorian opinion on the Eastern Question, and its learning on Balkan history still gives it weight beyond its moment of crisis.
frus-1861-d177:
On 20 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz for the second time in five days. The letter is document 177 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Madrid letters in five days show a post kept on a short rein. Schurz was able but new, and Seward guided him closely. The August notes form a small course in the Secretary's method: short, clear, and tied to one aim. A short rein in August gave Schurz room to grow without room to stray. Room to grow, on a short rein, is a fair sum of Seward's way with new men.
frus-1861-d277:
Seward heard from Mr. Angel on 4 June 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 277 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d77:
Charles Francis Adams sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 September 1861. It is document 77 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams and Seward again wrote on the same day, in ignorance of each other. Adams's page reports London as it stood in early autumn. His care with tone and fact made his reports the base on which Lincoln's cabinet judged British intent. His reports were later prized by scholars for their cool, exact prose. Cool, exact prose made his reports the base line for judging all other news.
frus-1862-d177:
Writing on 28 October 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report that appears as Document 177 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams spoke for the United States in London as its minister.

Reports written just before a mail steamer sailed tended to sum up the week, and this one closed October at the legation. The questions hanging over it were large: would Britain join France in pressing a truce, and would warships built in British yards reach the South? Adams's mail kept those questions in front of Washington. No working cable crossed the Atlantic in 1862, so every answer waited on a mail steamer.
frus-1862-d277:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton on 10 May 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 277 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter went by steamer to the Paris legation.

Mid-May 1862 found McClellan's army within sight of Richmond's church spires. Or so the phrase went, and Europe wondered if the war might end by summer. Seward's mail fed that hope where it helped and damped it where it hurt. Letters like this one were instruments of mood as much as of business, and Dayton knew how to use them. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d377:
On 4 September 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Viscount Treilhard, in a letter printed as Document 377 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter came five days after the Bull Run defeat.

Early September found Lee's army crossing into Maryland and the capital recovering its nerve. Seward's correspondence in that week, across all channels, worked to project calm resolve. His letter to Treilhard is part of that effort, filed just before Antietam gave Washington a stronger story to tell Europe. Formal calls between the two men were frequent, and their notes followed up the talks. French citizens and ships caught by the war gave the legation a steady stream of case work.
frus-1862-d477:
James E. Harvey, the American minister in Lisbon, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 June 1862. It is Document 477 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the first Portuguese report in the file.

Harvey reported from a capital whose importance lay in its ports and islands rather than its armies. Portugal watched the war with care, trading with America and ruling Atlantic stations where belligerent ships might seek coal or shelter. His reports told Washington how Lisbon meant to apply the rules of neutrality. For the reader, the Portuguese file opens a side door on the war: the legal, port-by-port struggle that ran beneath the famous battles.
frus-1862-d577:
James Watson Webb sent this report from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 July 1862, though the printed file places it after later papers. It is Document 577 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The Brazilian file's loose order reflects the mails: letters from Rio arrived in batches, months apart, and were printed as the office gathered them. Webb's July report covered the imperial court's view of the war and the practical questions of ports and shipping that Brazil's long coast raised. For Washington, his letters fixed the southern reference point of its wartime map. Read by date, the file shows a correspondence conducted in slow motion, each side answering a world already changed.
frus-1862-d677:
On 29 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame, the American minister to China. The letter is document 677 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It closes the spring set of orders in the China file.

Seward wrote knowing his words would not be read for months. That lag shaped the tone of all his far-off mail: clear aims, room for the envoy to judge, and news of home. This letter went out as the war at home turned grim. It is a fair sample of how the State Department kept faith with its distant posts when it could send them little else.
frus-1862-d77:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 7 June 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 77 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d177:
The American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, wrote this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 April 1863. It is document 177 of the 1863 volume of diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were busy in Britain buying ships, arms, and supplies. Reports from the London legation fed Washington's protests against that trade. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d277:
The mail from London dated 3 September 1863 brought Secretary of State William H. Seward this report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as document 277 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Adams dealt most often with Lord John Russell, Britain's foreign secretary. His letters home summed up those talks and the mood of the British government. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d377: On 29 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 377 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d477:
Among the day's business on 24 April 1863 was a letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d577:
In the flow of wartime mail, Secretary William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 24 June 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d677:
Dated 28 November 1863, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward went across the Atlantic to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams served as the United States minister to Britain. The letter is printed as document 677 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume.

Mail between Washington and London took days by ship, so each dispatch had to stand on its own. Seward used these letters to share news, set policy, and tell Adams what to say to British leaders. For a reader today, the value is the direct view. There is no retelling here, just the government's own words as they were sent during the war.
frus-1863p1-d77:
On 12 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 77 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet often held what would not fit the first: a talk recalled, a press cut, a name to note. Adams's pair of 12 February is of that kind. This letter is its second half. Set in the run, it shows how the London post turned a mass of news into clean, filed reports. A busy secretary could use them at once.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d177: Stettinius wrote to President Roosevelt on October 30, 1943, from his post as Acting Secretary of State. The letter is Document 177 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, in the Moscow section. While Hull closed the conference abroad, Stettinius closed the home end of the work, and this letter belongs to that handover day. The record names the two men and the date. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d277:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 26 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, open with Southeast Asia business. The chiefs approve amendments to paper C.C.S. 411 and order the revised plan sent to Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek through Lord Mountbatten without delay.

Reports from commanders follow, and General Eisenhower speaks first. He calls a single command for the Mediterranean absolutely essential, since air and naval commands already work that way. On the war there, he backs Italy as the main effort under a full push, with the Po valley as the goal and landing craft as his chief need. Under a limited push, he warns, only the line north of Rome could be held, on a strategic defensive with strong local attacks.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d377:
Harry Hopkins' handwritten notes, dated 1 December 1943 at one in the afternoon, jot the heads of a report by Foreign Secretary Eden from the foreign ministers' committee at Tehran. The notes break off in the middle of a page and appear incomplete, and no other Hopkins notes of the meeting have been found.

The surviving lines concern Turkey. Turkey should be asked to come into the war, and her president invited to Cairo to meet the President of the United States and the Prime Minister. Eden asked Marshal Stalin whether the Soviet government wished to send a representative to that meeting, and Stalin answered that he would send one. A proposed telegram to President Inönü was presented and discussed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d477:
The catalog heading misspells the form as “Memorandwn,” but the text is a memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff dated December 4, 1943. That was the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference. The State Department printed the paper in its Cairo-Tehran volume, among the records of the chiefs' sessions.

American position papers like this one gave the joint meetings their agenda and their friction. The United States chiefs used written memoranda to press their views on the combined body before decisions were entered in the minutes. A reader following the Cairo debate over strategy in Europe and Asia will find this paper part of the paper trail.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d77: Roosevelt answered Churchill on October 30, 1943, in a letter that is Document 77 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The exchange that day closed the Moscow chapter and opened the final planning for Cairo and Tehran, then four weeks off. The record states the parties and the date only. Readers can find the letter in the Foreign Relations volume, where the November papers begin soon after.
frus-1944-quebec-d177:
The McFarland minutes record the plenary session of September 13, 1944, where Churchill, at Roosevelt's request, opened the discussion. Since Sextant, he said, everything the United Nations had touched had turned to gold, with seven weeks of unbroken success. He congratulated the Americans on Dragoon, praised the integrated staff machine in France, and stressed that the British Empire's effort had reached its peak.

Churchill then pressed his Italian design. No forces should be withdrawn until Kesselring was beaten or on the run. Afterward the armies must not sit idle: he wanted a right-handed movement through Istria and Trieste toward Vienna, partly to reach it before the Russians. He also reviewed Burma's bitter campaign, where sickness had cost 288,000 men, and introduced Plan Dracula against Rangoon.
frus-1944-quebec-d277:
Two draft messages to Chiang Kai-shek, a long and a short version, were circulated on September 15, 1944, as C.C.S. 681/1. The longer draft, sent in Roosevelt's and Churchill's names, reports the Quebec decisions. Its delivery was tightly controlled: through General Stilwell and the two ambassadors in Chungking, closely paraphrased before presentation.

The message pledges all available resources toward the earliest practicable invasion of the Japanese homeland, with vigorous redeployment after Germany's defeat. For Southeast Asia, it promises continued operations under Mountbatten to secure the Myitkyina air bases and open overland communications between India and China. British forces would advance from Imphal toward Mandalay, Chinese and allied forces from Myitkyina, and Chiang's Salween armies toward Lashio, all under preponderant air strength.
frus-1944-quebec-d77:
Treasury Department officials prepared a memorandum dated September 1, 1944. The paper entered the files gathered for the Quebec Conference. The State Department later printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume. Treasury handled war finance and aid to the allies.

Financial questions ran through the Quebec agenda that September. Britain depended on American aid to keep fighting. Germany's future also raised money and trade questions. A Treasury paper gave officials shared facts before the talks. For readers, the memorandum shows finance staff shaping summit choices. Their work stood behind decisions the leaders announced later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d177:
A memorandum dated 21 November 1946 links two senior offices. The sender was the Commanding General of the Manhattan Engineer District, Department of War (Groves). The reader was the Atomic Energy Commission. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 177 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. The sender ran the wartime atomic bomb program, and the new Atomic Energy Commission was about to take charge of atomic work from the Army.
frus-1945-50-intel-d277:
On 20 May 1948, staff wrote up the discussion at the 11th Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. It is document 277 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

After key talks, an aide would write up what was said for the file. The result is close to the room itself. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d377:
A memorandum dated 24 March 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was the Assistant Secretary of State for Occupied Areas (Saltzman). It survives in print as document 377 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d77:
Secretary Byrnes wrote to McCormack on 23 October 1945. The secretary of state addressing his intelligence chief in person gave the young office a mark of standing. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

McCormack's interim service held the old OSS analysts, whose reports the secretary read with profit. Byrnes's letter shows the chief receiving direction from the very top of his department. Readers should weigh what that meant in the autumn contest. While the central fight ran on, the State office was quietly proving its worth to its own secretary. Its later eclipse makes these early marks of favor poignant reading.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d177:
London set a deadline for King Peter, and asked Washington's view of its next step. The Secretary of State's note to Ambassador Halifax of 23 January 1945 answers the British Embassy's inquiry of the day before. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Britain had asked what the United States thought of the course London proposed if the King failed to accept the Tito–Subasic agreement by midday. Stettinius points to the lines already sent to Ambassador Patterson on 17 January. Some points in the King's reservations, Washington holds, can be judged fairly only once the government is back in Yugoslavia. Friendly missions should also be set up in Belgrade at an early date. On the goal of a government returning home to work as one, the two capitals agree.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d277:
Hold your hand, Grew told the American officers drafting a prisoners agreement at SHAEF. His urgent cable of 27 January 1945 went to the embassy in London, for Murphy, and was repeated to Moscow. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

The Foreign Office had shared its cables on the proposed Soviet agreements covering freed prisoners and civilians. One British message shows SHAEF at work on a joint British-American text for the Big Three meeting. That text, Grew warns, stands at considerable variance with what the State, Army, and Navy committee is proposing to the Joint Chiefs. The American men at SHAEF must make no commitments until further instructions arrive, which Washington hopes to send through the Joint Chiefs on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d377:
Roosevelt's letter to Stalin of February 6, 1945, is among the most direct he wrote at Yalta. He says he has thought hard about their afternoon meeting. On the Polish government, he is greatly disturbed. The three great powers have no meeting of minds about Poland's political setup, and the world can see it.

Moscow recognizes one Polish government; Washington and London recognize another, in London. Roosevelt insists the split must not continue. People would think a breach had opened between the allies, which is not the case. He is determined, he writes, that there shall be no breach. Surely, he pleads, their differences can be reconciled.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d477:
China and Moscow move toward each other in these excerpts from Grew's cable of February 5, 1945. Chiang Kai-shek and T. V. Soong had told Ambassador Hurley that Moscow agreed to receive Soong as the Generalissimo's personal representative. The visit would come late in February or early in March. Talks would cover closer relations and Soviet participation in the war against Japan.

Korea, Manchuria, postwar economic matters, and the Sino-Soviet border filled out the agenda. Hurley relayed Molotov's September assurance: the Russians were not supporting the Chinese Communists, who, Molotov claimed, were not communists at all. Grew's digest gave the traveling delegation a window on the Far East bargain forming behind Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d77:
Trusteeship for dependent territories had been kept off the table at Dumbarton Oaks, and this 15 November 1944 memorandum explains why. Sent to the President by Acting Secretary Stettinius, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The paper asks permission to move the subject forward quietly.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff had not wanted the topic discussed while the war ran on. The Soviet, British, and Chinese delegations all wished to take it up later, and the State Department had draft proposals ready. Stettinius recommends further study with the military and naval authorities. If the President approves the proposals, they would go to the three allied governments before the founding conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d177:
Acting Secretary Grew sent Truman the State Department's full briefing agenda on June 30, 1945. His covering memorandum is document 177 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Truman had asked before leaving Washington for a fully documented agenda for the meeting in Germany.

Grew apologizes that the papers lack the clearance he would have wished, with no Secretary of State in place. But time is too short to hold them back. The attached memo has three parts. The first lists items the United States should raise, with the recommended American position on each. The second lists items the British intend to raise. The third covers other important matters likely to come up. The first item proposes no formal peace conference, and instead a council of foreign ministers of the great powers. Copies went to James Byrnes and Admiral Leahy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d277:
Winant sent on Britain's twin caveat on Austrian reparations in a cable dated July 7, 1945. The cable is document 277 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It quotes the words the British member gave his own government on July 4.

London accepts in principle that Austria must furnish reparations, the British words run. But London is not to be taken as settling in advance the form or sum of such payments, or Austria's capacity to make them. The group in London had no power to weigh the real question. London holds that the four powers should now take it up in light of Austria's economic prospects. The wording matches the U.S. caveat sent three days before.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d377:
A draft letter for President Truman, prepared by the American delegation, would report the Reparations Commission's progress to Stalin and Churchill. Pauley, the draft says, reports two main gains. The Commission's members have agreed on a percentage split of reparations among the three powers: 56 for the Soviet Union, 22 for Britain, and 22 for the United States.

To meet the proven claims of other nations, each of the three would give up part of its share in proportion. The members also agreed a procedure for dividing reparations among the other claimant countries. The draft further treats all property removed from Germany as reparations, save paid exports, war booty, and restitutions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d477: Three conditions for an Italian government's success are stated in an extract of Kirk's cable from Rome of July 6, 1945. The full text is printed as document No. 469. In present circumstances, Kirk writes, no government, however gifted, can prove its worth without three things. The armistice regime must be abolished. Allied troops must stay in the country, to give confidence to a people in a state of demoralization. And material aid must come at once, to prevent unrest through wide unemployment and hunger.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d577:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent a top secret report from Moscow on July 12, 1945. Addressed to the President and the Secretary of State, it is document 577 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It covers that night's talk between China's T. V. Soong and Stalin.

Harriman says Soong and Stalin agree on most points, but not on the railways and ports. Stalin gave way on guards, who will be Chinese, and on moving Soviet troops in Manchuria. He still demands a majority of railway directors, which Soong resists. Stalin also wants Dairen inside a Soviet military zone with a naval base. Soong offers Port Arthur as the base and Dairen as a free port under Chinese rule. Stalin wants a deal before he meets Truman, so the date of Soviet entry into the war can be set.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d677:
Ambassador Winant sent an urgent secret survey of the Tangier tangle from London on July 14, 1945. It is document 677 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. His source was again Hoyer Millar of the Foreign Office.

Millar said the Dutch had now pressed their interest in Tangier with some force. The Portuguese and Belgians had registered interest as well. Churchill himself was taking a hand from Hendaye, and London's line was fixed. Nothing could be done until after the Big Three meeting. In Paris, France talked of separate soundings to reconcile the four governments' views. London would discourage that course and saw any meeting before August as out of the question. Millar even weighed a Spanish exit with Sherifian troops moving in, which a tactful French approach might make acceptable.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d77:
General Eisenhower pressed Moscow for instant access to Berlin in an urgent telegram to General Deane on June 19, 1945. The message, sent from Frankfurt, is document 77 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Soviet officers wanted to delay the American survey party until Marshal Zhukov returned to Berlin on June 28.

Eisenhower calls that impossible. A meeting of this size cannot be arranged in two weeks, he says, and General Parks's party of some 275 men and 50 vehicles must go in the next day. He also demands open running rights on the Dessau-Berlin highway and the Halle-Berlin air route. Talks with Zhukov can wait, he adds; the groundwork cannot. The cable shows how tight the Potsdam timetable already was.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1077:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled the Secretary of State at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. Yugoslavia's Foreign Office had sent the American embassy in Belgrade two protest notes, dated July 18 and 19. They charge the Greek government with breaking the Atlantic Charter and the United Nations Charter in Aegean Macedonia.

Belgrade claims Athens fails to stop fascist gangs, backs them, and persecutes Slav Macedonians through its own forces. Testimony from 20,000 peasants who fled is cited as proof of a drive to expel or destroy them. Greek troops are also said to have fired across the Yugoslav border. Washington suggests the clash now needs joint international action, perhaps agreed at Potsdam itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1177:
The Soviet team tabled this proposal on 19 July 1945, the summit's third day. In the opening round, each side's papers staked out its starting demands. Only after all three hands were shown did the hard trading over words begin.

Moscow's papers pressed the Soviet case on the shape of postwar Europe. Borders, payments from Germany, and the rule of freed lands all ran through them. This proposal is the formal Soviet bid from that first round. Set beside the final protocol, it shows where Moscow started and how far the talks moved it, if at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1277:
The Joint Chiefs of Staff wrote to the President on 21 July 1945. Their messages to Truman ran through the summit on a steady rhythm. This one dates from the end of the first week, when the team had its full measure of the bargaining.

The chiefs wrote as the president's military house: forces, fronts, and the plans that bound them. Their word balanced the envoys' reports on the president's desk. This message is one turn of that exchange. It shows the commander in chief being served by his chiefs in writing, at the distance the summit imposed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1377:
Norman Brook, a senior secretary to the British cabinet, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on 28 July 1945. Brook served the British government at the staff level, much as Dunn served the American. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Staff-to-staff letters between allies are the grease of coalition work. Brook and Dunn could settle wording and timetables that leaders had no time to touch. This letter came just after Attlee took over the British delegation, when staff ties mattered most in keeping the talks smooth. Readers see here the level at which summits actually run: trusted aides passing paper so that principals can agree in public.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-77:
Department of State minutes record an informal foreign ministers' meeting of July 23, 1945, at 4 p.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Byrnes opened by returning to reparations and to his morning talk with Molotov.

The Secretary said he would not repeat all he had said to Molotov. He merely wished to state the U.S. view in Eden's hearing. Certain Soviet positions, he held, were hard to reconcile with an overall reparation plan. Since Maisky was present, Byrnes asked him to confirm or clarify the Soviet definition of war booty. As reported to him, it covered all supplies and equipment, plants and materials included. Molotov then handed in what he called the true Soviet definition, printed as an annex. Byrnes closed with a question: was it true that Soviet authorities had taken quantities of equipment from their zone?
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d777:
Kirk reported from Rome to the Acting Secretary of State on July 20, 1945, in document 777. The ambassador in Italy wrote during the Potsdam Conference's first week. Italy's place in the coming peace was unsettled. Kirk's report was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Rome's view reached Washington through Kirk's steady hand. He had served in many capitals and wrote with a cool eye. Readers get Italy as its government wished to be seen, filtered by a skeptic. The document shows a former enemy state lobbying for mercy while the victors met. Its timing ties the plea to the summit's first decisions.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d877: Emilio Collado cabled Willard Thorp and Jacob Reinstein from Babelsberg on July 23, 1945, in this secret telegram. Collado directed the Office of Financial and Development Policy. His news was blunt: four-power joint planning of imports, exports, and reparations now looked unworkable. The team was therefore drafting on a zonal basis instead. Western zones might still combine their handling and financing. Collado adds that he, McCloy, and Hilldring were drafting a directive on War Department financing duty.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d977: Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov answered Secretary Byrnes from Berlin on August 2, 1945. He agrees fully that the Potsdam reparations deal should be carried out as soon as possible. He also agrees the Reparations Commission should work closely with the Control Council and set up its organization in Berlin. One point he qualifies. The commission's permanent seat, he says, should naturally remain Moscow, as the Crimea Conference decided. He adds that the commission's work will bind it most closely to the Soviet Union, given the Berlin decisions.
frus-1948v02-d577: A 1948 FRUS document from the U.S. Military Governor for Germany. The occupation authorities reported from Berlin. This entry holds that report. Coming generations can find it. The historical record keeps it. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-295877: BTC Contract Services took its May 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297077: Haworth doubled its November 2005 protest — two case numbers, one furniture fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer each, and the record stays clean.
gao-gaoreports-b-298077: Critical Incident Solutions took its May 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.

gao-gaoreports-b-299577: Forest City Military Communities took its June 2007 housing-contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict.
