gao-gaoreports-b-400177: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by ECI Defense Group. The July 25, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-277: DOD's excess property was being wasted in 2005, and GAO's report says management control breakdowns caused substantial waste. The findings demand the fixes. The report warns that the surplus deserved better handling. The breakdowns had to be fixed. The surplus deserved better handling.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-377: Hardrock mining bonds needed better management in 2005, and GAO's report says BLM had to improve financial assurances for reclamation. The findings demand the guarantees. The report warns that the mined lands deserved real cleanup. The assurances had to be better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-477: Passport fraud detection needed strengthening in 2005, and GAO's report says improvements were required. The findings demand the vigilance. The report warns that the travel documents should not be faked. The improvements had to come. The travel documents should not be faked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-577: Disaster backup plans were better but not battle-tested in 2005, and GAO's report says agency plans improved, with oversight needed to finish the job. The review checks who could keep working through an emergency. The continuity plans were maturing. The continuity plans were maturing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-677: TSA's sensitive information designation needed clear policies in 2005, and GAO's report says oversight was required. The findings demand the rules. The report warns that the secrecy stamps deserved honest use. The policies had to be clear. The secrecy stamps deserved honest use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-777: E-rulemaking progress got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says centralized system development was advancing. The findings give the credit. The report shows the digital democracy was being built. The progress had to be sustained. The digital democracy was being built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-177: Energy workers' compensation needed better oversight in 2006, and GAO's report says adjustments had been made, though more planning was required. The findings balance credit and prodding. The report warns that the atomic workers deserved fair pay. The oversight had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-277: The 2010 Census buying was mostly sound in 2006, and GAO's report says the bureau generally followed good acquisition practices, though management needed continuing. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the headcount's contracts needed watching. The management had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-577: UN procurement controls were weak in 2006, and GAO's report says the internal controls needed strengthening. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the world body's shopping needed locks. The controls had to be fixed. The world body's shopping needed locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-677: The down-payment aid program's results were murky in 2006, and GAO's report says data limitations constrained the assessment of the initiative. The findings admit the fog. The report warns that the dream-home dollars needed proof. The data had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1077: Guarding bases and depots took more than fences in 2007 — GAO's report says the Pentagon's risk game needed sharper management. The findings press defense brass to run base protection like a discipline, not a checklist. In an age of asymmetric threats, the report argues, ad-hoc security is no security.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-277: America's logo on its aid needed measuring in 2007, and GAO's report says the agencies should better assess their marking and publicity efforts. The findings demand proof of impact. The report's question: did the flag on the grain buy any goodwill?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-677: Iraq's lights and oil needed one master plan in 2007 — GAO's report says the rebuild of the power and petroleum sectors wanted an integrated strategy. The findings demand joined-up thinking. The report's warning: megawatts and barrels rise or fall together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-77: Kidney-care payments needed bundling in 2007, and GAO's report says bundling Medicare's drug payments with all end-stage renal disease services would promote efficiency. The findings make the case. The report argues that one price for the whole treatment would curb the gaming. The bundle had to be tied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-877: Uncle Sam's ad buys got an audit in 2007 — GAO's report finds the established ad programs mostly served the White House's small-business push. The findings track where the government's marketing dollars went. The report asks whether the public's airtime served the public.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-477: The Government Accountability Office dug into traffic Safety: Improved Reporting and Performance Measures Would Enhance Evaluation of High-Visibility Campaigns in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-77: GAO found in 2007 that the aid agency and the space agency were slack about chasing wrong payments. A 2002 law tells each agency to size up, report, and claw back money paid in error — but both fell short. The report grades their thin efforts and presses both shops to hunt down mistaken payouts and get the cash back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-877: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Acquisitions: Department of Defense Needs Framework for Balancing Investments in Tactical Radios. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
how-to-teach-according-to-temperament-an: How to Teach According to Temperament, 1877. The phrenological teaching. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It awaits future readers. Kept for readers. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
jewett-deephaven-1877:
Deephaven, Jewett's first book from 1877, follows two young Boston women through a summer in Maine. They stay in a sleepy coastal town in a house left by a great-aunt. Contents name Kate Lancaster's plan, the Brandon house and lighthouse, and Lady Brandon among the early sketches.

City girls learn country wisdom as they meet weathered houses and salty local folk. Jewett tells the tale in linked sketches rather than one tight plot. The gentle comedy already shows her fine ear and her love of place. No one before her had written New England village life with such close and loving care, and critics saw a major talent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucifer-10177:
Lucifer, the name of the morning star, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Kaufmann Kohler. The word renders a Hebrew phrase in Isaiah, “the brilliant one, son of the morning,” whose fall is compared to the fall of the king of Babylon. Kohler treats the passage as a borrowed star myth.

The article links the proud star, hurled down from the mountain of the gods, to Greek and Babylonian tales and to the fall of the angels on Mount Hermon. It then shows how, in the century before Christianity, the myth passed to Satan, once an archangel cast down for raising his throne too high. Early Christian writers completed that identification. For readers, the entry traces one word from a Hebrew prophecy about Babylon to the later figure of Satan himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-paul-wil:
Paul Wilhelm Magnus, a German botanist, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Berlin on February 29, 1844, he studied at the university there and at Freiburg. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1870. In 1875 he became a lecturer at his home university, and assistant professor of botany in 1880.

The article stresses his work on the seas. He served as the botanist of the Prussian commission for exploring the oceans. He sailed on expeditions to the Baltic in 1871, the North Sea in 1872, and another voyage in 1874. His reports of those journeys were published by the government. His books treat the plant genus Najas, the form of certain seaweeds, and the fungi of a Swiss canton. The short entry records a botanist who carried his science from the lecture room onto survey ships.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mansion-house-a:
Mansion House and Guildhall Meetings, London's great protest gatherings for persecuted Jews, are described in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. The lord mayor summoned citizens to these meetings. The first met on July 3, 1840, against the blood accusation at Damascus. Two hundred ten leading residents had demanded it.

The article follows the meetings across fifty years. Daniel O'Connell and others spoke in 1840, demanding the accused men's release. The resolutions went to foreign ambassadors, and Russia's emperor replied favorably. In 1882 new meetings protested Russia's persecution of its Jews. The call bore names like the Archbishop of Canterbury, Cardinal Manning, and Charles Darwin. A fund of 108,000 pounds was raised for the victims. At the Guildhall in 1890 the city again deplored Russia's anti-Jewish edicts. A memorandum to the czar asked equal rights for Russian Jews. He refused to receive it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-kadosh-mei:
Meir Kadosh, born Meir ben Jehiel at Ungarisch-Brod in Moravia in 1593, earned his surname, "the saint," as a boy, and his Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906, by Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn, tells the story he himself wrote down. In 1608, aged fifteen, he set out with eight fellow students for a yeshivah in Poland. On the road the waywode, or lord, of Auspitz kidnapped him and held him prisoner for fifteen weeks, torturing him to force him to accept Christianity.

Meir held firm. The Jews of Cracow ransomed him and placed him in the yeshivah of Moses Meisels. In 1632 he published his account at Cracow as "Megillat R. Meir," the Scroll of Rabbi Meir, a short memoir of captivity and constancy. The entry notes that the tale rests on his own telling, catalogued by Steinschneider.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendoza-daniel-:
Daniel Mendoza was the Whitechapel boxer nicknamed the Star of Israel. Joseph Jacobs and Frank H. Vizetelly give him a full sporting biography in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Champion of England from 1792 to 1795, he founded a distinct school of boxing. Miles's history of the sport dates an era from Figg's championship "to the Appearance of Daniel Mendoza." The entry walks through his fights. It tells of the debut win over a Bath butcher in 1787. It tells of the three battles with Richard Humphries that made his name, and the two defeats of William Warr of Bristol.

Later life was quieter. He was sheriff's officer for Middlesex in 1806 and made exhibition tours. One last bout came in 1820, at fifty-seven, lost to Tom Owen in twelve rounds. He retired to keep the Admiral Nelson inn in Whitechapel. He died in 1836. He is remembered for bringing science to the prize-ring.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micah-book-of-1:
The Book of Micah, sixth among the Twelve Minor Prophets, is summarized chapter by chapter in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn, published in 1906. The book is ascribed to Micah the Morasthite and runs to seven chapters. A critical section after the summary takes up scholarly questions about the prophet's period.

Chapter one denounces the idolatry of Samaria and Jerusalem, and chapter two attacks oppression while promising Israel's restoration. Chapter three reproves cruel princes and false prophets, and chapter four turns to Jerusalem restored and victorious. The summary closes with reproof for injustice, a lament over corruption, and comfort that Israel will return to its land and triumph.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morais-henry-sa:
Henry Samuel Morais, born at Philadelphia on May 13, 1860, was a writer and minister raised inside American Judaism's founding family, as Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, Sabato Morais, gave him his religious instruction. He taught twelve years in Philadelphia's Hebrew schools before turning to print.

He was the principal founder of the Jewish Exponent and its managing editor for two years, with newspaper work at the Philadelphia Public Ledger beside. Pulpits followed at Mikve Israel, at Syracuse, and at Newport. His books made his name: Eminent Israelites of the Nineteenth Century at twenty, and in 1894 The Jews of Philadelphia, called here the most important local history of American Jews yet published.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-elija:
Moses ben Elijah ha-Levi was a Karaite scholar and poet of the Crimea in the eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn give him a brief entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Chufut-Kale, the old Karaite center in the Crimean hills.

His work Darosh Darash Mosheh gathers twenty-four treatises on various subjects. A dirge of his, written on the death of some scholar, is kept in the Karaite prayer book, the hazanya. That is nearly all the entry records. Even so, it names one writer from a small community whose literature is little known outside itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mostar-11177:
Mostar, capital of its district in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had one hundred sixty-four Jews in 1895. Gotthard Deutsch and Samuel Wessel wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on the town. The first Jews settled there only in 1850 and founded a community six years later. Until the Austrian occupation of 1878, all of them were Sephardic.

After 1878 Ashkenazic Jews arrived from Austria-Hungary, until the two groups stood about equal in number. The community rents a building for its synagogue and keeps a cemetery. It has no rabbi; the official who teaches religion in the city schools handles its religious affairs. The article stresses that the two groups, and their neighbors, lived in complete harmony.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-jacob:
Jacob Nathanson was a Polish teacher of chemistry. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Warsaw in 1832. He was educated at the University of Dorpat. He died at Warsaw on Sept. 14, 1884.

In 1862 Nathanson became professor at Warsaw's Szkola Glawna. He stayed until the academy closed seven years later. He wrote a number of works in Polish on chemistry. Beyond the classroom, he founded industrial schools. He also set up charitable societies for the city. At his death he left 30,000 rubles for authors. That gift formed an endowment to support their work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumegen-leopol:
Leopold Neumegen was an English schoolmaster from Posen. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1787 in that Prussian town. He died at Kew, near London, in April 1875. He first taught at Göttingen, in Germany.

About 1816 Neumegen removed to England to teach. He became principal of a boarding school at Highgate. For half a century his name was a household word. Hardly one noted Anglo-Jewish family lacked his pupils. Sir George Jessel and Professor Sylvester sat among them. Sebag Montefiore also learned under his care. Bad investments forced him to reopen a school at Kew. He began that fresh career at Gloucester House there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paltiel-11877:
Paltiel was a vizier to the califs of Egypt. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A vizier is the chief aide of a ruler. Paltiel lived in the last half of the nine hundreds. The one source for his life is a family tale.

That tale is the Chronicle of Ahimaaz ben Paltiel. It makes Paltiel kin to the poet Shephatiah of Oria. When Al-Mu'izz took Oria, Paltiel won his favor fast. He did so by his skill in the lore of stars. He told the calif he would rule three lands in time. The calif took him to North Africa on his march. He put the affairs of state in Paltiel's hands there. Paltiel fed the whole host on the march through sand.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pater-synagog-g:
Pater Synagogae means father of the synagogue in Latin. The title turns up often in the Jewish catacombs at Rome. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The words survive in stone inscriptions there. It named a man tied to the congregation.

Scholars read the title in two different ways. Berliner took it as the same as parnas, a community officer. Schürer, followed by most writers, saw a title of honor instead. On his view it praised men who served the congregation. A matching title, mother of the synagogue, honored women.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedigree-11977:
A pedigree is a table that shows a family's line of descent. Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews kept careful records of their family lines. Scattering and exile broke most of those records early. The article follows the record from Ezra to modern times.

Few families can trace their line back over two hundred years. Men named Cohen claim descent from Aaron, without proof on paper. After the Exile, proof of pure descent grew urgent. Priests could marry only women of proven clean stock. A court in Jerusalem heard disputes on such claims.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pierleoni-12077:
The Pierleoni were a noble Roman house of Jewish birth. Isidore Singer and Hermann Vogelstein wrote their entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A rich Jewish banker founded the line. Baptized, he took the name Benedictus Christianus.

His son Petrus Leonis gave the family its name. From castles he guarded the Tiber island and the popes. Urban the Second died under his roof. In 1130 his own son became Pope Anacletus the Second. A rival pope split the Church for eight years. The family kept its rank after the breach healed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinto-or-de-pin:
The Pinto were a great Portuguese Jewish family. Seven scholars shared this long entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its members were financiers, rabbis, scholars, and soldiers. They spread from Portugal across three continents. An early Pinto pleaded for Maranos at Rome in 1535.

Amsterdam held the family's richest branch in the 1600s. One Pinto left millions to Jews and Christians alike. Other Pintos rose in Brazil and Dutch Guiana. In Connecticut they joined the Revolution's cause. Aaron de Pinto backed Ayllon against Rabbi Ashkenazi. Aaron Adolf became a Dutch supreme court justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-siegfrie:
Siegfried Popper was an Austrian builder of warships, born at Prague in 1848. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at trade schools in Prague and Carlsruhe. He worked two years in machine shops. In 1869 he joined the Austrian navy as an assistant builder.

Popper rose to head of naval building work in 1902. In 1904 he became builder-general with admiral's rank. He watched over the building of many Austrian warships. They include the cruisers Panther, Leopard, and Tiger. They include armored cruisers and battleships as well. Nine of the largest ships were built from his own designs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-bar-bar-:
Rabbah bar bar Hana was a Babylonian teacher of the second set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a grandson of Hana, the brother of Hiyya. He went up to Palestine for his learning there. He sat under Johanan and passed on his words.

In his new land he was not held in high regard. Men took it for granted he would be passed by. Simeon ben Lakish would not greet him in public, it was assumed. After a time of mixed fortune he went home. The entry follows his trips and his standing at both schools. His name lives in tales told across the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rappaport-phili:
Philip Rappaport was an American lawyer and journalist born in 1845. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born and educated at Fürth in Bavaria. He moved to the United States in 1866.

The article says he first reported for a Pittsburgh German paper. He edited a daily at Wheeling while studying law. He entered the bar in 1870 and moved to Cincinnati. There he helped edit German papers as well. In 1874 he settled in Indianapolis to practice law. In 1881 he founded the Indiana Tribune. He owned and edited it for nineteen years. The entry joins newspaper work and law in one career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remnant-of-isra:
The remnant of Israel is a key idea in the Prophets. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The Hebrew words are she'erit Yisrael or she'ar. Isaiah's son Shear-jashub carries the idea in his name.

The article explains that most of Israel will fall or be exiled. Sin and disloyalty bring that severe punishment. Yet a remnant will be saved and will return. That remnant will trust God, not foreign alliances. Isaiah compares the survivors to grapes left after gathering. A shaken olive tree keeps a few olives too. Micah and Zephaniah teach the same doctrine, they say. The entry shows hope built into a message of judgment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-samue:
Samuel Rosenthal was a chess master born in Suwalki, Russian Poland, in 1838. Herman Rosenthal and A. Porter wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. After the last Polish rising he fled to Paris in 1864.

Rosenthal took up chess in Paris and improved with striking speed. Within a year he won first prize at the Café de la Régence tournament. He placed well at Baden in 1870 and at Vienna in 1873. At London in 1883 he won the brilliancy prize against Steinitz. In Paris he founded a chess circle and gave blindfold exhibitions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-julius-12:
Julius Sachs was an American educator born at Baltimore on July 6, 1849. Cyrus Adler and Louis H. Gray wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was educated at Columbia University and at Rostock, in Germany.

Sachs founded the Collegiate Institute in New York, a boys' school. He also taught secondary education at Teachers' College, Columbia University, as professor. He presided over the American Philological Association in 1891, among other bodies. He served the College Entrance Examinations Board as a secondary school voice. His writings treat school problems and classical philology and archaeology alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sacrifice-10877:
Sacrifice is the offering made to a deity for homage, favor, or pardon. Its six authors were Emil G. Hirsch, Kaufmann Kohler, M. Seligsohn, Isidore Singer, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, and Joseph Jacobs. The long entry begins with the Bible's own picture of the rite.

Scripture treats sacrifice as old as the human race itself. Cain and Abel stand for its two classes: vegetable gifts and animal ones. After the Flood, Noah offered of every clean beast and fowl. The patriarchs built altars across Canaan and offered at covenant moments. Abraham even believed himself commanded to offer up his own son.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samson-ben-sams:
Samson ben Samson was a French tosafist of the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He is called HaRaSH, and by anagram Ha-Sar, the prince of Coucy.

Many of Samson's explanations live inside the tosafot to the Talmud. He also commented on the Bible in his own right as scholar. He was brother-in-law to Moses of Coucy, who quotes him often. He studied under Isaac ben Samuel the Elder of Dampierre in France. Abulafia addressed his protest against Maimonides to Samson among leading rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sanger-adolph-l:
Cyrus Adler and Abram S. Isaacs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Adolph L. Sanger. He was an American lawyer and politician. Sanger was born at Baton Rouge, Louisiana, in 1842. He died in New York City on January 3, 1894. He graduated from the City College and from Columbia Law School in 1864. His rise in the law was rapid.

In 1885 Sanger was elected president of the board of aldermen. He served as a presidential elector for New York in 1880 and 1884. He sat on the board of education for three terms from 1886. He became its president in 1893. He first proposed Bryant Park as the site for a public library. In Jewish life he led the B'nai B'rith. He also presided over the Board of Delegates of American Israelites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-jos:
Josef Schlesinger, an Austrian mathematician, is profiled by Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman in this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. Schlesinger was born at Mährisch-Schönberg on December 31, 1831. His parents were very poor. He had to earn his living while still a mere boy. In 1858 he graduated from Vienna's Polytechnic Institute.

Schlesinger became an assistant at the Polytechnic in 1859. In 1866 he passed the state examination as a teacher of geometry. He taught in Vienna's schools. In 1870 he became professor of geometry at the forestry academy at Marienbrunn. In 1875 he moved to the agricultural academy at Vienna. In 1891 Vienna sent him to the Austrian Reichsrath. His books include a work on descriptive geometry from 1870. He also wrote on nature's spiritual mechanics and on the world's origin in ether.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seder-olam-rabb:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It treats the Seder 'Olam Rabbah, the oldest post-exilic chronicle in Hebrew. The Talmud quotes it simply as Seder 'Olam. Rashi and other early commentators cite it too. From the twelfth century the word Rabbah, greater, set it apart from a smaller namesake.

The work holds thirty chapters in three gates of ten. It runs from Adam to Bar Kokba's revolt under Hadrian. Only the stretch up to Alexander the Great is full. The rest is squeezed into one chapter's end. Scholars think a second part once existed and was lost. The author likely built the book to fix the era of Creation. His calendar system, adopted by the third century, still holds. He squeezed events into the shortest spans that fit the Bible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-nawa:
Shabbethai Nawawi was a rabbi and scholar living at Rosetta, Egypt, in the late seventeenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was a peer of Abraham ben Mordecai ha-Levi. Some of his responsa appear inside Abraham's book Ginnat Weradim.

Other writers quoted Nawawi's legal answers in their own works. Moses Israel and Judah Zain both drew on him. The bibliographer Azulai owned manuscripts of two Nawawi books. One dealt with law and the other with homiletic themes. The entry preserves traces of an Egyptian scholar whose work survives mostly through the books of others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shila-of-kefar-:
Shila of Kefar Tamarta was a Palestinian amora of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Palestinian sources call him simply Shila, with no place name. Babylonian sources add his Judean hometown to separate two men.

Shila gave public lectures on the Haggadah, the non-legal tradition. He is mentioned only in that connection, the entry says. Yet hints show he worked in legal study too. No legal sayings of his survive for readers today. His Bible readings came mostly from those public lectures. Each opens with the formula, Rabbi Shila has preached. The entry preserves a preacher known by the tag line that introduced his sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-tribe-of:
Emil G Hirsch, Caspar Levias, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article on the tribe of Simeon. It appeared in 1906. The tribe traced its line to Simeon, second son of Jacob by Leah. With his brother Levi he attacked Shechem over their sister Dinah. Jacob cursed both brothers with being scattered in Israel.

The tribe settled in the south, inside the land of Judah. Its towns are listed in Joshua and in Chronicles. Its numbers fell sharply between the two counts in Numbers. Later bands of Simeonites moved to Gedor for pasture in the days of Hezekiah. The article weighs these lists and tales with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-samuel-1:
Samuel Singer was a philologist born in Vienna on July 12, 1860. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the gymnasium and university of his home city. He took law and philosophy degrees in 1884 and 1885. In 1891 he began teaching at the University of Bern.

By 1905 Singer was professor of medieval German language and literature. His books covered German folk books and old epics. He wrote on Ulrich von dem Türlin and on Apollonius of Tyre. He also wrote notes on Wolfram von Eschenbach. His later work dealt with Middle High German written speech. Another book traced German culture through loanword meanings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-samuel-:
Samuel Spitzer was a Hungarian rabbi born in 1839 at Keszthely. Isidore Singer and Gabriel Schwarz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His father was rabbi of that town. He descended from Yom-Tob Lipmann Heller, the famed commentator. He studied at Prague and became rabbi at Esseg in 1856.

He was widely recognized as an authority on religious questions. Several humanitarian societies grew in his congregation from his work. Besides sermons, he published many works on ancient civilization. They covered army law, Jewish marriage, and communal order in turn. Others dealt with meals, baths, clocks, and letters among the ancients. He died in 1896, leaving a long list of books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-joseph-:
Joseph Strauss was an English rabbi born in Germany in 1848. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied at Stuttgart, Würzburg, and Tübingen. He earned his doctorate there in 1873. Ordained in 1870, he moved straight to England.

In England, Strauss became rabbi of the Bradford synagogue on Rowland Street. He still held that post in 1905. He lectured in German and Oriental languages at Bradford colleges. He taught for twenty-one years at Yorkshire College too. His books include Religion and Morals in English. A German work studies the religious philosophy of Ibn Ezra. It appeared in 1875 under a German title. The entry profiles a scholar-rabbi serving one northern town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szerencses-fort:
Emerich Szerencsés was a Hungarian deputy treasurer who died in 1526. Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Born Jewish, he faced ruin over a scandal with a Christian woman. To escape harsh punishment he accepted baptism. An archbishop baptized him with a palatine as sponsor.

As deputy treasurer, Szerencsés used his power for his former people. He warned Jews of danger in secret-code letters. He talked the king out of a ritual murder charge at Ofen. He won repeal of Prague's expulsion order at great cost. He saved two Jews condemned to die by fire. Every Friday he gave alms to poor Jews. Grateful rabbis honored his sons, who stayed Jewish. The entry tells of loyalty kept across a forced conversion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tayyib-14277:
Tayyib was a Tunisian family of rabbis and commentators. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It first appears in the later seventeenth century. Its members taught and wrote in Tunis for generations. Their books mostly comment on Talmud tractates.

Abraham ben Isaac Tayyib was rabbi of Tunis until 1741. His nickname was Baba Sidi among the people. He taught Isaac Lombroso, later Tunis's chief rabbi. His novellae on the Kodashim order were printed in 1810. Other notes of his sit inside colleagues' books. His grandson Abraham wrote a vast commentary called Hayye Abraham. It covers fifteen tractates plus notes on Maimonides. It was printed at Leghorn in 1826. The entry sketches three generations of one scholarly house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-translations-14:
Hebrew translations from Arabic form the backbone of this survey article. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. After Islam's rise, eastern Jews adopted Arabic widely. Rabbis had to write in Arabic to reach the masses. Learning later moved west to Spain and southern France.

Many Arabic works then passed into Hebrew dress. The oldest such translations date to the eleventh century. Isaac Albargeloni rendered Hai Gaon's book on buying in 1078. He also translated Ibn Janah's great lexicon. Moses ibn Gikatilla translated Hayyuj on Hebrew verb forms. Ibn Ezra translated grammar, astrology, and a book on lots. Judah ibn Tibbon judged the early versions faulty. Translators, he said, mixed in their own opinions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verein-zur-abwe:
The Verein zur Abwehr des Anti Semitismus fought anti Jewish hatred in Germany. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Twelve men formed the Berlin society late in 1890. Their appeal asked Jews and Christians to defend Jewish equal rights. It drew 535 signatures from leading Germans.

A sister society formed at Vienna in July 1891. Most support came from Christians, though Jews could join. By 1893 the Berlin group counted 13,338 members. They lived in 963 different places. Its presidents were the jurist Rudolf Gneist and later liberal leaders. The entry records an early, organized pushback against anti Semitism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-war-14777:
War in the Bible begins with kings fighting over the plain of Sodom. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this entry. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Genesis chapter fourteen tells that first recorded war. Chedorlaomer and his allies crushed five kings. Captives and goods became the spoils.

The entry surveys how Israel waged and limited war. Talks through messengers often came first. Hebrew law barred attack before a call to surrender. Armies consulted God before setting out. Spring was the usual season for campaigns. Later sections treat sieges, weapons, and battle order. The article builds a full picture from scattered Bible texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-hirsch-w-1:
Hirsch W. Wolf (1738-1820) was a German doctor who wrote on care and cures. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Lobsens in Posen, he took his degree at Giessen in 1779. He practiced first at Altona and then at Hamburg.

At Hamburg he served as doctor at the poorhouse for two years. His books treat the cures and fears of his day. One book deals with a plaster made from Spanish flies. One defends the early burial of the Jewish dead. Others treat smallpox, fever, and the force of life. His last book also treats animal magnetism, then a hot topic. The list shows a town doctor who wrote on each new claim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarza-samuel-ib:
Samuel ibn Seneh Zarza was a Spanish thinker of the late 1300s. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broyde wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Valencia in the east of Spain. His byname comes from a town whose name means thorn bush.

That word is the same in sense as the Hebrew seneh. No facts of his life are known to men now. One late note says he was burned at the stake there. That note blames a charge made by Isaac Campanton. Men of the past have shown that tale to be a mere myth. His peers held him in high awe in his day. A poet and a star man wrote verse in his honor. His chief work is a thought work on the Pentateuch text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zodiac-15277:
The zodiac is the band of sky holding twelve signs, through which the sun seems to travel each year. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Each sign spans thirty degrees, and the twelve divide the whole circle evenly. Astronomers use the signs, while astrologers use the star groups behind them.

The entry gives the Hebrew names of the signs, starting with Taleh, Aries, in the month of Nisan. It links the signs to the twelve tribes, whose camp standards matched them. It also ties the signs to parts of the body, as the Sefer Yezirah does. A slow shift, one degree in a hundred years, had already moved signs away from their star groups.
kabbala-denudata-knorr-tome1-1677:
Christian Knorr von Rosenroth published the first tome of his Kabbala Denudata at Sulzbach in 1677. The text is in Latin, the learned tongue of his Europe. Knorr gathered Kabbalistic writings, above all from the Zohar and the school of Isaac Luria, and rendered them into Latin with long introductions of his own.

Through this anthology, Jewish mysticism reached Christian scholars who read no Hebrew or Aramaac. Thinkers from Leibniz onward consulted Knorr's volumes on the sefirot and the souls of men. No English translation of the work is in the public domain. Tome one is the principal vehicle by which Lurianic Kabbalah entered the Christian West. Its influence on early modern thought is still being mapped.
la-tete-humaine-etudes-de-phrenologie-et:
Charles Rouvin wrote La Tête Humaine, printed in Paris in 1877. Its subtitle announces studies of phrenology and facial reading. He applies both to famous people of ancient and modern times.

The book carries many pictures set into the text. Rouvin had also written works on social fallacies and a thinker's manual. His motto says: judge the thing itself, not the words. Readers can see how nineteenth-century writers tried to read character from heads and faces. Famous heads from history serve as his test cases. Readers can watch the method applied, case by case, across the volume.
lalita-vistara-mitra-1877:
Rajendralala Mitra translated the Lalita Vistara into English in 1877. The Sanskrit text tells the Buddha's life as cosmic pageant. Mitra was a pioneering Indian scholar of the nineteenth century.

Miracles attend every episode of the ornate biography. A heaven-sent conception, a painless birth, and gods in attendance frame the story. The young prince's encounters lead toward the enlightenment beneath the tree. Beloved across Asia, the Lalita Vistara shaped Buddhist art for centuries. Mitra's translation captures its jeweled, devotional style in English. The work reads less as history than as devotion. Its gorgeous excess is precisely its point and charm.
lemery-course-of-chymistry-1677:
Nicolas Lemery was a Paris apothecary whose Cours de Chymie taught chemistry to fashionable crowds in his own laboratory. This 1677 English translation, A Course of Chymistry, was the bestselling chemistry textbook of the late seventeenth century. Lemery wrote for students, doctors, and curious householders alike.

He explains acids, alkalis, metals, and medicines with models of sharp and porous particles that a beginner can picture. Recipes and operations fill the course, from distilling spirits to preparing the drugs of his shop. The book's clarity helped turn chymistry from a secret craft into a public, teachable science.
mackenzie-royal-masonic-cyclopaedia-1877:
Kenneth Mackenzie built a vast word book of the craft in The Royal Masonic Cyclopaedia, out in 1877. Mackenzie was a sage of signs and rites in London. He later helped seed the Golden Dawn. Here he glosses each term, rank, rite, and tale of the Masons in A to Z form.

Lore of the craft sits by lore of the East and old myths. His own sly views slip in past the dry gloss. The book is a rich store for fans of rite. It shows the mind that shaped an age of magic. Mackenzie roamed the clubs and bands of the occult in his day. Few men of his age could match the breadth of lore packed here.
maclean-manual-antiquity-of-man-1877:
J. P. MacLean, an American writer on archaeology, published A Manual of the Antiquity of Man in 1877. The book is an early American synthesis of human prehistory for general readers. MacLean gathered what the 1870s knew of fossil man and the first ages of human life.

He surveys cave deposits with their extinct beasts, the shell mounds of the coasts, and the great earthworks of the mound-builders. European finds and American ones are weighed side by side. The manual's judgments belong to its decade, but its range is impressive. It stands as a snapshot of prehistoric archaeology while the field was still young and forming.
mccrindle-ancient-india-megasthenes-arri:
J. W. McCrindle collected Greek accounts of ancient India in his 1877 volume. Megasthenes' Indica and Arrian's Indica form the core of the book. McCrindle spent his career translating classical sources on India into English.

Megasthenes served as ambassador at Chandragupta's court around 300 BCE. His Indica survives only in quotations by later writers, which McCrindle assembled. Elephants, gold-digging ants, and seven castes fill the ambassador's report. Arrian's Indica adds Alexander-era knowledge and the voyage of Nearchus. Together they give the West's earliest systematic description of India. Wonder and sober reporting sit side by side throughout these fragments.
menghi-flagellum-daemonum-1577:
Girolamo Menghi was an Italian Franciscan exorcist whose Flagellum Daemonum, The Scourge of Demons, appeared in 1577. The book is a working manual of exorcism for priests facing possessed persons. It became the most reprinted Catholic exorcist's handbook of the early modern period.

Menghi gives the rites in order: prayers, adjurations, signs of the cross, and questions to put to the demon. He also teaches how to tell true possession from illness, fraud, and melancholy before any rite begins. Later exorcists copied his forms for two centuries, making his book the standard of the trade. Priests carried his manual into sickrooms and prisons across Catholic Europe.
miln-excavations-carnac-1877:
James Miln dug among the great stone rows at Carnac in Brittany in the 1870s. His book, printed in 1877, gives the first true dig report from the site. Carnac holds long lines of huge upright stones set in the far past. Miln worked at the Bossenno and Mont Saint-Michel sites.

He tells what the digs found layer by layer: tools, pots, and signs of old huts. Plans and views show the rows and the mounds near them. Miln's care set a mark for field work at such sites. The report launched the true study of Carnac.
mkultra-senate-hearings-1977:
The Senate dragged the CIA's mind-control program into the light in the summer of 1977. Project MKULTRA hearings, held jointly on August 3, laid out the agency's years of work on drugs and the mind. New-found money records had just shown the program was wider than first known.

Senators heard how the agency dosed men without their knowledge and hid the work behind cut-outs and shredders. The transcript prints the charges, the agency's defense, and the names of the dead and harmed. It is the base public record of the whole grim program. Later accounts of MKULTRA all build on this hearing.
morgan-ancient-society-1877:
Lewis Henry Morgan, a Rochester lawyer who studied the Iroquois for decades, published Ancient Society in 1877. His subtitle traces human progress from savagery through barbarism to civilization. The book is built on kinship systems, his great discovery as a fieldworker and theorist.

Morgan argues that mankind climbed one main ladder, marked by inventions: fire, the bow, pottery, farming, and iron. Family forms climb with them, from group marriage toward monogamy. Marx and Engels read the book closely; Engels built his Origin of the Family on it. Modern anthropology rejects Morgan's single ladder but honors his kinship work. The book is a foundation stone of American anthropology.

B. Abelev and the ALICE Collaboration reported this measurement. It appeared in Physical Review Letters in January 2013. The team smashed protons into lead nuclei at CERN. They counted charged particles across a wide angle range. The measure is called pseudorapidity density in the paper.

The average density at midrapidity is reported per colliding pair. It fell below the value expected from proton collisions. It stood far above older gold collision results, they note. Models of particle production must now match this value. The data help separate first-moment effects from later ones. Such checks clarify how hot matter forms in collisions.
openalex-w2784936077:
Sergej Nowoshilow, Siegfried Schloissnig, and Ji-Feng Fei lead a large team sequencing the axolotl genome in Nature in 2018. The Mexican axolotl is a star laboratory salamander, famous for regrowing lost limbs and tissues. Its genome, though, is gigantic and full of repeats, which long blocked assembly. At thirty-two billion letters, it dwarfs the human genome tenfold.

The team combined long-read sequencing with optical mapping and built a new assembler, MARVEL, for the job. The finished assembly anchors regeneration research in actual gene sequences. Comparing its tissue-formation regulators with other animals illuminates how such genes evolved. Salamanders anchor studies of development and evolution across four-legged animals. A reliable axolotl genome gives those fields their missing reference. It should speed the search for the genetic switches behind regeneration.
openalex-w2891646477:
Alex Y. Doets, Christine Verboon, and Bianca van den Berg lead this 2018 study in Brain, comparing Guillain-Barré syndrome across world regions. The IGOS Consortium followed the first one thousand patients in its international cohort. Guillain-Barré paralyzes patients after infections trigger immune attacks on nerves. Doctors suspected presentation and recovery differ by geography, but worldwide data were lacking.

Patients entered within two weeks of onset at one hundred thirty-five sites in eighteen countries. Teams recorded symptoms, spinal fluid results, and nerve conduction studies on a shared schedule. Follow-up visits ran through a full year of recovery. Electrophysiological tests classified each case as demyelinating, axonal, or another subtype. Comparing regions on identical measures reveals genuine variation rather than reporting habits. The study gives neurologists a global baseline for this rare, dangerous disease.
openalex-w2904186977:
Dylan Nelson, Volker Springel, and Annalisa Pillepich lead the IllustrisTNG team's public data release paper, in Computational Astrophysics and Cosmology in 2019. This paper opens the flagship simulations' full data to everyone.

The release covers the TNG100 and TNG300 runs, with TNG50 to follow. Each run ships with halo catalogs, merger trees, and one hundred snapshots of cosmic time. The accessible volume already reaches about seven hundred fifty terabytes. A web API offers on-demand visualization and analysis without massive downloads. A JupyterLab interface lets users compute beside the data in a browser. The team also lists scientific caveats for using the simulations wisely. Few datasets in astronomy are shared this completely.
openalex-w2943031177:
Nádia Noronha, Amanda Mizukami, Carolina Caliári-Oliveira, and colleagues wrote this 2019 review in Stem Cell Research and Therapy. The authors review priming, ways of preparing the cells before treatment so they work better. Limits in the field include poor cell survival after infusion, source and donor differences, and uneven culture methods. Priming options covered include cytokines and growth factors, low oxygen, drugs, biomaterials, and changed culture conditions. The review weighs each approach for future clinical use.
openalex-w2951276077:
Günter Blöschl, Marc Bierkens, António Chambel, and colleagues published this community paper in Hydrological Sciences Journal in 2019. It names twenty-three unsolved problems in hydrology, the science of water on Earth. The list came from a field-wide effort to focus research on shared questions.

The team ran a public consultation online, then held two workshops to gather, rank, and merge candidate questions. About two hundred thirty scientists took part in total. Despite that range, the process showed a taste for continuity rather than sharp new directions. The final questions center on process-based understanding of how water varies and what causes those changes, across all scales.
openalex-w2951287977:
Swastika Chandra, Paul Ward, and Masoud Mohammadnezhad published this study in Frontiers in Public Health in 2019. It examines patient satisfaction at outpatient clinics in the Suva subdivision of Fiji in 2018. Happy patients tend to follow treatment and prevention advice more closely, so satisfaction matters for health outcomes.

The team used both surveys and interviews in a mixed method design. Four hundred ten patients filled in a structured survey, and three hundred seventy-five replies were analyzed. The survey covered waiting time, doctor communication, and patient trust. Twenty patients also took part in recorded interviews. The authors report that most patients were generally satisfied, and they identify the factors linked to satisfaction.
openalex-w3035590377:

Searching five databases, the team found ninety studies covering barriers, helpers, and programs for ages ten to nineteen. Stigma and negative views of services and professionals were the barriers named most often. Past good experiences with care and better mental health knowledge helped teens come forward. Most programs taught mental health basics through classes, media, or peer training. The review gives services a map of what to fix first.
openalex-w4384652177:
Marcela Uliano-Silva, João Ferreira, Ksenia Krasheninnikova, and colleagues present MitoHiFi, a tool for assembling mitochondrial genomes, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2023. Modern PacBio sequencing reads are long and highly accurate. In animals and fungi, the small mitochondrial genome is captured alongside the main genome, often many times over. No dedicated tool existed to pull it out of such data and build it cleanly.

MitoHiFi takes raw reads or draft assemblies and returns the finished mitochondrial sequence with its genes labelled. It keeps variant copies separate and rejects look-alike pieces inserted in the main genome. The tool has already built hundreds of mitochondrial genomes for large biodiversity projects. It is written in Python and freely shared, with repeat regions newly reported in many species.
openalex-w7204159777:
Luan Filipe Viana Saldanha, of Hospital Agamenon Magalhães in Brazil, led a Portuguese-language case report published in 2026 on thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura in a patient with HIV. In this rare, potentially fatal disorder, autoantibodies disable a protein that keeps blood from clotting in tiny vessels. In HIV patients it is hard to separate the immune form from vessel damage caused by the virus itself, and the distinction changes treatment.

The patient was a thirty-five-year-old man with severe anemia from destroyed red blood cells and very low platelets, who tested positive for HIV. A standard score indicated high probability of the immune form. Daily plasma exchange and corticosteroids raised his platelets sharply and cut a damage marker within five days, before antiretroviral therapy began.
openalex-w7204194277:

Built under Brazil's new high school guidelines and the state curriculum, the proposal aims at scientific literacy and student protagonism through hands-on investigation of the body and self-care. Nine meetings join physics, chemistry, and biology around tasks such as computing body mass index, reading nutrition labels, and measuring blood pressure. The sequence ends with a Health Day at School outreach action. The authors expect genuine student engagement and social-emotional growth, with the teacher acting as a strategic mediator between science and daily health.
openalex-w7212010777:
Gerson Ferreira de Farias and Ana Celia Querino ask whether environmental law in Brazil stands as a field of its own. Their article traces care for nature from the ancient world to the present day. It then weighs the norms and institutions that now protect the environment. The goal is to judge how well the law balances use of natural resources with their care.

Concern for nature is old, they note, but sharper rules came after the Industrial Revolution sped up extraction. In Brazil, the 1988 constitution made a healthy environment a basic right. Since then, laws and treaties have grown fast. The authors conclude that environmental law has its own science and norms. They call it key to fair and lasting protection for people alive now and yet to come.
openalex-w7212545577:
Ana Lucia de Souza Almeida studies play as a tool of school work, and the bars that keep staff from its use. The study ran in a town school in Olinda, Pernambuco, with staff of the late grade years. Talks and close watch of class work gave the data.

Staff, she finds, prize play on the whole. They say it draws kids in, wakes talk, and feeds gains in class. Yet its use stays spotty. The bars she logs: thin training, few tools at hand, no time to plan, and rooms in poor state. Play, in this light, is a craft the school must back with time, tools, and skill, or it stays a wish.
openalex-w7213147277:
Andryne Evinlin Alves Nunes leads a team that took a zoo show to town squares in Teixeira de Freitas, Brazil. Class zoology can feel far from life: few tools, thin staff skill, dull books. The show brought the beasts to the street. Skins, bones, and beasts held in jars let guests touch and ask. More than two hundred guests of all ages came through.

Wrong takes on the beasts surfaced as guests talked. So did poor habits toward the wild world. Each false take was a chance to teach on the spot. Guests left with myths peeled back and a fresh care for wild life. The show thus did the work of a lab, a class, and a fair at once. For schools short on gear, it points a way: take the beasts to the folk, and let the street be the school.
openalex-w7213443277:

On those assumptions, yearly output comes to roughly sixteen thousand tonnes of green hydrogen. That equals well over a thousand tonnes per month on average. The authors conclude that Cascavel holds relevant potential for solar-based hydrogen. Real production would still depend on technical progress and falling production costs. The estimate is offered as a contribution to planning debate on new energy in the region.

They see room to grow that work by tying physics of colour to social and cultural contexts.

Nascimento reflects on what that reshaping means for the university's wider duty to society.

Teaching children to write, the authors argue in effect, is not the same as students appropriating writing as their own tool, and the campaign's limits appear exactly in that gap.
openalex-w7216573577:
Rosângela Pereira da Silva Barros and André Manoel Correia dos Santos reviewed, in 2026, whether ultra-processed foods expose pregnant women to bisphenol A. Bisphenol A is a chemical used in plastics and can linings that disrupts hormones. Searching two databases, they selected twenty-seven articles from 2015 to 2026 on people. Most exposure to it comes through food, they report, above all canned foods and products packed in plastic, as the substance migrates into contents faster with heat and worn containers.

The chemical crosses the placenta during pregnancy and is associated with restricted fetal growth, low birth weight, premature birth, and altered fetal metabolic programming. Substitutes sold in BPA-free products showed endocrine risks of their own. Frequent ultra-processed food consumption in pregnancy is therefore a plausible exposure route, the authors conclude, strengthening the nutritionist's role in guiding women toward fresh and lightly processed foods.
openalex-w7221152977:
Zeneide Brito Mendes and five co-authors report a school intervention on waste and responsible consumption, published in 2026. About sixty Brazilian elementary students took part in talks, videos, and sorting games meant to connect daily buying and throwing away with the solid waste problem.

Students began shyly, then joined in once everyday examples and hands-on activities took over, reflecting on impulse buying and the difference between need and desire. A broken projector cable forced quick improvisation from the team. Because learning was never formally measured and habits were not followed up, the authors claim awareness and dialogue, not lasting change. They recommend built-in evaluation and links to school recycling practice.
peirce-fixation-belief-1877:
The Fixation of Belief, published in 1877 in Popular Science Monthly, opens Peirce's series Illustrations of the Logic of Science. It is the paper in which pragmatism begins, though the word itself comes a year later.

Peirce asks how beliefs get fixed, and finds four methods: tenacity, authority, the a priori method of taste, and the method of science. Only science, he argues, ties belief to something real outside our wishes, and so only science settles doubt for good. The essay's calm logic hides a revolution. Every later pragmatist, James and Dewey included, built on this paper.
plos-pbio-0020077:
Gregory C. DeAngelis and William T. Newsome studied how the brain reads its own visual maps in PLOS Biology in 2004. In area MT, neurons respond to both motion direction and depth. The two kinds of information are woven into the same patch of cortex.

The puzzle is how a later brain area picks out one kind of signal without mixing in the other. The authors test how well the joint map supports judging depth from motion cues. Their work speaks to a broad problem in brain science: tidy readout from messy, mixed signals. Lessons from MT apply to many areas where one cell group carries several kinds of news at once.
plos-pbio-0020277:
Chung-I Chang, Sébastien Pili-Floury, Mireille Hervé, and their team solved the shape of a fly immune sensor in PLOS Biology in 2004. The sensor spots peptidoglycan, a mesh material in bacterial cell walls. Its structure shows a groove where that mesh fits, like a key in a lock.

The same protein also has an odd cutting activity that can trim the bacterial material it detects. Sensing and trimming in one molecule is a compact design. Structures like this show how insect immunity, which lacks antibodies, still tells friend from foe with precision. They also offer drug design lessons, since bacterial wall pieces are classic antibiotic targets.
plos-pbio-0020377:
R. Daniel Rudic, Peter McNamara, Anne-Maria Chang, and their team linked body clocks to blood sugar in PLOS Biology in 2004. BMAL1 and CLOCK are core gear proteins of the circadian clock, the daily timer in our cells. Mice with broken clocks showed faults in how they handle glucose.

The finding connects two systems once studied apart: daily rhythms and sugar control. Organs like the liver and pancreas run on clock time, and their sugar work follows the day. When the clock breaks, that work slips. The study helps explain why shift work and broken sleep raise diabetes risk. It also suggests the time of day may matter for diabetes care.
plos-pone-0000077:
Samantha Kerry, Michael TeKippe, Nathan C. Gaddis, and their team hunted an immunity gene in PLOS ONE in 2006. Their study organism fights off bacterial and fungal infections with the help of GATA transcription factors, proteins that switch gene groups on. One such factor proved required for a working defense.

Without it, the host could not mount the proper response to either kind of germ. A single switch controlling defense against both bacteria and fungi marks it as a high-level control. That makes it a strong lead for understanding immune failure. It may also point to ways of boosting defense, in crops or in animals, by tuning one central switch rather than many small ones.
plos-pone-0000177:
Benjamin A. Onwuegbusi, Jonathan R. E. Rees, Pierre Lao-Sirieix, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. In oesophageal adenocarcinoma, a cancer of the food pipe, they study the TGF-beta signaling pathway. The title reports that losing the Smad-dependent arm of that pathway stops cells arresting their cycle and instead promotes invasion.

A pathway that normally restrains growth can be cut in a way that frees the tumor. The authors show this selective loss in cancer cell lines. The result helps explain how this aggressive cancer spreads, and it marks a step that future treatments might target.
plos-pone-0000277:
Bénédicte Lafay and Jeremy J. Burdon published this plant microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Legumes house bacteria in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air, fertilizing the plant. The authors survey the molecular diversity of those root-nodule bacteria in Kakadu National Park in Australia's Northern Territory, a landscape little sampled for such microbes.

Australia's native legumes and their bacteria evolved apart from the farm species most studies use. Cataloguing their diversity shows what nitrogen-fixing partnerships exist in wild ecosystems. The work also supplies baseline data for a protected landscape, useful as climates and land use change.
plos-pone-0000377:
Sean O. Sean O. Henderson and colleagues tackled a public health question in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They asked why death rates from heart and blood vessel disease differ between racial groups. Known causes like smoking, blood pressure, and cholesterol are often blamed only in part. The team tested how much of the gap those established risk factors can explain.

Their analysis concludes that the established factors account for most of the racial differences in deaths from cardiovascular disease. That finding points prevention efforts toward the known, changeable risks rather than toward unknown causes. It also frames unequal exposure to those risks as a central reason the death rates differ.
plos-pone-0000477:
Kirsten Moll and colleagues described a new piece of the malaria parasite's surface machinery, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, sticks to human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. The team identified a novel DBL-domain of the parasite's 332 molecule and proposed it is involved in erythrocyte adhesion.

Sticking to red cells helps the parasite hide from the spleen and cause disease. A domain that does the sticking is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines meant to break the grip. Malaria surface proteins are notoriously variable, so each well-mapped piece adds to the search for stable targets.
plos-pone-0000577:
Tal Murthy and colleagues built a checked gene library for a dangerous germ, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and is feared as a possible bioweapon. The team built a full set of its protein-coding genes, each one checked by reading its sequence.

A checked set like this lets any lab order a gene and test what its protein does. No one has to clone genes from the live germ to start work. That speeds the hunt for drug targets and tests. Papers that build shared tools like this rarely win fame, but they lift the work of a whole field.
plos-pone-0000677:
François Meurens, Mustapha Berri, Richard H. Siggers and colleagues studied how gut bacteria relate to two immune signals in the intestine. Their 2007 PLOS ONE subject was chemokines, small proteins that call immune cells to a location. TECK, also called CCL25, and MEC, or CCL28, are made mainly in the thymus and in mucosal surfaces. Their receptors, CCR9 and CCR10, sit mostly on T and B lymphocytes.

In humans, mice, pigs, and sheep, these chemokines help sort immune cells into the gut. Commensal bacteria, the normal residents of the intestine, are the variable under study. If resident microbes tune these signals, the gut's immune traffic partly answers to its own bacteria.
plos-pone-0000777:
Sander H. Diks, Kaushal Parikh, Marijke van der Sijde and colleagues asked how small the core set of protein phosphorylation sites might be. Reversible phosphorylation, run by enzymes called kinases, is probably the most important regulatory mechanism in eukaryotes. The team studied phosphorylation in vitro with peptide arrays. The arrays carried most protein sequences held in the PhosphoBase database. Cell lysates supplied the enzymes that act on them.

Their title poses the question of a minimal eukaryotic phosphoproteome: a basic set of sites that many species share. If such a core exists, it defines the essential wiring of cell regulation. Comparing lysates from representative species tests how universal that wiring is.
plos-pone-0000877:
Hua Wong, Jean-Marc Victor and Julien Mozziconacci built an atom-by-atom model of the chromatin fiber, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inside the cell nucleus, histone proteins wrap DNA into a packed, ordered structure. That packing controls which genes can be read and when.

The team built their model from known structures: the nucleosome core, plain DNA and part of a linker histone called H5. Their fiber includes those linker histones, which many simpler models leave out. The result is a flexible structure whose shape shifts with the spacing between nucleosomes. Such models help turn static pictures of DNA packing into testable ideas.
plos-pone-0000977:
Frederic Pincet examined how pulling scaffold proteins to the cell membrane drives specific signaling, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. A cell must answer each signal with the right response, not a generic one. Scaffold proteins help by holding the right partners together, steering the signal down one path.

Pincet focuses on the step where scaffolds are recruited to the membrane, the cell's inner surface. That move can decide which response fires. The paper works at the level of molecular mechanisms, the physical details of binding and place. Getting those details right is what separates a true explanation from a diagram.
plos-pone-0001077:
Etay Ziv, Ilya Nemenman and Chris Wiggins measured how network shape affects signal handling in small gene circuits, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A transcriptional network has to sense environmental signals and answer well. The team quantify how the network's topology, its wiring pattern, influences that ability.

They pose the problem in information theory terms, which frees the analysis from assuming one specific function. A wiring pattern can then be scored for how much signal it can carry. Small biochemical networks are the kind synthetic biologists actually build. General rules for their design, not tied to one job, are the paper's aim.
plos-pone-0001177:
Leishmania donovani is a parasite that causes visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly disease also called kala-azar. Rosario Díaz González and colleagues studied one of the parasite's enzymes, DNA topoisomerase IB, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The parasite's version of this enzyme differs substantially from the human one, which makes it a promising drug lead.

The authors deleted parts of the enzyme to search for the smallest working form, a minimal functional heterodimer. Mapping which pieces are essential shows where a drug might grip. Structural differences between the parasite and human enzymes are exactly what selective drug design needs.
plos-pone-0001277:
Microsporidia are intracellular parasites with some of the smallest genomes known, highly derived relatives of fungi. Nicolas Corradi and colleagues compared the genomes of three species, Encephalitozoon cuniculi, Antonospora locustae, and Enterocytozoon bieneusi, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Despite fast sequence evolution, far-related microsporidia can share much the same gene order.

The authors describe patterns of genome evolution across the three parasites. Only two microsporidian genomes had been studied before. Matching compacted genomes shows what a parasite can throw away and what it must keep. It is a lesson in how small a genome can get.
plos-pone-0001377:
Timothée Masquelier, Rudy Guyonneau, and Simon Thorpe published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how nerve cells learn from timing. When one nerve cell fires just before a second one, their link tends to grow strong. When the order flips, the link tends to grow weak. The team built a model based on this timing rule.

In their tests, the model learned to spot the start of a pattern that repeats in a stream of spikes. It did so without being told what to look for. The result shows how a simple timing rule can pull order out of noise. It may also hint at how real brains pick up rhythms and habits.
plos-pone-0001477:
Emmanuel Boucrot and Tomas Kirchhausen wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on cell size during division. Using films of single cells, they found that a cell shrinks as it rounds up to divide. The smallest size comes at a key stage, just before the split. Size then grows back fast as the cell moves to part.

A set size dip during division had not been charted this clearly before. It hints that cells shed or take up fluid on a strict clock. That clock may help the split go right. The work adds a plain but new fact to the base account of how cells divide.
plos-pone-0001577:
Stephanie Prady and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how well acupuncture trials are reported. Two rule sets had been issued to lift trial reporting: one for all trials, one for acupuncture. Poor reports block readers from judging a trial's worth. The team rated reports from before and after the rules came out.

They checked whether scores for report quality rose over that span. Gains would show the rules work in practice, not just on paper. Weak gains would urge stronger steps by journals. Either way, the study tests a cheap tool for lifting science quality across the field.
plos-pone-0001677:
Lucia Banci, Ivano Bertini, Mirela Boca, and their co-authors studied a protein tied to a fatal nerve disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The protein is SOD1, short for copper, zinc superoxide dismutase 1. About 100 single-letter changes in its gene are known to cause the familial form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS. In that disease motor neurons die and muscles waste away.

The changes are scattered across the whole protein, which makes their shared harm hard to explain. The team focused on oligomerization, the tendency of SOD1 copies to clump together. The full text gives the protein measurements and how mutants differ from the normal form. If stray clumping is a common thread among mutants, it offers one target for drugs across many forms of familial ALS.
plos-pone-0001777:
Sander L. J. Wijers, Patrick Schrauwen, Wim H. M. Saris, and their co-authors measured heat production in human muscle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Mild cold and overfeeding raise energy expenditure in mammals, a process called adaptive thermogenesis. In small animals it comes mainly from mitochondrial uncoupling in brown fat, where energy is burned as heat instead of stored.

The team asked whether human skeletal muscle contributes through mitochondrial uncoupling of its own. They report that muscle uncoupling is associated with cold-induced adaptive thermogenesis. The full text gives the cold exposure tests and the muscle measurements. Muscle is most of body mass, so even a small uncoupling there could matter for weight control research.
plos-pone-0001877:
Takaoki Kasahara and co-authors tested a bold treatment idea in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The mice carry a fault in the DNA of their mitochondria, the small power units inside cells, placed only in nerve cells. The fault models a human eye and muscle disease whose patients at times also have mood disorders.

The mutant mice showed acts much like those seen in bipolar illness, such as a warped daily rhythm. The team then gave the mice brief electric shocks to the brain, a lab form of a therapy used in human care. They report a marked effect on the odd acts. The work links faulty cell power to mood-like change.
plos-pone-0001977:
Jeremy Peirce and co-authors built a better math tool for mapping genes in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Advanced intercross lines are mouse groups bred over many generations. Their gene shuffling is dense, which lets traits be mapped to fine spots on the genome. Standard mapping methods from simpler crosses were often applied to them, followed by naive shuffle tests.

The pair of problems can bias results. Their method, called GRAIP, reshuffles genomes in a way that fits these lines, for both simulation and significance tests. Sharper tools mean gene hunts in mice land on the right spots more often.
plos-pone-0002077:
Debby Vissers and co-authors simulated preventive HIV drugs across whole epidemics, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, means taking HIV drugs before exposure to block infection, and it looked promising, above all for women. Demand for rollout was expected the moment trials proved it works, so planners needed long-term forecasts.

The team simulated the impact of PrEP on HIV transmission and epidemics in Africa and India. Models can weigh how coverage, adherence, and risk change alter the gains over years. Forecasts like these help health systems spend on the mix of tools that cuts new infections most.
plos-pone-0002177:
Kristin Olesen and Anthony Auger studied how brain chemistry in newborn rats can switch on hormone receptors, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hormone receptors in the growing brain shape cell processes that last into adult life, changing both behavior and body function. Earlier work suggested that dopamine, a brain messenger, can control progestin receptors in set regions of the adult brain.

The authors asked whether dopamine can also switch on estrogen receptors in the newborn female brain. They found that it does, in limited regions, and that this triggers a marker gene called Fos. The result shows hormone systems in the infant brain can be turned on by brain signals alone.
plos-pone-0002277:
Beth McNally, Joanne Trgovcich, Gerd Maul, and co-authors studied a cancer-linked protein found outside the cell nucleus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The PML gene was discovered through its part in a chromosome swap that causes a form of leukemia. Inside the nucleus, PML protein helps control cell growth, tumor suppression, and cell death.

A separate pool of PML sits in the cytoplasm, the cell's outer compartment. The team reports that this cytoplasmic PML helps cells resist viral infection. The finding gives an old, well-studied protein a second workplace and hints the cell stations some of its antiviral defense outside the nucleus.
plos-pone-0002377:
Xin and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Dedong Xin, Landian Hu, Xiangyin Kong, among others. Its subject is alternative Promoters Influence Alternative Splicing at the Genomic Level. More and more experiments have shown that transcription and mRNA processing are not two independent events but are tightly coupled to each other.

Both promoter and transcription rate were found to influence alternative splicing. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002477:
Amsili and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Shira Amsili, Hagit Zer, Stephan Hinderlich, among others. Its subject is uDP-N-Acetylglucosamine 2-Epimerase/N-Acetylmannosamine Kinase (GNE) Binds to Alpha-Actinin 1: Novel Pathways in Skeletal Muscle?. Hereditary inclusion body myopathy (HIBM) is a rare neuromuscular disorder caused by mutations in GNE.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002577:
Beveren, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Nico J. M. van Beveren, Lieuwe de Haan, among others. Its subject is a Visual Metaphor Describing Neural Dynamics in Schizophrenia. In many scientific disciplines the use of a metaphor as an heuristic aid is not uncommon.

A well known example in somatic medicine is the ‘defense army metaphor’ used to characterize the immune system. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002677:
In 2008, Seong Il Choi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about protein solubility and folding enhancement by interaction with RNA. The catalog record names Seong Il Choi first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. While basic mechanisms of several major molecular chaperones are well understood. A further point appears in the abstract. Here, we report a chaperone type of protein folding facilitated by interaction with RNA. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002777:
Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of neutrality and the response of rare species to environmental variance. Authorship is credited in the record to Lisandro Benedetti-Cecchi and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Neutral models and differential responses of species to environmental heterogeneity offer complementary explanations of species abundance distribution and dynamics. A further point appears in the abstract. Under what circumstances one model prevails over the other is still a matter of debate. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002877:
Srinivasan Krishnamoorthy mapped a signaling network in fruit fly cells for PLOS ONE in 2008. Adding a phosphate group to proteins is one way cells switch signals on and off, and about a third of cell proteins carry such marks. The study focused on receptor tyrosine kinases, a key family of signal receivers.

Using Drosophila S2 cells with the ErbB1 receptor, the author charted which proteins gain phosphate marks after signaling starts. That chart is called a phosphor-proteome. The result reveals new network links, in the paper's own terms, and gives cell biologists a parts list for how this signal spreads inside the cell.
plos-pone-0002977:
Carlos Barcia, Nicholas Sanderson, Robert Barrett and co-authors watched T cells change astrocytes in 2008. Astrocytes are star-shaped brain support cells that usually swell in response to trauma, stroke, or degeneration. Their response to a direct immune attack by T cells was poorly understood.

Effector T cells form tight contacts called immunological synapses with target cells. The PLOS ONE study reports those contacts induce polarization of astrocytes, both in living animals and in dishes.
