That is a novel response mechanism to cellular injury, with relevance to brain diseases where T cells attack. Details of samples, measures, and analysis are set out in the full article text.
plos-pone-0003077:
Vera Levina, Adele Marrangoni, Richard DeMarco and co-authors enriched lung cancer stem cells with drug selection in 2008. Cancer stem cells are thought to regrow tumors after chemotherapy, though direct confirmation was still forthcoming. The team asked whether drug treatment could enrich and maintain such cells.

They then examined the enriched cells' cytokine network plus tumor-forming and metastatic properties. Published in PLOS ONE, drug-selected cells model the survivors that relapse is made of. Studying them is a step toward treatments aimed at the cells chemotherapy leaves behind. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003177:
Michiteru Kitazaki, Hisashi Kobiki and Laurence T. Maloney test how depth cues affect lightness judgement in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. How light a surface looks is affected by how the scene is interpreted. Some evidence suggests perceived lightness under two-eyed viewing differs from that in actual scenes, while other reports say viewing conditions have little effect.

The authors compare pictorial depth cues, binocular disparity cues, and motion parallax cues in three-dimensional virtual scenes. Readers learn which kinds of depth information change how bright a surface seems. The work matters for vision science and for building virtual scenes that look right.
plos-pone-0003277:
Kellie J. Hall, Matthew T. Harper, Karen Gilio and colleagues analyse a kinase in platelets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. PKC theta is a novel protein kinase C isozyme predominantly expressed in T cells and platelets. T cells lacking it show reduced activation, and mice lacking it are resistant to autoimmune disease, making it an attractive therapeutic target for immune modulation. Collagen is a major activator of platelets.

The team carry out a genetic analysis of the role of protein kinase C theta in platelet function and thrombus formation. Readers learn whether an immune drug target also affects clotting. That safety question matters before such inhibitors reach patients.
plos-pone-0003377:
Venkateswara Rao Simhadri and colleagues traced messages between immune cells in this 2008 paper. Dendritic cells are scouts that show threats to the rest of the immune system. Natural killer cells destroy infected or cancerous cells on contact. The study asked how a protein called BAT3 passes signals between these two cell types.

The scouts were found to shed tiny bubble-like packets loaded with BAT3. These packets, called exosomes, reach killer cells and switch on their response. The signal works through a surface sensor named NKp30 on the killer cells. The finding shows how immune cells can guide each other without direct contact.
plos-pone-0003477:
Nadège Bault, Giorgio Coricelli, and Aldo Rustichini studied how rank shapes choices in this 2008 paper. Animal societies rest on dominance orders, high over low. People likewise care about their standing among others. That care should bend economic choices, not just feelings.

Their work treats each person's payoff as tied to others' payoffs. Experiments showed social ranking changes what people pick. Gains feel smaller when a rival gains more. The results matter for pay, markets, and any group with a pecking order. Pay deals at work often turn on rank as much as on raw amounts.
plos-pone-0003577:
J. William Critchfield and co-authors mapped HIV-specific T cells in the gut in this 2008 study. The intestinal mucosa shows strong virus replication in HIV infection. It also suffers pronounced loss of CD4 T cells early on. HIV-specific CD8 T cells may modulate the disease course.

The team measured responses in the rectal mucosa during chronic infection. Their size and complexity reflected the patients' clinical status. Strong local battles mark how the disease is going. Vaccines may need to protect where the virus hits hardest. The gut is where HIV does much of its early and lasting damage.
plos-pone-0003677:
Anna Kuparinen, Robert B. O'Hara, and Juha Merilä published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. As organisms grow, they pass turning points such as maturation at rates that vary by chance. Earlier models of these transitions worked only in fixed time steps. The authors wanted a model that flows in continuous time.

They built probabilistic models for such ontogenetic transitions, keeping the randomness that real growth shows. The framework extends reaction norms, the patterns that link genes and environment to timing. It gives ecologists a sounder way to predict when individuals will make their big life changes.
plos-pone-0003777:
Chunyu Yang, Guangchun Cao, Yang Li, and colleagues published this waste treatment study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Black liquor is the alkaline wastewater left from pulping wheat straw for paper. Its high pH and heavy pollution load make it very hard to treat. It causes serious environmental problems.

The team built an alkaline consortium, a chosen crew of microbes that thrive in such conditions. They tracked how the crew's makeup changed while it treated black liquor with a very high pollution load. The study shows a designed microbe team tackling one of industry's toughest effluents.
plos-pone-0003877:
Joseph Kagaayi, Ronald H. Gray, Heena Brahmbhatt, and co-authors reported on infant feeding and HIV in 2008. Their PLOS ONE study followed babies born to HIV-positive mothers in Rakai District, Uganda. Mothers could feed by breast or by formula under a local program. Data comparing the two routes in real program settings were scarce.

The team tracked 182 infants and compared death rates between the feeding groups. They also tracked how many babies stayed free of HIV. Such evidence helps programs advise mothers where both feeding routes carry risks. The study adds ground-level data from rural Uganda to a hard policy choice.
plos-pone-0003977:
Olga Björklund, Johan Kahlström, Peter Salmi, and co-authors gave caffeine to pregnant mice in 2008. Worry persists about caffeine use in pregnancy and early infancy. Early exposure might leave lasting changes in behavior. The team gave pregnant mice modest caffeine doses of 0.3 grams per liter.

Their PLOS ONE article traces the effect to receptors on the mother. Caffeine acted on maternal adenosine A1 receptors, not the pups directly. Offspring still showed long-lasting behavioral changes afterward. The result reframes how early caffeine may shape the developing brain. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004077:
Bin Zhang and Jian-xing Ma studied a protective protein in eye cells in 2008. SERPINA3K is a serpin, a protein that blocks protease enzymes. Its levels fall in the retinas of diabetic rats. That drop may contribute to diabetic retinopathy, a blinding disease.

Their PLOS ONE article reports SERPINA3K prevents oxidative necrotic cell death. It does so by inhibiting calcium overload in the cells. Calcium flooding is a final common path to cell death. A natural protector against it could inspire new eye treatments. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004177:
Ghibom Bhak and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alpha-synuclein is the protein that clumps into Lewy bodies, the deposits found in the brains of people with Parkinson's disease. Learning how it forms amyloid fibrils, long ordered protein fibres, is key to any plan to stop the disease.

The team studied how shear stress, the force of flowing or stirred liquid, affects that process. They report that the protein first gathers into granules, and that this granular assembly speeds up fibril formation under shear. The finding shows how physical forces in a cell's world can hurry a disease protein along.
plos-pone-0004277:
Michel Henry and colleagues published this hepatitis B study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hepatitis B virus DNA is vulnerable to editing by human APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases. These enzymes mutate viral DNA, though HBV is edited far less than HIV. The team analysed and compared editing by all seven APOBEC3 enzymes.

Using a quail cell line that makes no APOBEC of its own, they tested single-domain versions of each enzyme against HBV. They examined the recombinant nature of APOBEC3G, the family's best-known member. Mapping which enzymes can edit HBV clarifies a natural defence the virus must dodge.
plos-pone-0004377:
People who eat less often lose weight, then stall. Leanne Redman, Leonie Heilbronn, Corby Martin, and co-authors measured why, in free-living adults. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper came from the CALERIE study of calorie cutting. Forty-eight overweight adults, average age near thirty-seven, joined for six months. They were split into four groups with different intake targets.

Earlier work had not measured daily life responses in an objective way. The team tracked both metabolic change and behavior change. Bodies can burn fewer calories than expected. Habits can also shift in ways that blunt a diet. Knowing both responses helps explain stalled weight loss. It also helps set honest targets for diet programs.
plos-pone-0004477:
Nerve cells that serve the zebrafish sense of water flow are picky about direction, show Adele Faucherre, Jesus Pujol-Marti, Koichi Kawakami, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Fish sense movement in water through a line of organs along the body, called the lateral line. Their sensors are hair cells, like those in our inner ear, with tiny bristles all tipped one way.

That shared tilt lets a whole group of hair cells read motion coherently. The team found the afferent neurons, which carry signals to the brain, are strict selectors: each connects to hair cells of one orientation only. Keeping the two directions in separate channels lets the fish tell which way the water moves. The rule may hold in ears as well.
plos-pone-0004577:
Making a step look taller can make people step more safely over it, show David Elliott, Anna Vale, David Whitaker, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Tripping is a common factor in falls, which injure many older people. A typical safety strategy is to lift the foot higher over a step edge.

The team asked whether a visual illusion could increase the perceived height of a step. If the step looks bigger, people may clear it with more room to spare. Their title gives the outcome: the illusion led to safer stepping behavior. A painted pattern costs almost nothing. If it prevents even a fraction of falls on stairs, it is a cheap public health tool drawn from vision science.
plos-pone-0004677:
Yong Zhang and colleagues screened for insect only microRNAs in the silkworm for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny bits of RNA that tune how genes are used after they are copied. They play a large part in how insects grow and change form as they mature.

The team ran a large screen in the silkworm, a moth raised for silk for ages. They hunted for microRNAs found in insects but not in other animal groups. Such finds can reveal steps that guide larva to moth change. They may also offer targets for pest control that spare other species.
plos-pone-0004777:
Michalis Aivaliotis and colleagues profiled protein phosphorylation in an archaeon from the third domain of life, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Phosphorylation is a major control tag on proteins in complex cells. Its origin and evolution are open questions, and archaea hold a lead role in that debate as a distinct, ancient domain.

Many studies show archaeal proteins do carry phosphate tags. The team mapped tags on serine, threonine, and tyrosine in a salt loving archaeon. A full map tests how old this control system is. It may show that complex regulation predates complex cells. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings.
plos-pone-0004877:
Núria Gavara and Richard Chadwick studied collagen based mechanical anisotropy of the tectorial membrane and hair bundle coupling, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tectorial membrane in the mammalian cochlea displays anisotropy where mechanical properties differ along directions. Anisotropy arises from collagen fibrils organized in fibers running radially across the membrane in the inner ear. Shaping how sound driven motions couple rows of outer hair cells.

Directional stiffness tunes hearing sensitivity and frequency selectivity. Collagen architecture is functional, not incidental. Defects may explain some hearing losses. Bioinspired sensors could copy the design. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004977:
The midbrain holds important dopamine neurons. They sit in the substantia nigra and the ventral tegmental area. These neurons die in Parkinson's disease. Scientists grow similar neurons in culture to study them. Dario Greco and colleagues asked how faithful those cultures are. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

They compared gene expression in embryonic midbrain tissue with neuronal primary cultures. The profiles show where dish-grown neurons match the real thing. They also show where the cultures drift. The comparison guides better lab models of the dopamine system. That matters for Parkinson's research, which leans heavily on such cultures.
plos-pone-0005077:
Tumors often live in low oxygen. A protein called HIF-1 alpha is their master switch for surviving it. Ekaterina Moroz and colleagues built tools to watch that switch live. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They made two chimeric reporter systems. The reporters glow as HIF-1 alpha builds up or breaks down.

Real-time imaging follows stabilization and degradation in living cells. Many factors tune this protein in cancers. Watching it live reveals how cancer cells adjust the switch. Drug hunters gain a way to see their target in action. Compounds that destabilize HIF-1 alpha become easier to find. The tools serve both basic research and screening.
plos-pone-0005177:
All living things deal with carbon dioxide, which shifts back and forth into bicarbonate in the body. That shift is slow on its own, but enzymes called carbonic anhydrases speed it up. Elleuche and Pöggeler studied the beta form of these enzymes in the fungus Sordaria macrospora in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The pair found these enzymes play a part in building the fungus fruiting bodies and in helping spores sprout. So a gas-handling enzyme also guides growth and new life in this species. The finding widens what scientists expect these common enzymes to do inside cells.
plos-pone-0005277:
Antiretroviral therapy can suppress HIV, yet many treated patients still show abnormal immune activation and low CD4 counts. Jacobson and colleagues asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether other herpesviruses help explain that lingering activation.

The team explored ongoing replication of cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, and the Kaposi sarcoma herpesvirus in suppressed patients. These viruses are common and can flare quietly. If they drive the activation, treating them could calm the immune system and protect the CD4 cells patients still need. These other viruses hide in most adults for life. Flare when the body is weak, so they are a smart place to look when the main virus is held down yet the body still burns with low-grade fire.
plos-pone-0005377:
Climate swings repeatedly expand and shrink where species can live. Those range shifts are proposed as a major force shaping life history traits and global biodiversity. Léotard and colleagues tested the idea in an equatorial three-species symbiosis in PLOS ONE in 2009.

In a symbiosis, three species live bound together, so one partner's spread affects all. Range expansion drove the evolution of dispersal traits in their system. The case links biogeography, where species live, to the evolution of how far their young travel. Three lives bound as one are a strict test of spread, since a slow partner can hold back a fast one. And the range edge is where such checks shape what lives where.
plos-pone-0005477:
Josefin Madjidian and Åsa Lankinen studied conflict between the sexes in a plant, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Males and females of a species can want different things from mating, and that clash can drive traits to change over time. Most tests of this idea had used animals, not plants.

Their work on an annual plant looked for signs that male and female traits push against each other over generations. Plants offer a fresh test because pollen and seeds play roles unlike those in animals. What they found helps show how wide the reach of sexual conflict may be.
plos-pone-0005577:
Jiayun Lu and co-authors studied a stem cell factor called SALL4 in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. SALL4 helps embryonic stem cells stay able to become any cell type. It also plays a role in leukaemia, where stem-like cancer cells keep growing.

The team searched for proteins that work with SALL4 and found a repressor complex it uses. Through that complex, SALL4 switches off two genes, PTEN and SALL1. Switching off PTEN, a brake on growth, may be one way SALL4 keeps stem cells, and cancer cells, dividing. A factor shared by stem cells and cancer stem cells is watched closely, since blocking it must not harm healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0005677:
Devi Stuart-Fox and colleagues studied lizards split into hidden lineages in a 2009 field and lab study. Gene tests now reveal many cryptic species: groups that look alike but differ deeply in their DNA. One such zone in this study mixes two lineages where their ranges meet.

Across that hybrid zone, the team compared body traits, parasite loads, and how well males compete. They ask whether the lineages have truly parted ways in form and habit, not just in genes. The answers help explain how new species form while still looking the same. They also warn that looks alone can hide real diversity.
plos-pone-0005777:
Suzana Gispert and co-authors followed aged mice lacking PINK1 in 2009, modeling a genetic form of Parkinson's disease. Loss of PINK1, a mitochondrial protein kinase, causes a recessive variant of the disease. The team bred mice without it and watched them into old age.

The mice developed a Parkinson-like phenotype with worsening mitochondrial faults, yet without the neuron death many expected. That split is telling: failing power plants alone can disturb movement before cells die. It suggests treatment windows may open earlier than neuron loss. The study refines what PINK1 loss does over a full lifespan.
plos-pone-0005877:
Venkata Sabbisetti and co-authors found in 2009 that a guardian protein keeps cells alive partly by switching on a fat-making enzyme. The protein p63, especially its delta form, is central to skin development and to many tumors. How it promotes cell survival was only partly mapped.

The team showed p63 drives fatty acid synthase, an enzyme that builds fats cells need to grow. Survival signals and fat supply turn out to be linked. Tumors often crank up fat synthesis, so the link may matter in cancer. The study fills a gap in how a major developmental protein sustains cells.
plos-pone-0005977:
A fungal colony is a web of threads with shared inner fluid, or so it seemed. Arend van Peer, Wally Müller, Teun Boekhout and colleagues revisited that view in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the fungus Schizophyllum commune, whose threads are split into rooms by walls called septa, each pierced by a large pore.

Fluid and even cell parts can stream through open pores, making the colony act as one body. Yet the team shows the fungus can close its septa when conditions call for it. That shutter control revises the old picture of an always-open colony and suggests fungi can seal off damage or stress room by room.
plos-pone-0006077:
TB can hide inside the body for years, dormant and shrugging off drugs. Chirajyoti Deb, Chang-Muk Lee, Vinod Dubey and colleagues built a better model of that hiding state in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper subjects Mycobacterium tuberculosis to several stresses at once in the lab, mimicking the harsh spots it meets inside a host.

The stressed germs became lipid-loaded, dormant and drug-tolerant, much like hidden TB in people. A faithful model is the missing tool in the hunt for drugs that kill latent germs, the main barrier to curing TB for good. The system lets teams screen compounds against the enemy in its toughest form.
plos-pone-0006177:
Breathing illnesses have long disrupted military missions, and troops abroad face extra risk. Bryony Soltis and colleagues surveyed United States troops sent to Iraq and Afghanistan for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Close living quarters, stress, and fresh exposure to germs all raise the odds of catching a chest illness while deployed.

Troops reported their own illness episodes and symptoms, giving rates and burden that records alone had missed. Few solid data existed on this problem before the survey. The results help medical teams plan supplies, rest, and prevention for future deployments. They also show how much duty time simple infections can quietly consume.
plos-pone-0006277:
H5N1 bird flu has grown steadily more deadly in poultry, and human cases keep mounting. Hongbo Zhou and colleagues focus on the neuraminidase protein, one of the virus's surface tools, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its stalk region varies a lot between strains and may track with virulence.

A special stalk motif is responsible for increased virulence and disease severity, the title states. Pinpointing a short pattern behind deadliness helps surveillance labs flag dangerous strains early. It also gives vaccine and drug researchers a defined feature to watch. The result links a small structural detail to a global health threat.
plos-pone-0006377:
Radiation stress rewrites the small RNA controls inside cells. Nicole Simone and colleagues measured micro RNA expression after ionising radiation in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Micro RNAs are small, conserved, non-coding RNAs that adjust protein output and regulate many processes, including stress responses.

Oxidative stress from radiation altered the micro RNA profile, per the title. Those shifts may steer how cells survive or die after exposure. Radiation is used in cancer therapy, so response markers have clinical value. Micro RNA patterns could one day predict which tumors resist treatment.
plos-pone-0006477:
Daniel Glass and colleagues measured vitamin D and skin color in the United Kingdom for PLOS ONE in 2009. Vitamin D may protect against many diseases. Public health advice urges people to avoid sun to cut skin cancer risk. But avoiding sun may also lower vitamin D, with harms of its own. The balance may differ by skin type.

The authors report low vitamin D levels in fair skin types in the United Kingdom. That result is counterintuitive, since fair skin makes vitamin D more easily. Behavior, such as staying out of the sun, may outweigh biology. The study feeds a debate on how sun advice should vary between people.
plos-pone-0006577:
James Harper, Gillian Gile, Erick James, and colleagues questioned species definitions in microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. For the majority of microbial eukaryotes, protists and algae, there is no clearly superior species concept consistently applied. In the absence of a practical biological species concept, researchers rely on morphology, outward form. The authors argue morphology is inadequate for species and genus delineation.

Their example comes from a paramecium-related group. Form can mislead because distant relatives converge and close relatives diverge. DNA-based evidence often redraws the tree. The paper is a call to rebuild microbial taxonomy on genetic grounds.
plos-pone-0006677:
Yukari Takahashi and colleagues studied two small RNA molecules in lung cancer cells for PLOS ONE in 2009. The molecules are microRNAs named MiR-107 and MiR-185. MicroRNAs are short strands that lower gene activity. They can silence a message or trigger its breakdown. Researchers suspected these two might slow cancer cell growth.

The team tested the microRNAs in human non-small cell lung cancer cell lines. Both molecules were able to induce cell cycle arrest. Arrest means the cells stop dividing at a checkpoint. Stopping division is one way a tumor's growth can be restrained. The findings suggest these microRNAs could inform future lung cancer research and treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0006777:
Art F. Y. Poon and colleagues built a grammar-based method for parsing social network surveys in PLOS ONE in 2009. People tend to form ties with others sharing their attributes. Some attributes are ambiguous, stigmatized, or illegal. They create hidden populations whose members are hard to identify. Surveys of such groups yield messy, incomplete network data.

The authors used stochastic context-free grammars to parse that data. Grammars, borrowed from language analysis, model structured patterns with randomness. Applied to networks, they can infer likely missing structure. Better parsing improves estimates of hidden population size and links. That helps health outreach reach groups that standard surveys miss.
plos-pone-0006877:
Aylin Yilmaz and colleagues measured an HIV drug in spinal fluid in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is raltegravir, an integrase inhibitor. It was used in patients whose virus resisted other drug classes. HIV can shelter in the central nervous system. A drug must reach that shelter to work fully.

The team measured raltegravir concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma. Comparing the two shows how well the drug penetrates the nervous system. Poor penetration could leave a viral reservoir untreated. Good penetration supports regimens for patients with brain involvement. The measurements guide dosing where the blood-brain barrier limits access.
plos-pone-0006977:
Cunyou Zhao, Zhiwen Xu, Feng Wang, and colleagues studied a brain receptor gene in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene, GABRB2, builds part of the GABA A receptor, a key calming receptor in the brain. Quiet variants in this gene had been linked to schizophrenia. Those variants also tracked with how the gene's message is cut and joined.

The team examined splicing in one region, exon ten. They catalogued new isoforms, alternate forms of the gene's product. Then they weighed links between those forms and psychotic disorders. Such splicing shifts could change how the receptor works in the brain.
plos-pone-0007077:
Nicolas Moniaux, Christophe Nemos, Shonali Deb, and colleagues studied a transcription partner protein in PLOS ONE in 2009. The human PAF complex travels with RNA polymerase II as it reads genes. It regulates several steps of gene expression. In yeast, its counterpart controls a set of cell-cycle genes.

The team examined one member, hPaf1, in human cells. They found it acts as a regulator of cell-cycle progression. A factor that times both gene reading and division is a natural control point. Its failure could help explain how some cells slip into uncontrolled growth.
plos-pone-0007177:
Joydeep Mukherjee, Nicole Webster, and Lyndon E. Llewellyn wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on disease in a Great Barrier Reef sponge. The sponge is Rhopaloeides odorabile. Reports of marine sponge disease were rising worldwide when the study appeared, with risks for reefs and other sea life.

The authors purify an enzyme from a sponge pathogen and describe its properties in detail. The enzyme breaks down collagen, a tough structural protein. Their work gives marine biologists a concrete agent to study when they ask how sponge infections damage their hosts. The enzyme's traits are reported from the pathogen itself, not inferred from relatives.
plos-pone-0007277:
Justin A. Green, Chau T. H. Tran, Jeremy J. Farrar, and colleagues studied a steroid treatment for tuberculous meningitis in 2009. Adding dexamethasone to treatment reduces deaths from this brain infection. How the steroid produces that benefit was not known when the study began, leaving a gap in care.

Matrix metalloproteinases drive tissue damage in many inflammatory brain diseases. The authors measure their concentrations in spinal fluid during treatment. They relate those levels to clinical outcomes. Their PLOS ONE paper tests whether calming these enzymes explains part of the steroid benefit.
plos-pone-0007377:
David Fouchet, Guillaume Leblanc, Frank Sauvage, and colleagues modeled a cat virus across fifteen populations in 2009. Feline immunodeficiency virus spreads through bites between cats. Cat density and sex ratio can strongly affect how often cats fight, and hence how often the virus transmits between individuals in a population.

The authors use dynamic stochastic modeling to estimate population risk factors. Stochastic models include chance events, which matter in small populations. They apply the method to fifteen natural cat populations. Their PLOS ONE example shows how modeling can separate real risk factors from random variation.
plos-pone-0007477:
Marianne Seney and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on African mole-rats, rodents whose societies range from solitary living to fully eusocial colonies. The naked mole-rat, the most social species, shows almost no external difference between male and female genitalia. The team compared genital anatomy across species with different social systems. They asked whether anatomy tracks how a species lives.

Across the family, genital morphology followed social structure. The more eusocial the species, the smaller the sex differences tended to be. In colonies where most animals never breed, strong sexual signals may matter less. The pattern ties mating anatomy to social organization in a measurable way. It offers a rare case where society's shape is written on the body.
plos-pone-0007577:
Inna Djagaeva and Sergey Doronkin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how neurons grow their branches. Dendrites, the branching arms that receive signals, must form precise shapes for the brain to wire correctly. Misshapen dendrites appear in several disorders of the mind, from schizophrenia to intellectual disability. The team studied a protein complex called the COP9 signalosome in fruit fly neurons. It is part of the cell's protein-recycling machinery.

The signalosome regulates dendrite growth in two directions at once. That dual control gives the neuron both a gas pedal and a brake from one complex. Balanced control produces the arbor shapes that synapses need. When the balance fails, the wiring suffers. The study helps explain a defect shared by many brain disorders. It also shows recycling machinery moonlighting as an architect of neurons.
plos-pone-0007677:
Lasse Folkersen and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a DNA region tied to heart disease. Large scans had linked a stretch of chromosome 9, called 9p21, to coronary artery disease. How that stretch raised risk was still unclear.

The team studied gene activity data from five different sets and tied the risk versions to changes in gene use. They also found eight new splice variants of ANRIL, a long RNA made at that site. Those variants may be a step in the path from DNA to disease.
plos-pone-0007777:
William Farrugia and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks whether metal ions help an antibody grip its target. The target, Lewis Y, is a sugar marker found on most epithelial cancers. That makes it promising for antibody-based cancer therapy.

A humanized antibody against Lewis Y had already shown encouraging safety in trials. Antibodies read sugar clusters on cell surfaces, a hard recognition task. The authors explore how metallic ions might assist that recognition. Understanding the grip at atomic level could improve antibody drugs. It could also guide the design of new ones.
plos-pone-0007877:
Timothy Dunn and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines chemical signaling inside mouse eye cells. Retinal ganglion cells carry vision signals from eye to brain. During development, activity shapes how these cells grow and connect.

A key cascade uses calcium to switch on protein kinase A, an enzyme that relays signals. The authors found the calcium-driven rise in kinase activity is mediated by several adenylate cyclases. Those enzymes make the messenger molecule cAMP. Having multiple routes to the same switch adds robustness. The finding refines how scientists picture activity-dependent development in the visual system.
plos-pone-0007977:
Leo Garcia Flores and colleagues tried a new scan for pancreatic cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease is often found too late for surgery to help. Their scan used PET/CT imaging aimed at a sugar-binding protein that shows up in tissue around the tumor.

Lighting up the tissue near the tumor, rather than the tumor alone, may make small cancers stand out sooner. Early finds raise the odds that a surgeon can remove the growth in full. The early results support more testing of this aim-at-the-neighborhood approach in people at high risk.
plos-pone-0008077:
Gilles Guerrier and colleagues counted hunger and death among war-torn families in eastern Chad for PLOS ONE in 2009. Violence had driven more than two hundred thousand people from their homes in three years. Some lived in camps, others in villages or towns, displaced and host families side by side.

Surveys weighed children and gathered death records in each setting. Malnutrition and death rates told a grim, uneven story across the three kinds of place. Relief teams can use such maps to send food and care where the need is worst, rather than where access is easiest.
plos-pone-0008177:
Till Steiner, Yaochu Jin, and Bernhard Sendhoff presented a new computing method in PLOS ONE in 2009 called vector field embryogeny. The work deals with artificial embryogenies, computer systems that grow forms in steps like an embryo. Most such systems rely on maps of gene networks. Their method skips those maps entirely.

Instead, the approach shapes the flow of the system itself, known as its phase space. The authors showed the idea works by evolving cell differentiation, where cells take on distinct roles. Growing patterns emerged from the shaped flow. The result points to a fresh route for evolving complex forms in the computer.
plos-pone-0008277:
Takumi Kayukawa and Yukio Ishikawa studied cold hardiness in an insect in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The onion maggot, Delia antiqua, survives winter as a pupa. Pupae in winter diapause show strong cold hardiness. So do pupae acclimated to cold outside diapause. The team investigated which genes switch on during this hardening.

They linked a chaperonin protein to the insect's cold tolerance. The protein works by repressing the breakdown of actin at low temperatures. Actin gives cells their structure, so protecting it protects the cell. The finding explains one mechanism behind insect survival in winter.
plos-pone-0008377:
Wendy W. Hwang-Verslues and colleagues profiled breast cancer stem cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Cancer stem and progenitor cells can give rise to different forms of cancer. That heterogeneity was well shown in leukemia. For solid tumors, including breast cancer, the concept was not yet established. The team analyzed solid tumor cells using stem cell markers.

Profiling revealed multiple lineages of human breast cancer stem and progenitor cells. Distinct lineages could explain why breast cancers behave so differently. They might also respond differently to treatment. Identifying them is a step toward targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0008477:
Matthew Hemming and co-authors hunt for targets of an enzyme in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme is BACE1, also called beta-secretase. It cuts proteins near cell membranes and sheds their outer parts. BACE1 is best known for its role in Alzheimer disease. It makes the first cut that leads to amyloid buildup. But it likely cuts many other proteins too.

Using quantitative proteomics, the team list proteins cut by BACE1. Proteomics measures many proteins at once with high precision. A fuller target list helps explain what the enzyme does in health. It also warns what blocking it might disrupt in treatment.
plos-pone-0008577:
Viswanathan Palanisamy and co-authors study tiny vesicles in human saliva in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The vesicles are called exosomes. Cells release them, and they carry proteins and RNA to other cells. They occur in most body fluids, including milk, blood, and urine. Saliva exosomes had not been mapped in detail. The team collect them and study their structure at nano scale.

They also list the RNA and protein cargo the vesicles carry. That catalog shows what messages saliva exosomes could deliver. Such vesicles may serve as markers of oral and body health. They could one day carry drugs as natural delivery packets.
plos-pone-0008677:
Daniel Costa, Patrick Robinson, John Arnould, and colleagues tackled a tracking problem in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Biologists often follow seals and sea lions with ARGOS satellite tags. The tags report where an animal is, but each fix carries some error. Knowing the size of that error matters for any claim about travel or feeding.

The team compared ARGOS fixes with Fastloc GPS readings taken at the same time. GPS served as the trusted yardstick for animals swimming at sea. Their checks show how far off a satellite fix can be. Wildlife researchers can use those numbers to judge how much trust a track deserves.
plos-pone-0008777:
Victoria Gonzalo, Juan José Lozano, Jenifer Muñoz, and colleagues linked chemical tags on DNA to multiple colon tumors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most cases of several separate colorectal cancers trace to inherited syndromes. Sporadic cases, with no family syndrome, were less understood. Faulty methylation tags near gene switches can silence protective genes. That silencing drives many colon cancers.

The team compared tag patterns in patients with multiple tumors and controls. Certain promoters carried abnormal tags again and again. Those patterns may flag people who need closer screening. Finding them clarifies how sporadic multiplicity arises.
plos-pone-0008877:
Benjamin Groves, Hilde Abrahamsen, Heather Clingan, and colleagues found a brake on the cell's self-eating system. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Macroautophagy lets cells wrap and recycle their own worn parts. The mTOR pathway is one of its main drivers. Faulty control of this recycling links to cancer and brain diseases. A G-protein regulator called AGS3 was the suspect brake.

Raising AGS3 levels slowed the mTOR-driven recycling in their tests. The protein thus works against, not for, this cleanup route. A mapped brake helps explain how cells pace their recycling. It may also offer a handle for drugs in recycling-linked diseases.
plos-pone-0008977:
Arantza Rico and co-authors warned plant scientists about a side effect of a routine lab trick, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The trick, agroinfiltration, uses Agrobacterium bacteria to slip genes into tobacco leaves. Researchers use it to test plant genes quickly, including genes for fighting disease. The study used the tobacco species Nicotiana tabacum.

Leaves treated with the bacteria ended up with lower levels of the hormone ABA. The treatment also blunted salicylic acid, a defence signal plants raise against Pseudomonas bacteria. So the test method itself dampens the very defences researchers want to study. Anyone using the trick must allow for that hidden effect.
plos-pone-0009077:
Nigel Wood and co-authors gave enriched cages to mice bred with Huntington's disease and watched who benefited, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Enriched housing means bigger cages with toys, tunnels, and chances to explore. Such housing improves brain function in lab animals and has been proposed as therapy. The R6/2 mouse is the standard model of Huntington's.

Benefits from enrichment were not the same for every mouse. Males and females responded differently to the livelier cages. The animals' exact genetic makeup also shaped the effect. A one-size therapy may fit poorly if sex and genotype steer the gains.
plos-pone-0009177:
Jeffrey H. Schwartz and colleagues published this archaeology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It asks a heated question about ancient Carthage, the Phoenician city in North Africa. Old accounts claimed the Carthaginians routinely killed infants as religious offerings. The authors tested that claim against the bones themselves.

Carthage had two kinds of burial ground. One held older children and adults, while the other, called the Tophet, held urns of cremated infant remains. By studying the ages and remains in those urns, the team judged whether the pattern fit sacrifice or natural infant death. Their answer was no: the remains do not support systematic sacrifice of infants.
plos-pone-0009277:
João Pedro Pereira, Jason Cyster, and Ying Xu published this immune cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Young B cells are born in the bone marrow, then leave to patrol the body. A fat-like signal called S1P guides older B cells out of lymph organs. Whether it also drives the first exit from the marrow was not fully known.

Using mice that lack S1P or its receptor S1P1 in set conditions, the team tested that exit step. They report a role for both the signal and its receptor in immature B cell egress. Completing that picture matters because B cell traffic shapes the whole antibody defense.
plos-pone-0009377:
Bernd Fritzsch and co-authors published this mouse ear study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene Prox1 helps build the lens, retina, pancreas, liver, and lymph vessels. It is also active in the inner ear's support cells and neurons. What exactly it does in the ear was the team's question.

Using standard and conditional mouse mutants, they removed Prox1 activity in the developing ear. Growth of the balance canals' cristae then faltered. Nerve fibers also failed to extend properly to the outer hair cells of hearing. The study shows one gene coordinating both the ear's balance and hearing wiring.
plos-pone-0009477:
Mara Marongiu and colleagues studied a protein that guides ovary growth in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is FOXL2. Faults in it cause a syndrome with eyelid defects and can lead to early ovarian failure. The team found that FOXL2 gets tagged with small proteins called SUMO. This happens in both human and mouse cells.

The tagging changed how stable the protein is. It also changed where the protein sits in the cell and how well it works. So a small tag acts as a control dial on a key protein. Faults in that control could add to the diseases tied to FOXL2.
plos-pone-0009577:
Mirko Zimic and co-authors built a low cost microscope for tuberculosis work in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding TB early saves lives, but many clinics in poor regions lack good equipment. One culture method, called MODS, grows the germ so it can be seen under a microscope. Inverted microscopes for that job are costly. The team designed a cheaper version for the task.

Their device lets lab staff spot the germ's early growth in culture. Lower cost puts the test within reach of more clinics. Faster diagnosis means faster treatment and fewer new infections. The paper is a piece of practical engineering aimed at a deadly, widespread disease.
plos-pone-0009677:
Jeremy Lundholm and co-authors tested plant mixes for green roofs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Green roofs cover buildings with living plants. They cool the building, soak up rain, and shelter urban wildlife. Not every plant mix does those jobs equally well. The team grew roofs with varied species and functional group combinations. They measured how each mix performed key ecosystem functions.

Certain combinations of species and groups outperformed others across several functions. Diversity in plant type, not just in species count, drove much of the gain. The results give planners an evidence based planting guide. Better mixes mean roofs that cool more, drain better, and support more life.
plos-pone-0009777:
Maxime Cazorla and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study presents cyclotraxin-B, a new compound that blocks TrkB, the receptor for a brain growth factor called BDNF. Drugs for brain disorders have changed little in recent decades, and small blockers of TrkB had been hard to build.

The compound bends the receptor so it cannot signal, blocking both driven and resting activity, the team reports. Given to mice, it reached the brain and eased anxious behavior, with no lift in mood tests. The authors offer it as both a research tool and a lead for new drugs for brain disorders.
plos-pone-0009877:
Broken DNA strands are among the most dangerous injuries a cell can suffer. Donghong Ju and colleagues studied a repair pathway and a protein that must be cleared for it to work. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The repair route is nonhomologous end-joining, which glues broken ends back together. The protein is Rpn4, normally destroyed by the proteasome, the cell's disposal machine. When that degradation was inhibited, end-joining repair of double-strand breaks suffered. The result shows timing of protein cleanup matters for genome safety. Double-strand breaks can kill a cell if left unrepaired.
plos-pone-0009977:
PAX3 is a gene that helps build pigment cells early in life and stays active in adult skin. Sandra Medic and Mel Ziman mapped where it appears in normal skin and in moles and melanomas. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Melanocytes are the pigment-making cells of the skin. Melanocytic lesions include naevi, common moles, and melanomas, the dangerous skin cancers. Comparing PAX3 expression across all three shows where the gene switches behavior. Such maps help separate harmless moles from cancers. Skin color comes from melanin made by these cells.
plos-pone-0010077:
Barry J Thompson, writing alone in PLOS ONE in 2010, rechecks a claim about growth control in fruit flies. A recent report said a gene pair, Mal and SRF, plus a regulator named Pico, are needed for cells to multiply and tissues to grow. The pair is known for roles in cell movement.

Thompson found that mutating Mal or SRF did not affect cell growth in the fly wing. He also could not repeat the reported body-size effects of raising or lowering Pico. Forcing Pico or Mal on did swell wing tissue, where SRF is most active. His verdict: the pair can drive growth when overactive, but normal growth does not need it.
plos-pone-0010177:
The authors were Shinsuke Ohnuki, Satomi Oka, Satoru Nogami, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study screened drug effects in yeast using images. Drug discovery depends on learning what a compound does inside cells and what it targets. New imaging tools can record many cell events at once, in fine detail and at large scale.

The team built a high-content, image-based screen to find drug targets in yeast. Yeast is cheap, fast, and shares much core biology with human cells. A screen that reads cell pictures can flag promising compounds and their targets early, before costly animal work.
plos-pone-0010277:
Shan Deng and colleagues survey a stem cell marker across human cancers in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. The marker, ALDH1, is an enzyme used to find cancer stem cells, the rare tumor cells thought to seed and sustain growth. Its normal pattern across tissues was largely unknown.

Staining hundreds of tumors of six types and many normal tissues, the team found each cancer's ALDH1 pattern mirrored its tissue of origin. Enzyme levels matched protein levels, and long lab culture did not change them. In ovarian cancer, high ALDH1 linked to worse outcomes, and marked cells resisted chemotherapy. The marker suits cancers whose normal tissues show little of it.
plos-pone-0010377:
Daniel Weiller, Robert Märtin and Sven Dähne argued that movement should shape how senses encode space, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sensory systems aim to capture what matters for behavior. What matters depends on what an animal or robot can actually do. A sense that ignores its owner's abilities may waste effort on useless detail. The authors built that idea into a learning model.

In their setup, representations of sensory space formed with motor limits in mind. The resulting codes differed from those learned by senses alone. This matters for robotics, where cameras and limbs are designed separately too often. It also matters for brain theory, since bodies and senses evolved together. The paper asks designers to start from the whole agent, not the sensor.
plos-pone-0010477:
Jing Jie Yu and colleagues examined eye tumors in HIV patients in East Africa for PLOS ONE in 2010. Squamous cell carcinoma of the conjunctiva, the eye's surface, had grown much more common there alongside HIV. Its behavior in that region seems distinct from elsewhere. Causes were suspected to involve both human papillomavirus and a growth receptor called EGFR. The team tested tumor samples for both factors.

Sorting out which drivers act in these tumors guides treatment choices. EGFR can be targeted by existing cancer drugs in some settings. HPV involvement would raise questions about prevention. The study serves a patient group often left out of cancer research. It also shows how infection and cancer intertwine in the HIV era.
plos-pone-0010577:
Jiabing Ji and Janet Braam introduced a new laboratory method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Geneticists often insert a known tag into DNA, then need to read the unknown DNA next to it. Finding that neighboring stretch has usually been slow and unreliable.

Their method, called restriction site extension PCR, reads outward from the tag in a more direct way. Tests showed it could recover flanking DNA quickly and in larger numbers than older approaches. A faster route from a tag to a full gene should help researchers link mutations to the traits they cause.
plos-pone-0010677:
Mark Littler, Diane Littler, and Barrett Brooks surveyed seaweeds on Saba Bank, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bank is a flat-topped seamount in the Dutch Windward Islands, twenty to forty-five meters deep in its shallow parts. Its plant life was among the least known parts of its reef system.

The team collected and named macroalgae across the bank's habitats. Many records were new for the area, and the flora proved richer than expected for a single seamount. Seaweeds feed and shelter much reef life, yet surveys often skip them. A full plant list makes the bank's living wealth harder to overlook in protection plans.
plos-pone-0010777:
Nuria Andreu and colleagues tuned glowing reporter systems for tuberculosis research, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacteria that make their own light let scientists follow infection without killing the animal or germ at each check. Standard light-making systems worked poorly in these waxy-coated bacteria, so the signal needed work.

The team tested several luciferase systems and adjusted how they are expressed. The best setups shone brightly and stayed stable in mycobacteria. Glowing germs can be counted quickly in drug and vaccine tests. A brighter, steadier signal shortens experiments and reduces the number of animals that long infection studies require.
plos-pone-0010877:
Timo Homeier, Torsten Semmler, Lothar Wieler and co-authors published this bacterial evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some E. coli strains leave the gut and cause disease in the brain, bladder, or blood, in both people and birds. A stretch of DNA called GimA, carrying an invasion gene, helps some of them enter brain lining cells.

The team screened hundreds of isolates from patients, animals, feces, and a reference collection for the GimA island. Alongside the full island and its complete absence, they found a third pattern: a short remnant, as if the island had been partly deleted. The full island appeared almost only in certain family lines of the bacterium. Homeier and colleagues use this patchy record to ask whether losing DNA tracks where a strain lives and what disease it causes.
plos-pone-0010977:
Patricia Guillaumot, Céline Luquain, Mouhannad Malek and co-authors published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cholesterol is vital in cell membranes, and its level is tightly controlled by mechanisms that are still partly unknown. Screening a special membrane fraction, the authors identified an uncharacterized protein and named it Pdro.

The protein sits mainly on late endosomes and lysosomes, the cell's sorting and recycling stations, anchored by fatty tags at one end. Changing its amount changed the cell's free cholesterol content. Guillaumot and colleagues also note that other groups found the same protein under different names, tied to cell movement machinery and lysosome control. Pdro emerges as a new handle on cholesterol balance, relevant to diseases from heart disease to rare storage disorders.
plos-pone-0011077:
Yeh, Xie, Langdon and colleagues reported a mouse study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They used mice bred to make extra amounts of a protein that triggers histamine release. Histamine drives many allergy symptoms, so the team wanted to see what too much of this factor does across the body.

By tracking the bred mice, the team charted wide effects linked to the extra protein. Their results help show how one immune factor can shape allergy and swelling in many tissues. The work gives later studies a clear animal model to test. It may also point toward treatments that calm an overactive immune response.
plos-pone-0011177:
Levi, James, Nelson and colleagues used fat derived cells to heal skull bone in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fat tissue holds stromal cells that can form other tissues. The team placed human cells of this kind into large skull defects in mice, wounds too big to heal on their own.

The human cells healed those critical defects by forming new bone. Using a patient's own fat as a source would ease supply and rejection worries. Skull repair after injury or surgery is a real clinical need. The result brings fat to bone repair closer to practical testing in people.
plos-pone-0011277:
Bergstedt, Tingskov, Thierry-Carstensen and colleagues ran a first human trial in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tuberculosis skin tests are old and often unclear, since prior BCG vaccination confuses results. The team tested a new reagent combining two proteins specific to the TB germ in volunteers for the first time.

A specific skin test could catch TB sooner and sort true infection from vaccine effects. That distinction matters in countries where BCG is routine. The trial checks safety and response as first steps toward clinic use. Better detection helps curb spread by finding infectious people earlier.
plos-pone-0011377:
Shuqi Xiao and co-authors read the full gene response of pig lungs infected with PRRSV in 2010. The virus causes a costly reproductive and lung disease in pigs worldwide, and vaccines control it poorly. Using deep sequencing, the team recorded which lung genes switched on or off across the whole genome during infection.

The response map revealed broad changes in immune and tissue genes as the virus took hold in the lung. Patterns in that map point to pathways the virus provokes or evades, and to stages where treatment might help most. Veterinarians and breeders gain a resource for picking drug targets and for breeding pigs that resist infection better. The study also shows how one deep sequencing run can replace years of gene-by-gene work in farm animal disease.
plos-pone-0011477:
Johan Lorenzen and co-authors followed kidney patients over time in 2010 to test whether repair cells in the blood predict heart trouble. Chronic kidney disease greatly raises the risk of heart attacks and strokes, beyond what standard risk factors explain. Endothelial progenitor cells, which help repair vessel linings, circulate in the blood and can be counted at a clinic visit.

The prospective study measured those cells and then tracked who suffered cardiovascular events during follow-up. Testing the idea prospectively, with the count taken before events occur, is what separates a real warning sign from hindsight. If repair cell counts forecast events, nephrologists gain an early-warning readout to guide closer monitoring and earlier treatment. The study design itself is the point: kidney patients need predictors proven by waiting and watching, not by looking backward.
plos-pone-0011577:
Thierry Chaminade and co-authors scanned people's brains in 2010 as they watched a humanoid robot move. Robots built like people are entering homes and hospitals, and designers need to know whether human social brains treat them as people. The team measured brain responses to the robot in the areas that read human emotional gestures, the movements by which people read feelings.

The neural verdict was mixed in an informative way: some social circuits answered the machine much as they answer a person, while others held back. That split predicts where human-robot interaction will feel natural and where it will feel eerie. Gesture designers can aim at the circuits that accept the machine, rather than polishing appearance blindly. The study also serves basic science, using the robot as a controlled, repeatable almost-person to probe how gesture perception is built.
plos-pone-0011677:
James Hadler and co-authors estimated how deadly the 2009 pandemic flu was in New York City, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging a new pandemic strain's severity quickly is vital for planning the response. A novel H1N1 virus was recognised in late April 2009, and the city saw an intense first outbreak peaking in late May.

Instead of counting only confirmed cases, the team used population estimates of flu-like illness from May and June. Dividing deaths by that fuller total gave more realistic fatality rates. Their accounting gave officials a truer sense of the virus's toll while the pandemic was still unfolding.
plos-pone-0011777:
Michael TeKippe and Alejandro Aballay compared immune defences in sterile worms, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making eggs and sperm costs resources that cannot then be spent on other trials. In the worm C. elegans, growing a germline cuts lifespan and raises the odds of falling to germs, so worms that lack a germline are oddly hardy.

The team infected germline-free mutants and mapped their response tools. The mutants used a mix of defences shared with normal worms and tools distinct to their state. That split lays bare the hidden immune cost of breeding in plain terms.
plos-pone-0011877:
James Boyd, Eric Oldenburg, and Geoffrey McMichael built in 2010 a color photo guide to how fall Chinook salmon embryos develop. Development speed in fish eggs depends strongly on temperature, summed as accumulated thermal units. Knowing the link lets biologists estimate when eggs in a natural gravel nest were fertilized.

Few staged photo references existed, so the team paired pictures of each embryo stage with the thermal units reached by then. A shared visual scale helps hatchery staff and field crews judge embryo age the same way. For wild salmon, better aging of eggs sharpens estimates of spawning time, which feed into river management and protection plans.
plos-pone-0011977:
Robert Glaser and Mark Meola reported in 2010 that a bacterium living inside insects helps them resist West Nile virus. Wolbachia is a widespread insect endosymbiont already known to raise virus resistance in fruit flies and in mosquitoes that do not normally carry it. The question was whether native Wolbachia does the same in its natural hosts.

In both Drosophila melanogaster and the mosquito Culex quinquefasciatus, hosts carrying their native Wolbachia resisted West Nile infection better. Culex mosquitoes spread the virus to people, so a natural resistance factor in them is more than a curiosity. It supports strategies that use Wolbachia to make mosquito populations poorer virus carriers.
plos-pone-0012077:
Maria Danoviz and co-workers tried in 2010 fat-based stem cells as a mending crew for hearts hurt by a heart attack, in rats. Heart cell grafts face a blunt flaw: most cells put in wash out or die in days. The team drew stem cells from rat fat, an easy source, and asked if soft gel-like helpers called biopolymers could keep more of the cells in place.

Put in with the gels, more cells stayed put, and the hurt hearts worked better than those of rats left with the harm alone. Heart shape and pump strength both moved the right way. A cheap, rich cell source joined to a stay-put trick meets the two big blocks at once, and points to heart mending built from a patient's own fat.
plos-pone-0012177:
Daniel Vilceanu and Cheryl Stucky investigated how mouse sensory neurons feel mechanical force, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Touch, pressure, and pain from squeezing or stretching all begin when force opens special channels in nerve endings. Which channel carries the main current in these neurons was still unknown, and one candidate was a channel already known for sensing irritating chemicals and cold.

They recorded the electrical currents that flow when sensory neurons are physically pushed, testing that candidate's role. Their measurements tie the candidate channel to part of the force response. Knowing the true touch sensors matters for treating pain where normal touch hurts, a problem current painkillers handle poorly.
plos-pone-0012277:
Hans Lomholt and Mogens Kilian sorted the acne bacterium's family tree in PLOS ONE in 2010. Propionibacterium acnes lives on nearly everyone's skin, sick and healthy alike, which long made its role in acne doubtful. The authors tested a sharper idea: only certain lineages of the species cause trouble, while their cousins live peacefully on clear skin.

Their population analysis found a distinct subpopulation and epidemic clones tied to acne. If the disease belongs to particular strains, treatment can aim at them instead of carpet-bombing the skin's whole community. It also explains decades of confusing results in which the same species seemed both guilty and innocent.
plos-pone-0012377:
Nathalie Stroeymeyt, Fernando Guerrieri, Jelle van Zweden and colleagues watched ants make fast choices in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Animals often must choose quickly, trading accuracy for speed when danger or hunger presses. Ants face such choices when picking a new nest or a food route, and each side of the body gathers its own clues.

The researchers tracked how ants weigh clues seen on each side when they judge a path. The ants combined the clues fast and still chose well, showing a neat way to beat the speed-accuracy trade-off. Their method may inspire designs for robot swarms and other systems that must decide well under time pressure.
plos-pone-0012477:
Claudia Hoffmann, Marlies Galle, Sabrina Dilling and colleagues studied how Salmonella triggers an inflammatory alarm in macrophages, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Macrophages are immune cells that eat invaders; when Salmonella injects proteins through its needle-like secretion system, the cell fires caspase-1, an enzyme that launches inflammation. A bacterial whip protein, flagellin, was thought to be required for that alarm.

The team showed the alarm can fire without flagellin when the bacterial effector SopE and the secretion system are at work. Redundant triggers make the alarm hard for bacteria to evade. Understanding the wiring helps explain severe Salmonella inflammation and may guide anti-inflammatory strategies.
plos-pone-0012577:
Delia Goletti, Alamelu Raja, Basirudeen Kabeer and colleagues tested a new TB marker in people living with HIV, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Standard TB blood tests rely on interferon gamma and lose sensitivity in people with weakened immunity, exactly the group most at risk of TB. An alternative marker, IP-10, is released in larger amounts and might read more reliably.

The team assessed whether IP-10 accurately detects the TB-specific immune response in HIV-infected persons. A dependable test for this group would close a dangerous diagnostic gap, since TB is a leading killer of people with HIV. Their evaluation informs which assays clinics should adopt for co-infected patients.
plos-pone-0012677:
Hilimire, Mounts, Parks and co-authors used scalp recordings to separate two forces that guide visual attention. Attention boosts what matters and filters the rest, but two ideas compete to explain it. One stresses how much an item stands out, the other where it sits in space.

Their 2010 brain-wave study timed the responses to tease those forces apart. The signals showed salience and space acting at different moments. Settling how attention splits its work helps explain disorders where focus fails, and sharpens basic vision science. Such timing work is hard to get from behaviour tests alone.
plos-pone-0012777:
Glasser, Taneri, Feng and co-authors used population models to compare targeted flu vaccination plans. Mathematical models suit this task because rival plans can be run on the same virtual population. Their 2010 study insisted the models be checked for credibility before their rankings are trusted.

They tested strategies that aim vaccine at different age or risk groups. Which group to favour depends on whether the goal is fewer deaths, fewer cases, or keeping schools and hospitals running. Their framework helps officials match a flu plan to a stated goal.  Several flu seasons of spread informed the model runs.
plos-pone-0012877:
Silveira, Barlow, Louzada and co-authors counted leaf-litter insects in Amazon forests with different fire histories. Fire is used across the Amazon to clear land for cattle and crops, and those fires often escape into nearby forest. Their 2010 study compared unburned forest with forest burned three times in seasonally dry areas.

They measured which factors set the abundance of arthropods living in fallen leaves. Leaf litter animals drive soil health and feed many larger species. Knowing how repeated fire thins them helps judge the true cost of escaped burns.
plos-pone-0319877:
Shengying Wan and colleagues measured the fruits of camphor trees from eleven source populations across Jiangxi Province, China, to map how much the species varies. One hundred seventy trees were scored on ten fruit traits, from size ratios to peel thickness and seed weight. Camphor is an economically important tree, and breeders need to know where the useful variation lives.

Nearly three-quarters of the variation sat between populations rather than within them, meaning the source stand matters more than the individual tree. Diversity scores were high overall, and peel thickness varied the most of any trait. For selecting superior planting stock, the message is to sample widely across provenances, since each holds a distinct slice of the species' variation.
plos-pone-0327077:
Meng-Jung Lin asked whether the body's molecular age clocks change how well older adults weather marriage's upheavals, such as widowhood or divorce. Using a large American retirement study of more than sixteen hundred older white adults. The team combined thirteen DNA-based ageing clocks with records of marital transitions, depressive symptoms, and death. They adjusted for genetic and social background.

Marital change itself tracked with more depressive symptoms but not, directly, with higher death risk, and it barely touched the clocks. The interesting action sat in the combinations: for death risk, several clocks significantly altered how transitions played out, mostly among men, with biologically older men paradoxically showing more resilience. Lin suggests the clocks may capture a lifetime's accumulated adaptation, not just wear, and calls the resilience reading a hypothesis worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0327277:
Abigail Kusi-Amponsah Diji and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on outpatient care at a Ghanaian university hospital. Fragmented services and rotating doctors there break the bond between patients and providers. Twenty-eight people, clinicians and care recipients at the hospital in Kumasi, were interviewed in depth about the current system and a proposed Family Practice Model. That model would give each patient a dedicated doctor.

Two themes captured the mood. Participants described the present system as therapeutic disconnection: impersonal, rushed consultations, poor records, and never seeing the same provider twice, all eroding trust. Against that stood the wish summed up in the second theme, a doctor to call my own. Stakeholders backed a relationship-based model promising continuity, smoother processes, and long-term connection. The model, they conclude, could transform outpatient care and, by strengthening primary care, help Ghana toward universal health coverage.
plos-pone-0337677:
Tomohiro Udagawa and co-authors grow miniature kidney filters in a dish to test whether injury to some filtering cells spreads to their untouched neighbors. These podocyte cells wrap the kidney's filters, and their loss drives chronic kidney disease. The team mixed two mouse cell lines into mosaic organoids, one line vulnerable to a targeted toxin and one tagged and safe, then poisoned only the vulnerable cells.

Targeted cells were injured as intended, and their safe neighbors inside the same tiny filter also weakened, losing a key protein and quieting their identity genes. When the two organoid types grew side by side in separate clusters, no spread occurred. Udagawa and colleagues conclude the damage passes by direct contact within a shared filter, a mechanism that could help explain how kidney disease advances.
plos-pone-0338277:
Testing a patient's genes before prescribing can prevent bad drug reactions, but health systems ask whether the tests pay for themselves. Taichi Ochi and colleagues gathered seventeen earlier systematic reviews on that question into one umbrella review, published in PLOS One in 2026.

Searches across three databases, with a fresh update in 2025, fed the summary, and each review's quality was graded with a standard checklist. As the number of studies has grown, the balance of evidence has leaned toward the tests being worth their cost in several drug areas. The authors say cost questions should no longer block careful rollout where guidelines already support testing.
plos-pone-0342577:
Yutaro Nishikata and colleagues fed cholesterol-rich food to rats bred to have high blood pressure and strokes, and got a counterintuitive result. Cholesterol is normally a villain in heart disease, yet earlier reports said these rats lived longer on such a diet. Three groups of young rats ate plain food, cholesterol-enriched food, or the same diet plus a drug that blocks the body's own cholesterol making, for twelve weeks.

The cholesterol-fed rats ended with blood pressure about a tenth lower than controls, alongside wide changes in tissue fats, including plant sterols and lower levels of a fat linked to inflammation. Kidney tissue was also checked for damage. The rat paradox will not rewrite diet advice for people, but it shows cholesterol's effects depend heavily on context.
plos-pone-0343577:
Francisco Chamera and five colleagues work out how much fishing the catfish of Lake Malawi can bear, in this 2026 study of the lake's southeast arm. Catfish support a valuable commercial fishery, but effort has grown for decades. Using catch and effort records stretching back to the start of the century, the team applied a classic bioeconomic model that weighs stock growth against costs and prices.

Their analysis shows the stock survives only if yearly effort stays below a clear ceiling. The most profitable sustainable level sits far below current effort, at only a few hundred trips a year. Observed fishing far exceeds that level. The authors recommend deliberate cuts in effort so the fishery keeps producing both income and fish over the long term, rather than mining the stock down.
plos-pone-0346077:
Erica Christensen and colleagues tackle chronic wasting disease in this 2026 PLOS ONE wildlife study. The fatal prion disease spreads among deer through contact and through contaminated ground. The team followed mule deer fitted with GPS collars across Wyoming and tested them each year. It then modeled which landscape features raised the yearly chance of infection.

Deer favored spots near secondary roads, and those same spots carried higher disease risk, linking risk to how deer use the land. Risk also rose where the terrain collects moisture, even though deer did not prefer those areas, which points to prions lasting longer in damp ground. The findings aim to help managers target testing and disease control.
plos-pone-0346777:
Yingquan Ao and seven colleagues published this optics study in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rather than building a device, they used computer modeling to test a light filter made from stacked graphene sheets separated by thin insulating layers. The spacing between the layers changes gradually along the stack, a pattern called a chirped grating.

Their simulations show the stack lets longer wavelengths of light pass while blocking shorter ones, acting as a low-pass filter. The cutoff point and the width of the passing band can be adjusted by changing the number of layers, the spacing gradient, or the electrical state of the graphene. The authors suggest uses in spectral scanning and adaptive optics.
plos-pone-0347777:
Angelina Sutin and colleagues surveyed nearly two thousand adults on their sense of purpose in life and the strategies they use to handle stress. People with a strong sense of purpose tend to feel less stress, and the team tested whether better coping explains part of that link. Depression, anxiety, and current stress levels were also measured.

Purpose came with more active coping and more seeking of support, and with slightly less giving-up coping. Those ties looked much the same across age, sex, race, and education. One wrinkle mattered: among people currently in distress, purpose was linked to more disengaged coping, not less. The results caution against one-size advice, since coping habits seem to change under strain.
plos-pone-0347877:
Sabrina Harris and colleagues report a rare bright spot in climate change biology, from a gentoo penguin colony at Martillo Island, Argentina, near the species' northern limit. A time-lapse camera watched the colony from 2013 to 2024. Heat is dangerous for cold-adapted penguins, and the record includes chicks dying within the hour on a day that hit twenty-four degrees.

Across the study years the penguins advanced their breeding season by about two days each year. Breeding earlier means chicks fledge before the worst summer heat, cutting the number of dangerously hot days they endure. The authors are careful: hotter futures may overwhelm this shift. For now, a warming-driven change is shielding chicks instead of exposing them.
plos-pone-0348077:
Md Mafizer Rahman and colleagues built a maths model of dengue fever in Bangladesh that treats medical care as a moving part, not an afterthought. Many models assume everyone recovers alike, but their version separates people who recover on their own from those whose recovery depends on treatment. It also lets mosquito biting rise and fall with temperature. They fitted the model to case and weather data from each division of the country.

Where treatment was scarce, outbreaks peaked far higher, while prompt supportive care blunted epidemics even when transmission ran hot. Forecasts singled out metropolitan Dhaka as both a hotspot and the place where better treatment access would matter most. The authors offer the framework to other low-resource settings planning for seasonal surges.
plos-pone-0348177:
Xiuyu Tang and colleagues test how to keep small dental tools clean between patients in this 2026 PLOS ONE laboratory study. Reusable burs and flexible root-canal files must be cleaned before sterilizing, and keeping them moist after use stops debris from drying on. The team compared plain water, an enzyme cleaner, and a professional transport gel.

Instruments went through four rounds of use and reprocessing, then were checked under microscopes and with a test that detects leftover biological residue, plus surface imaging for wear and contamination. The professional moisturizer produced the cleanest instruments. The results give dental clinics practical guidance on a step that affects both patient safety and how long delicate tools last.
plos-pone-0348277:
Ayla Ahmed and co-workers study how smoke from home cooking fires relates to severe pneumonia in young Ugandan children. Pneumonia with low blood oxygen is a leading killer of children under five. Their 2026 study reviews cases at twenty hospitals, covering more than seven hundred children, and estimates each child's exposure from fuel type, cooking time, kitchen shape, and airflow.

Nearly every child lived with fine particle levels far above the world health limit. Higher exposure went with more breathing trouble, lower oxygen on arrival, longer oxygen treatment, and worse severity scores. Eye and nose irritation also rose with exposure. The links strengthen the case for cleaner stoves and better home ventilation in Uganda.
plos-pone-0348377:
Antje Lorenz and Elisabeth Beyersmann ran word-recognition experiments on how German speakers process compound nouns, words built from two nouns like water bottle. In German every noun carries a grammatical gender, and a compound takes the gender of its second part, its head. The question was whether the first part's gender also wakes up in the mind during reading.

Volunteers judged words flashed on a screen, preceded by the German word for the, matched either to the head's gender, the first part's gender, or neither. Primes matching the head sped recognition in both experiments; primes matching the first part did nothing. Minds, it seems, store the head's gender as the compound's own and let the modifier's gender sleep.
plos-pone-0348577:
Youssef El Khatib and Farangiz Mukhamedova propose a different goal for building investment portfolios, one that punishes wobble directly instead of rewarding return per unit of risk. Classic methods chase the best ratio of gain to volatility, which can still leave investors with deep drops. Their formula rewards expected return while dividing by portfolio volatility in a way that favours calm paths, and it stays inside mainstream preference theory.

In rolling tests on standard stock portfolios, with trading costs and no short selling allowed, the method produced clearly calmer results and shallower worst drops than the classic benchmark. Its average performance stayed in line with simpler strategies. The advantage held through the financial crisis, the pandemic crash, and the twenty twenty-two rate shock. The authors offer it to investors who value a smooth ride.
plos-pone-0348677:
Mohamed Metwaly and Abdullah Alshami map where ancient people likely settled around Al-Madinah in Arabia and which caravan routes fed the oasis city once called Yathrib. Their 2026 study scores the land with six factors, from slope to distance from water channels, then computes the cheapest walking paths toward major old sites and a coastal port.

Nearly a third of the study area rated highly suitable for settlement. Water access, gentle slope, and soil type governed the pattern most. Modeled routes matched known historical trade stations well when checked. The method can be reused across dry lands to predict where ruins wait and how goods once moved between desert wells.
plos-pone-0348777:
Ali M Alshhre reads sixty Saudi proverbs about women as a small archive of home life and nature. Proverbs come from the Saudi National Encyclopaedia regional records.
