Many use bread, heat, pots, pests, kohl, and henna to talk about mothers, wives, and home duty. Close reading joins feminist tools with attention to things and the living world.

Praise often hides a price. Sayings that honour mothers and home builders also lock women into heavy work and blame. Warning sayings police where women go, how they look, and how much freedom they claim, using images of want, risk, and loss. Everyday speech, the author shows, quietly governs gender through the language of the home.
plos-pone-0348877:
Nobukazu Nameki and co-authors solved the structure of a mouse protein piece bound to ubiquitin in 2026. The piece comes from proteins that help clear ribosomes stuck on faulty messages, a cleanup job vital to healthy cells, but its grip on ubiquitin was only guessed.

Using nuclear magnetic resonance, the team mapped the three helix bundle and its contact with ubiquitin's sticky patch, finding a grip much like that of known ubiquitin readers. One loop, though, had a distinctive double turn found in no close cousin. The detail refines ideas about how stuck ribosome cleanup crews recognise their targets.
plos-pone-0349377:
Wilson Castro and colleagues tested whether the electrical behavior of chicken breast meat can reveal its quality grade without cutting or tasting it. Ninety-six samples of Creole chicken were classed by acidity into the standard three grades: pale and soft, normal, and dark and dry. The team then swept the meat with radio-frequency signals and recorded how it stored and absorbed the energy.

The electrical spectra differed by grade, most clearly at low frequencies, where the dark, dry grade stood apart, and modeling separated two relaxation processes with grade-specific timing. Only three samples fell in the palest grade, so the authors call the work preliminary. A fast electrical probe that grades meat on the line would help producers sort quality without destroying product.
plos-pone-0349577:
Oswaldo Cadenas presents a streaming method for shrinking huge two-dimensional point sets without changing their convex hull, the smallest convex shape wrapping all the points. Hull calculations underpin mapping, graphics, and robotics, and on massive data most input points sit uselessly inside. His reduction examines points as they arrive in a single pass and discards only those provably interior, each backed by a local geometric certificate.

On synthetic data the filter kept only about one point in ten, and on large real-world sets under one in a hundred. Yet the hull of what remains is exactly the hull of the original. Throwing away the interior safely lets downstream hull algorithms run fast on streaming data that never fits comfortably in memory.
plos-pone-0349777:
Margarita Osuna and co-authors asked how the way diabetes and high blood pressure are counted changes later life estimates in Colombia, in 2026 work. Self reports and direct measures give very different rates, and policy built on the wrong one will mislead.

Using a national ageing survey from 2015, the team built rates three ways: reported diagnosis, measured risk, and both combined. They also split cases into controlled, uncontrolled, and unaware, then estimated years lived with each disease after sixty. Combined counting gave the longest time lived with diabetes. The spread shows why surveys should measure, not just ask, when planning care for older adults.
plos-pone-0349877:
Deaths recorded as involving antipsychotic medicines in England have been rising, and Muhammad Umair Khan and Syed Shahzad Hasan examined the pattern using national prescription data from 2015 to 2023. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered all seven English health regions.

Recorded deaths climbed from about ten to about fourteen per million prescribed items, growing a few percent each year. London saw the steepest rise while the Midlands fell. Poorer areas carried higher rates, and areas with larger Asian populations showed lower rates. The authors stress these records link medicines to deaths without proving cause, but the uneven map argues for closer local review of prescribing safety.
plos-pone-0350277:
Yizhou Chen and Jie Zhang surveyed more than three thousand Chinese university students to unpack why active students report fewer depressive symptoms. Exercise is known to protect mood, but the mental pathway was unclear. Their 2026 online survey measured activity levels, depressive symptoms, and grit, meaning the perseverance and passion people bring to long-term goals, then tested whether grit carried the effect.

More active students did report milder symptoms. Statistically, though, the whole benefit ran through grit: once grit was accounted for, activity alone showed no direct link to symptoms. The authors suggest that programs pairing exercise with grit-building elements, such as goal setting and persistence training, may protect student mental health better than exercise promotion alone.
plos-pone-0351077:
Prompt engineering became a public buzzword almost overnight. The term covers wording requests to AI systems skillfully. Reuben Ng and Ting Yu Joanne Chow analyzed the public conversation. They gathered nearly three hundred thousand English posts. The posts came from X and Reddit. All mentioned the term during one year from May 2023.

Discussion spiked around product news and viral claims. Themes and mood shifted quarter by quarter. Some posts hailed a new profession. Others mocked the hype. Sorting the chatter shows a public negotiating meaning in real time. The authors say educators should track such talk. Platforms should track it too. Fast-moving AI vocabulary enters everyday speech quickly.
plos-pone-0351177:
Reading with a toddler, pausing to ask questions and chat, is called dialogic reading. Ming Yean Sia and colleagues asked whether that early talk leaves a mark on the brain years later, in this 2026 PLOS One study following children from age two to age five.

Parents' engagement during shared reading was measured at two. At five, children's forehead brain activity was recorded with light-based scanners while they played a card-sorting game testing mental flexibility. More early dialogue went with stronger activity in regions handling planning and control, even after accounting for mothers' education and children's vocabulary. The authors suggest shared book talk helps build the brain's control systems.
plos-pone-0351477:
Mattia Ronca and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for an imaging study of kidney tumors at the University Hospital of Bordeaux. Ordinary CT scans do not measure how stiff a tumor is, yet stiffness may help characterize tissue. Fifty adults scheduled for kidney tumor surgery will receive CT, MRI-based stiffness mapping, and ultrasound stiffness checks in the days before their operation.

Because this is a protocol, it sets out a plan rather than findings. The main aim is to learn whether plain CT density values can predict stiffness measured by the specialized methods, using machine learning models checked by repeated cross-validation. Secondary work will compare the imaging methods with each other and with the final pathology results, and judge how feasible the extra scanning is in routine care.
plos-pone-0351577:
Older adults on the edge of diabetes lose muscle and grow frail, and hard exercise is tough for many to keep up. Hui-Ying Luk and colleagues present the HEAT trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing whether warming the legs locally can guard blood sugar and muscle, alone or before interval training.

Heat is expected to improve blood vessel growth and energy factories inside muscle, the same features that support sugar control. The two-phase trial compares real heat against a sham version, then checks whether heated muscle adapts better once training starts. The protocol reports design only; results will come later.
plos-pone-0351877:
Zeki Taş and five colleagues gather views on school sports from the people who live them in this 2026 study. Eighteen participants at one public high school in the Turkish province of Sakarya took part. Six were students, six were parents, and six were physical education teachers. Each group met separately for focus group interviews. The questions concerned how sports shape school achievement and commitment to school.

Across the three groups, sports were seen as a positive force. Participants linked participation to better perceived achievement. They also tied it to stronger attachment to school life. Because the study is qualitative, it reports perceptions rather than test scores. That is its strength. Policy about school sports usually counts medals or grades from above. These voices show how the value is actually experienced day to day, by teenagers, the parents cheering them, and the teachers organising it all.
plos-pone-0351977:
RETRACTION: The PLOS One Editors retract a study of magnesium oxide nanoparticles made with the plant Saussurea costus. The study claimed the particles kill microbes and breast cancer cells. It also claimed uses in photocatalysis. After the work appeared, readers raised concerns about many of its figures. This notice withdraws the study in full.

The problems were not small slips. Panels overlapped with panels in other papers. Some overlapped with other panels in the same paper, under new labels. Still images of cells treated one way were presented as another way. Repeated patches showed inside single images as well. When the pictures carry the proof and the pictures are recycled, no claim in the study can stand.
plos-pone-0352577:
Daniel Wychrij and six colleagues test a broad fungal vaccine in monkeys in this 2026 study. Recurrent vaginal yeast infections trouble an estimated one hundred thirty-eight million women each year. Standard antifungal drugs often fail to stop recurrences. No fungal vaccine is approved anywhere. Rodent models translate poorly to human immunity. The team therefore built the infection model in Japanese macaques, then vaccinated the animals.

The macaques, like women, developed genuine infections with visible fungal filaments. Natural infection produced weak antibody responses. It also failed to protect against reinfection. Vaccination changed the picture. Immunised animals mounted strong antibody levels in blood and mucosal tissue. Their fungal burden after a fresh challenge dropped clearly. A single vaccine candidate guarding against many fungi could matter well beyond this one infection, and the primate model gives developers a realistic testbed.
plos-pone-0352677:
Selina Limmen and seven colleagues study how decisions get shared in children's physiotherapy. Their 2026 Dutch study ran in two phases. Six focus groups heard from adolescents, parents, and therapists separately. A survey of forty-six more therapists checked those findings. The goal was practical: when should families help decide, and what helps or hinders that teamwork?

Sharing, the groups said, can start at the very first meeting. Goal setting is a natural moment to involve children and parents. Involvement should then continue, adjusted to each family's wishes. Comparing treatment options, visit frequency, and home practice all invite joint choices. The team folded the lessons into an existing goal-based decision model. They also matched rollout strategies to known implementation barriers. Young patients get a real voice, without dumping adult-sized responsibility on them.
plos-pone-0352877:
Khurshid Ataniyazov and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One genetic study of high blood pressure in Uzbekistan. The study region is Karakalpakstan. The Aral Sea crisis hit that area hard, and salty conditions strain health there. The team compared more than six hundred patients with high blood pressure to one hundred eighty controls. They tested nine gene variants tied to blood pressure control.

Six of the nine variants linked to the disease after strict checks. Some raised risk, and others seemed protective. The team also checked effects across sex, age, and weight groups. A seventh variant looked promising before the strict checks, but did not survive them. The authors say so plainly. They present the findings as a regional genetic profile. It may help explain why high blood pressure is so common in this stressed region.
plos-pone-0352977:
Almalki and colleagues surveyed burnout among front-line clinic staff in Al-Khobar, Saudi Arabia, in a 2026 study. More than one hundred doctors, nurses, and other providers completed a standard burnout inventory. About one in five met the study's burnout mark.

Feeling detached from patients scored highest, followed by emotional exhaustion. Exhaustion ran higher in women, in lower-paid staff, and in those seeing many patients daily. Some drivers were personal and some were workload based, the authors note. Cutting patient load pressure and supporting lower-paid staff are concrete steps clinics can take before burnout drives skilled workers away.
plos-pone-0353177:
Yinqin Liu and colleagues use worldwide health data to chart a neglected overlap: heart failure caused by long-term lung diseases. Their 2026 PLOS ONE analysis covers adults aged fifty-five and older across three decades, from 1990 to 2021. The lung conditions involved include chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, scarring lung diseases, and dust-related lung damage.

Total cases and years lived with disability climbed sharply over the period, even though rates per person changed only modestly. The burden grew steepest after age seventy-five and ran higher in men than in women. Mapping where this combined burden concentrates can help health systems plan clinics, staff, and long-term care for ageing populations.
plos-pone-0353277:
Muhammad Ahsan ul Haq and four colleagues redesign an electric motor so it needs no brushes or separate exciter, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. Their wound-rotor synchronous machine uses a stator winding split into two unequal sections. That imbalance creates an extra magnetic ripple, which a second winding on the rotor harvests and converts to direct current to power the rotor's own field winding.

Simulations of an eight-pole design validated the scheme. Against the existing design, the new machine produced slightly more power and torque while drawing about half the input current — and it runs from a single inverter instead of two. Brushless, efficient motors of this kind suit pumps, fans, and electric drivetrains.
plos-pone-0353377:
Ibrahim L Kadigi, Lazaro Kagata, and Stefan Sieber simulated rice farming across Tanzania. They tested which input combinations best protect harvests as the climate shifts. Their 2026 study drew on a national farm census of more than six thousand rice farms. It modeled yields under uncertainty. Farms were sorted by seed type and fertilizer practice, on the mainland and in Zanzibar.

Improved seeds paired with manufactured fertilizer performed best. That pairing gave a real chance of top yields. It also gave the lowest risk of falling below food security lines. Local seeds responded weakly even when fertilized. Organic fertilizer helped soils more than immediate harvests. Mainland farms gained far more than Zanzibar's. The authors recommend prioritizing farmer access to improved seed and fertilizer.
plos-pone-0353477:
Trinidad and colleagues, in a 2026 review, gather what schools have done to teach swimming over the past twenty-five years. Swimming lessons build child development and help prevent drowning, yet programs vary widely. The team searched major research databases and screened studies by set rules, keeping sixteen that fit.

Most programs focused on technique and practical skills, with little link to the wider school curriculum and limited input from physical education teachers. Work centered on younger children, from infants through primary school, and was scarce at secondary level. Program length, session frequency, content, and testing tools all differed a lot between studies. The authors conclude that school swimming needs stronger backing from institutions, better teacher training, and a more joined-up approach for each age stage. Without that, they argue, gains in water safety and skill will stay patchy.
plos-pone-0353677:
Maher Abdessater and five colleagues test whether one day of simulation training can prepare new doctors for a common bedside procedure, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Inserting a urinary catheter is routine, but most complications come from beginners. Forty fresh interns at a university hospital first answered a knowledge and confidence survey — only a small minority felt ready, and basic facts about catheter sizes and technique were widely missed.

After lectures, videos, and hands-on practice on male and female models, knowledge, confidence, and self-belief scores all jumped sharply. Six months later the group had performed hundreds of real catheterisations with a high success rate and few complications. Practice off the patient, the authors conclude, pays off on the ward.
plos-pone-0353777:
Alrashood and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Saudi Arabia, ask whether artificial intelligence in science teaching can strengthen, rather than dilute, students' cultural identity. Forty-seven experienced science teachers in two regions were interviewed and observed in class. The worry behind the study is that imported digital tools may flatten local culture out of lessons.

Teachers did not see AI as a mere delivery pipe for facts. They described using it to root science ideas in local settings, stories, and values, making lessons more interactive and group-based, and helping them judge learning in more responsive ways. The authors are careful: these are teachers' perceptions and observed practices, gathered through an inductive thematic analysis, not proof of student outcomes. They frame AI as a cultural bridge when teachers steer it deliberately, and call for designs that build local content in from the start.
plos-pone-0353877:
Xolelwa Dyani, Olanrewaju Oladimeji, and Moreoagae Bertha Randa publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for strengthening school teams that support teenagers' mental health in South Africa's Gauteng province. About one in seven adolescents worldwide lives with a mental health condition, and schools are where help can reach them earliest. The study focuses on the support teams already inside secondary schools.

The plan unfolds in stages: questionnaires to map how common learners' difficulties are, a review of existing interventions, then interviews with team members about what works and what fails. From that evidence the team will build and roll out a quality-improvement intervention. The protocol matters because it designs the fix with the schools, not for them.
plos-pone-0354177:
Shaoshuai Hou and six colleagues study how to quieten herringbone planetary gearboxes, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering paper. These compact gear systems drive wind turbines, aircraft engines, and ship propulsion, but vibration and noise limit them. The team examined a design whose teeth are staggered in phase between the two halves of the herringbone pattern, and derived formulas for how mesh stiffness changes over time.

Staggering the teeth clearly improved vibration behaviour in their models. Speed changes and manufacturing errors mattered too, and one error type, a tangential slip on a single tooth, dominated the rest. The findings give gearbox designers a practical lever for smoother, longer-lasting transmissions.
plos-pone-0354277:
Sukpornsawan and colleagues, in a 2026 study, explore how computers can recognize antibiotic packages in Thai pharmacies. Look-alike packaging is a safety risk when staff check medicines by eye under time pressure. Their approach reads both the look of a package and the words printed on it.

Thirty-six products were photographed and measured for traits such as image complexity, how much of the package is printed area, and how confidently a text reader could read the words. A clustering method sorted the packages into nine groups with shared traits. Packages in a middle range for complexity and printed area were recognized most consistently, and text reading confidence mattered too. A second analysis rated which groups used their inputs most efficiently. The authors offer their framework as a structured way to judge packaging for automated checking systems.
plos-pone-0354377:
Oluwakemi Tomobi and co-authors tested clinical simulation as a booster for basic science learning among pre-health students. Interest in science fades through schooling in the United States, most sharply for underrepresented students, and weak science foundations block health careers. Their 2026 study added team-based emergency simulations after traditional lectures.

Students rotated through healthcare team roles in four scenarios, from drug overdose to stroke and cardiac emergency. Checklists assessed their performance, and tests before and after measured understanding and recall. Tomobi and colleagues examined whether the format was feasible and welcomed by students. They frame simulation as an equity tool: vivid practice may hold the students whom lectures alone lose.
plos-pone-0354477:
Verma and colleagues present a 2026 profile of WHiSE 2.0, a study of Indigenous people who use drugs in three northern Ontario cities. Indigenous people face deep health gaps tied to colonial history. The study, led with Indigenous guidance, asks what harm reduction, meaning steps to cut the harms of drug use, looks like in their lives.

About three hundred fifty people in Sudbury, Thunder Bay, and Sault Ste Marie answered an hour-long survey. Most identified as First Nations. Housing was shaky for many: large shares slept on the street, in shelters, or on couches. Smoking drugs was the most common route, with injecting also common. Even so, most people knew what harm reduction meant, and most had been tested for HIV and hepatitis C. Many took part in ceremonies, and some said cultural teachings shaped their safety practices. The profile sets up follow-up work on regional service gaps.
plos-pone-0354677:
Youngjae Lee and four colleagues published this 2026 pilot trial on helping older adults recover balance after a trip. Thirty community-dwelling volunteers practiced either a simple step training that needs no special gear, standard treadmill trip training, or no training, then faced induced trips on a laboratory walkway.

The step training group recovered with a longer and faster first step than the untrained group. Lee cautions that the sample was small and harness use differed between groups. Still, a low-cost routine that sharpens the rescue step could bring trip training beyond specialized labs if a bigger trial confirms it.
plos-pone-0354877:
Jenny Paola Alfaro-García led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of how dengue virus can damage blood vessel walls from a distance. Fluid taken from infected cells was applied to vessel lining cells, and gene activity plus computer network modeling traced the response over time.

The fluid briefly switched on inflammation, then turned toward repair and tissue rebuilding, while pushing lining cells toward a different cell identity. Two molecules, a signaling protein and a structural one, sat at the network's center. Alfaro-García links this sequence to the leaking vessels of severe dengue.
plos-pone-0354977:
Aditi Moudgil, Shalli Rani, and Fazlullah Khan tackle computing decisions for connected vehicles in this 2026 paper. Cars now offload heavy computation to roadside edge servers, but someone must decide which tasks go where, fast, and in a way engineers can audit. Their framework optimizes task placement and resource allocation together, driven by an algorithm they call GTGO, and adds a module that explains how much each decision variable mattered.

As the number of task-generating vehicles grew, the framework improved overall system welfare by roughly a fifth over baseline approaches and cut average task delay a lot. The optimizer settled quickly, within a few dozen rounds, and the explanations came without hurting performance. The authors present the package as a clear option for smart transport systems.
plos-pone-0355277:
Helene Smith and co-authors interview professional staff about why women in and just out of prison in New South Wales, Australia, struggle to get contraception care. Women with prison histories face higher rates of pregnancy and abortion and poorer birth outcomes than other women, pointing to unmet need. A dozen health and case staff described what helps and what blocks care during custody and the fragile weeks after release.

Staff pictured fertility as interrupted by prison itself, then swamped by unstable housing and competing demands after release. They asked for options that are easy to reach, reversible, and gentle, plus counseling that respects the woman's own timing. Inside prison, service structure itself blocked access in ways the interviews detail. Smith and colleagues argue release planning must treat contraception as core health care.
plos-pone-0355377:
Qianqian Jia and colleagues run in 2026 a blinded trial of a chest wall nerve block for patients having keyhole surgery to clear the bile duct. One group received the block guided by ultrasound before general anaesthesia, and the other received none. Pain scores and use of a patient controlled pain pump in the first day were the main measures.

Pain at rest and on movement was lower in the block group at several early time points, and pump use fell as well. The block covered the expected skin zones, and one strong pain drug was needed less during surgery. By one day, pain scores no longer differed.
plos-pone-0355477:
Shazia Humayun and co-authors asked whether feeling called to one's work lifts whole teams, not just individuals. They surveyed workers in Pakistani manufacturing, gathering answers from nearly two hundred employees grouped in forty-nine teams. Their 2026 study drew on field theory to trace how personal calling might travel into team results.

Calling did reach team performance, and the bridge was collaborative crafting, where teammates reshape their work together in a self-managing way. The effect grew stronger where leader-member exchange, the quality of the boss-worker relationship, ran high. Humayun and colleagues say calling research should move up a level: meaning at work pays off partly through what teammates build jointly.
plos-pone-0355677:
Jong Yun and colleagues present in 2026 a trial plan for patients having stomach cancer surgery in Korea, testing whether extra protein in vein feeding aids recovery. People having planned removal of the stomach will receive either protein rich or standard vein feeding around surgery. Feeding goes through a vein in the arm for several days.

The main check compares how well the body holds onto nitrogen, a sign of protein balance, a few days after surgery. Other checks cover nutrition, muscle size, blood sugar, problems after surgery, and return to function. As a protocol, it gives methods and reasoning, not results.
plos-pone-0356177:
Tao Zhao and five colleagues test how printer settings affect the strength of 3D-printed carbon fiber composites, in this 2026 study. Their material mixes continuous carbon fiber into a common biodegradable plastic and is printed layer by layer. The team varied the printer nozzle size and the share of fiber in the part, then pulled specimens apart and examined the breaks under an electron microscope.

Parts with fiber snapped with almost no stretching, while plain plastic deformed visibly first. The larger nozzle produced much stronger parts, and strength rose steadily as fiber content increased, thanks to even fiber placement and tight bonding between fiber and plastic. Weighing strength against cost, the authors name a mid-level fiber share as the sweet spot. They see the lightweight, partly plant-based composite suiting uses from vehicle parts to custom medical devices.
plos-pone-0356277:
Zahra Toghiyani and co-authors asked what shapes sexual joy for newlywed couples in Iran. Social rules and private life both play a part, but local proof was thin. Their 2026 study spoke with thirty-one newlyweds, some as couples, till no new themes came up in the talks.

Three themes ran through the talks. Rules learned before marriage, with strong taboos, still weighed on couples. Each partner's deep beliefs about sex shaped ease and hopes. Power and choice formed the third theme: who starts, who decides, and how fair it feels. Toghiyani and colleagues say classes before marriage should deal with these social and private layers head-on, not teach body facts alone.
plos-pone-0356377: Shallal and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on students teaching bioethics to fellow students. The teaching happened during clinical rotations, when students work with real patients. From this case study, the authors draw three lessons meant to travel to other schools. They frame the lessons with a tool called CFIR, used to study how new practices take hold.
plos-pone-0356477:
Xinru Guo and three colleagues ask whether a soy compound changes how a blood marker of vessel stress relates to heart risk, in this 2026 analysis. The marker, called EASIX, reflects stress on the endothelium, the lining of blood vessels. The team compared people's estimated ten-year cardiovascular risk across levels of genistein, a plant compound from soy, measured in urine. Statistical models adjusted for other influences and tested how the relationships curved.

Higher vessel stress scores went with higher estimated risk overall. The link differed modestly by genistein level: a significant interaction appeared, though the association was only slightly weaker in the high-genistein group, and the shape of the curve differed between groups. The authors are explicit that these are hypothesis-generating findings from a single analysis, not evidence that soy intake changes anyone's risk.
plos-pone-0356777:
Maciej J Ejsmond led a team of six authors studying common eider ducks in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Ducklings of this sea duck can suffer from a lack of thiamine, a vitamin vital for nerves and energy. The team asked how the mother's diet affects that risk in her young.

Ejsmond's group found that risk rises when females eat large prey. That prey-size link gives conservation staff a concrete dietary factor behind poor chick health. Where eider numbers are falling, understanding food links helps target protection. The study also shows how a mother's foraging choices, shaped by changing seas, can pass effects to the next generation before the ducklings feed at all.
plos-pone-0356877:
Luya Yang, Min Zhang, and Yaxian Gao built a three-part system for spotting defects on steel plate surfaces in real time. Flaws hide in low-contrast images on the factory floor. Genuine defect photos are also scarce. Their 2026 study attacks both problems. An adaptive step boosts contrast by merging color channels by information content. A generative network then synthesizes extra defect examples for training.

The detector itself is a slimmed-down version of a current YOLO model. It uses ghost convolutions and attention to stay fast. Together the pipeline lifted detection accuracy by several points. It cut parameters by about a fifth. It reached strong scores at a few milliseconds per image. Steel makers could run such a system on the line without slowing production.
plos-pone-0357077:
The PLOS One Editors retracted this systematic review and meta-analysis in 2026. The review had pooled studies claiming that sensory art therapies ease anxiety around root canal treatment in highly anxious dental patients. A retraction means the journal has withdrawn the article as unreliable, and its conclusions should not be used.

Editors found the review lumped together very different interventions, from virtual reality and aromatherapy to yoga and aerobic exercise, so any pooled effect could not be credited to a specific therapy. Several included studies also failed the review's own eligibility rules, enrolling routine dental patients or testing exercise rather than art therapy. With its evidence base misassembled, the analysis could not support its claims.
plos-pone-0357277:
Kristina Anna Djupvik Aakvik leads a team of eight linking birth records to later physical activity in Norway, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Babies born early face many health questions, and whether they grow into less active children and adults was unclear. The researchers joined the national birth registry to a large regional health study, giving nearly thirteen thousand participants aged thirteen to fifty-two whose movement was measured by wearable sensors for a week.

Each extra week of gestation predicted slightly more light activity per day, an effect clearest in females, and more total activity among adolescents. Birth weight, by contrast, showed no relationship with later movement once examined on its own. The differences per week are small, but across a population they suggest early birth leaves a faint, lasting fingerprint on everyday activity. The authors frame it as one more reason to support activity in those born preterm.
plos-pone-0357377:
Mingyu Ji and coauthors published a 2026 diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE on a single-tube test that names six common respiratory pathogens at once. Since the COVID pandemic, respiratory infections have resurged, and treatment depends on knowing which germ is responsible. Their assay combines real-time PCR with melting-curve analysis of fluorescent probes, distinguishing two flu types, respiratory syncytial virus, rhinovirus, adenovirus, and a mycoplasma bacterium in one run.

Against a panel of fifty-seven other pathogens, the test never gave a false identification, and it detected each target at very low copy numbers. Repeat measurements were tight and consistent. On several hundred throat samples, it matched or beat a commercial kit, with agreement statistics near perfect, and it proved more sensitive for several of the targets and more precise for rhinovirus. The assay is proposed for hospital laboratories needing fast, high-throughput answers during respiratory virus season.
plos-pone-0357577:
Melissa Lagger and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a Swiss cohort study on a timely question. Do GLP-1 receptor agonists, the blockbuster diabetes and weight-loss drugs, affect pancreatic cysts that can turn cancerous?? These cysts, called IPMNs, are increasingly common findings, and the same drugs are now taken by millions, yet their effect on existing pancreatic lesions is unknown. Three Swiss hospitals will pool records from 2010 to mid-2026.

Patients will be sorted into four groups by drug exposure and cyst status, and cyst progression will be judged by international radiological criteria. The study also tracks tumor markers, pancreatitis episodes, progression to advanced precancer or cancer, and operations triggered. The authors are frank about limits: with only a few dozen patients expected in the key group, the study may be too small for firm answers. Even so, a carefully measured signal beats the current evidence vacuum.
plos-pone-0357977:
Anvar Sadath and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a systematic review on what happens after non-suicidal self-injury. Self-injury without intent to die is common in young people and linked to later suicide attempts, but past reviews blurred distinct outcomes together. The planned review insists on time order, including only studies where self-injury clearly came before a later attempt or death.

The team will search five major databases for observational studies, with two reviewers extracting data and rating bias independently. Because the studies will likely differ too much for pooled statistics, results will be synthesized as a structured narrative. The review will also track whether features of the self-injury, such as frequency or method, track with graver later outcomes. The registered protocol's sharper focus, its authors hope, will improve risk assessment and safety planning in clinics.
plos-pone-0358077:
M. Kristen Hall and coauthors published a 2026 cell study in PLOS ONE on how sugar chains on proteins shape neuroblastoma, a childhood nerve-cell cancer. Cancers often carry simpler sugar coatings, and the team focused on the enzyme that starts branching these chains. Using gene editing, they crippled that enzyme in a human neuroblastoma cell line, then compared growth, sticking, and invasion against the original cells.

The mutants carried more of the simple sugar type and fewer branched forms, and restoring the enzyme reversed that. Their growth changed surprisingly: slower when sparse and unattached, yet faster in crowded dishes and three-dimensional cell balls. They also clung together more strongly and invaded more aggressively. Fed a growth signal, the mutants responded far more strongly than the parent line. Weakening this enzyme, they say, makes these cancer cells more dangerous in several ways, a caution for sugar-targeting therapies.
plos-pone-0358177:
Kevin Thomas leads a team of eight laying out the PANEM trial in PLOS ONE in 2026, a large test of digestive enzyme supplements after stomach removal surgery. Patients who lose part or all of the stomach often digest food poorly, because meals and pancreatic enzymes no longer meet in the right order. Weight loss, discomfort, and fatty stools follow. Whether routinely swallowing replacement enzymes with meals improves life quality has never been settled in a proper trial.

PANEM will enroll one hundred eighty-eight adults across several centers and assign them by chance, in secret, to enzyme capsules or identical placebos taken with meals. The main yardstick is cancer specific quality of life, especially physical functioning, after six months. Weight, extra nutrition use, and blood measures of nourishment count as secondary outcomes. The protocol gives surgeons and dietitians the design from which a long missing answer should come.
plos-pone-0358477:
Dipika Chandra leads a team of five reviewing why elderly villagers in Bangladesh struggle to use primary health care, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The reviewers registered their plan, searched several databases in March 2026, and sifted more than two thousand articles down to nineteen that met their rules. Barriers were then sorted through a social ecological lens, which stacks causes from the individual outward to national policy.

Five levels of obstacle emerged. Personal barriers included failing physical capability, empty pockets, and not knowing what services exist. Family barriers included weak family connection, relatives controlling health decisions, and gender inequality inside the household. Organizational, community, and policy barriers stacked above those. The authors argue that fixing clinics alone will not move elderly patients who are stopped first at home. Effective reform in rural Bangladesh must work on every level of the stack at once.
plos-pone-0358777:
Yan Zhu and four colleagues tackle a weakness in synthetic voices that must sound emotional, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Zero shot systems can copy a new speaker. Yet feelings often blur into the words. Their fix separates the two streams. Text meaning and emotional tone travel through parallel attention paths and merge only at a controlled gate, so neither corrupts the other during generation.

They also built a fine grained emotion space of sixteen classes, sorted from pitch and energy patterns in speech. During training, the system dwells on its hardest examples. Samples with unusually high loss get extra weight. Tested on speakers the system had never heard, using a standard emotional speech collection, it produced words with a low error rate and clean sound measures. The design targets expressive voices for media and assistance tools.
plos-pone-0358877:
Md Parvej Hussain leads a team of six measuring how a small start in life shadows children's nutrition across South Asia, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The authors used recent demographic and health surveys from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal, and the Maldives. They matched children of low birth weight with similar children of normal weight. The total passed one hundred forty-seven thousand cases. Then they compared five forms of malnutrition.

About sixteen percent of the children had been born small. After matching, low birth weight was significantly associated with every form examined: stunting, wasting, underweight, having at least one form, and suffering several at once. The pattern held country by country with one exception, wasting in Bangladesh and the Maldives, where the link lost significance. The authors say preventing low birth weight itself, through maternal care, is the lever that moves all five outcomes together.
plos-pone-0359277: Santo and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the microbes of the horse gut. They profiled the small compounds those microbes make along the whole digestive tract. Horses were fed in three ways: pasture, hay, or rations with added oats. Diet shapes the gut's chemistry, and those compounds affect the horse's health. The profiles give vets and owners a fuller picture of feeding effects.
plos-pone-0359577: Kotan and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on filling gaps in health data. Records often miss values, and the reason for the gaps changes what fix works. The team tested a method called CHIT, a cyclical hybrid approach, under three missing-data patterns. They used health data sets as the test ground. Honest tests of gap filling matter because filled values quietly shape later findings.
plos-pone-0359777:
David Calzada, Laura Martín-López, and Jerónimo Carnés published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus, the house dust mite whose droppings trigger many allergies. The authors use genetic and microbiomics approaches to monitor the growth of mite cultures and the environmental influences on them.

Laboratories grow these mites to produce allergy test and treatment materials, so culture quality matters. Tracking both the mites' genes and their microbes can reveal why batches thrive or fail. Allergen manufacturers and researchers standardizing mite material are the readers for monitoring methods of this kind.
plos-pone-0360077:
Randa Al-Kharabsheh and Muayyad Ahmad built in 2026 a large scale artificial intelligence analysis to predict which neurology patients will return to hospital without planning to. Unplanned readmissions are costly and often signal that something in the first stay or the discharge plan went wrong. The authors use CHAID decision trees, a method that sorts patients into risk groups through a branching series of questions.

A decision tree has an advantage over many AI tools: doctors can read its reasoning and see which factors drove a prediction. If such a model proves accurate, hospitals could aim follow up calls, home support, and medication reviews at the patients most likely to bounce back. The work joins a wider push to make hospital prediction tools explainable.
pmc-10517477:
Alowais, Alghamdi, Alsuhebany, and co-authors survey how artificial intelligence is entering clinical practice. Health care is complex for patients, doctors, and hospitals alike. The authors argue that fast gains in these computer systems could improve care and daily life for patients if used well.

Inside, the review walks through where such tools can plug into medical work, from reading scans to easing routine tasks. It also weighs the care needed before hospitals trust them widely. For clinicians and students, the piece offers a broad, plain map of a fast-moving field and the choices it now forces.
pmc-13122077:
Yan-Bo Fu is first author on a 2026 randomized trial of a traditional Chinese herbal formula for leg artery disease. In lower limb arteriosclerosis obliterans, leg arteries narrow and harden, and reopening them by catheter often fails again over time. The formula, Danggui Sini Decoction, was added to standard care.

Thirty-eight patients at one hospital were split evenly between standard vessel reopening alone and the same care plus the decoction. At one month, overall success rates were alike, though quality of life improved more with the formula. At six months, the formula group had higher success and better vessel openness rates. The authors claim mid-term benefit and lower re-narrowing risk.
pmc-13196977:
John Owuoth and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study on new HIV infections in western Kenya. HIV rates in Kisumu County run over four times the national mean. The team enrolled adults with more than one recent sexual partner to measure how often new infections occur.

They followed 619 adults without HIV, testing them every three months for up to two years. Eleven new infections occurred over the follow-up span. The rate was lower than the team expected. Having four or more partners and forced sexual activity linked to higher risk in early checks. The authors credit prevention work, wider treatment, and regular counseling for the lower rate.
pmc-13197277:
Chernkhuan Stonsaovapak and colleagues wrote a 2026 review with network analysis on sensory cues for walking in Parkinson disease. Parkinson disease slows gait and shortens steps. External cues, such as lights, sounds, or touch pulses, can steady walking, but which type works best was unclear.

The team pooled thirty-three trials with more than eleven hundred patients. Touch-based and visual cues each raised walking speed versus control care. Visual, touch-based, and sound cues each lengthened stride. Rankings put touch cues first for speed and visual cues first for stride length. Both beat sound cues alone. The ranking gives clinics a clear order for choosing cue types.
pmc-13197477:
Christian Hoehne and colleagues ran a 2026 training study with a printed model for gum splinting. Periodontal splinting binds loose teeth to steady neighbors. Dental students need safe practice before treating patients, so the team built a low-cost printed jaw with movable front teeth.

Forty-three fourth-year students each made two splints in a crossover course, using two fiber materials in random order. Students rated the course good and highly relevant to real care. Felt readiness rose from poor before the course to good after it. Tooth placement accuracy did not differ by material or by session order. The cheap model offers repeatable practice under lifelike looseness.
pmc-13201077:
Yuuki Y Watanabe and colleagues tracked Greenland sharks after longline release in a 2026 study. Greenland sharks grow extremely slowly and mature late, so fishery bycatch could threaten them. Few studies had combined stress measures with long survival tracking in one species, so the team did both in Arctic waters.

They used hook timers, blood tests, motion sensors, and acoustic plus satellite tags. Blood stress markers sat within normal ranges for kin species. Released sharks swam faster with quicker tailbeats at first, then settled after about ten hours. Nine of ten tagged sharks survived past thirty days, with one tracked for years. Careful handling, they stress, keeps survival high.
pmc-13241377:
Geng and co-authors at Qilu argue hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries need start-to-finish thinking. Hard carbon's graphitic patches, nanopores, and defects jointly decide sodium storage. Most studies tune one stage, feedstock, firing, or coating, on its own. Those lone gains often fade once combined.

The review maps how early choices shape what later steps can achieve. Coupling points between stages offer the real gains for synergy. Factory output needs steady batches, which piecemeal tuning cannot deliver. The authors call for hard numbers linking structure to performance, and joint design across stages, in future work.
pmc-13242477:
Jazmín Viteri-Echeverría and co-authors asked how well nuts and seeds digest for people with cystic fibrosis. Their paper appeared in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2026. Cystic fibrosis disrupts digestion, so high-energy foods like nuts could help if the body can break them down. The team simulated digestion and colon fermentation in the lab for almonds, hazelnuts, peanuts, and sunflower seeds, using conditions modeled on the disease and gut microbes from child donors.

Sunflower seeds came out best, matching peanuts on fat breakdown and leading on protein breakdown under cystic fibrosis conditions. Their fermentation also shifted gut microbe mixes and raised output of helpful short-chain fatty acids. Almonds digested poorly, possibly because of natural compounds that block enzymes. Hazelnuts fell between the extremes. The authors single out sunflower seeds as a promising food for children with the condition.
pmc-13242977:
Harris Butler, John Rice, and Nichole Carlson compared statistical methods for watching whether doctors follow safety rules on a risky pain drug. Their paper appeared in Learning Health Systems in 2026. Tapentadol extended release, an opioid under a federal risk program, was tracked in Colorado claims data from 2012 to 2019. The cohort held 2,702 first-time patients, and the surveillance watched prescribing rates and dosing correctness every two weeks.

A classical control-chart method and the team's modified version were run side by side at the same false-alarm setting. The modified method, which watches for the model going wrong rather than raw counts, flagged more genuine shifts. Its detections also lined up better in time with outside policy actions affecting the drug. The authors propose the approach for regulators who want their own early warning on prescribing behavior. It complements, rather than replaces, the drug makers' own safety assessments.
pmc-13243177:
Vidya Mullangi and colleagues describe how a fast-clearing drug bridged a mother to a cesarean after a heart attack in pregnancy. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. At twenty-nine weeks pregnant, the thirty-nine-year-old woman suffered a heart attack from a blocked front artery of the heart. A stent restored flow, and she started two blood-thinning drugs that protect stents but complicate surgery.

Her earlier cesarean had used a vertical cut, so a cesarean was required less than three months after the stent. Stopping the thinners risked a clot; continuing them risked bleeding. The team bridged the gap with cangrelor, a platelet blocker given by vein that wears off within hours. The cesarean at thirty-seven weeks went ahead under that cover. Four months later she remained free of complaints. The authors believe this is the first bridge reported for cesarean birth.
pmc-13243877:
Keyuan Chen, Wulin Ma, and Lei Lei traced an outbreak of colistin resistance through a captive breeding center for the endangered crested ibis. Their study appeared in Transboundary and Emerging Diseases in 2026. Colistin is a last-resort antibiotic, and its resistance gene mcr-1 rides plasmids that jump between bacteria. From 2017 to 2024 the team screened 2,660 ibis samples at the center in Deqing, China, and sequenced what they found.

Resistance flared only once: detected in spring 2021, it peaked that summer in a quarter of samples, then faded by autumn. Wild egrets visiting the site carried the same gene at even higher rates, and one egret strain matched an ibis strain to the last core gene difference of zero. A staff dog and the center's sewage also tested positive; water and feed fish did not. Every deep-checked isolate resisted multiple drugs. Egrets, the authors conclude, were the likely couriers.
pmc-13246777:
Guo and Xue review mitochondria as command centers of innate immunity in this 2026 Communications Biology article. Mitochondria are famous as the cell's power plants, but under stress or infection they also release internal molecules that act as danger signals. Those signals feed three major defense pathways, including the cGAS-STING alarm, the NLRP3 inflammasome, and an antiviral relay anchored on the mitochondria themselves.

Because the pathways meet on one organelle, the cell's energy state and its immune state stay tightly coupled. The authors argue this hub role helps explain inflammatory and autoimmune disease when the signaling misfires. They call for new imaging tools that can watch danger signals leave mitochondria in living tissue, opening routes to targeted immune therapies.
pmc-13248977:
Kong and colleagues engineered a two-in-one nanoparticle against liver cancer, reported in 2026. The carrier is a porous polydopamine particle loaded with evodiamine, a plant alkaloid with anticancer activity but poor uptake, plus a dye that heats up under near-infrared light. Two added tags steer the particle first to tumors and then to mitochondria, the cell's power stations.

Under laser light, the particles imaged tumors clearly and attacked them with heat and drug together. The combined hit collapsed mitochondrial voltage and released signals that trigger cell suicide. Tumors in animals shrank strongly. The authors present the design as a template for pairing imaging with combination therapy.
pmc-13249777:
Dörr and colleagues compare two kinds of older epilepsy patients in Berlin clinics, in a 2026 Journal of Neurology study. Some people reach old age having lived with epilepsy since youth, while others develop it late. The records of two hundred forty-three patients aged sixty-five and over, seen between 2010 and 2025, were split by age at onset to test whether the groups still differ.

Half of the lifelong group were seizure free, against more than two thirds of the late-onset group. Lifelong patients also carried a higher total drug dose. The authors suggest that in seizure-free older patients with decades-old epilepsy, carefully trimming medication may be worth considering, a decision usually avoided for fear of relapse.
pmc-13249977:
Neumann, Diekmann, and Lauenstein measured joint fluid messengers across arthritis stages in dogs, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. Their dogs developed osteoarthritis after a torn knee ligament, and the team scored joint damage during surgery. The guiding idea is bold: osteoarthritis may be less a wearing-out than a bone repair process gone wrong, resembling fracture healing that never finishes.

One messenger, interleukin-6, fell significantly as damage advanced, fitting a shift from inflammation toward repair. Three bone-related markers moved in stage-consistent directions without reaching significance. The authors read the combined picture as support for the repair-gone-wrong view, while asking for bigger, longer studies to confirm it.
pmc-13250177:
Chehab and co-authors study whether ethnicity shapes outcomes for patients with a leaking heart valve in South London. Their 2026 Open Heart paper follows adults with moderate or worse mitral regurgitation, where blood flows backward through the mitral valve. Records came from one large hospital center and covered diagnoses made between 2010 and 2023.

Among more than six thousand patients, Black patients were younger, poorer on average, and more often had valve leaks caused by other heart disease. Crude death and surgery rates differed between the ethnic groups. After statistical adjustment, ethnicity itself was not linked to death or to receiving an operation, while poverty measures were. The authors urge better valve detection in minority communities and action on the social drivers of heart health.
pmc-13250877:
Hamza and a large team test fatty acid compounds as possible prevention or treatment for throat gonorrhea. Their 2026 Emerging Microbes and Infections study responds to rising drug resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae and few options for throat infections. Five throat and mouth cell lines were infected with two gonorrhea strains in the laboratory.

Two arginine-based fatty acids stood out, killing bacteria fast without harming any of the cell lines at tested doses. Applied after infection, they cleared more than nine tenths of bacteria within thirty minutes to two hours in most cell types. Applied before infection, one compound prevented most infections within half an hour. The authors propose topical use around sexual exposure as a future transmission reducer, pending human studies.
pmc-13251077:
Yılmaz and Yeşil publish this 2026 correction in BMC Oral Health for their study of short-term dental work made by three methods. The first paper weighed edge fit and fracture strength across printed, milled, and handmade methods. Two microscope images in the paper turned out to be wrong.

On re-checking their first image set, the authors found that two scanning scope images had been copied by mistake while the figures were put together. They picked out the right image for the aged milled group, and the fixed figure appears with this notice. The authors regret the slip and stress the error was limited to the figures alone. Results and findings stand as they were.
pmc-13253877:
Zebing Mao and a large team build a self-aware tensegrity robot in a 2026 study. Tensegrity structures mix stiff bars with stretchy cables, making light, strong frames suited to rough places. Their six-bar version carries 24 flexible sensors and a fine-tuned large language model, a type of AI trained on text and images.

The system can rebuild its own shape from its sensing tendons, with no outside sensors. It sends data to an iPhone for wireless checks and uses the AI model for fault finding and plain-language answers. The authors see promise for exploration tasks where human help is far away.
pmc-13253977:
Fahmida Akter and colleagues measure newborn sepsis in a 2026 study in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Sepsis is a life-threatening body-wide infection, and newborns in low-income settings face high risk. The team studied 125 babies in a neonatal intensive care unit at a tertiary hospital from December 2023 to July 2024.

Sepsis was found in 69.6 percent of the babies, with early-onset cases at 60.9 percent. Low birth weight raised the odds sharply, as did lower mother schooling, low family income, and home delivery. The authors urge stronger mother education, more births in facilities, and wider studies across centers.
pmc-13254377:
Tim Lehmann and co-authors study balance control after knee surgery in a 2026 paper. Athletes who had anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, 17 in total, were compared with 13 healthy controls. All stood through 100 surprise platform shifts while hip motion and brain signals were recorded by mobile EEG.

The surgery group showed higher hip acceleration during early adjustment and late re-stabilizing. Brain response signals were larger, and information flow in a front-central network dipped early then rose later. The authors read this as more effortful, less automatic control, which may raise re-injury risk.
pmc-13257677:
Alexandr Shchemelev and colleagues hunt for the parts of HIV-1 that barely change, however much the virus mutates elsewhere. Stable regions matter because they keep the virus working and could anchor future drugs or vaccines. Their 2026 study scores conservation across every major viral protein.

They analyzed more than a thousand full viral genomes spanning the main subtypes. An entropy score flagged columns where sequences stayed nearly identical, and two search methods mapped the conserved stretches. The Pol and Gag proteins held the most, including enzyme centers and binding sites. The authors present these stretches as candidate targets needing lab validation.
pmc-13257777:
Lukas Kühn leads the authors of a 2026 protocol for a three-round Delphi study on advanced practice physiotherapists in German tertiary care. Tertiary care means highly specialized hospital care. Advanced practice roles for physiotherapists are well tested in basic muscle and joint care, but are still new in German hospitals. The study aims to name the best practice areas for these roles and agree on the skills and core abilities they need.

Experts will answer online surveys over three rounds, rating items on a seven-point scale, with agreement set at seventy percent or more. Data collection ran from January to May 2026: 98 experts were invited, 37 finished round one, 34 round two, and 32 round three. The findings are meant to guide how these roles are built in Germany.
pmc-13258677:
Samet Tosun and Emre Çulha asked two chatty AI models to name dental instruments from photographs. Identifying root-canal files by eye is a small but real clinical skill. Their 2026 study pits ChatGPT-4o against Gemini 3 Flash on five file systems, fifty rounds each.

Both models also had to justify each call by describing the tool's shape. Gemini 3 Flash recognized more files correctly and answered far more consistently across repeats. ChatGPT-4o wobbled notably between identical viewings. Neither, the authors conclude, is steady enough to work unsupervised in a clinic yet. The contest does show how fast visual AI is closing in on specialist tasks.
pmc-13260777:
Sophia S Muhali leads a 2026 case report of pregnancy with complex heart disease present from birth, not yet repaired. Her condition, pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, means the lung artery is missing and a large hole connects the heart's lower chambers, so lung blood flow depends on side vessels. Survival to adulthood without repair is rare. At thirty-two weeks, the 22-year-old came in with worsening breathlessness, heart failure, and blood oxygen of only seventy-four percent.

Imaging showed the defect, an overriding aorta, and non-joined lung arteries arising from the aorta. She had a caesarean delivery as her state worsened, then heavy bleeding after birth needing hysterectomy. Ten days later she suffered a stroke from blocked blood flow, but improved with blood-thinning drugs and supportive care. She remained stable at six months. The authors stress advice before pregnancy and full-team care in such cases.
pmc-13261977:
Miu Suzuki and colleagues explore a little-studied exercise molecule in the urine of healthy young adults. BAIBA, released by working muscle, has been linked in animals to fat browning and better glucose handling. Their 2026 brief report measures it in blood and day-long urine from fifteen volunteers.

Blood levels registered in only a third of participants, while urine captured the molecule in everyone. People with measurable blood BAIBA excreted about five times more in urine. Habitual breakfast skippers also showed higher urinary levels. Urine may track the body's BAIBA status more faithfully than blood, the authors suggest, pending bigger studies.
pmc-13262577:
Yujing Gu and colleagues ask what gives nursing students a firm professional identity. Three hundred sixty-one nursing interns in mainland China completed questionnaires on life meaning, death attitudes, and peer support. Their 2026 cross-sectional study models how these inner resources connect.

Students richer in life meaning held stronger professional identities, as did those at peace with death. Fearful death attitudes pulled identity the other way. Both kinds of death attitude partly carried meaning's effect into identity. Friends' support strengthened the direct link between meaning and identity, though it did not change the death-attitude routes. Mentoring and meaning-making both look like useful levers.
pmc-13263277:
Jia-Shu Chen and co-authors review the brain mapping protocol used during glioma surgery at their San Francisco center in a 2026 journal article. Gliomas are brain tumors, and removing as much as possible while sparing movement and language is the goal. Mapping means stimulating the brain during surgery to find tissue that must be preserved. Their protocol has evolved over decades.

Before surgery, brain scans and function tests are loaded into a navigation system used throughout the operation. During removal, electrical stimulation tests of movement and language guide each step, under awake or asleep anesthesia as the task requires. Decisions to keep cutting rest on constant feedback as functional pathways near. Afterward, scans and exams help judge whether any deficits will be temporary or permanent.
pmc-13264577:
Alefe Luiz Caliani Carrera led a 2026 pilot trial in dogs of a stem cell product injected into the knee joint after bone surgery. The dogs had a common knee operation that levels the shin bone top after ligament damage. The product holds the helpful fluids stem cells release, without the cells themselves.

Twenty pet dogs were split by chance into a treated group and a dummy injection group, with neither owners nor vets knowing which was which. Treated dogs were less lame and in less pain by day 15, while the other group caught up near day 60 to 90. Joint wear scores rose in the control group but fell in the treated group. Bone healing at day 30 was also better with treatment. The authors see promise as an add-on therapy.
pmc-13264877:
Eva Kagenaar and co-authors wrote a 2026 protocol for the SORT study, which compares two strong treatments for bladder cancer that is confined to the organ but has grown into muscle. Both follow chemotherapy first: one removes the bladder, the other uses high-dose radiation and keeps it. A randomized trial failed to recruit, so proof must come from records.

The team will use the UK National Cancer Registry for patients treated from 2015 to 2021, linked to hospital, radiation, and drug records. They will copy a trial's rules on real-world data, a method called target trial emulation, and adjust for baseline differences. The main outcome is death from any cause at three years. Costs and cost-effectiveness will also be compared, along with death rates at five years.
pmc-13264977:
Zhanna Sarbassova led a 2026 report on a pilot training program in autism care for health workers in Kazakhstan. Children with autism need joined-up care from many professions, yet local training was scarce. A mixed team of specialists and parents built a 60-hour course covering detection, management, rehabilitation, and family support.

The pilot ran in Astana with 49 health professionals in two cohorts. After training, correct use of the newer diagnosis code system rose from about 74 to about 88 percent, and all doubt about that system vanished. Knowledge of autism subtypes grew, and recognition of who leads team care rose from about 29 to about 46 percent. Staff also reported better grasp of referral routes and family support tools. The authors present the course as a scalable model for Kazakhstan and similar settings.
pmc-13266577:
Li-Jia Liu and colleagues describe a new plant species in a 2026 paper from Sichuan, China. Field work in Yajiang County found a mint-family plant much like a known species but with clear differences. Its leaves, flower spikes, and small leaf-like bracts did not match the known plant.

The team checked 12 leaf and flower traits and read more than a thousand genes from 45 plant samples. Both lines of evidence marked the plant as a separate species, named Elsholtzia yajiangensis after its home county. It is known only from that one site so far. The authors list it as data deficient and warn that diversity in the Hengduan Mountains may be undercounted.
pmc-13267277:
Vittoria Vardanega and colleagues model prenatal testing for sickle cell disease in England in a 2026 paper. Current screening tests the mother, then the father, then offers invasive testing when both carry the gene. When the father cannot be tested, women may wait or miss out. A blood test of the mother alone, called non-invasive prenatal testing, could fill the gap.

Using a decision tree, the team set the lowest test accuracy a future study should demand. One scenario allowed under 10 missed cases a year nationally; a stricter one allowed at most 2. The stricter bar needed about 99 percent sensitivity. Both scenarios implied study sizes too large for a single forward-looking study. The authors suggest design workarounds for rare conditions.
pmc-13267977:
Yuya Saruta and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare liver growth in a young adult. Mesenchymal hamartoma is a harmless liver lesion usually seen in infants. Their patient was a 31-year-old woman whose screening ultrasound found a small liver mass. A year later it had grown from 23 to 68 millimeters, raising concern.

Her long use of birth control pills pointed doctors toward a hormone-linked liver tumor called adenoma. Scans showed a well-edged mass almost 75 millimeters wide near a large liver vein. Judging the growth risky, surgeons removed the rear section of the liver with robot help, vein included. Tissue study showed the harmless hamartoma, with fibrous tissue, spindle cells, and stray bile ducts, and no cancer. The case shows how this rare lesion can fool imaging.
pmc-13269177:
Yuki Morita and co-authors published a case series in 2026 on stomach surgery for patients with many small hormone-linked stomach tumors. These tumors often grow alongside an immune attack on the stomach lining. Removing the lower stomach cuts a hormone that feeds the tumors, but its value was unclear.

Eight patients treated from 2005 to 2023 were reviewed, with a median age of 60 years. Before surgery, most had more than 20 tumors, and hormone levels were very high. After surgery, the median hormone level fell from 4,800 to 68. Tumors shrank in two patients and vanished in six, with no return of disease or deaths during follow-up.
pmc-13269377:
Andres Marmol-Perez and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on muscle loss in young survivors of childhood cancer. This loss, called sarcopenia, combines weak grip strength with low muscle mass. The study asked whether survivors with muscle loss report worse quality of life.

The study included 116 survivors with an average age of 12.1 years. Grip strength and body scans sorted them into no, probable, and confirmed muscle loss groups. Most quality-of-life scores were alike across the groups. One clear gap stood out: girls without muscle loss scored better in total, physical, mental, and school life than girls with confirmed loss. No such pattern was reported for boys.
pmc-13269577:
Lukas Zierke and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on a cargo protein called CLN8 in acute pancreatitis, a sudden painful inflammation of the pancreas. CLN8 normally ferries digestive enzymes from their making site toward storage compartments. Using mouse cells and mice lacking the protein, the team watched how the disease unfolded without it.

Loss of CLN8 softened the early phase of the illness but did not prevent it. The key enzyme still reached its compartments and was partly activated, pointing to backup delivery routes. Later, injury grew worse, with more cell stress and more self-eating of damaged cell parts, shown by raised marker proteins. The authors say those later stress responses drive severity.
pmc-13269977:
Adam Wawrzeńczyk and co-authors published a review in 2026 on biomarkers for monitoring eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic immune disease of the food pipe. Symptoms match tissue activity poorly, so patients need repeated camera scopes. The review sorts candidate markers by body compartment: tissue, fluids near the tissue, and blood.

Signals tied to type 2 inflammation define the disease but measure weakly in blood. Tissue gene signatures and markers sampled close to the food pipe tracked inflammation and treatment response far better. Structural markers showed that tissue healing does not always mean the lining is restored. The authors propose combining molecular and low-burden tools to cut scope use, after prospective testing.
pmc-13270477:
Jaouad Nguadi and co-authors published a case report in 2026 about a 65-year-old man with advanced heart failure who received a CRT-D device, a pacemaker-defibrillator that resynchronizes the heart. The procedure used 50 milliliters of iodinated contrast dye and succeeded. Four hours later he developed spinal myoclonus, sudden generalized muscle jerks sensitive to touch.

His consciousness stayed clear and brain-wave tests were normal. Brain and spine MRI on day three showed no stroke, bleeding, or inflammation. Kidney function stayed stable. Fluids and clonazepam, a calming drug, brought complete resolution within 72 hours. At three months he had no nerve after-effects. The authors call it the first such case after this device procedure.
pmc-13270877:
Yulena Osorio-Navarro is lead author of a 2026 journal article reporting the whole genome of a new fungus species, Xylaria chamelensis. Specimens were collected from a legume family pod in tropical dry forest in Jalisco, Mexico. Xylaria fungi mostly live on dead matter, though some live inside plants or cause plant disease.

The team grew the fungus in pure culture, sequenced its genome, and compared it with relatives. The assembly spans 51.93 million DNA letters and predicts 11,238 protein-coding genes. Shape evidence plus genome evidence support naming it a new species, forming its own line in the Xylaria family tree. The data serve future work on fungal naming and plant links.
pmc-13271477:
Clare T. M. Doherty is lead author of a 2026 process study inside the STRENGTH trial. That trial tested a behaviour change programme inside cardiac rehab for people with heart disease. The study explored how participants experienced activity. It also asked what helped or hindered staying active, and how context shaped engagement.

Interviews and focus groups covered both trial groups. Attendance records and diaries checked how faithfully the programme was delivered. Both groups valued social support, staff oversight, and set sessions. The programme group added tailored support, outside accountability, and self-monitoring. Those raised awareness and confidence. Low exercise confidence, though, may have held back activity done alone.
pmc-13272977:
Liyang Jiang leads a 2026 real-world study of adebrelimab-based treatment as a first therapy for extensive-stage small cell lung cancer in China. This fast-growing lung cancer often spreads to brain or liver, groups often excluded from trials. The study enrolled 149 patients with brain spread, liver spread, or fluid around the lung.

Median time before the cancer grew was 6.47 months, and median survival was 13.77 months overall. Results were close to trial results for brain spread and fluid cases, but benefit looked limited for liver spread, where median survival was 10.51 months. Severe side effects occurred in 42.3 percent of patients, with no new safety signals found.
pmc-13273877:
Chen and colleagues argue that a very high ejection fraction in heart failure is a warning sign, not a strength. Their 2026 journal article studies 200 patients with supranormal ejection fraction. That means the heart pumps out 65 percent or more per beat.

Patients split into two phenotypes by cause. Group A, with 88 patients, had valve or blood pressure overload. Group B, with 112 patients, had intrinsic heart muscle disease. That group included hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and cardiac amyloidosis. Both groups had a median ejection fraction of 69 percent. Group B patients were younger, at 56.0 years on average versus 68.8 years in group A. Their hearts were stiffer, with worse event-free survival. The adjusted hazard ratio for that outcome was 3.91 in the fully adjusted model. The authors urge a red-flag workup for such patients.
pmc-13274077:
Christine Chin-jung Hsieh and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on a possible treatment for tuberous sclerosis complex in mice. The inherited disease switches a growth signal called mTOR too high, harming brain wiring and the myelin coating on nerve fibers. Many patients develop learning and behavior problems.

The team gave a drug named J4, which raises levels of the brain chemical adenosine, to mice carrying one faulty copy of the Tsc2 gene. Treated mice showed better thinking, less anxiety-like behavior, and healthier white matter on brain scans. Myelin looked stronger under the microscope, and key myelin proteins rose. Two overactive brain markers also fell toward normal.
pmc-13278477:
Dala N Daraghmeh leads a 2026 survey of pharmacists in Palestine on probiotics and prebiotics. These are products that add helpful gut microbes, or feed them. Pharmacists are easy-to-reach advisers on such goods, but their knowledge had not been measured locally. Four hundred of them filled in a survey on knowledge, attitudes, and daily practice.

Most showed moderate knowledge. About a third reached the high band, and about a tenth scored poorly. Views were positive: most believed the products give health benefits and were willing to recommend them. Advice habits varied, with weak access to proof and low confidence as barriers. Age, training on the topic, and prescription volume showed modest links to knowledge in adjusted analysis.
pmc-13279177:
Abdulwahid M. Salih and colleagues report a 2026 review built around two cases of thyroid cancer change. The cancer is papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer type. In rare cases it can shift to a harsher form inside neck lymph nodes, the glands that filter fluid. Both patients were women with neck swelling.

Each woman had full thyroid removal with neck node surgery. Tissue tests showed cancer that had changed form in the nodes, in one case to a squamous type and in the other to a high grade type. The team also reviewed seven past cases, with ages from fifty six to seventy nine years. Signs were most often neck lumps. The report warns that changed cancer in nodes needs prompt, full treatment.
pmc-13279277:
Tammy C. T. Lan and colleagues report a 2026 study of how aging breaks timing in the mouse ovary. The ovary cycles through egg growth, release and repair hundreds of times in life. How age upsets that fine team work in space and time was unclear. The team used a spatial gene read method that maps gene use at near cell scale.

They mapped twenty two mouse ovaries across cycle stages and ages, with more than six hundred thousand spots in all. New software let them track hundreds of eggs, egg sacs and post release bodies. Aging warped the place and time order of egg sac growth before cycles stopped. Immune cell shifts, swelling signals and loose tissue order all played a part. The maps show how local cell groups run ovary work.
pmc-13279477:
Anna Sofie Buhl Rasmussen and a large team report a 2026 study of a cancer drug in spinal fluid of young patients. The drug is imatinib, used in a blood cancer called acute lymphoblastic leukemia with a gene join. The cancer can return in the central nervous system, the brain and spinal cord. Adult data show imatinib enters spinal fluid poorly, yet child data are sparse.

The study ran at many centres and drew paired blood and spinal fluid samples over time. A precise lab method weighed the drug and its main active break down product in both fluids. Math models tracked levels across fluids and across visits. Young patients held the gene join type or a like type that may also respond. Sound child data can guide dose and choice of drugs that reach the brain better.
pmc-13279877: Soojung Jo and colleagues issue a 2026 correction to their study of political ideology and HPV vaccine awareness, based on a national health trends survey. The error sat in the author affiliations, where three units at Purdue University were merged in one line by mistake. The notice splits them back out: the School of Nursing, the Department of Public Health, and the Regenstrief Center for Healthcare Engineering, each in West Lafayette, Indiana.
