Author order and the study content stand as first published.
pmc-13280577:
Ade Herdian Putra and team write a 2026 letter on mental health care in palliative oncology nursing. They reply to a 2026 study by Ibrahim and Zaghamir, where a structured six week nurse led palliative intervention improved quality of life in older adults with cancer. The program cut distress and symptom burden as well. Its multi part design addressed physical, social, functional and spiritual domains at once. The letter raises a question the study invites but does not address.

Sessions three to six hold cognitive behavioral techniques, mindfulness strategies and emotional expression work. Coping with uncertainty and spiritual counseling also feature. These are structured interventions that, in most clinical and research contexts, call for special training in talk therapy or counseling. The letter asks what training nurses need to deliver such parts responsibly, safely and with fidelity. Clear competency frames guard patients and nurses.
pmc-13281077:
Rina Nishiyama and Tetsushi Nonaka studied how singers lock in time with a partner in a 2026 set of tests. Thirteen women sang a carol chorus in unison through earphones. At times the other voice was a real singer. At times it was a fake voice made by singing software. Video of the partner was shown in half the trials and hidden in the rest. The team tracked how the two voices lined up over time.

With a human partner, singers matched more closely and sang a touch ahead of the beat. That forward lean grew stronger when video was on. With the fake voice, the lean and match were weaker. The authors say small wobbles in a real voice, plus sight of the body, help singers guess what comes next. Fake partners, they add, give fewer of those clues.
pmc-13281777:
Xinhui Li and colleagues presented a new math method for brain scans in a 2026 paper. Brains are read in unlike ways, by shape scans and by activity scans. Tying the two together is hard, since the data are vast and tangled. Older tools often force simple rules and blend all people into one map. The new method hunts for hidden bundles of signals in each scan type. Bundles can be any size and can link across types or stand alone.

The method also lets each person's map vary at fine scale. Tests on fake data with known answers showed it found the true bundles. It was then run on two large real datasets of shape and activity scans. Its bundles tracked with age, sex, and illness traits in later checks. The authors say the tool can expose joint and solo patterns that older tools flatten away.
pmc-13281877:
David G Armstrong and colleagues tested a soaking wound dressing in people with diabetes in a 2026 study. Foot ulcers are a heavy burden in diabetes and drag down daily life. The dressing pairs soft silicone with a super-absorbent core that drinks wound fluid. Twenty-eight adults with shallow, clean ulcers joined at eight Polish centers. Care ran up to six weeks with pressure-relief footwear. The team tracked wound size, life quality, benefit felt, and movement.

More than three in four wounds shrank by at least a fifth. About one in five closed fully with new skin. Life quality scores improved a great deal, most in mood and daily life. Patients' felt benefit rose as well. Movement levels held steady, and footwear use topped ninety-five in one hundred hours. No harm was tied to the dressing in the report. The authors call the early results hopeful.
pmc-13282277:
Serkan Arslan and co-authors report a 2026 case of a young child whose gene fault caused both widespread tuberculosis and early lupus. A change in the STAT1 gene made its signal overactive, weakening defence against some infections while stirring autoimmunity, where the immune system attacks the body. The patient was a four-year-old girl first treated for appendicitis, a swollen appendix.

During surgery, surgeons found swollen belly lymph nodes carrying tuberculosis bacteria, confirmed by a lab test. Her history held shingles and repeated mouth thrush, and immune tests showed weak virus-fighting cells. Gene testing found a new variant in STAT1, not inherited from either parent. A year later she developed lupus, a body-wide autoimmune disease, and then a dangerous immune overreaction syndrome. A targeted drug brought partial improvement. Stem cell transplant, the definitive option, was planned. The case widens the known picture of this gene disorder.
pmc-13282677:
Wei Huang and co-authors present a 2026 study on how thyroid hormone levels relate to fatty liver disease, and whether iodine status changes that link. Past research conflicted. The team used nationally representative United States survey data from 2009 to 2012 on adults, building several adjusted statistical models. The liver condition, shortened to MAFLD, is fatty liver tied to metabolic problems such as excess weight and diabetes.

Higher levels of one thyroid hormone, FT3, and a higher ratio of the two main hormones, were linked to greater odds of fatty liver. Lower FT4 pointed the same way. Liver enzymes, a good cholesterol marker, and body weight may carry part of the effect. The pattern shifted with iodine, a nutrient the thyroid needs: under low iodine, one hormone showed the inverse link; under excess iodine, others came into play. The authors say iodine status may modify the thyroid-liver link, pending further validation.
pmc-13282877:
Lisha Kuang and Pantao Shu wrote a 2026 letter to the editor on airway pressure treatment for asthma with obesity. The letter responds to a trial by Anne E Dixon and colleagues. It reviews why obesity may worsen asthma and why pressure support might help.

The writers note that fat tissue can press on the chest and shrink lung capacity. They also list non-mechanical factors such as stress on cells and inflammation. The trial idea is that added pressure can raise lung volume and hold airways open. The letter places that idea within past clinical and genetic work. It argues that clinical use still needs more proof.
pmc-13282977:
Van Charles Lansingh and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter on virtual reality in eye surgery training. The letter responds to a review by Ahuja and colleagues. It praises the review while raising points on scope, word use, and proof of training value.

One point concerns an academy app that teaches facts more than surgical skill. The writers say it should sit outside a surgical training review. They also praise clear use of virtual and augmented reality as distinct terms. Training proof should cover more than skill gaps between novices and experts. Face and content checks matter too, and future studies should state which proof they seek.
pmc-13283177:
Sound beacons barely steady blindfolded steppers whose inner ears are electrically perturbed, Assan Mary Cedras's 2026 lab tests find. Balance uses sight, inner ear signals, and body sense together. Sound may also guide stance, but its role in moving tasks was less known.

Twenty young healthy adults stepped in place while blindfolded with heads tilted forward. A mild electric signal to the inner ear faked a turning signal. Trials ran with no sound or with a fixed sound source nearby. Without the fake signal, sound did not cut heading drift or its spread. The fake signal pushed drift toward the active side in both sound setups. Sound alone was a weak guide here.
pmc-13283377:
Sympathetic sprouting and a spinal immune receptor act as one pain axis in rats, Tingting Yu's nerve injury experiments argue in 2026. After nerve injury, sympathetic fibers can grow near pain fibers and worsen pain. The team asked whether outer nerve drive and spinal immune signals form one linked axis.

Rats got nerve ligation, sham surgery, or added drug treatments in groups. Pain was tested with fine filaments, and spinal tissue was checked for immune markers. Blocking sympathetic drive eased pain and calmed spinal immune signals. Blocking a spinal receptor called P2Y12 also eased pain in the model. Combined blocking gave no extra gain, which supports one shared pathway.
pmc-13284477:
Fidel Rampersad and co-authors present a 2026 case report of two bile duct problems found together in a woman in her mid-60s. Mirizzi syndrome occurs when a stone stuck in the cystic duct presses on the common hepatic duct. The patient also had stones in the lower common bile duct, a pairing the authors call uncommon and hard to judge before surgery.

Ultrasound first spotted the problems, and CT plus MRCP imaging confirmed the compression and the duct stones. Surgery included gallbladder removal, bile duct exploration with a scope, and a bypass join to the bowel. The case stresses how cross-section imaging can reveal paired bile problems early and shape a safer surgical plan.
pmc-13284877:
Nur Düzen Oflas and a large co-author group report a 2026 multicenter study comparing heart risk scores in obese adults in Türkiye. Most risk tools were built in groups with few severely obese people, so their fit for this population is unsure. Records for 6,378 obese adults from seven regions were scored with SCORE2, SCORE2-DM, and AHA PREVENT models.

Risk estimates were compared across regions and between models, with checks for agreement and for traits such as age, smoking, and diabetes. Clear regional differences appeared in smoking and other traits in the early results reported here. The study asks whether guideline cut points sort the same patients alike, a key point for fair prevention care.
pmc-13285277:
Ricardo R. Figueiredo and co-authors track ringing in the ears after COVID-19 in a 2026 clinical cohort study. Tinnitus can follow viral illness through ear harm, inflammation, or drug effects, and hearing loss is its main risk factor. The study followed 233 adults with COVID-19, split into tinnitus and non-tinnitus groups, with symptom, treatment, hearing, and mood data.

Post-COVID tinnitus showed distinct traits and shifted in character across pandemic phases, the authors report. The cohort work maps how common the symptom was and its toll on mental health, using handicap and anxiety scales. The authors stress joint checks of hearing and mental health after COVID-19, since ear symptoms and distress often travel together.
pmc-13285677:
Cal J. Halvorsen and co-authors expand a shared dataset on generations teaming up for social good in a 2026 update article. Cogeneration means younger and older people working side by side on shared causes. The base survey polled 1,549 Americans aged eighteen to ninety-four in March 2022 through a standing national panel, by web and phone.

Five held-back items now join the file: faith labels, from Protestant and Catholic to agnostic and atheist, plus how often people attend services. The wider set still centers on paid and unpaid cross-age work, drive to join, blocks in the way, and top social concerns such as schools, planet, and mental health. The file now holds 188 measures for reuse.
pmc-13286077:
Pavol Mikolas leads a 2026 study that forecasts daily functioning in young adults with mental health symptoms. Early help works best when teams can spot who will struggle at work and in daily life years ahead. Baseline facts from interviews and brain scans fed several smart models, whose calls were then checked against functioning one and two years later.

The sample held 357 help-seeking adults aged 18 to 35, drawn from nine sites across Germany. Plain interview facts alone sorted later functioning fairly well, and a slim tree model using just five items did even better. A large language model, used with no extra training, matched the classic model almost call for call. Brain scan measures added little on their own, which favors cheap clinical facts as the core of early warning tools.
pmc-13286377:
Veronica Biga and co-authors catch two rival gene switches sharing a cell in a 2026 developmental study. HES1 and HES5 each repress the other in spinal cord progenitors, a setup expected to force an either-or fate. Both also pulse on and off in cycles. Live imaging of mouse cells tested whether the rivals truly exclude each other as the classic picture demands.

Knockdowns confirmed the pair do repress one another in these progenitors. Yet imaging found cells carrying both at once, their pulses marching in step, a hybrid state the textbook switch forbids. Computer models showed the shared state holds while repression stays balanced, then tips to a single winner when strengths skew. Tissue checks matched that arc, with brief double expression fading into single-factor domains as the cord matures.
pmc-13286577:
Regina Cardoso de Moura and colleagues build the first validated yardstick for dentists' grasp of minimal intervention dentistry in a 2026 instrument study. The approach favors prevention, early catches, and repair over drill-and-fill habits, yet no sound tool measured whether dentists know, can do, and embrace it. Items drafted with expert review and focus groups were fielded to dentists across Brazil's Federal District.

After revisions, 454 dentists took the questionnaire and 404 responses fed the factor analysis. Statistics settled on two factors mirroring the competency frame of knowledge, skills, and attitudes together. Reliability cleared the adequacy bar, and fit measures mostly behaved, though one error index ran high and a single-factor reading was firmly rejected. The authors offer the tool as a common ruler for training programs and policy checks.
pmc-13287277:
Cristina M Justice and colleagues searched family data in 2026 for inherited variants behind attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Two family collections were combined, covering more than two thousand people. Tests looked both at single variants passed within families and at broad chromosome regions shared by affected relatives.

Three variant signals passed strict thresholds, near or inside genes called TFRC, GSDME, and TRIM31. One shared region on chromosome 19 held another strong signal. Gene sets also overlapped with brain surface size and with resting brain network measures. The authors say family designs can surface risk genes that ordinary case comparisons miss, and can start linking those genes to brain traits.
pmc-13287477:
H I Abdel Rahman and Doaa Eid built a long-memory time model in 2026 to forecast monthly sunspot counts, using records from January 1749 to October 2025. Their chosen model, with three past terms and two error terms, fitted past data closely, matching observed values with a correlation the authors report as 0.989.

Forecasts place the peak of the current cycle near 224.7, close to the observed high around 216 in August 2024. The next cycle is expected to top out lower, near 179.3 around March 2035. Error measures were small in validation checks. The authors offer the model for space weather planning tied to solar activity.
pmc-13288177:
Sachiyo Igata and co-authors measured timing spread in the right heart chamber in 2026 in 30 patients with high pressure in the lung arteries from narrowed vessels. Scans, ultrasound speckle tracking, and direct pressure readings through a catheter were combined in one visit.

Wider timing spread tracked with higher artery pressure and higher flow resistance, and with weaker matching between chamber and artery. After adjustment, artery pressure alone predicted the spread, covering about a quarter of its variation. Chamber size and pumping share did not. Dyssynchrony appeared even when chamber function was only mildly reduced. The authors propose the ultrasound measure as a stand-in for invasive pressure checks.
pmc-13288577:
Michael J Stein and a large team hunt shared blood proteins for multimorbidity in 2026. Data came from the EPIC cohort in Europe. It holds 13,270 people. A SomaScan test read their plasma proteins. Steps from health to first and second illness were modeled.

Hundreds of protein signals overlapped across diseases. The diseases were heart disease, diabetes, and cancer. In all, 38 signals tracked steps to a second illness. Most meant higher risk as levels rose. SEMA6A raised risk at each step. NLGN1 pointed the other way. UK Biobank checks broadly agreed. The signals may show shared paths to illness.
pmc-13288677:
Jyun-Jie Li, Chen-Hung Hsiao, and Duen-Ren Hou describe a mild, metal-free way to place two acetate groups on one carbon of aryl methyl ketones in a 2026 chemistry paper. Their reagent is nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate, and the changeover runs under gentle conditions across a wide range of starting ketones.

Substrates bearing varied electronic character on the aryl ring all reacted, with slightly electron-poor rings giving the best returns. Tests of how the reaction proceeds point to a radical route that begins when a single electron transfer lets the nitrosonium ion nitrosate the enol form of the ketone. The products, geminal diacetates, are handy as protecting groups and as building blocks for further bond making.
pmc-13288877:
Ji Won Lee, Thorsten Bach, and Biki Ghosh report a light-driven way to add fluorine to carboxylic acids without cutting the acid group off, in a 2026 chemistry paper. Iridium photocatalysis activates the fluorinating agent Selectfluor, and a range of primary and secondary acids gained fluorine at positions from beta to epsilon along the chain.

Keeping the carboxyl group intact matters because older routes sacrifice it to make the radical that carries fluorine in. Tests of the pathway suggest light first reduces Selectfluor, freeing a nitrogen-centered radical that pulls hydrogen atoms from the acid and keeps a radical chain running. Site-selective fluorination of cheap, common feedstocks could ease access to drug-like building blocks.
pmc-13288977:
Asilay Seker and colleagues study mood swings in autistic youth and youth with ADHD. Their 2026 study mines health records in London. Software pulled mood notes from free text. Records covered 21,906 children and teens. Care ran from 2008 to 2022.

Unstable mood linked to more clinic use each year. The link held in all three groups. It held for autism, ADHD, and both. Discharge came faster only in the ADHD group. The effect was strongest without ADHD drugs. Stable mood did not speed discharge in autism. The authors urge checks for mood control. Such checks could shape care plans early.
pmc-13289077:
Asebe Hagos and colleagues study child vaccine gaps in Ethiopia. Their 2026 study reuses a national survey. Data ran from 2019 to 2021. Five regions fed the data set. The weighted set held 1,888 children for full cover. A smaller set tracked dropouts.

Only 29.1 percent of one-year-olds were fully covered. Two in three had partial cover instead. Dropout between first and third doses hit 34.3 percent. Rich and city children fared better. Poor and rural children fared worse. Mothers with no schooling saw the worst rates. Gaps also split sharply by region. The authors call for fair catch-up work.
pmc-13289177:
Sheila Agyeiwaa Owusu and colleagues study stool tests for child TB in The Gambia in 2026. Sputum is hard for children to give. Stool may be an easier sample. The team spoke with teens, caregivers, and staff. All had taken part in a test study.

In all, 27 people were interviewed. Staff and officials called stool testing workable. Collection was easy, they said. It could fit current work flows. Caregivers were willing to give samples. Some were surprised stool could show TB. Teens felt shy about giving stool. Staff liked stool more than sputum. Steady supplies and outreach are needed, they said.
pmc-13289377:
Elvio Henrique Benatto Perino and coauthors measured a 2026 cost of making surfactin, a soap-like compound from Bacillus subtilis with strong cleaning and antimicrobial power. Making it drains energy and raw materials from the cell, which limits factory yields. The study focused on the large srfA gene cluster that builds the compound without ribosomes.

Three strains were compared: a normal producer, one missing the whole srfA cluster, and one keeping the cluster but missing a helper gene. Math first estimated energy and helper molecule needs for building surfactin from scratch. Growth, sugar and nitrogen use, and protein profiles were then measured in culture. The producer grew slower and yielded less biomass, while the strain without the cluster grew fastest.
pmc-13289477:
Shaya Akbarinejad and colleagues introduce a 2026 computing pipeline, called DEEPctMUT, for finding tumor DNA in blood without first sequencing the tumor itself. Blood-based cancer tracking is gentle and repeatable, but tumor-free methods often miss faint signals. Tissue-based methods are sharper yet slower, pricier, and need tumor samples that may not exist.

The pipeline pairs molecular barcodes with three error-cleaning steps: machine learning suppression, deep learning noise filtering, and removal of blood-cell and inherited variants using matched white cells. Tests on cell lines, spiked samples, healthy blood, and colorectal cancer plasma showed detection down to very low variant shares as reported. Pre-surgery cases were all caught in one comparison, beating a commercial kit.
pmc-13289777:
Marcello Maida and coauthors test a 2026 concern that GPT-5 overstates colorectal guideline advice. Language models follow guidelines closely, yet they may turn cautious recommendations into firm orders without showing evidence strength. Four European colorectal guidelines supplied the test material, with every statement, its strength, and its evidence grade extracted for fair judging.

For each statement, a case vignette and question went to the model under plain and guideline-focused prompts. Three experts rated fit to guideline content and fit to strength wording separately. Content fit was high, but strength fit lagged, worst for weak advice and low-grade evidence in the results. A tuned prompt lifted both scores sharply in a follow-up test.
pmc-13290077:
Joanna M. Lukasiewicz and Marinus J. M. Smulders review a 2026 market overview of gene-edited plant varieties and products. Editing tools change DNA at precise spots to create new traits, and many countries now regulate such plants, called new genomic techniques, more lightly than classic transgenic crops. European Union rules remain under debate, creating a patchwork market landscape for breeders and farmers.

The review explains how each edit type is regulated worldwide and lists products already marketed, approved, or in field trials. Buyer perception may challenge uptake, the authors note. Otherwise edited varieties face the same hurdles as conventional launches: farmer and processor needs, competition, and consumer taste. Clear rules will decide rollout speed.
pmc-13290577:
Predicted body makeup, not just weight, tracks fatty liver risk in a Chinese case-control study by Shuang Liang and colleagues from 2026. Metabolic-associated fatty liver disease keeps spreading, and few studies have separated the roles of fat mass and lean mass.

The matched study paired 1,683 patients with the disease against 1,683 controls and estimated fat mass, body fat percentage, lean mass, and their ratio from standard equations. Every measure ran higher in the patient group. After adjustment, people in the top quarter for fat mass, fat percentage, or the fat-to-lean ratio carried roughly two to nearly three times the risk of the bottom quarter. Even lean mass pointed the same way, a result the authors treat cautiously. Links ran stronger in younger, non-obese, and normotensive people.
pmc-13290877: A brief correction notice from 2026 by Haoxue Yang and colleagues fixes the title of their article in Inflammation. As published, the title ended mid-thought at 'Exacerbates'; the corrected one adds 'Ulcerative Colitis'. The title now names the disease the study covers: a form of bowel inflammation driven by immune cells the protein NMI pushes into an attack state. The notice gives nothing else: no data, methods, or results.
pmc-13291177:
Tropical forests soak up mercury that industry releases far away. Longyu Jia leads a 2026 global model study of this uneven trade. Leaves take in mercury from the air. Leaf traits shaped by climate change how much they hold.

The model adds those leaf traits to world forest maps. Rainforests in South America and Africa show the highest uptake rates. Both regions have little industry of their own. Warm climate leaf traits boost mercury capture at low latitudes. Total forest uptake is now pinned down far more tightly than before. The authors urge a fresh look at global mercury rules. Forest loss could also free stored mercury again.
pmc-13291277:
Leaf extract can make zinc particles for farm use. Hassan Iqbal leads a 2026 study using Cassia absus leaves. Chemical fertilizers and sprays carry health and nature costs. A plant-based route may offer a safer swap.

The green-made particles were checked with many lab tools. Their shape was mostly round and size stayed in the nano range. A charge test showed the mix stays stable in liquid. Dish tests then fought three plant disease bacteria. Clear kill zones formed around the particles. The largest zone hit one target germ. Roles as both feed booster and germ fighter are proposed. Field proof must still follow.
pmc-13291777: Chengxin Liu and co-authors published a 2026 correction fixing author affiliations on their study of gene activity and treatment options in dengue fever. One affiliation for Yong Jiang was wrong and has been replaced with the Shenzhen Hospital of Integrated Traditional Chinese and Western Medicine. Two omitted affiliations were added, one for Ming Zhong and one for Bei Ye. The notice covers affiliation details only, and the source article now carries the fix. Nothing beyond the correction itself is available here, so the study's findings cannot be summarized from it.
pmc-13292077: Kavin Palanivelu and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of the oriental fruit fly Bactrocera dorsalis infesting Indian jujube. The notice says Figure 1c, which shows the fly's wings, was wrong as published, along with its legend. A corrected figure and caption appear in the notice, describing the head, thorax, and wing pattern of the adult fly. The authors state the fix does not alter the article's scientific conclusions in any way, and the original version has been updated. Only the correction is available here.
pmc-13292377:
Zoë Tess Lara Lindhorst and co-authors screen a 2026 batch of German raccoons for gut parasites people can catch, framing the work as One Health surveillance. Raccoons, an invasive species around Saxony's pond farming country, may seed water with zoonotic protozoa. Fecal samples from 104 culled raccoons, collected from 2020 to 2022 across six aquaculture areas, got antigen tests plus PCR and sequencing.

Giardia duodenalis assemblage B, sub-assemblage BIV, turned up in 24 percent of samples, with rates varying significantly by location and by fish farm. A Cryptosporidium skunk genotype appeared in 2 percent of samples without clear patterning. The authors cast raccoons as genuine reservoirs in wet production landscapes. They recommend folding wildlife monitoring into pond management and invasive species control.
pmc-13292477:
Xiulian Huang's team tests a 2026 light-activated attack on Vibrio parahaemolyticus biofilms fouling stainless steel in food plants. The treatment pairs curcumin with blue light, a photodynamic method that generates reactive oxygen inside the biofilm. The team aimed squarely at exopolysaccharides, the glue sugars holding the biofilm's protective matrix together.

At 60 micromolar curcumin under 9.17 joules per square centimeter of blue light, the treatment erased over 60 percent of biofilm mass and killed 5.0 log units of cells per milliliter in their tests. Chemistry showed the light-driven reaction snipped sugar linkages and shrank the glue molecules, collapsing their hydrogen-bond networks. The matrix turned less water-shy, less sticky, and less cohesive, so the biofilm broke apart. The authors offer the mechanism as design guidance for stronger photodynamic sanitation.
pmc-13292577:
Jeff Bierwagen's team tests a 2026 immune relay: tiny sacs shed by bacteria priming human macrophages, whose signals then armor lung cells against SARS-CoV-2. Packets from five pathogens, including Klebsiella pneumoniae and E. coli, were fed to blood-derived macrophages. The team measured cytokine and interferon responses, then passed the macrophage media to Calu-3 airway cells before viral challenge.

Material from Klebsiella, E. coli, and Salmonella provoked strong inflammatory and interferon-driven gene programs through Toll-like receptor 4 signaling. Legionella and pneumococcus packets barely stirred the cells. Media from the strongly primed macrophages switched on antiviral genes in the lung cells. Virus output tended to fall in cells pre-treated with Klebsiella or E. coli vesicle media. The authors frame the relay as a blueprint for immune-modulating or vaccine strategies.
pmc-13292777:
Mohammed Yousuf and co-authors studied heat stress in Hararghe Highland sheep in a 2026 field report from Ethiopia. Sheep support rural families through meat, wool, and live sales, yet hot and humid weather can harm growth, breeding, and immunity.

Body measures in the sheep shifted by season and by time of day, and lowland animals showed the highest values, pointing to greater heat strain. The team tested ten heat stress indices against body measures and found strong links for most of them. Three comfort indices predicted stress best, while simpler climate indices were put forward for farm use. The work helps farmers spot heat load early.
pmc-13293377:
Sarah H Gordon leads a 2026 randomized trial testing whether simpler mailings can draw new Medicaid members in Maine into primary care. New members often lack a regular doctor, though steady primary care supports prevention and chronic care.

From March 2021 to January 2022, new adult members got either a standard text-heavy packet or that packet plus two plain visual mailers naming one nearby doctor. Over 12 months, the extra mailers changed nothing measured: visit rates, emergency or hospital use, enrollment length, or preventive services such as flu shots. Barriers beyond mail design must drive low engagement, the team suggests.
pmc-13293477:
Mahlet Misrak Argaw and co-authors test, in a 2026 pilot study, whether adding game elements to a virtual reality task lifts engagement in young adults with mild anxiety. Standard care can work well, yet access and sticking with it remain hard for many.

A total of 50 adults aged 18 to 39 in northern Sweden were split at random between game and plain versions of a virtual cleaning task called Cleanify. Each person had one 15-minute headset session, then rated focus, immersion, and overall experience. The game group reported higher engagement and immersion than the plain group. Full outcome detail is limited in the record, so gains should be read as early signs.
pmc-13293577:
Plant extracts used in Benin against diarrhea are put to an animal test by Edna Hounsa and colleagues in a 2026 study. Water and alcohol-water extracts came from Khaya senegalensis bark and Anacardium occidentale leaves, two traditional remedies where drug access can be limited.

Male Wistar rats were given castor oil to trigger diarrhea, then treated with extracts at set doses. The alcohol-water extracts delayed diarrhea onset, cut stool frequency and water content, and lowered a purging score. One Khaya dose matched the standard drug loperamide on some measures, though stool weight did not fall. Antioxidant action tied to plant polyphenols may help explain the effect.
pmc-13293877:
Amani Y. Alhalwani heads a 2026 retrospective case-control study on inflammation in people who have both abnormal blood lipids and dry eye disease. Records for 214 patients diagnosed at King Abdulaziz Medical City between 2016 and 2023 were split into lipid disorder alone versus lipid disorder with dry eye. Blood counts fed an aggregate inflammation index, alongside C-reactive protein checks.

Patients with dry eye showed higher neutrophil and monocyte counts. Their inflammation index rose with C-reactive protein and fell weakly as HDL and total cholesterol rose. After accounting for age, sex, and body mass index, the index showed no independent link to dry eye, so the authors call for prospective work.
pmc-13293977:
Saborni Chowdhury, Avery J Kruger, and Liza M Roger study the heat shock protein HSP60 in three cnidarians for 2026. The animals are the coral Pocillopora acuta, the anemone Exaiptasia diaphana, and the jellyfish Cassiopea xamachana. Despite that shared structure, control of the protein differed by lineage and by setting. Such variation helps explain why close relatives handle heat stress so differently. The authors connect the pattern to coral bleaching risk as oceans warm, where a conserved defense can still fail if its regulation is mistimed.
pmc-13294377: Kaisheng Zhou and coauthors are named on a 2026 editorial expression of concern for their 2024 Scientific Reports article proposing IRF1 as a marker of nucleus pulposus cell necroptosis in disc degeneration. Editors warn that the article shows an unusual citation pattern, with references 8 through 14 not clearly relevant where cited or to the overall topic. Readers are urged to judge those references with caution. Every author agrees with the notice. The item is only an editorial warning, with no new experiments or revised findings.
pmc-13295177:
Runhong Yao and colleagues probe light plus vibration treatment in older adults with mild thinking problems in a 2026 study. Mild cognitive impairment alters brain rhythms and blood flow, while mobility limits block exercise based options for many. A seated, effort-free stimulation pairing was explored as an alternative.

Twenty-seven volunteers received flickering light at 40 cycles per second together with gentle low-frequency vibration. Blood signal measures fell after treatment in both front brain halves, sooner on the right than the left. In a smaller recorded subgroup, frontal fast rhythms eased while slower rhythms rose elsewhere. The pattern suggests short sessions shift brain activity in timed, uneven ways.
pmc-13295577:
Yi-Luen Shen and colleagues test bacterial tail weapons against stubborn Pseudomonas infections in a 2026 study. Pyocins, virus-tail-like proteins made by the germ itself, kill close relatives by locking onto surface sugars.

Altogether 109 intensive care isolates from central Taiwan were typed and challenged with eight purified pyocins. Sensitivity followed surface type closely, with some groups shielded by long, dense sugar chains that hide the target. Pairing two pyocin families killed resistant strains together more strongly than either alone, supporting tailored cocktail treatment for resistant infections.
pmc-13295777:
Jiahao Wang and colleagues find hidden targets that explain immune strength in kidney cancer in a 2026 study. Renal cell carcinoma answers immunotherapy well despite carrying few mutations, a puzzle for cancer science. Many such antigens appeared across patients, and the T cells chasing them sat in worn-out groups inside tumours, a sign of constant stimulation. Engineered T cells carrying the matching receptors killed tumour cells strongly in dishes and in animals. The work names a fresh target family for cell therapies.
pmc-13295977:
Carlos Marques-Gomes and colleagues review, in 2026, new drug hopes for Sjögren's disease, a long-term autoimmune condition causing dryness and fatigue. No treatment yet changes the disease course, and care still mainly eases symptoms.

Approaches include tuning B cell survival, blocking antibody recycling and cutting co-stimulation between immune cells. Early results encourage, though people with mainly gland problems remain underserved. Sharper outcome measures and patient grouping are flagged as next needs.
pmc-13296377:
Minal M. Kshirsagar and colleagues survey, in 2026, how well parents understand children's dental health and whether that understanding tracks with decay. Nearly seven hundred parents of children aged two to twelve completed a fourteen-item literacy scale while children's teeth were scored for decay, missing and filled teeth.

Literacy scores varied by sex, area and job status. Children of parents with stronger understanding had clearly less decay experience, and city children fared better than rural ones. The authors urge targeted dental education for rural and low-literacy parents as a direct route to healthier children's teeth.
pmc-13296777:
Marina Russo and co-authors pilot, in 2026, a molecular signature in osteoporosis, linking two sugar-binding proteins to the tiny RNAs thought to control them. Bone and blood from twenty-three joint replacement patients, thirteen with osteoporosis, were compared for both protein and RNA levels.

Osteoporotic bone showed less of the first protein and more of the second, with matching shifts in both RNAs. Blood patterns broadly echoed the bone picture. The authors suggest the combined signature could become a marker of fragile bone change. They stress the small pilot scale and call for larger confirmation work.
pmc-13296977:
Beatriz Medeiros-Fonseca and a large toxicology team feed, in 2026, bracken fern extracts to mice, including animals carrying a cancer-linked virus, for four weeks. Bracken is eaten by people and livestock worldwide yet holds known toxins, so underground stem and young shoot extracts were compared in water and diet.

Stem extracts hit harder, especially in skin, liver and spleen, and effects grew in virus-carrying mice. Young shoots were tolerated better. Weight and intake were watched throughout. The authors warn that plant part and preparation change risk, urging caution over bracken as food.
pmc-13297277:
Duygu Baykal and co-authors test, in 2026, whether richer MRI reading can pick who should get shunt surgery for suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus, a fluid buildup mimicking dementia. Eighty-four symptomatic patients were split by later management after spinal fluid testing, with fifty healthy scans for comparison.

Usual size ratios, including the Evans index, separated patients from controls but not surgical from conservative cases. Tightness at the top of the brain stood alone as a predictor, and combined models scored best. The authors say shape features reflecting fluid dynamics beat size alone for surgical choices.
pmc-13299177:
A vitamin C derivative calmed the protein turmoil that ultraviolet light stirs inside skin cells, report Agnieszka Gęgotek and co-authors in a 2026 proteomics study. They grew keratinocytes and fibroblasts together, exposed them to UVA radiation, and tested whether a day of pretreatment with 3-O-ethyl ascorbic acid at 150 µM protected them.

UVA pushed both cell types toward inflammatory protein profiles and weakened antioxidant and growth signals, including in the fluid the cells shared. The derivative largely restored protein levels toward those of unirradiated cultures. The authors conclude the compound defends both skin layers and the signaling between them, supporting its candidacy in sun-protection products.
pmc-13299377:
Parks lift how much people move, most of all where streets beg for walks in any case. Ghazal S Fazli and her team show that link in a 2026 study from Canada. They tied survey replies from 41,945 Ontario adults to parks near home and a score for how fit the streets are for walks.

In walk-fit zones, one or more small or mid parks near home raised the odds of free-time sport by 29%. The lift for free-time plus trip moves was 48%. Both marks stand next to unwalkable zones with no parks. In low-walk zones, parks moved the marks by just 4% to 7%. High walk fit plus rich large-park reach also tied to less fat in the round.
pmc-13299677:
Not all joint-lining stem cells are equal, and where in the synovium they come from shapes what they can do, find Moiz Ahmad and colleagues in a 2026 systematic review. Synovial mesenchymal stem cells are prized for cartilage repair, but the joint offers several harvest sites, from membrane to fluid.

Filtering 2,312 papers down to ten studies, the review found real differences in growth rates, surface markers, and differentiation power between sources. Cells harvested near blood vessels performed better, and membrane-derived cells outgrew fluid-derived ones. The authors say choosing the right synovial source could matter for regenerative therapies, though the molecular reasons remain to be worked out.
pmc-13300977:
Long medication lists in older diabetics may signal blood-sugar trouble more than frailty, Funda Datlı Yakaryılmaz and Ayten Eraydın report in a 2026 geriatric assessment study. They examined 278 adults aged sixty-five and older with type 2 diabetes, scoring function, thinking, nutrition, mood, frailty, and walking speed. Polypharmacy meant five or more concurrent medicines.

Just over half the group, 54.7 percent, met that threshold, and they carried clearly higher HbA1c and fasting glucose. Each rise in HbA1c multiplied polypharmacy odds nearly fivefold, while frailty status showed no link at all. HbA1c alone separated the groups sharply, with an area under the curve of 0.898 in the analysis.
pmc-13302877:
A two-metal shim tames the weld between titanium and steel, Tong Wu and colleagues show in a 2026 joining study. Two-millimeter titanium and steel plates were resistance spot welded through a niobium-nickel bi-interlayer meant to block brittle iron-titanium compounds. Weld cross-sections were examined and joints pulled apart to measure shear strength across currents and times.

Two joint types emerged, one with separate nuggets and nickel-niobium layers, one where the metals mixed at the center. Strength rose then fell as energy input grew. The best joint, using foils of 0.05 and 0.04 millimeters at 11 kiloamps, carried about 8.7 kilonewtons. Matched interlayer thickness and settings are the key, the authors conclude.
pmc-13303777:
Shasha Du and Michael Ohsfeldt study how China's middle class gains social honor through study abroad choices in a 2026 interview-based article. Destination rankings for overseas study act as more than school choices, carrying signals about family standing.

Drawing on Riesman's theory of social character, the authors sort family reasoning into three patterns. One stresses practical gains and group values, one stresses passing culture across generations, and one stresses visible experience and online display. These patterns mix and clash as families negotiate, rather than acting alone. Honor appears as a shared, contested product shaped by rapid social change.
pmc-13304177:
Heng Yin and co-authors develop concrete that holds back its own early heat in a 2026 materials study. Fresh mass concrete warms as it sets, and uneven heat can crack large pours such as bridge foundations.

Part of the coarse stone was swapped for steel-wrapped beads holding water-rich gel that soaks up heat as it changes state. Half-insulated tests showed lower and later heat peaks. Computer models rebuilt the full heat history and matched the measured curves well. In a bridge pile-cap simulation, the best mix cut peak core heat, heat gaps, and heat stress together.
pmc-13304477:
Laydy Mitsu Mena-Chacon leads a 2026 study of essential oils from plants in northeastern Peru as natural food protectors. Foodborne germs sicken hundreds of millions yearly, and plant oils vary greatly in strength by species and origin.

Six oils, including lemon verbena and two forms of a root vegetable relative, were profiled chemically and tested against four standard germ strains. Lemon verbena oil and one root oil stopped both major germ groups best, likely thanks to rich oxygen-bearing scent compounds. Oils heavy in a different compound class worked weakly. Dose tests backed the ranking for future food safety use.
pmc-13304977:
Eşe Aslan Başbulut, Demet Yavuz, and Tülin Demir test whether past Lyme disease exposure links to unexplained kidney failure in northern Türkiye in a 2026 early case-control study. Lyme germs damage dog kidneys clearly, but human kidney links rest on rare case reports.

Forty-five dialysis patients with kidney disease of unknown cause were matched with 45 healthy controls. Antibody screening with blot confirmation found past exposure slightly more often in patients than controls, but the gap was not statistically firm. Every confirmed patient lived rurally, farmed or kept animals, and recalled repeated tick bites.
pmc-13306077:
Pablo Maya studied food, pain and early memory change in older women in a 2026 survey from the Valencian Community in Spain. Women aged 50 or more were recruited through pharmacies and health centres, and diet was scored from a standard food questionnaire.

Complete data covered 470 women for memory outcomes and 328 for pain in the reported counts. A higher dietary inflammatory score linked consistently to worse outcomes, while Mediterranean-style patterns differed from each other in strength of link. The authors caution that not every diet carrying the Mediterranean label behaved the same against inflammation, pain or word fluency.
pmc-13307377:
Rui Wang and Xiaoshuai Li write a 2026 letter on a faculty training course that taught Web 2.0 tools with Universal Design for Learning in medical schools. Use of all nine tools rose after training, yet two months later few teachers used them often in class.

The letter calls that gap a know-do divide and argues that lost class control, not just time or weak tech support, helps explain it. Interactive tools shift power toward students, which can feel like a threat to expert standing. Training that ignores that identity strain, the authors warn, will keep seeing weak uptake after the course ends.
pmc-13307677:
Lady Johana Hernández-Sarmiento and co-authors study in 2026 how two cannabis related compounds act on human macrophages infected with Mayaro virus, a mosquito borne virus that causes fever and lasting joint pain. Cells were treated before or after infection, and gene activity plus virus growth were checked at 6 and 24 hours.

The lab made compound WIN 55,212-2 cut virus growth at 24 hours when given after infection, without killing virus directly on contact. Its effect tied to stress signals inside the cell, not to the usual interferon alarm path. The compound also calmed many swelling related genes and shifted the mix of signals the cells released into their fluid.
pmc-13307877:

Mycobacterial DNA turned up in 421 samples, and most of those held drug sensitive tuberculosis strains in the test. A small share showed resistance, led by isoniazid only resistance, and a few held non tuberculosis germs alone or mixed. Big hospitals yielded far more positives than front line clinics. Wider use could speed matched care and help national plans to end tuberculosis deaths.
pmc-13308677:
Madeleine A Gaidimas and co-authors set up in 2026 a high speed work flow that maps how rare earth metal organic frameworks grow, a space too wide for hand trials alone. Robots ran mixed heating runs while fast X-ray, vision, and element checks read the goods at scale.

In all, 1488 unique runs were done, with more than 800 diffraction reads and more than 13,000 vial images scored by a trained vision model. Five new rare earth frameworks came to light, and phase maps charted 18 goods by heat, acid, metal, and linker choice. A mixed metal bath then yielded one chosen crystal type, which shows the maps can guide picky growth.
pmc-13309477:
Karen B. Gessler led a 2026 mouse study on whether a common cholesterol drug harms energy centers in the front part of the brain. The prefrontal cortex, a region tied to thinking, had been little studied.

Male mice took the drug by mouth for seven days at a set daily dose, while others took a plain substitute. Treated mice moved a bit more in activity tests, and memory checks at two time points showed no loss. Tissue tests then probed breathing rates of cell energy centers and chemical balance. The authors report no sign of harm to cell viability in this short course.
pmc-13309577:
Wenbin Tan and colleagues chart world research on gut microbes joined with cancer immune therapy in a 2026 mapping study. Work on how gut microbes help or hinder immune drugs has grown fast, yet its shape and hubs were unclear. Counts and citation links offer one way to draw that map.

Output grew about 23 percent per year on average, and China plus the United States supplied 60.1 percent of the total share in this field. Three research lines and three knowledge paths stood out. The authors offer the map to guide new teams toward gaps and partners.
pmc-13310377:

The authors note the germ can infect with as few as 10 to 50 organisms, yet stays rare in the region. They urge clinicians to weigh tularemia when lung disease shows dead, swollen lymph nodes, even where cases are few.
pmc-13310677:
Lian Li and co-authors test whether frailty carries the link between poor nutrition and thinking decline in older Chinese adults in a 2026 study. Each of the three problems is common after 65, and they likely feed each other. Their three-way weave had rarely been measured in one community sample.

Cluster sampling recruited community elders in Ningbo, screened with short tools for nutrition, frailty, and dementia risk. Rates came out at 17.04 percent for malnutrition, 32.37 percent for frailty, and 13.02 percent for cognitive decline in the sample figures. Poor nutrition tied significantly to frailty in adjusted models. Mediation analysis then weighed how much of the nutrition-to-thinking path runs through frailty, with matched comparisons as a check. The authors urge joint screening.
pmc-13310977:
Wenya Bi and colleagues survey advance care planning among emergency staff in China in a 2026 study. Emergency rooms often treat dying patients, so staff must know how to learn care wishes ahead of crisis. Knowledge, views, and intent to act were measured across many hospitals.

Valid replies came from 686 doctors and nurses at 54 hospitals in Anhui Province in December 2024. Knowledge scores were low, while attitude scores ran higher. Age, experience, schooling, past exposure to planning facts, and end of life care work shaped scores. Training that reaches younger and less exposed staff may lift practice intent.
pmc-13311277:
Tal Sella and co-authors report a 2026 real-world study of lighter treatment for young women with early hormone-sensitive, HER2-positive breast cancer. The question was whether single-drug chemotherapy plus hormone therapy gives results as good as stronger mixes.

Hormone therapy type, with or without ovarian suppression, also made little difference. The authors suggest many young patients may do well without treatment build-up, though follow-up must continue.
pmc-13312077:

The team measured udder traits in 84 milking goats and 72 dry goats, with yield records spanning 2022 to 2024. Horizontal teat placement in dry goats was the only quality trait tied to higher yield. pmc-13312477:

Finite element analysis then tracked stress across the lunate's joints with the scaphoid, radius, triquetrum, and capitate in bending and extension. A flatter lunate facet inclination angle strongly raised stress at the lunocapitate joint, while steeper angles shifted load toward the scaphoid joint. The authors propose adding these angles to the usual measures when judging risk and planning surgery.
pmc-13312577:

The team hunted for the transcription factors among oxygen-response genes that carry prognostic weight, drawing on bulk and single-cell data and mapping how tumor cells talk to their neighbors. From those regulators they built a predictive model that sorts patients into risk groups by expected survival. The authors argue the key factors illuminate how this cancer works under low oxygen. pmc-13313177:

Rates of a few spine and lung diseases were higher in vaccinated women. Yet the authors could not show the vaccine caused them, since other factors and wrong codes may explain the gap.
pmc-13314577:

Treating organs as medicines could shake the gift basis of donation and public trust, they argue. The piece urges lawmakers to keep organs as non-commercial goods while rules catch up with science.
pmc-13314777:
Obhuli Chandran M. and colleagues test deep learning rebuilding of head CT scans in a study issued in 2026. Non-contrast head CT is the standard scan for brain ills, but repeat scans stack up radiation and cancer risk over a life.

The team set three arms side by side. One used low-dose scans rebuilt by a deep learning tool called Precise Image. One used low-dose scans rebuilt by the older iterative method. pmc-13315177:

Neck rotation and side bending improved sharply by final follow-up, and scoring covered head tilt and face balance. The method avoids a visible neck scar.
pmc-13315677:

Adding atrial strain and gene data aims to flag decline earlier.
pmc-13316277:
Sriram Gubbi and colleagues explore in 2026 whether faults in the MRN DNA repair complex drive some thyroid cancers, a role rarely considered beside the usual MAP kinase drivers. A query across three thyroid cancer data collections found MRN harmful variants in 35 of 762 patients, a share of 4.6 percent in the reported count, and all such patients had anaplastic cancer. Repair defects may matter in that aggressive subtype.
pmc-13317777:
Zhiquan Li and co-authors chart, in a 2026 bibliometric study, research where eczema and inflammatory bowel disease meet, two barrier illnesses that share immune and microbe faults. No map of this joint field existed, so they counted and clustered its literature.

pmc-13318477:
Hassami Sawadogo and co-authors report a 2026 case series on children's urological emergencies treated at the regional hospital in Dédougou, Burkina Faso, where published data from regional centres are scarce. Records covered one year, from April 2025 to March 2026.

Only 28 children aged up to 15 years were included, almost all boys, with an average age of 8.22 years across the series. Injuries made up the largest share, including scrotal trauma and three cases of goring by cattle, followed by testicular torsion and blockages. Torsion cases arrived after long delays, and two-thirds needed removal of the testicle, yet every child survived. The authors call for community awareness and staff training.
pmc-13318577:

pmc-13318777:

Where changes land across genomes is not fully random. Repair pathways and existing biases shape where changes land. New tools expand what scientists can see. CRISPR editing and single-cell sequencing now reveal these processes in fine detail. The author calls for continued watch and lab study to predict how bacteria adapt.
pmc-13319077:
Yanhu Ji and colleagues present a 2026 time-series study of air pollution and hospital admissions for ischemic stroke in Zhangzhou, China. Each 10-unit rise in fine particles carried a relative risk of 1.0356 in their model. Effects ran stronger in men, in people under 65, and in the cold season. Overall, 7.0 percent of admissions, some 854 cases, traced to pollution above WHO guideline levels.
pmc-13319377:
Walter Mdekera Iorjiim and co-authors test a plant compound in fruit flies in a 2026 study of aging harm from an HIV drug. The drug can speed up wear on body function and shorten fly life. The compound, drawn from moringa leaves, is known for guarding nerve cells and fighting cell damage.

The dose that killed half the flies in tests is also reported for safety context.
pmc-13319677:

pmc-13320277:

Coated gels helped cells cling, grow, drift, and mature, and gene reads showed a growth path switched on as the driver. pmc-13320477:

pmc-13320677:

pmc-13321377:
