Threshold values for spread were derived for each group, and sensitivity checks flagged the strongest drivers. Simulations showed strong, wide vaccination cut spread and human cases, while less bird to human contact also helped. Combined sanitation and targeted poultry culling gave the largest drop in spread under optimal control tests.
pmc-13322277:
Margot Evelin Bernedo-Itusaca leads a 2026 study of thinking skills at high altitude in Peru. Life under chronic low oxygen raises red cell counts and blood thickness, which may starve the brain of oxygen. The team studied 200 healthy young adults, 50 each in Lima, Arequipa, Puno, and La Rinconada, cities from near sea level to 5100 metres.

Blood oxygen fell and haemoglobin rose with altitude, peaking at 19.47 grams per decilitre in La Rinconada, where oxygen saturation dropped to 81.64 percent in the study. Moderate to severe thinking impairment appeared only in that extreme altitude group, where just 10 percent tested unaffected. Sleep quality was also weighed beside altitude effects.
pmc-13322677:
David A. Connor and co-authors validate automated home cage monitoring for early drug safety checks in a 2026 rat study. Brain related side effects sink many drug candidates, and the standard observation battery relies on brief, subjective human scoring. An automated Home Cage Analyzer watches rats in their own cages around the clock.

In a crossover design where each rat served as its own control, three known drugs were tested: amphetamine, diazepam, and chlorpromazine. The system caught expected stimulant and sedative effects across light and dark phases. At the top amphetamine dose, floor movement fell while rearing rose sharply, a nuance brief checks could miss. The team backs the tool as a first line screen.
pmc-13322877:
Shuping Liu and colleagues test whether acupuncture links to faster recovery in Guillain-Barre syndrome, in a 2026 prospective study. They enrolled 128 patients admitted between April 2025 and March 2026, all receiving standard care, with 58 also receiving acupuncture and 70 not.

After two weeks, more patients in the acupuncture group met the set gains on the Hughes disability scale and on summed muscle strength scores. Starting features were well balanced between groups, and several statistical checks supported the link. Acupuncture stood as an independent predictor of short-term improvement in their models. The authors frame the result as added benefit on top of immunoglobulin therapy, not a replacement for it.
pmc-13325377:
Doretta Cuffaro and colleagues devise a color test for dopamine in banana peel waste in a 2026 study. Banana peel is rich in dopamine, and measuring it cheaply could turn food waste into a valued resource.

In a magnesium and ammonium buffer at pH 9.4, dopamine forms a purple-blue pigment that absorbs strongly at 595 nm. Plate readings gave 5000 micrograms of dopamine equivalent per gram of dry peel, close to the 5700 from a chromatography check. The test stayed linear with a detection limit of 1.8 micrograms per mL. It runs at tiny scale with almost no sample prep. Farms and processors could screen waste streams quickly with it.
pmc-13326077:
Denzil Johnson, Nkiruka Umaru, and Cathal T. Gallagher set out a research agenda for reforming pharmacy discipline in the United States in a 2026 article. Weak or slow discipline of unfit pharmacists puts patients at clear risk.

Boards weigh cases through panels that seat practicing pharmacists with heavy workloads and little regulatory training. That setup leans toward coaching and rehabilitation over firm sanctions, which may underplay public protection. The authors map the United States framework of practice law, entry standards, and board powers. They argue the transatlantic comparison can show where decision design fails and which reforms deserve testing first.
pmc-13327877:
Chiara Catelli and co-authors check lungs from multi-trauma donors for transplant in a 2026 review of 125 recipients. Donor lungs are scarce and donors are growing older, while trauma donors are often young yet may carry bruised lungs. The study compared 36 recipients of trauma-donor lungs with 89 recipients of other donor lungs, treated from 2013 to mid-2024.

Early results, including graft dysfunction and intensive care stays, looked alike, and six-month survival ran higher in the trauma group before adjustment, at 91.7 percent against 75.3 percent in the raw figures. After matching for age and other gaps, survival, lung function, and long-term airway decline matched closely. Trauma lungs, chosen with care, should not be turned away on origin alone.
pmc-13328377:
Navazh Jalaludeen and a large team test outcome predictors in stiff-heart heart failure in a 2026 exploratory study. Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction resists simple forecasts. The team measured left atrial stiffness by speckle tracking, walking distance, and blood markers in 43 patients, whose mean age was 77.2 years.

Over a mean follow-up of 24.5 months, five patients died and 21 were hospitalized. Atrial stiffness predicted death independently, with a hazard ratio of 1.81 in their model, alongside the standard natriuretic peptide marker. Six-minute walk distance and growth differentiation factor 15 predicted hospital stays. Combining chamber mechanics, fitness, and blood signals may sort risk better than any single test.
pmc-13330577:
Zian Liu and colleagues link body weight, blood thickness, and brain rhythms at high altitude in a 2026 study. Long-term residents of Lhasa, Tibet, had resting brain waves recorded with a 64-channel system. Body mass index came from measured height and weight, and blood viscosity was estimated from blood indicators with a validated altitude model.

In total, 123 residents entered the study, with main analyses run on 118 people after the small obese group was set aside. Four standard brain microstates were mapped. Higher body mass tied to thicker blood, and thicker blood tied to rarer appearance of one microstate. A mediation model supported that indirect path. Altitude brain adaptation may run partly through blood flow traits.
pmc-13331277:
Ryohei Ono and colleagues report kidney recovery after months without urine in a heart attack case in a 2026 article. A 57-year-old woman had heart attack with both cardiogenic and anaphylactic shock, then lasting no-urine kidney failure needing dialysis. Pump support through the skin kept circulation going for over 4 months.

Urine flow returned after 2 months of no output, letting dialysis stop in the reported course. A durable heart pump was implanted on day 138, and she stayed dialysis-free afterward. Kidney failure often bars durable pump use in the authors' country. Lasting flow support can still rescue kidneys in select cases, they argue.
pmc-13331777:
Maryam Masjedi Esfahani and colleagues present a 2026 case report of POEMS syndrome, a rare disorder driven by an abnormal plasma cell clone that is often mistaken for other nerve diseases. Their patient was a 37-year-old man with growing limb weakness and swollen groin lymph nodes.

Scans showed enlarged liver and spleen, widespread lymph node swelling, and thickened spinal nerve roots. Bone lesions mixed worn and hardened areas, a pattern that pointed away from a simple inflamed nerve condition. Electrical nerve tests confirmed a damaging polyneuropathy, and a node biopsy revealed Castleman disease of mixed plasma cell and hyaline vascular type, sealing the diagnosis. The authors argue that spotting this scan pattern early can speed clone-directed treatment and spare patients long delays.
pmc-13332477:
Ranakishor Pelluri and a large team pooled real-world studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026 asking whether gabapentinoid drugs worsen flare-ups in people with COPD or asthma. These sedating pain and seizure drugs could plausibly harm patients whose breathing reserve is already thin, but the evidence was scattered.

Four cohort studies, reported across seven papers, met the review's rules after a search running to January 2026. Taken together, gabapentinoid use showed no significant link to flare-ups, with a hazard ratio of 1.12 and wide uncertainty. Split by drug, though, gabapentin at 1.27 and pregabalin at 1.37 each carried significantly higher risk, while mirogabalin did not, and event rates ran higher in users with an incidence ratio of 1.41. The authors call for long-term studies that can explain the drug-level differences.
pmc-13332777:
Matteo Gelardi wrote a 2026 letter to the editor responding to the BRISA study of severe asthma typing, which combined nasal cell sampling, induced sputum, blood, and circulating markers. Gelardi congratulates the authors and agrees that nasal sampling alone cannot replace sputum, but argues that verdict should sharpen, not shrink, the nose test's role.

Nasal cytology, he notes, directly shows the upper airway lining, revealing not just counts of eosinophils, mast cells, and neutrophils but also cell activation, lining damage, mucus output, and mixed patterns. In the BRISA group, 72 percent had allergic rhinitis and 50 percent had sinus disease with polyps, conditions that give the nose its own inflammatory character. The poor match between nose and sputum results, with a kappa of −0.0862, may reflect real differences between airway compartments rather than a weak test. He places nasal cytology as a complementary window inside precision care.
pmc-13333177:
Lu Huang and Jean-Pierre Djukic review spin crossover in metal complex catalysts in a 2026 survey. Some transition-metal complexes can flip reversibly between low-spin and high-spin states when pushed by heat, light, pressure, or fields. The trick was long studied for materials but only lately for speeding chemical reactions.

Flipping spin reshapes the metal's electron layout and stretches or tightens its bonds, which can redirect or accelerate a reaction. The review first covers the basics of the phenomenon and the main triggers, then walks through recent homogeneous catalysis studies with different transition-metal complexes, tracing how spin switching changes reaction pathways. Because a spin flip can quietly alter behavior, the authors recommend that anyone testing new catalysts built on common 3d metals should routinely check whether spin crossover is at play.
pmc-13333277:
Chuanhao Zhang and colleagues compared radiation alone against radiation plus chemotherapy for early head and neck cancers with small lymph node spread, in a 2026 multicenter cohort study. Adding chemotherapy is standard for advanced disease but brings heavy toxicity, and whether small-volume cases need it was unsettled.

The study gathered 240 patients with stage T1–2, N1–2a squamous cancers from centers in China and Canada, with a median age of 57.8 years and 21 percent HPV-negative, and balanced the groups by treatment weighting. Combined treatment did not significantly improve overall survival, with a hazard ratio of 0.50 and wide uncertainty, but it did improve freedom from progression, with a hazard ratio of 0.42. The pattern matches the NRG-HN002 trial's drop in local failure. The authors advise weighing the control gain against toxicity case by case and call for larger prospective trials.
pmc-13333377:
Tomáš Hanousek and co-authors assemble a three-part 3D forest dataset for Central European trees in a 2026 data paper, built to train and test the algorithms that read forest scans. Ground truth of this depth is what machine learning for tree measurement has lacked.

The core is a library of 3,618 individually cut-out tree point clouds from laser scanning campaigns at 47 Czech sites between 2009 and 2025. It covers 12 species with and without leaves, each tree paired with field traits and model-derived structure numbers. Second come 15,718 virtual airborne scanning scenes of 50 by 50 m, simulated with the HELIOS++ tool from procedurally grown forests at two point densities, with exact metadata for every tree. Third, 273 trees were fully rebuilt in 3D, woody skeletons from structure models plus realistic foliage. The authors host the collection in the Czech National Repository for segmentation, species naming, and virtual forest experiments.
pmc-13333477:
Chunyan Hu evaluates an ultrasound-guided swallowing program in a 2026 study of elderly patients recovering from radioactive therapy for medullary thyroid cancer. The 131I-MIBG treatment that targets MIBG-positive tumors can injure mouth and throat tissues and weaken swallowing muscles, leaving patients aspirating food and losing weight.

Eighty patients aged 65 and over with swallowing difficulty after therapy were compared over eight weeks. Forty received conventional nurse-led rehabilitation. Forty received a phase-based program using ultrasound imaging to watch the throat muscles and hyoid bone move, guiding exercise as recovery progressed. The guided group gained on oral intake, swallowing difficulty scores, and quality-of-life ratings, with suprahyoid muscle thickness up by a quarter and hyoid movement up by a fifth. Aspiration events fell from 15 to 9 percent and pneumonia readmissions from 15 to 5 percent, with no harms. Hu presents the approach as safe and scalable for cancer rehabilitation.
pmc-13335177:
Won Ju Hwang, Jungyeon Lee, and Zhengxiao Sun studied what nursing students learned from a COVID-19 disaster simulation in a 2026 qualitative study. Their aim was to shape a standard disaster nursing module.

Seventy-eight senior nursing students sent in reflective journals through an online platform after the simulation. Two researchers coded the journals on their own and merged their coding, drawing 235 core statements into four themes. The themes were experiencing disaster situations and learning, gaps in disaster nursing competency, understanding community resources and nursing roles, and professional growth with future educational needs. Students plainly showed gaps in crisis leadership and clear communication. The authors call for hands-on training formats that keep students safe and distanced, including lifelike virtual reality.
pmc-13336577:
Xiaolin Jiang and co-authors describe a 2026 chemistry advance for releasing hydrogen from formic acid, a liquid that stores hydrogen well. The hard step is removing a key hydrogen atom without making carbon monoxide. Their catalyst pairs one palladium atom with two silver atoms, held by a phosphorus-based frame and formate bridges.

Working in open air at 60°C, the pair beat single-metal versions and gave clean hydrogen with no carbon monoxide. Computer models and live spectra confirmed the two metals stay close and share the work through the reaction. The catalyst could be reused with good results. Clean, fast hydrogen release matters for portable fuel and green energy systems.
pmc-13336877:
Lina Zhu and co-authors reveal a guardian ring that keeps the cell's ribosome factory intact in a 2026 study. The nucleolus, a membrane-free zone inside the nucleus, builds ribosome parts. A gene-silencing complex called PRC2.1, tied to marked silent chromatin, gathers around it in a ring.

One part, PCL2, forms droplets whose fluidity it controls through a floppy region. PCL2 helps the nucleolar protein NPM1 assemble into five-part units and links nucleolar parts together, keeping ribosome RNA and protein output running. Cells need this support to keep growing. The work shows surrounding silent chromatin actively maintains the nucleolus rather than sitting idle nearby.
pmc-13337777:
Adilai Abula leads a 2026 rabbit study of a mixed scaffold for fixing gum and jaw bone defects. Five material options were compared, led by a blend with antler powder, chitosan, and platelet-rich fibrin. A commercial bone powder served as the positive control, and one group received nothing.

Fifty-four rabbits were split into six groups of nine, each with a one-sided defect. Animals were checked at 4, 8, and 12 weeks by eye, imaging, and tissue study. New bone area, ligament width, and mineral strength were measured. Implanted groups kept healthy gum form with shallow probing depths, setting up comparison of which blend rebuilt bone best.
pmc-13338677:
Myungsung Kim and colleagues evaluate Fruto, a campus mental health app, in a 2026 mixed methods study. College students face high distress but seek professional help at low rates. Fruto joins screening, information, counseling access, and campus directions in one place tied to the counseling center.

First, 16 students tried scenario prototypes and gave interviews that shaped revisions. Then students used Fruto for eight weeks while attitude and belief measures were taken before and after. The study checks both whether students accept the tool and whether help-seeking attitudes shift. Linking an app to real campus services is the core test.
pmc-13340677:
A large ovarian cyst in a young girl traced back to thyroid failure, in a 2026 case report by Maysam Jehad Yousef Hamarsheh and coauthors. The 7-year-old arrived with sudden lower belly pain, and imaging showed a large, mildly complex cyst on the left ovary plus a smaller one on the right, with blood flow intact.

Blood tests revealed severe primary hypothyroidism with raised prolactin and estradiol and delayed bone age, fitting Van Wyk–Grumbach syndrome. The big cyst was removed keyhole-style and proved benign. Thyroid replacement normalized her hormones, and the remaining cyst shrank away, a reminder to check thyroid function before planning surgery.
pmc-13341077:
Two fusion strategies for two-level lumbar stenosis are compared in a 2026 study by Xiaoyang Sun and Dichao Huang. Records covered 124 patients treated between January 2023 and October 2025, split between bilateral laminectomy with fusion and total laminectomy with fusion.

The bilateral group left hospital sooner, lost less blood, and walked earlier. Their pain, disability, and function scores also improved more at every follow-up, with excellent or good results in 95% versus 91% under the MacNab criteria. Complications included three cases of nerve root irritation and two mild epidural issues. The findings favor the bilateral approach for this two-level disease pattern.
pmc-13341177:
Radioactive iodine use in thyroid cancer is changing, and Kyeong Jin Kim compares the newest Korean and American guidance in a 2026 commentary. The 2024 Korean Thyroid Association and 2025 American Thyroid Association guidelines appeared in sequence, inviting a side-by-side reading.

Both move away from routine postoperative iodine toward selective, risk-fitted use. They agree on easing treatment in low-risk disease, matching dose to risk, wider use of recombinant human TSH preparation, and adding SPECT/CT after therapy. Kim argues the real shift is precision: aligning purpose, dose, preparation, and follow-up checks with each patient's recurrence risk rather than simply using less iodine.
pmc-13342277:
George M. Rodgers reviews treatment options in 2026 for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a rare clotting disorder caused by lack of the enzyme ADAMTS13. The review covers both the inherited form and the immune form, where the body attacks its own enzyme and small clots damage organs.

Plasma infusion or lab-made ADAMTS13 can replace the missing enzyme in the inherited form and prevent its high death rate. Standard care for the immune form combines steroids, plasma exchange, and rituximab, sometimes with caplacizumab, yet stubborn cases remain. Rodgers surveys newer choices, including gene therapy, plasma cell drugs such as bortezomib and daratumumab, and fresh blockers of von Willebrand factor.
pmc-13342877:
Anton Sokolov built Nekropolis, a 2026 dataset gathering public records of research and digital items that were retracted, withdrawn, revoked, or shut down. The corpus spans computer science publishing and nearby AI governance systems, placing very different endings under one shared record format.

In total, 14,923 artifacts from 2018 to 2026 carry category, lifecycle dates, stated reasons where sources give them, and cautious inferred cause labels. Journal retractions drawn from Retraction Watch form 90.5 percent of the release, joined by preprint withdrawals, benchmark closures, and wallet pilot endings. Sokolov stresses the set describes one curated slice, not overall rates, and suits tests of evidence extraction and time-aware search.
pmc-13343977:
Bhawna and co-authors study how cell defenses shift as Chandipura virus floods cultured cells in 2026. The virus causes deadly brain outbreaks in India. Defenders have two main arms, interferon signaling and killing infected cells. The team varied how many virus particles hit each cell at once.

Rising dose lifted virus yield up to a point, then output mysteriously fell at the highest dose tested. Modeling and knockout cell infections showed interferon rules at low dose, but at saturating dose cell death does the heavy lifting by destroying the virus's breeding ground. The dose-dependent handoff may guide when anti-inflammatory care helps most in viral disease.
pmc-13344477:
Bokang Yuan and co-authors design a jelly electrolyte to fix the two big flaws of zinc-iodine batteries in 2026. Iodine species wander between electrodes and zinc grows spiky dendrites, so the team built a polyzwitterionic hydrogel carrying both positive imidazolium and negative sulfonate groups in one network.

The negative groups repel wandering iodide and lock up free water, while the positive groups even out zinc plating and catch escapee iodide. Cells ran over 4,500 hours in symmetric tests and kept 71.48 percent capacity after 10,000 cycles, and a flexible pouch cell kept working under harsh bending. Paired charges inside one gel, the authors show, can tame both failure modes at once.
pmc-13346377:
Rami Zalfou and Anna Tegunimataka study when young people with Middle Eastern backgrounds leave the parental home in Sweden, using register data issued in 2026. Records cover ages 17 to 35 from 1998 to 2022, and a competing risks model separates moving into independent living from moving directly into marriage.

Youth of Middle Eastern origin left for independent living less often than native Swedes and moved into marriage more often. Gaps ran wider for the second generation and for women. Family income and schooling explained only a small part of the gap, while high joblessness in a neighbourhood was tied to slower moves into independent homes.
pmc-13347077:
Charlotte Blease and colleagues argue, in a 2026 viewpoint, that young people are too often left out of designing digital mental health tools they use most. Co-design and public involvement are widely praised. Yet youth input is described as patchy, shallow, or sought only late, which risks tools that miss how young users actually live and what they fear.

Three linked causes are named, starting with tangled language about what participation even means across fields, and the piece uses a life cycle view from problem setting through testing. Concrete steps are proposed so youth voices shape generative systems early and throughout, not as a final check before launch.
pmc-13347677:
Gopiga Ilango and colleagues sort a hospital drug store by cost and need. Their inventory study appeared in 2026. The store serves a tertiary care hospital. All 1,402 drugs bought in one year were classed. The year ran from April 2018 to March 2019. One scale ranked spending share. Another ranked vital, essential, or desirable status. A matrix then crossed both scales.

Just 135 items ate up most of the spend. Their share was 70.11 percent of yearly costs. Vital drugs numbered 373 items. They took 37 percent of costs on their own scale. The crossed matrix flagged 458 items. Those items form the top watch group. Managers now hold a clear list for strict stock control.
pmc-13348077:
Muhammad Musiyam, Siti H.N. Hafida, and Siti Aisyah rate how ready high schools are for disasters when fairness is counted, in a survey study from 2026. Questionnaires from 995 people across five schools scored disaster unit readiness and how fully gender, disability. Social inclusion ideas were built into plans, since drills often ignore unequal risk.

Readiness varied widely, with public schools ahead of private schools on both unit strength and inclusion in the reported scores. Stronger disaster systems also carried stronger inclusion, a linked pattern from regression checks. Which suggests fixing the base system first gives fair practice a place to stand in school safety work.
pmc-13349877:
Sinan Ersan and colleagues compared complication risks after eye surgery in a 2026 records study of people with primary open-angle glaucoma. Using the TriNetX network, they identified adults who had cataract removal with lens implant, either on its own or with a minimally invasive glaucoma procedure added.

After matching patients on background traits, the team tracked four problems over 90 days: bleeding inside the eye, swelling at the retina's centre, retinal detachment, and eye infection. Relative risks compared the two surgical routes at several time points. Adding a small glaucoma procedure aims to lower eye pressure, but patients and surgeons need clear numbers on whether it raises early complication risks.
pmc-13349977:
Linfang Li and colleagues built a deep learning detector for lung nodules in CT scans in a 2026 methods study. Small lung lumps vary in size, shape, and density and hide among normal structures, yet finding them early guides treatment.

Their network, DAFNet, uses a two-branch sampling module that gathers features at several scales with less computing cost, plus an attention block that weighs channels and positions. It was tested on a local set of 2,172 images from 1,060 people and on the public LUNA16 benchmark. Accurate automatic detection could lighten the load on radiologists who screen large numbers of chest scans.
pmc-13350177:
Theodore Kindong and co-authors developed a security-by-design framework in 2026 for AI-run energy management systems. Smart, decentralised power systems lean on artificial intelligence, but each data flow opens security and governance gaps.

Using a design science approach over academic and industry literature, they traced data through sensing, model building, and deployment, sorting the security problems found at each stage. Four design principles were drawn up to answer those weak points, with responsibility spread across the many parties who build and run such systems. Trustworthy energy infrastructure must be designed in from the start, they argue, not patched afterward.
pmc-13351877:
Yuxin Jiang leads a 2026 study of how chronic obstructive pulmonary disease shapes outlook in widespread small-cell lung cancer treated with chemotherapy plus immune therapy. Markers that predict benefit in this combined group are not defined. All patients at Jinling Hospital had lung function tests before treatment, and survival was the main outcome.

The team gathered lung measures such as vital capacity and one-second volume, plus blood values including albumin and cell counts. Stepwise survival models, group comparisons, and landmark checks were used to find predictors. A goal was to spot which patients with lung disease gain most from immune-based care. Findings may guide more personal choices in a group often left out of marker studies.
pmc-13351977:
Serhat Özgün leads a 2026 study of hard diagnoses and possibly needless invasive tests before pneumoconiosis is recognised. Dust lung disease is often mistaken at first for cancer or infection because scans look alike. Records covered 121 patients from 2021 to 2025 who had invasive tests before dust disease was considered.

Work exposure, scan patterns, and decision paths were reviewed alongside test results and harms. Scan patterns tied to cancer or infection strongly linked to invasive testing. Greater scan burden linked to worse lung function, with a P value below 0.001. Working diagnoses often failed to match invasive findings. The authors argue earlier attention to job history could spare patients risky procedures.
pmc-13352477:
Jaeyoung Yoon and co-authors test strong, fast electric pulses on human brain slices in 2026. Brain stimulation treats epilepsy, but how it quiets seizures at the cell level is unclear. Slices came from patients with drug-resistant epilepsy, and recordings targeted three cell types in cortex layers 2 and 3.

At higher pulse rates, fast-spiking interneurons fired more and more selectively and kept firing faithfully, while pyramidal and other interneurons faded fast. Synapse weights also shifted, roughly doubling the relative drive-to-brake conductance at fast-spiking cells only. Basic cell excitability barely changed. pmc-13354477:
Rojan Singh Dangol and co-authors report a rare case from 2026 in which a teen boy had bowel trouble at two sites at once. In this illness, one part of the bowel slides into the next part and blocks it. Scans pointed to trouble in the small bowel, and an operation was needed to find the full picture.

Surgeons found growths on stalks that had pulled the bowel inward at both sites. They fixed one site, cut out a short piece of bowel, and made a stoma for the other site, and the boy left the hospital on day 12. The case shows why the whole bowel must be checked during surgery, since a second site is easy to miss.
pmc-13356077:
Ahmed S Kenawy and co-authors tracked in 2026 how men with type 2 diabetes and prostate cancer took their oral diabetes drugs in the year before and after cancer diagnosis. Using United States insurance data for 7,864 patients, they modeled adherence paths over time. Three paths appeared before diagnosis: steady high, steady decline, and steady low.

After diagnosis, a fourth path of moderate decline emerged, and over 61 percent of men changed path. More than half of the steady-high group slipped lower, while many in the low groups improved. Older age and fewer diabetes drugs linked to better adherence. The authors call for targeted support for diabetes care during cancer treatment.
pmc-13357077:
Caiping Tian and co-authors explored in 2026 whether a growth protein called BMP5 can help diagnose lung adenocarcinoma and predict its course. The protein's role in this common lung cancer was unclear. Using large cancer datasets, they checked BMP5 levels, survival links, immune ties, and drug responses, then tested its effect in lab-grown cells.

BMP5 was low in lung adenocarcinoma, and low levels meant worse survival, while the protein predicted outcomes accurately. It tied to many immune features and to how well several drugs worked. Adding BMP5 in lab tests curbed tumor growth, likely by slowing the cell cycle. The authors propose it as a marker and treatment guide.
pmc-13358477:
Ji Hoon Kim and co-authors compare two operations for very sweaty palms in a 2026 study from Seoul. Surgery on chest nerves stops the sweating, but many patients then sweat more on the back or legs, a problem called compensatory sweating. The team compared two nerve cut points to see which causes less of it.

They reviewed patients treated in 2023: 44 had the T3 method and 225 had the R4 method. Both groups were checked for new sweating and for how pleased they were weeks and months after surgery. The results help surgeons pick the cut point that dries palms while keeping side effects low.
pmc-13361677:
Alaa M S Azazz and Ibrahim A Elshaer studied social media addiction and mental health in Saudi university students in a 2026 paper. Heavy social media use is now part of daily student life, and addiction-like use raises worry about stress, anxiety, and depression. The team surveyed 600 students and modeled the links with a statistical method suited to complex surveys. They also asked whether a student's field of study changes the pattern.

Two sides of addiction linked clearly to worse symptoms: trouble managing time and performance, and seeking comfort in social contact online. The time and performance side showed the strongest tie to distress. The results suggest that how students use social media, not just how long, tracks with their mental state. Universities could target those habits in support programs.
pmc-13362377:
Kellina Maduray and Jingquan Zhong report a 2026 review of hospital records on ketones and a fast, uneven heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation. Using a large United States care database, they compared more than ten thousand intensive care patients with more than thirteen thousand ward patients. None had the rhythm problem when they arrived.

In intensive care, patients with ketones in their urine or blood had lower rates of the rhythm problem than those without. On general wards the pattern flipped, and ketones went with higher rates. The split shows the same body signal can mean different things in different settings, a point doctors should weigh when they read ketone tests.
pmc-13362977:
Ioanna Aggeletopoulou and colleagues offer a 2026 review that builds an ethical, patient-centered framework for irritable bowel syndrome care. Many patients with this gut-brain condition feel brushed off or confused about their symptoms, which erodes trust and follow-through. The authors treat clear, kind communication itself as part of the therapy, not a side extra.

Their framework rests on naming the condition without stigma, being open about what is not known, and letting patient values steer shared choices. Diet advice is handled with care to avoid harsh food limits, and patient-reported outcome scores are used to track what matters to patients. Stigma and doubt get direct attention. The goal is care that patients can stick with over the long haul.
pmc-13364077:
Xiaohui Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study on spraying trehalose, a protective sugar, on tea plants facing heat stress. Using two broad metabolite screens on leaves from control, heat-stressed, and sugar-treated heat-stressed plants, they catalogued hundreds of changed compounds and the pathways they belong to. Shared core paths centered on amino acid handling and the building of flavonoid pigments.

It also shifted flavonoid output toward stronger antioxidant forms while trimming wasteful extra decoration of others. Total flavonoids fell versus stressed plants, which the authors read as relief: the plant needed less emergency defense. The sugar emerges as a candidate heat shield for tea.
pmc-13364377:
Assemgul Sadvakasova and co-workers test 2026 microbe mixes to shield rice from a Fusarium fungus that wilts young plants. One mix used a lone Bacillus strain. A second paired that strain with a light using Nostoc strain. The team tracked plant harm and the microbes in soil, roots, and leaves.

Treated plants showed up to half less disease while their dry weight held. The gain came not from more microbe kinds, but from a reshaped mix in each plant zone. The work guides the design of sprays that guard crops with no harsh chem use.
pmc-13371877:
Salima Serroukh and co-authors followed living kidney donors in Rabat, Morocco, for 26 years in a 2026 study. The group held 154 people who gave one kidney to a close kin from 1998 to 2024. Checks tracked kidney work, blood pressure, and heart risk over the long term.

Most donors were women, with a mean age of 43 at the time they gave. The team used blood tests to watch how the one left kidney coped with the years. Long data like this is rare from the region. It helps clinics set fair rules for who can give, and how donors should be checked for life.
pmc-13379377:
Gebreselema Gebreyohannes and co-authors report a 2026 study on using bacteria from textile factory waste water to break down dyes. Henry Steel Olcott, co-founder with Helena Blavatsky of the Theosophical Society, kept a diary of the movement's birth. Old Diary Leaves turns that diary into a history told by a man who was there. Olcott was an American lawyer, soldier, and journalist before he was an occultist.

He recalls the first meetings in New York, the move to India, the masters and marvels claimed around Blavatsky, and the work of building lodges worldwide. His tone is plain and often wry, even about wonders. As the participant's own memory of the early society, the volumes remain a first source for its history.
tob-4146-15477:
Volume four of Ganguli's Mahabharata carries the epic from book thirteen to its close in book eighteen. The aged Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, delivers long teachings on dharma, the law of right conduct. Those lessons form one of the epic's great storehouses of wisdom.

In time the Pandavas lay down their kingdom and walk toward the mountains and heaven. A stray dog joins them and proves more than he seems. One by one the heroes fall on the road. The longest story ever told ends quietly, with the claim that truth alone endures. Ganguli's full translation remains a landmark of patience.
tob-4177:
Catherine of Siena, a dyer's daughter who became a counselor to popes, dictated her Dialogue in states of prayer in the 1370s. She speaks with God the Father, and he answers at length. The record here follows the 1919 checked edition of her spiritual testament.

The talks range over the soul's growth, the corruption of the church, and the call to reform it from within. Catherine's image of Christ as a bridge between heaven and earth carries the whole design. Her tone is fierce, tender, and utterly assured, often in one page. Few medieval women wrote with such authority, or kept it.
tob-4277:
Lewis Spence, a Scottish writer on myth and folklore, turned to Mexico for a study devoted only to its gods. Where his companion work on Mexico and Peru told the myths, here the focus stays on the divine cast itself. Each major deity of the Aztec world gets close attention.

Readers meet the feathered serpent, Tezcatlipoca the smoking mirror, and Tlaloc the rain god, along with many lesser powers. Spence explains what each god ruled, how priests honored them, and what their images meant. The result is a clear guide to a faith that Spanish conquerors worked hard to destroy.
tob-9052-15477:
Ganguli's fourth volume closes the Mahabharata with books thirteen through eighteen. Bhishma, the dying elder, teaches dharma from his arrow bed: how kings should rule, how people should give, forgive, and prepare for death. His lessons form a small library inside the epic.

At last the Pandava heroes renounce the world and climb toward heaven, falling one by one on the road. A faithful dog walks with them to the end. The poem closes on how to die well and what survives a person. With this volume, Ganguli's immense labor of translation stands complete.
turgenev-virgin-soil-1877:
Virgin Soil, Turgenev's last novel, appeared in 1877 and is given here in R. S. Townsend's translation of 1917. Young Nezhdanov joins the populist movement, whose members went to the people with hopes of rousing the peasants. He lodges as a tutor on an estate while spreading pamphlets in secret.

Beside him, Mariana shares his ideals and his growing doubts about their mission. The peasants prove wary, officials close in, and Nezhdanov's faith in himself gives way. Turgenev treats the young rebels with sympathy and clear sight at once. The novel records a real movement of the 1870s at close hand. Townsend's version stands as a distinct translation beside Garnett's.
un-ga-res-55-177:
Guatemala's fifth year of peace brought a fresh UN mandate in Resolution 55/177, passed in December 2000. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2000 by a vote of 1999. In late 1999, the land held its first general vote since the peace was signed. Power passed in peace from one chief to the next, a mark of real growth toward a free state open to all.

Yet core parts of the peace still waited to be done, the text stresses. A fresh timetable from the follow-up team was called for. Both sides had asked the UN to back the firming of peace to 2003. The mission's tenth and eleventh reports on human rights are weighed in the text.
un-ga-res-a-69-77:
One of the UN's three arms bodies has gone quiet, and Resolution A/69/77, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, takes stock of it. The Disarmament Commission is the Assembly's own debate body on arms, set up to study questions in depth and to send firm counsel back. The Assembly had the commission's report before it, and recalls the bids of 2006 to make its work bite.

The text notes a blunt fact: in fifteen years, the commission has sent no firm counsel to the Assembly at all. Its revival is urged for the next three-year cycle. Talks should be tight and aimed at results. Background papers from the UN's disarmament study arm may help spark the debate back to life.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly resolution 55/177 was adopted on 19 December 2000. It carries the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala into its fifth year. The mission monitors the peace settlement that ended the country's civil war. The Assembly draws on the mission's verification reports and on reporting by the Secretary-General and Guatemala's peace commission.

The mandate is renewed for the whole of 2001. The resolution notes the national elections held in late 1999 and the peaceful transfer of power that followed. It calls on both the government and the former insurgent movement to meet their remaining peace commitments. That way the accords can be fully carried out. Continued verification gave the settlement an external check while its hardest reforms were still pending.

Resolution 69/77, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the report of the Disarmament Commission. It notes that the Commission has produced no substantive recommendations in fifteen years. It encourages work to revitalize it. It sets its next substantive session for 6 to 24 April 2015. A report is due to the Assembly's seventieth session.
un-sc-res-1377:
Foreign ministers of the Security Council met on 12 November 2001 to declare a common stand on terrorism. Two months after the September attacks, the Council recalled resolutions 1269 (1999), 1368 (2001), and 1373 (2001). It declared that acts of international terrorism form one of the most serious threats to peace and security in the twenty-first century. Such acts, it said, challenge all states and all of humanity.

The declaration condemns all acts, methods, and practices of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, whatever their motive. Financing, planning, and support for terrorism are declared contrary to the Charter, like the acts themselves. The Council says a sustained joint effort by all member states is essential to beat the threat. It calls on states to join the anti-terrorism conventions as soon as possible. It also links the fight to easing regional conflicts and tackling development problems.
un-sc-res-1477:
The Rwanda tribunal needed a new pool of temporary judges in 2003. Nominations for ad litem judges had reached the Secretary-General. On 29 April 2003 the Security Council forwarded the list to the General Assembly. The tribunal's statute sets that step. The Assembly would elect from the names sent. Candidates came from many states across Africa, Europe, and beyond.

Ad litem judges sit for single trials rather than full terms. They let a busy court run more cases at once. The Arusha tribunal faced a heavy docket from the 1994 genocide. Extra judges were key to its plan to finish trials on schedule. The forwarding act is brief, but it staffed real courtrooms.
un-sc-res-1577: Resolution 1577 dates to 2005 in the Council's numbered output, and this entry reproduces the record text via Wikisource. Votes on such texts need nine of fifteen members, with no permanent member opposed. What passed that bar is preserved here in full, so readers can weigh the decision in the members' own chosen words.
un-sc-res-1677:
Violence shook Timor-Leste in late April 2006, and the Council reacted within weeks. On 12 May 2006 it extended the United Nations Office in Timor-Leste, UNOTIL, until 20 June. The government in Dili had opened an inquiry into the April incidents. The Council noted that step. It stayed committed to lasting stability in the young country.

The Secretary-General owed an update by 6 June 2006. It would cover the situation and the future United Nations role after UNOTIL ended. The Council urged Timorese institutions to tackle the causes of the violence. UNOTIL would help within its current mandate. Events soon forced a far bigger mission than anyone planned that May.
un-sc-res-1777:
UNMIL's next year came with planned cuts on 20 September 2007. The Secretary-General's report of 8 August 2007 guided the Council. Liberia's police were being rebuilt and deployed, and a new army was taking shape. Governance gains and control over natural resources continued. Ex-combatants still needed steady jobs. UNMIL and the Côte d'Ivoire mission coordinated across the border.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate until 30 September 2008. It endorsed the Secretary-General's advice for a staged reduction of the mission's troops, by some 2,450 over the year. A cut of about 498 in the police element was endorsed as well. The Secretary-General would track progress against core benchmarks, from security handover to the rule of law. The Council planned to review his findings before the mandate expired. Liberia's calm held through the drawdown, a sign the peace had begun to carry its own weight.
un-sc-res-1877:
On 7 July 2009, the Council acted on the Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal by adopting Resolution 1877. The court had admitted it could not finish all its work by 2010. Three permanent judges had resigned. Appeals work was set to swell once the last trials ended.

The Council extends the terms of the sitting permanent and temporary judges to 31 December 2010. Judges named to fill the empty seats get the same term. The Secretary-General may add one extra temporary judge for a short period, above the normal cap of twelve. The statute is amended so trial judges can move up to the Appeals Chamber as cases close. The court must still finish as fast as it can.
un-sc-res-277:
Southern Rhodesia's white regime proclaimed a republic in March 1970. The move aimed to cement its illegal rule. On 18 March 1970 the Security Council condemned the proclamation. It restated its line of resolutions against the regime since 1965. Sanctions already in force stayed in effect. Reports from the sanctions committee informed the decision. Spain cast the lone abstention.

No state could recognize the illegal regime or help it. Acts of its officials and bodies deserved no recognition anywhere, courts included. Britain held the primary duty to let the people of Zimbabwe choose self-determination. The text tightened the legal isolation of the Smith regime. Majority rule in Zimbabwe still took another decade to arrive.
un-sc-res-377: Security Council business produced Resolution 377, catalogued in this library as a 1975 record in the DECLASSIFIED group. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-477:
Security Council Resolution 477, adopted on August 14, 1980, recommended Zimbabwe for membership in the United Nations. The southern African land had won legal independence from Britain that April, after a long guerrilla war against the white minority regime that had called the country Rhodesia. Free elections brought Robert Mugabe to power as the first prime minister of the new state.

The Assembly seated Zimbabwe eleven days later. The council's brief text closed a fifteen-year saga in which the UN had treated Rhodesia's rebel regime as illegal and backed sanctions against it. Few admission votes carried such a sense of a wrong formally undone and a people's long fight recognized.
un-sc-res-77: Work on limiting conventional weapons reached the Council in the autumn of 1949. Its Commission for Conventional Armaments had sent a second progress report. The report covered the first items of the commission's plan of work. On 11 October 1949 the Council told the Secretary-General to pass the papers on. The General Assembly and member states would receive them. The record of the Council's own debate went along. The short act kept the disarmament file moving between bodies.
un-sc-res-977: Holding number 977 in the Council series, this resolution carries a 1995 date in the library catalog. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Resolution 1377, adopted unanimously on 12 November 2001 at a meeting of foreign ministers, is a declaration on terrorism issued two months after the September 11 attacks. It builds on the binding counter-terrorism duties the Council had imposed in September. Ministers declared that acts of international terrorism rank among the gravest threats to world peace in this new century.

The declaration calls terrorism a challenge to all states and to humanity, and condemns every act, method, and practice of it as criminal and unjustifiable, whatever the motive. Financing, planning, and support for attacks are likewise condemned. It argues that only a sustained, comprehensive campaign, with every member state taking part under the Charter and international law, can defeat the threat.

A long slate of names fills most of this text. They are picks for stand-in judge at the Rwanda war crimes court. The court sat in Arusha, Tanzania. It tried the men blamed for the 1994 mass killings. Full-time judges could not hear all the cases. Stand-ins filled the gaps. Resolution 1477 passed with no dissent on 29 April 2003.

The Council sent the slate to the General Assembly. The Assembly would vote the judges in. The names came from all over the world. Chad, Turkey, Cameroon, Uganda, and Poland are among the states on the list. Some picks would never sit. The slate had to be wide so the Assembly could choose. The text is dull at a glance. It still shows the vast, slow grind of bringing a genocide to trial.

Burundi's United Nations operation, ONUB, is extended until 1 June 2005 in this text of 1 December 2004. The mission had deployed in June 2004 to support the Arusha peace process. Burundian parties had since agreed a power-sharing deal in Pretoria, and parliament had adopted an interim constitution in October giving guarantees to all communities.

ONUB stays in place to help carry the transition through to free and fair elections. Governments and parties in the region are urged to reject violence and cooperate with ONUB and the Congo mission in ending impunity. Congo and Rwanda are called on to help Burundi complete the inquiry into the Gatumba massacre and bring those responsible to justice.

Timor-Leste's slide into crisis bought its UN office a month of life in 2006. On 12 May, the Council adopted Resolution 1677. Clashes inside the young state's security forces had erupted in late April. The text names the incidents of 28 and 29 April. People had died, and thousands had fled their homes in Dili. The state the UN helped build looked fragile.

The text extends the small UN office, UNOTIL, just to 20 June 2006. The Secretary-General must report by 6 June on the state of play. His report must also scope the UN role past that date. The government and state bodies must tackle the roots of the violence, with the office's help. A far larger mission followed within weeks.

Uganda's path into the United Nations runs through Resolution 177, adopted on 15 October 1962, with every member in favor. The Council had examined the East African country's bid for membership. Uganda had become independent from Britain only days earlier, on 9 October, and joining the UN was among the first acts of the new state.

In a single operative sentence, the Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Uganda. That recommendation was the required first step, because the Charter gives the Assembly the final vote on new members but only on the Council's advice. The brief record captures Uganda taking its place in the wave of African states entering the UN in the early 1960s.

Resolution 1777, adopted on 20 September 2007, extends the UN mission in Liberia while approving its gradual slimming. The Secretary-General's August report described steady government progress against corruption and in recovering control over natural resources. The Liberian police were being rebuilt, equipped, and deployed, and restructuring of the armed forces had begun, though much remained to do.

UNMIL's mandate was renewed until 30 September 2008. With that year secured, the Council endorsed the Secretary-General's plan for a phased drawdown of the mission's troops and police as Liberian forces took over. It pressed Liberia and its partners to speed up police and army reform and the building of a national security framework.

The Yugoslavia tribunal's bench is reinforced and its judges extended in Resolution 1877, adopted on 7 July 2009. Its Completion Strategy Report admitted it could not finish work in 2010, three permanent judges had resigned, and the Appeals Chamber faced a rising workload.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Trial Chamber permanent judges and all ad litem judges, serving and unassigned alike, until 31 December 2010. It runs until their cases finish, if that is sooner. The Appeals Chamber judges' extension will be reviewed by 31 December 2009. It lets the Secretary-General appoint ad litem judges beyond the statutory twelve, up to thirteen at a time until the end of 2009, so a reserve judge can sit. It amends Article 14 of the Statute. Up to four extra permanent judges can join the Appeals Chamber as their trials complete. They include judges drawn from the Rwanda tribunal.

Rhodesia's white rulers claimed the rank of a republic in 1970. The move aimed to lock in rule by a small white class. The Council's bans had not yet brought the revolt to an end. Some states still traded with the banned regime. South Africa and Portugal kept it fed. Resolution 277 passed on 18 March 1970 by fourteen votes to none. Spain held back.

The claim to republic rank was damned as void. No state could grant the regime a nod of law. All ties had to snap: trade, posts, and travel links alike. Cars, trains, and planes to the land were to halt. South African police and troops had to leave at once. Aid for Zambia, hurt by the bans, was urged. States had to report their steps by 1 June.

Western Sahara, a territory on the coast of West Africa ruled by Spain, drew the Council's attention in the autumn of 1975. Spain had written to the Council about the situation. Rival claims to the territory were raising the temperature in the region. Resolution 377 was adopted by consensus on 22 October 1975.

Acting under Article 34 of the Charter, the Council decided to look into the dispute. That article lets the Council investigate situations that might endanger peace. The Secretary-General was sent on a mission to the area and to the parties concerned. The Council appealed to all of them to show restraint and moderation. Calm conditions would let the mission go ahead well. The General Assembly's decisions on the territory, including its call for decolonization, stayed fully in view.

The shelf label on this text points at Jerusalem. The page itself tells a far happier tale. Zimbabwe had just won its freedom. White rule in Rhodesia ended after a long bush war. Free polls in 1980 chose a black-led state. Its bid for a UN seat came next. Resolution 477 passed with no dissent on 30 July 1980.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Zimbabwe. The Assembly did so weeks later. Robert Mugabe led the new state at its birth. The seat closed one of Africa's last colonial files. Few votes in 1980 carried such joy. A state the UN had shunned as a rebel colony now took its lawful place in the hall.

Paperwork moved the early arms debate forward in 1949. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had delivered its second progress report. Annexes covered the first items of its work plan, settled back in August 1948. Resolution 77 was adopted on 11 October 1949. Nine members voted yes, with the Ukrainian and Soviet delegations abstaining.

The Secretary-General was told to forward everything to the General Assembly. The report, its annexes, and the Council's own debate record all went across. The Assembly would read them for information. Nothing was decided about weapons themselves. The text captures the UN's division of labor. The Council's commission studied conventional arms, then reported upward to the full membership.

The war crimes court for Rwanda needed a home, and the Council chose one on 22 February 1995. The court had been set up the previous November, by Resolution 955. It would try those behind the genocide of 1994. The choice of its seat had been left to the Council. Resolution 977 was adopted unanimously.

On the advice of the Secretary-General, the Council decided that the court would sit at Arusha. Arusha is a town in the United Republic of Tanzania. The choice depended on proper arrangements between the United Nations and Tanzania's government. Those arrangements had to be acceptable to the Council. Rwanda's government had said that it would work with the court. Fixing the seat let the new tribunal start building its courtrooms, staff, and case files.
webster-displaying-of-supposed-witchcraf:
John Webster, a physician and schoolmaster, published The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft in 1677. The huge book sets out to debunk supposed witchcraft by natural causes alone. Webster had seen the trials up close in the north of England, and he writes as a doctor who trusts observation over accusation.

He explains fits, visions, and strange cures by disease, fraud, and fear. Case after case receives a physical reading. The work is the great Restoration skeptical summa, massive and methodical. Webster answers Glanvill point by point in the same years. His Displaying shows how far a determined natural philosophy could go in emptying the witch belief of its evidence.
works-on-phrenology-physiology-and-kindr: Works on Phrenology, Physiology, and Kindred Subjects, 1877. The kindred works. This book preserves that catalogue. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
wright-philosophical-discussions-1877:
Chauncey Wright was a sharp American thinker whose work spread mostly through essays and talk. After his early death, Charles Eliot Norton edited his Philosophical Discussions in 1877. Wright had defended Darwin in America with unusual force. Charles Sanders Peirce counted him as a mentor and sparring partner.

The essays take up evolution, science, and the methods by which minds gain truth. Wright writes plainly and cuts hard against loose or wishful reasoning. His pages show the tough style that shaped the first American pragmatists. The volume preserves a mind that print almost lost. It explains his quiet fame among peers.
zola-lassommoir-1877:
Zola opens L'Assommoir with Gervaise waiting up for Lantier until two in the morning. For a week he has sent her to bed with tales of hunting for work. That night she thinks she sees him enter a bright ballroom with Adele, a pretty brunette.

He sleeps out for the first time, and Gervaise wakes at five in wild sobs. Her bare furnished room holds a broken bureau, three straw chairs, and a greasy table. Hope still lies ahead: honest work builds her a small laundry in time. Her husband's drinking then dissolves it all, in the starkest portrait of drink and poverty in French letters.
